## The King.

Whereas on behalf of you, **Friar Thomas de Mercado**, of the **Order of Preachers** <note>Also known as the Dominicans, an order of monks famous for their scholars and theologians.</note>, Master of Sacred Theology, a report was made to us stating that you had written a book titled **Deals and Contracts of Merchants** <note>Original: "Tratos y contratos de Mercaderes."</note>. And because it was very useful and necessary, and you had spent much time in its creation, you petitioned us to have it reviewed and, should it be found worthy, to grant you a license to print and sell it with a privilege for fifteen years, so that within that time no other person could print it, or as our mercy should decide.
This request was reviewed by those of our Council, and after the required diligence was performed on the said book as prescribed by the royal ordinance <term>pragmática<note>A royal decree with the force of law. This refers to the strict 1558 law governing the censorship and licensing of books in Spain.</note></term> recently enacted by us, it was agreed that we should order this our decree <term>cédula<note>An official document or warrant issued by the king or a high authority.</note></term> to be given to you for this purpose, and we held it to be right.
And by the present document, we grant license and authority so that you, or whoever holds your power of attorney, may print the said book mentioned above, and so that for the period of the first ten years following—which shall be counted from the date of this our decree forward—you, the said **Friar Thomas de Mercado**, or the person who holds your power, may sell the said book.
And we command that no person without our license during the said period of ten years may print or sell it, under penalty of losing all the books they may have printed, plus twenty thousand **maravedís** <note>A common unit of account and copper coinage in 16th-century Spain; this was a significant fine meant to deter book piracy.</note> for our treasury.
And we command that after it is printed, it may not be sold until it is first brought to our Council, along with the original that was reviewed, which is rubricated <note>Signed with a flourish or "rubric" to prevent unauthorized changes.</note> and signed at the end by **Juan de la Vega**, our court clerk <term>escriuano de camara<note>A high-ranking official responsible for certifying royal documents and council proceedings.</note></term> among those who reside in our Council, so that it may be seen if the said printing conforms to the original, and the price at which each volume must be sold may be set <term>tasse<note>The "tasa" was a government-fixed price for a book, calculated per page, to ensure merchants did not overcharge the public.</note></term>, under penalty of falling into and incurring the penalties contained in the said royal ordinance and the laws of these kingdoms.
And we command those of our Council, the President and Judges of our High Courts <term>audiencias<note>High courts of justice that also held administrative and legislative power.</note></term>, the Mayors and Bailiffs of our House and Court, the Chanceries, and all the governors, assistants, chief magistrates, ordinary mayors, and any other judges and justices of all the cities, towns, and places in our kingdoms and lordships, and each and every one of them, both those who are now and those who will be from here on, to observe and fulfill this our decree and favor which we thus grant you, and with

# Dedicatory Epistle

I judge it a great oversight that any congregation of traders—such as those here in Seville, or in Burgos, Medina, and Lisbon—does not have determined by some university of theologians what is lawful and unlawful in the business matters most commonly practiced among them. This would ensure that in the common and principal aspects of trade they might not err, even if in some rare or unusual business they might lack this light or this resolution. Although this is as necessary a thing as natural reason itself dictates, I do not see that any <term>consulate</term> <note>Original: "consulado." A powerful guild of merchants that also functioned as a commercial court to regulate trade and resolve disputes.</note> has been diligent in this matter.

For, in my judgment, I do not believe there is greater anguish for a man than to occupy himself all his life with what he does not understand. Because man naturally desires to know, and he desires most effectively to know that which he most deals with and has most often in hand. And not to know in a business deal what is just and what is its opposite is to understand nothing of it. For this is the first thing that a Christian must know about any business, so as not to lose eternal good while dealing with temporal matters.

For this reason, desiring the utility and true honor of these <term>steps</term> <note>Original: "gradas." This refers to the stone steps of the Cathedral of Seville, the traditional meeting place for the city's merchants before the construction of a formal exchange building.</note>, I ensured that although I alone composed the work, many men more senior in age and learning than I were almost its authors—namely, all the <term>professors of theology</term> <note>Original: "cathedraticos en Theulugia." The senior academic chairs at the University of Salamanca, then the intellectual heart of the Spanish Empire.</note> at the University of Salamanca and many other masters of great erudition, as named above, who examined it once composed and approved its doctrine. Each of whom reviewed it personally and provided a <term>censure</term> <note>In the 16th century, a "censure" (censura) was a formal review by an expert to certify that a book contained no theological or moral errors.</note>.

# Dedicatory Epistle

# Prologue.

<image-desc>A square woodcut decorative initial 'O' featuring a central circular floral or stellar motif surrounded by ornate scrollwork and geometric patterns.</image-desc>
There is a very strict obligation, as the **Gospel** says, for those to whom divine clemency has communicated some <term>grace freely given</term> <note>Original Latin: "gratis data." In theology, this refers to spiritual gifts given to an individual for the benefit of others rather than for their own personal sanctification.</note> to serve His people with it, in those areas where the people have the greatest need. And it is a most singular condition for those who were granted the gifts of knowledge and understanding (true riches if well employed) to serve their <term>commonwealth</term> <note>Original: "republica." At this time, it referred generally to the organized community or the "public thing," rather than a specific form of representative government.</note> by teaching the methods that must be taken in the business affairs that most frequently occur within it, as a body of teaching that will be profitable to many. For it is characteristic of wisdom—making its seat in one, or at least in few—to communicate itself as a divine good and allow itself to be enjoyed by many. Its communication consists of guiding and directing the business of all through the words of these few, whom wisdom chooses among all mortals as a temple where it might dwell and from which it might respond, as the glorious **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), one of the most influential Latin Church Fathers.</note> affirms. In this, created wisdom imitates the eternal wisdom from which it derives. God always had the habit of showing Himself to men very rarely, but those to whom He appeared He would anoint and establish as princes or prophets among the multitude of the <term>common people</term> <note>Original: "vulgo."</note>, so that they might govern and teach them. Thus He revealed Himself to **Abraham**, to **Jacob**, to **Moses**, **Joshua**, and **Gideon**, who, having received revelation and being instructed from heaven, defended the **Israelite** people from the fury of their enemies and showed them how to live under a sovereign <term>governance</term> <note>Original: "policia." In the 16th century, this term referred to the civilized order, administration, and moral conduct of a city or state.</note> with most holy laws. He did the same among the **Gentiles**, despite their being unfaithful. For His infinite piety never abandoned the human race in such a way that He did not show them, through various paths, some means to achieve true salvation. He revealed His justice and truth to those ancient **philosophers**, as the **Apostle** <note>St. Paul.</note> teaches in his writing to the **Romans**, so that through their mouths and preach-

# Prologue.

[Obliga]tion so that it might come to the notice of the whole world. In this way, our human wisdom—which is also found firmly established in only a few—possesses a most effective desire within its very core to benefit all, as we find through experience, both in our own times and in those of the past, if we consider all the wise men who flourished in various ages and parts of the world. 

As soon as they reached the summit and height of knowledge and drank—as **Persius** <note>Aulus Persius Flaccus (34–62 AD), a Roman satirist known for his difficult but stoic-influenced poetry.</note> says—from the fountain of **Parnassus** <note>A mountain in Greece which, according to mythology, was sacred to Apollo and the Muses; drinking from its springs was a metaphor for receiving poetic or intellectual inspiration.</note>, they felt within themselves a nearly natural instinct to be useful and helpful to their people. They enlightened their ignorance and pointed out, as if with a finger, the path to happiness that they themselves had already found. For this is what everyone generally lacks, and what men desire and seek with the greatest effort in all their works. 

And they apply the teaching according to the disposition in which they find their citizens. The principal intent is always one; the means are diverse. The end is that of wisdom itself (that is to say, to live a just life); they choose these means in accordance with the capacity of the people. For even in showing men their own good (toward which they are naturally inclined), it is necessary to use ingenuity and art, according to what is natural to them: to guide themselves and be guided by reason.

[Ly]curgus <note>Lycurgus (c. 820 BC) was the legendary lawgiver of Sparta, who established the communalistic and militaristic reforms of the city-state.</note> sought to show how beautiful equity and modesty were. **Plato** took as his undertaking the task of making all his **Athenians** equal; **Numa Pompilius** <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing the city's religious and legal calendar.</note> aimed to endear the **Romans** to religion and divine worship through great ceremonies. **Xenophon**, seeing how great a need there was in the world for a most prudent prince, studied how to depict one, taking as his exemplar **Cyrus**, Monarch of the **Persians**. 

Of our sacred doctors, who can say with how much greater effort and skill they follow this destiny, always teaching men what is most appropriate according to the time? Certainly, only someone who perfectly understands how much more these men participate in true wisdom (the specific nature of which we are explaining) than those first ancients could ever explain it. Even our God, who is wisdom by essence, prides Himself on this quality through **Isaiah**. "I am," He says, "the Lord your God, who teaches you useful and profitable things." <note>A reference to Isaiah 48:17: "I am the Lord your God, who teaches you what is best for you, who directs you in the way you should go."</note>

And following them, the apostolic men who succeeded them in office, all strive for the benefit and health of souls, preaching and writing what was necessary according to their time.

We see that Aristotle followed this style in writing Logic, the first of the <term>liberal sciences: the traditional academic subjects of the medieval and Renaissance periods, including grammar, logic, and rhetoric</term>, where he speaks to beginners, teaching more through rules and divisions than through effective demonstrations. Even the very nature of reason and discourse he taught more through precepts and examples than through abstract reason. He judged wisely that when speaking with novices in letters, no quality could be better for his doctrine than facility and plainness. For nothing is more necessary in any work than to make oneself understood by those for whom one writes. For this reason, it is very right to shorten it, expand it, adorn it, or break it down, according to their <term>ingenio: the natural intellect, wit, or capacity of a person</term>. 

Therefore, I judged it correct to make the work plain <note>original: "suelta," meaning loose, free, or unencumbered by dense academic structure</note>, fearing—and I believe with good cause—that if it were to come out perfect and showy, it would lack, despite all its beauty, the "fortune that is best" (as they say). Because it would not achieve the intended good, nor would its reading be savory to the merchant. One single finery, it seems, our entire brevity could have, which would give it no small grace: namely, the excellence and elegance in words, which the work also lacks in parts. For the other garments and trappings of which we stripped it are so pompous and ostentatious that it is clearly understood to have been a good decision to remove them for someone speaking with people who are very busy and distracted by business. 

But this vivid color of elegant speech not only did not hinder, but rather would have added (as is usual) an extreme beauty. # Prologue to this second
### Addition.

THIS work comes forth so much more expanded than before that it appears new; for this reason, we ought to give a new explanation of our labor in a new prologue. But no one should criticize either the initial brevity or the extension of this second version. For human works acquire their growth and perfection in the course of time, being, after all, the products of men, of whom (as the proverb says) none was born great, nor has anyone ever emerged fully accomplished in any art suddenly. Little by little, progress is made in them, until good practice takes root through use and talent. Also, as this <term>Summa: a comprehensive manual or compendium of knowledge, usually regarding law or theology</term> was composed for people very busy in business, I took great care not to be too long-winded, so as not to cause <note>original: "ahitar" — literally to cause indigestion; here used metaphorically for mental exhaustion</note> weariness with the reading. Thus, being cautious, the work remained short in some parts. Afterward, it was received by both the learned and the unlearned with such goodwill that it seemed to me I could safely expand many of the initial resolutions a bit more. Especially since highly esteemed doctors had advised me to do so from the beginning. And to speak the truth, moral cases, being acts of the will, are a bottomless sea. Every day new ones present themselves, and new aspects of the old ones come to our attention. It would be poor judgment to keep silent about what is newly offered if it is as beneficial as what was first published. Thus, almost all the subjects of the first, second, and third books come forth well-explained, with new reasons and persuasive arguments for the truth, and new resolutions of business matters important to commerce and common contracts. Those of the fourth book remained almost as they were at first, because they are of such a nature that it was not our profession to treat them as the main intent of our work. In addition to these additions inserted into the original questions and subjects, it became necessary to explain separately the <term>Pragmatic of Wheat: a royal decree or legal regulation issued by the Spanish crown to control the price and trade of grain</term>. Therein I believe we have perfected the subject of buying and selling...

<meta>This page continues the author's preface to the second edition, shifting from the reasons for expanding the general work to the specific addition of a treatise on natural law and its relationship to divine and human legislation.</meta>

Therefore, so that whoever reads the entire work may not be ignorant—if they retain its contents—of anything concerning this very general treatise, I added (with no less cause and necessity) a short treatise on **natural law**, which is the foundation within man for all **positive laws** <note>Positive laws are specific statutes "posed" or decreed by a legislature or authority, as opposed to inherent moral laws.</note>. Eternal law, which exists from eternity, comes first, but it does not bind us unless it is promulgated and notified to us; it is promulgated through natural, divine, and human positive laws.

Of all these, natural law is the first within us. Thus we see that when **God** on **Mount Sinai** gave the law to **Moses**, where He taught him what is just regarding God and one’s neighbor, the first precepts were those of natural law; and these He gave with greater authority and more ceremonies. That is to say, speaking them to him by word of mouth and giving them written on two tables of stone. All the other judicial and ceremonial precepts, concerning His worship and the temple, He established <term>vocis oraculo: by the oracle of the living voice; a legal term referring to an oral decree as opposed to a written one</term>, as they say. 

And on the tablets, although the first three commandments belonged to His honor, they are also in part natural. For the **natural light** <note>A theological term for human reason and conscience</note> shows us—and through it we understand—that there is one sole almighty God, and that it is unjust to swear by His holy name in vain, and very just for man to rest and free himself for a time to know and revere Him. 

And since man must measure and regulate his acts by the laws, which are his rule and level, it is fitting that he should not be ignorant of the first and principal among those that bind him. Especially since most of the justice and rectitude of human **contracts** belongs to natural law. For if positive law ordains many things regarding them, most of those concern formalities and required circumstances. The substance, for the most part, arises from natural law. For this reason, it is impossible, if one is ignorant of it, to understand their <term>quiddity: the inherent nature or "whatness" of a thing</term> and equity. Therefore, it seemed most necessary—there being such ignorance of it among many—to treat and explain it. I hope in our Lord that as this edition comes out more perfect, so it will be received with no less goodwill.

### ¶ CHAPTER ONE: WHAT
### *Natural Law is; its causes, power, and virtue; and how the commutative justice of Contracts rests upon it.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap "A" featuring two figures, possibly scholars or legal authorities, positioned within and around the letterform.</image-desc>

HAVING TO TREAT IN this work, in both general and specific terms, of all human contracts (excepting Marriage), addressing not only their practice <note>original: "praxis"</note> and style but principally the justice and equity with which they must be conducted: it seems very appropriate to reveal to merchants <note>original: "tratantes," referring to those who engage in trade and legal dealings</note> the fountainhead <note>original: "principio fontal"</note> from which flow so many conditions, rules, and distinctions as contracts require and as we shall set forth. I do not doubt that upon reading these our resolutions, someone (and perhaps many) may desire to understand from where so many obligations arise for merchants, such as those we explain here. And who is it that obliges them to trade under these conditions, seeing as they are free men? To this end, it seemed very opportune for me to explain here the causes of all these rules and the principal foundations of this justice that we shall teach. Through this, everyone may understand that in this entire work, and in no part of it, do we bind anyone by our sole authority or will.

# What natural law is, and what its principle is
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

[authori]ty; but by another greater one, which is effective and powerful enough to bind all men: that of God, of nature, of the Church, or of the republic. And firstly, regarding reason and natural law: for it is from here that all this doctrine is most closely derived, as it is the most fitting measure and rule of human works. It is also that which, until now, merchants <note>original: "tratantes," referring to those engaged in business and trade</note> discuss and understand the least. Hardly any of them consider or judge a contract to be licit or illicit based on its conformity or repugnance to natural law; even when they hear these words, they understand them no more than if they were Greek. For this reason, it will be beneficial to inform them of this firm foundation upon which all their business rests, and to stir up in them this light. Since it always burns within them, they ought to follow it perpetually, as it is the star that guides us through the dark and gloomy night of this life.

<margin>The human race lives by art and reason. <note>original Latin: "Hominum genus arte, & ratione viuit."</note></margin>
Aristotle, in the first book of the *Metaphysics*, teaches us a truth well-proven by experience: that animals move by natural instinct, but men live by reason and art. Although we could also say that all are governed by reason, with the difference that brute animals are ruled by the reason of God, who placed in them this natural instinct (which, without any freedom of their own, awakens, moves, and impels them), while man is ruled by his own rational reason—which is also a divine gift. God placed a natural instinct in the brutes, and in men the light of reason, which (as David <note>referring to King David in the Psalms</note> says) is a portrait, though imperfect, of the divine light. God is infinite and inaccessible spiritual light.

For if one were not free, it would no longer be an obligation, but rather force or captivity. 

But some might ask, how does reason oblige man if it cannot punish the one who disobeys it? I say first that to oblige, it is not necessary to have the power to punish the disobedient. For we see that many times one man obliges himself to another, without either of them having the <term>jurisdiction<gloss>the legal power or authority to administer justice</gloss></term> to punish himself or the other. It is enough that there is a judge who compels the parties to stand by what they have obligated themselves to. Thus we can say that if reason does not punish the one who is rebellious and <term>contumacious<gloss>stubbornly or willfully disobedient to authority</gloss></term>, God, the supreme judge, punishes the transgressors of His precepts most severely. Solomon says that the good man receives great joy from practicing virtue. If bodily peace is a sufficient goal for the dangers, costs, and labors of a long war—because (as Plato says) kings do not fight except for the peace of their subjects—how much better a reward for virtue will be the spiritual peace and tranquility of the soul? This peace was so great a good to Job that it consoled him in the midst of all his labors. He said: "never has my heart reproached me." And Saint Paul held this testimony, which a good conscience gives to the one who obeys reason, not only as a consolation for his great hardships, but even as solid and true glory. 

And, on the contrary, the harsh and grave rebuke of the conscience, which follows immediately, is a great punishment for an evil deed. Saint Isidore says that there is no greater penalty than that which a bad conscience gives, because no one can live happily while following what is evil. And Seneca says that the most severe punishment for any sin is to have committed it, since a great penalty is annexed to the evil itself. It is so great that, even in the midst of his vicious joy, it makes the wicked man sad and waters down his contentment with pain. 

The ancient philosophers, knowing for certain that by justice a reward was owed to virtue and punishment to vice, and seeing most of the virtuous poor, troubled, and dejected—and many of the vicious with rest and honor—asked how virtue in the former lacked a reward, and a bad life in the latter lacked a penalty. And this doubt is so apparent that it moved Isaiah and King David (the most excellent of all the Prophets) not a little, and made them think and labor to answer and satisfy the question. ### how great its virtue and obligation is.

[Those without the] name of faith <note>The text likely reads "sin nombre de fe," referring to the ancient philosophers who lacked Christian revelation.</note> (which points to the reward of heaven and the fire of hell) replied that the contentment that virtue brought with itself was sufficient payment. This is approved by Saint Ambrose, saying that the tranquility and peace of conscience is sufficient happiness and reward for the labors of the virtuous. And it is a great judicial penalty, the unpleasantness and disgust that the soul receives from vice. For even if it is tasty to the senses, it cannot help but be more bitter than gall to the soul. 

But we (who by divine clemency) possess both philosophies, the natural and the divine, say both things: namely, that reason has two rewards and two harsh punishments. One in this life (which is the peace or the restlessness of the conscience) and another in the future (which is glory or eternal torment). Saint Augustine used to say:

> Lord, you have justly ordained that a restless and vicious soul should be its own punishment. <note>A paraphrase of Augustine's *Confessions*: "You have commanded, and so it is, that every disordered soul should be its own punishment."</note>

In all of this, we shall recognize how narrow and necessary is the obligation that reason places upon man: for with such abundance and perpetuity is the fulfillment of it rewarded, and with such severity is the breaking of it punished forever. The excellent prize for observance, and the most severe penalty for transgression, clearly show the great obligation of man to obey and keep the **natural law** <term>Natural Law: The moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</term>. For no one would be so rigorously punished by reason unless they broke that which they were obliged to do by clear justice. 

Thus, to necessarily carry out any work, it is enough that reason commands it. There is no need to seek another emperor or another legislator. It is true that, since God placed reason almost as his **vicar** <term>Vicar: A representative or deputy; here, reason acts as God's direct representative within the human soul.</term> in the soul, He also expressly commands what reason dictates, and even makes particular mention of it in His Gospel; therefore, to act against reason is to go against God. Thus, the natural law (which is that which reason teaches) is, and is simultaneously called, [divine] law...

For just as man is now inclined and ready to eat when he can and is hungry, or to sleep when he feels like it, or to preserve his life through honest means, so man was then ready and quick to perform all acts of virtue and natural justice. For this reason, God only gave him one statute—not to eat of the tree—so that by obeying Him in a matter to which he was not naturally inclined, and which was not a matter of natural law, he might acknowledge God as his Lord through his obedience.

But by falling, man was left so dazed by the blow he received that it is now necessary to bring the natural law back to his memory; and God is content if man obeys that to which he was already naturally obligated. ->### how great is its virtue and obligation.<-

...to give to each what is fitting and what comes to them by right: this is what theologians call "creating equality." Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the "Angelic Doctor" whose writings formed the basis of Catholic legal and moral thought.</note> (who is our prince) says it is the specific property of justice to create equality in human contracts. And equality consists of balancing two dissimilar things. Just as a horse and one hundred ducats <note>A gold coin used widely in Europe and the Spanish Empire during this period.</note>, though so different in their essence, come to be equal in their **esteem** (that is, their market value) if the horse is worth that much. And justice demands that when the horse is traded, one hundred ducats are given for it, and no less—even if it could be obtained for less through some deception or force. In this way, each person is given what belongs to them with equality. To the one who buys, his horse; to the one who sells, an equal amount of money (as I said) in value. And if a slave, being worth two hundred escudos <note>A Spanish gold or silver coin.</note>, is traded for that amount, the buyer and seller remain equal: the former with his black slave <note>original: "negro"; the author uses this term interchangeably with "eſclauo" (slave) to discuss a commercial transaction, reflecting the era's legal treatment of enslaved people as commodities.</note>, and the latter with his escudos. But if less were given, the seller would remain unequal, not being given as much as he gave. Indeed, the buyer would take more, receiving a value of two hundred escudos—which is the slave—while giving the seller only one hundred and fifty (as we are supposing). This inequality is, and is called, injustice. In such a way, for a contract to be just, it requires equality—not in the persons who are contracting (for they can be, and usually are, very different), but in the things that are contracted. And these things are equal not in their nature, but solely in their value and esteem.

From all this it is inferred that to deal with justice is to establish equality and equity in contracts. To this we are bound by the **natural law**, which issues from our reason. It dictates: that we should wrong no one. The observance of this law binds all mortals without exception. In such a way that in any contract, it is enough to reveal its inequality to demonstrate its injustice. And once discovered, one must know that it is to be avoided and fled from, without any need to ask further who condemns or forbids it. For we show here general—

->### That it is natural law, and what its principle is<-

That is, reason commands us to uphold justice and detests injustice. And it is the same to act against one's conscience as it is to act against the will of God, who inscribed and infused this natural light within us. Thus says the Apostle <note>Saint Paul the Apostle; the author refers to Romans 14:23: "Everything that does not come from faith is sin," often interpreted by Scholastics as acting against one's conscience.</note>: everything a man does against the dictate of his own conscience is sin. I do not say this because we will not later provide the reasoning and authority for what we shall affirm. For as we are among the last to write on this subject, we will not offer any resolution that has not first been given by many others whose wisdom was solid, whose learning was well-founded, and who possessed great authority. We certainly do not take pleasure in new and strange doctrines, but rather in those venerable ones of antiquity. However, I wished to open this trench and lay this foundation for the entire work—namely, that it is a matter of <term>natural law</term> <note>Universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, independent of written laws.</note> to maintain equality with one's neighbor in our business dealings, and that to do the opposite was against the very light of the soul that gives us our being. It only remains for us in this third chapter to descend further into particulars, extending this doctrine with various examples from which no small utility will be gained. And to speak clearly, nothing more remains in this entire work than to specify this supreme rule, for in its entirety, it only teaches how to deal with one another without causing grievance.

<header>how great its virtue and obligation.</header>
B 2

This justice should rightly reside in any ruler <note>original: "rector"</note> of a multitude: such as a prince, a prelate, or a magistrate <term>corregidor</term> <note>A crown official in Spain who exercised both administrative and judicial powers over a district.</note>, for they are the ministers of the laws. They are not to govern the subject people according to their own recent whims <note>original: "aluedrio"; refers to arbitrary will or unchecked discretion.</note>, nor judge their cases according to their own personal opinion, but rather by the written laws. In those matters that the laws have already provided for, the result will always be what is just and true.

It is a question much debated among philosophers, both ancient and modern, as to which is more beneficial and appropriate for the commonwealth <term>republica</term> <note>In the 16th century, this term referred to the "public thing" or the state as a whole, regardless of whether it was a monarchy or a republic.</note>: that a man should reign within it, or the law. That is, whether they should be governed by the judgment of a single wise man, or by the law established by as many wise and learned men as gathered together to create it. And all agree with Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher whose "Politics" argued that "the rule of law is preferable to that of any individual."</note>, who determines that it is best for the law to reign primarily, and then the man. The law exists to show what must be done, and the prince exists to ensure the law is kept and to put into execution what the law directs. 

It is very harmful for a ruler to follow his own will while abandoning the rectitude of the laws, even if they are the very laws he himself established. For he likely established them with greater counsel and less passion than he feels in the present moment. Speaking generally, the law judges much better than a man. Firstly, this is because many wise men ordained the law, and they understand affairs better than one man alone. Secondly, those lawgivers were not moved by the passions of love or self-interest (which tend to blind even the most perceptive judgment), which might perhaps move a prince or a judge who lives today and knows the parties involved in a lawsuit. Toward one of those parties, there may be a thousand considerations of friendship, blood, social interaction, or appearance that might sway him. But those ancient inventors of the laws could not be blinded by hatred or love for those living now, whom they never knew. # That natural law is its origin.

...will err, whoever abandons through his corrupt appetite that which is provided with such integrity and virtue by right.

It is a great benefit to a youth—and even if he is wise, no small satisfaction—to be guided by the opinion of his wise and discreet father; and it is a great danger to leave paternal governance. This happens most often as it did to the prodigal son of the Gospel <note>A reference to the Biblical parable in Luke 15:11-32, where a son leaves his father's house only to fall into ruin.</note>. And we should believe that those first princes and learned men were given from heaven to the commonwealths <term>republicas</term> as fathers. And since, with such good intention and so much consideration, they studied the equity and justice with which people were to be governed, current governors and judges should be glad that in matters so tangled and arduous—such as the rule of a city or a kingdom, or the resolution of lawsuits—they are governed and guided by the knowledge and prudence of the ancients. For what greater joy is there than to be certain, in the most important matters, that one is doing right? And one achieves this by following the law, which almost never errs. It is true that the prince has, and must have, the power to establish new laws, and to repeal those established, and to grant dispensations from them. But I say that just as much counsel and prudence is required to establish a new law for a people, and just as many causes and reasons are necessary to justify it, so much and no less is required to repeal one already established, or to choose not to follow it. However, we do not treat this "legal justice" in this work. It is discussed and taught in much larger volumes.

There is another particular kind of justice, which we call **commutative justice** <term>justicia cõmutatiua</term> <note>This refers to the justice governing private transactions and exchanges between individuals, ensuring that what is given and received are of equal value.</note>. This ought to be present in everyone, both princes and vassals alike: it shows and inclines a man not to wrong <note>original: "agrauiar"; to cause offense, harm, or legal injury to another.</note> another. In the absence of this virtue, the first kind [legal justice] becomes necessary. For if no one wronged another, a judge who judges would be superfluous. But because it is impossible, given our [fallen] state—

### how great its virtue and obligation.

...corrupt, a thousand grievances, injuries, thefts, and acts of violence would occur. And because justice makes a man just, and since there are two types of it, there are also two ways of being just: namely, a just judge and a just citizen. A judge is just when he rightly gives each party their due. And the private individual is just when he does not harm his neighbor.

This commutative justice <term>justicia commutatiua</term> <note>Commutative justice is the branch of justice governing private exchanges between individuals, ensuring that the value of what is given equals the value of what is received.</note> is practiced and shines most brightly in the contracts that men celebrate with one another. These are so numerous that not all of them even have a name. Some have acquired one; others have lacked one until now. Thus, there is a very famous distinction among learned doctors between contracts that are "named" and others that have no proper name. For example <note>original: "V.g." for the Latin *verbi gratia*</note>, if you give me some Chrysostoms <note>Likely referring to editions of the works of St. John Chrysostom, which were valuable scholarly items in the 16th century; the context of "ducats" implies a commercial transaction for books.</note> and I give you eight ducats for them, it is a contract (which we both make) properly called "sale and purchase." There are not a few of these, although I believe they have not been named because they are not currently as frequent or common as the named ones, which are very continuous. It is enough that we treat them in this chapter, providing examples and showing that for all of them to be just and lawful, they must contain equality—that is, that what is traded is equal in value and price. ### That it is natural law, what its principle is

...as we discussed at length in the second book. Since all the established rules aim at this goal: that the price equals the goods. 

In selling on credit <term>al fiado</term> <note>original: "al fiado"</note> for more than the current price, all injustice consists in an inequality—which is taking more than what the merchandise is worth in itself. And the effort spent there is in declaring this disparity. For neither the delay of the payment nor any of the other pretexts <note>original: "colores," literally "colors," used here to mean rhetorical excuses or justifications</note> that traders usually give for their defense makes them equal. A Flemish pound <note>The "libra de Flandres" was a unit of account used in international trade and banking, particularly between Spain and the Low Countries.</note> is worth one thousand seven hundred. This is, at that time, its just value. But it is sold on credit for one thousand nine hundred. It already exceeds the value on one side by two hundred; consequently, the price creates an inequality. Thus, justice is broken by not giving to each what belongs to them. Rather, it takes away what they already had: which are these two hundred that were charged in excess. They give as a reason the waiting for payment. But by proving (as we prove in its proper place) that none of these titles increases the value of the pound, it remains evidently clear that the goods and the price are still unequal.

When selling with advanced payment, it is common to give less than what the goods will be worth at the time of delivery—which is the measure and level of its just value. By taking a little away from that value, the inequality that is created appears very clearly. We explained this contract in its place.

In the loan, despite it being such an excellent work <note>The author refers to a "mutuum" or simple loan, which in Christian tradition was ideally an act of charity.</note>, only the interest (which is usury) is condemned, because only this causes excess and disproportion in the contract. For if one lent one hundred ducats, and they return one hundred and ten, the amount paid already exceeds what was received by ten. And consequently, those ten are the injustice.

In real currency exchanges <term>cambios reales</term> <note>These were financial contracts involving the exchange of different currencies in different locations, often used as a way to circumvent usury laws.</note>, where in order to gain some profit, it is necessary for the withdrawal and the payment to be unequal in quantity...

To this (as we have proved extensively), we are obligated not only by divine law but also by natural law itself. It is a more than sufficient reason to reject any business deal—no matter how great the profit—if it does not conform to the right dictates of reason. ## What natural law is, and what its principle is

...they ordain many necessary things according to the time and circumstances. It was not right for the first laws to determine or interfere in these matters, as they were temporary and brief; for the primary laws must be immutable. What God and nature command is perpetual. It cannot be changed, but **positive law** <term>derecho pofitiuo</term> <note>Human-made laws established by a government or church, as opposed to natural law derived from reason or divine law.</note> varies with time. We are also obliged to avoid or execute these laws for as long as they endure.

Beyond this, many things are left for the **Republic** <term>republica</term> <note>Referring generally to the civil state or the organized political community.</note> and the **Church** to determine, in one law as much as in another. In these matters (as is evident), they will have the force to bind their subjects. It is divine law that a man must confess all his sins; but the law does not specify when he is obliged to confess. It leaves this to the Church to determine. It is also a divine precept that we fast and mortify ourselves, but it does not explain when or how; all this remains to the declaration of His Church, which commands that this abstinence be practiced on certain days in **Lent** <term>quarefma</term>, during the **Ember days** <term>quatro tẽporas</term> <note>From the Latin "quattuor tempora" (four times). These were seasonal periods of fasting and prayer in the liturgical calendar.</note>, and on the vigils of the apostles, abstaining from meat and not dining. It is also a matter of **natural law** that a thing be sold for its just price, but it does not designate the specific just value of every kind of clothing. It leaves this to the Republic to set the price <note>original: "tasse" - referring to a fixed price or valuation set by authorities.</note> when it seems convenient. Thus, these ecclesiastical and secular powers and authorities can oblige us to celebrate our contracts and business dealings with certain circumstances and conditions—and even forbid us from certain contracts which, though they may be naturally licit in general, are not suitable at this time, or in this land, or for these people. All of this is entrusted to the prelates and princes, so that they may provide for and declare it.

# Author’s Purpose

...sums: such that neither Tyre nor Alexandria, in their own times, were equal to it. And in any of these dealings, one cannot avoid—given human malice and greed—certain deceptions and a thousand clever tricks, at times so hidden that a particular wit is needed to understand them, and even the help and favor of God so that, when the opportunity arises, one does not commit or plot them. 

Both these things—namely, the great commerce of these <term>Gradas <note>The "Steps" of the Cathedral of Seville, which served as the city’s informal commercial hub where merchants gathered to trade before the construction of a formal exchange building.</note></term> and the business interests found there, and the great amount of sin and error committed through what I believe is often ignorance—and the great desire I have seen (and still see) in many to do what is right, moved me to compose this little work along with those that follow. I intend for these to serve them as a light and a torch, so they may see the treacherous steps on the dangerous path of their profession. 

In this work, with all possible brevity, I will treat the state and condition of merchants—especially those of this <term>republic <note>In the 16th century, "republic" (república) referred generally to the "commonwealth" or the organized body politic of the city/state, rather than a specific form of government.</note></term>—and their businesses and dealings. I have written and published this specifically and particularly for their benefit and convenience in their mother tongue and the vernacular. In this way, without need of an interpreter, they may read and understand how they must buy and sell, form their partnerships, manage their commissions, send and sort their cargoes, and divide costs, interests, and profits.

<margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Part 2-2, Question 66, Article 2: "Each person is more careful to provide for something that belongs to himself alone than for what is common to all or to many." <note>original: "S. As **Aristotle** says, the delight a man receives from occupying himself with his own business is ineffable. It cannot be easily explained how much it matters, in terms of doing something with joy, for a man to consider that a thing is his own. On the contrary, great is the lukewarmness with which common business is treated.

<margin>Human affairs are handled more orderly if the particular care of some specific thing is assigned to individuals... <note>original: "Ordinatius res humana tractatur si singulis immineat propria cura alicuius rei pro-" This continues the citation from Aquinas regarding why private property leads to a more organized society.</note></margin> In such a way that, once that first charity was lost, it was necessary for each person to have some share in temporalities, whether in real estate or movable goods. It happened that, as not every kind of good fell to every person, but rather various kinds—vineyards to some, olive groves to others, livestock to others, clothing, linens, and cloth to others...

But this type of negotiation was as limited and insufficient as was natural for it to be, being the first of its kind. For all human things in their beginnings are either small, weak, coarse, or simple; and with the passage of time they grow and gain strength. This imitates man himself, who at the beginning of his existence is almost repulsive to think how much he is nothing. Thus, this method of trade was "lame," for the things necessary for life could neither be obtained nor found easily. It happened (as the law says) that while I might need what you had, I might not have anything that was of use to you; or if I did have it, I might need it just as much myself. Thus, no barter could take place between us, and consequently, no one could sufficiently provide for his house and family. 

It is true that despite all its insufficiency, this mode of trade lasted for great lengths of time in many places. ## On the Beginning and Origin

<margin>
Paulus, Law 1 of the Digest, on the contracting of sales: "The origin of selling and buying began with exchanges, but because it did not always nor easily happen that when you had what I desired, I in turn had what you were willing to accept, a material was chosen—a public and perpetual valuation—which would remedy the difficulties of exchanges and the proportions of quantity." <note>original: "P.I.C.in.l.1 ff. de cōtra. empt. origo vẽdēdi emē diq, a permutationibus cœpit, sed quia nō semper, nec facile occur rebat vt cũ tu haberes quod ego de siderarẽ, in uicẽ ego ha berẽ, quod tu accipere veles, electa materia est publica, ac perpetua stimatio, q̃ difficultati bus permu- tationum & qualitate quantitatis subueniret." This is a foundational legal text by the Roman jurist Paulus, explaining why money was invented to solve the "double coincidence of wants" problem in bartering.</note>
</margin>

<margin>
Aristotle, as cited above. "When help was sought from more distant [lands]..." <note>original: "Arift. vbi supra. Cū a re motioribus quæreretur auxiliū im-" This refers to Aristotle's Politics, where he explains that as communities grew and traded over longer distances, the transport of bulky goods became impractical.</note>
</margin>

[Through human] ingenuity and organization, necessity compelled them to seek another form of negotiation—one that was broader, more capable, and sufficient to ensure that necessary things could be obtained with ease, plenty, and abundance. And they invented buying and selling at a just price, valuing and assessing each thing on its own according to how it could serve mankind. They established silver and gold as the common and general price for all things. In this way, without having to give up the provisions, furnishings, or valuables that one already possessed and used, a person could find what they newly required. This was the origin of buying and selling, and of the invention of money, as <term>Paulus<gloss>Julius Paulus, one of the most influential Roman jurists, whose writings make up a large portion of the Digest of Justinian.</gloss></term> testifies and affirms in the Law.

This was a trade that pleased everyone, except for <term>Lycurgus<gloss>The legendary lawgiver of Sparta, famous for his austere reforms.</gloss></term>. In the laws he gave to the <note>The text attributes these laws to the "Parthians and Lydians," likely following a specific interpretation of St. Thomas Aquinas, though Lycurgus is traditionally associated with Sparta.</note> Parthians and Lydians—as **St. Thomas** records in his twentieth *Opusculum*—he prohibited buying and selling, commanding that nothing be sold, but that everything should be bartered. However, this was a very blind law, which no one afterwards accepted.

This new invention of commerce was also brought about by the passage of time—especially after the <term>General Flood<gloss>The Biblical Deluge (Noah’s Flood).</gloss></term>, when this <term>worldly machine<gloss>An early modern phrase referring to the complex structure or "engine" of the physical world and human society.</gloss></term> began to be populated anew. There were provinces and kingdoms that were sterile and lacked every kind of provision or clothing. In some parts, olives, vines, silk, or <term>cochineal<gloss>A precious scarlet dye produced from insects; highly valued in the Spanish Empire.</gloss></term> did not grow; in other parts, there was no cattle or sheep. We see many provinces lacking these things even today, despite all the industry, diligence, and labor that has been applied to produce them without success; they remain lacking in many necessary things.

To provide for an entire kingdom or city, it was impossible to transport a great quantity of these goods by carriage. It was a most troublesome business to carry an equal amount of goods from here to there for barter, and it incurred great costs. For both these reasons, men agreed to choose a pair of metals that would serve as the price for everything sellable, so that in a small volume and weight, the value of much could be carried.

<margin>See the Decretals regarding clerics or monks avoiding business and the benefits of the clergy, book 1, distinction 88; also on fornication; and St. Thomas [Aquinas], *Summa Theologica* 2-2, question 40, article 2; also question 77, article 4; question 187, article 2; and Sylvester [Prieras], under the word "cleric," point 3. <note>These are legal and theological citations from Canon Law and the works of Thomas Aquinas and Sylvester Prieras regarding the moral restrictions on the priesthood.</note></margin>
To raise horses, and once they are raised, to sell them at a fair: this is the business of squires <note>lower-ranking nobility or landowners</note>. To buy a great quantity of grape juice <note>must</note> so that, once it has become wine, it may be sold for a profit: this is a common cleverness shared by everyone, not the profession of a merchant. This is because the wine improves in itself and is almost transformed. But to buy any kind of clothing or provisions and, without any change occurring in the item itself, to sell it again because the value has increased or it has moved to another place: this is trading and negotiating. And this alone, and only in this sense, are clerics forbidden from being merchants—namely, that they should not engage in buying to then immediately sell again for a profit without the item itself being changed. A cleric cannot buy wheat and store it <note>original: "encamarallo"</note> to sell it, nor oil, nor wine already made, nor jewels, nor slaves, nor anything already perfect in its kind. But they are not forbidden from sowing, tilling, or breeding, even if it is for sale; because in all of this (as Aristotle says) there is a great conversion in nature and a great change.

Returning to our purpose, it is clear that merchants are a very ancient people who began almost as soon as the world was created; although, as their occasion <note>their origin or necessity</note> was sin, they have always gone on multiplying it with malice. It is true that in ancient times (as Plutarch says), when men desired and sought what is worthy of being desired—which is to see and to know—merchandise was held in high reputation, especially practicing it in remote parts as those from Spain do. And there were then most eminent men who applied themselves to trade, taking the opportunity to carry curious and costly goods to other kingdoms in order to see people and cities, and to acquire favor with great princes and kings. Because these rulers, to obligate the merchants to bring exquisite jewels and treasures from their lands, honored and cherished them greatly. Solon and Thales <note>original: "Talete"</note>, the two wisest of the Seven Sages of Greece, were merchants throughout their youth, and afterward great philosophers; and Solon was a very powerful prince

# ...and the Antiquity of Merchants.

...and a prudent governor. Hesiod, a most ancient author, and Plutarch, affirm that in those times no way of life that man followed, nor any occupation in which he engaged, nor trade, nor office in which he practiced, was as highly esteemed and regarded among the people as commerce <term>merchandise</term> <note>original: "mercācia"</note>, because of the great convenience and profit it brings, both to the traders and to the entire body of the commonwealth <term>republic</term> <note>original: "republica," referring to the state or organized society</note>. 

First, this art provides cities and kingdoms with an infinite variety of things that they do not possess within themselves, bringing them from abroad; these things serve not only for luxury, but are often necessary for the very preservation of life. 

Second, there is a great abundance of every kind of clothing, both native to the land and foreign, which is a great benefit. 

The individual traders also enrich themselves entirely and perfectly in body and soul. Because by conversing with many people, being in distinct kingdoms, dealing with various nations, experiencing different customs, and considering the diverse governance and civil order <term>policy</term> <note>original: "policia," meaning the refined administration and social order of a city</note> of different peoples, they become universal men, well-traveled and fluent <term>ladinos</term> <note>referring to being linguistically and culturally skilled in foreign environments</note> for whatever business may come their way. They acquire and increase great prudence and experience to guide and govern themselves, both in private and general matters. They are useful to their commonwealth because of the great knowledge of various things they have seen and heard in their travels <note>original: "peregrinaciō," literally pilgrimage, but here meaning world travels</note>. 

We see that very excellent men have emerged from the ranks of merchants who, with their prudence and power, often saved their homeland from grave evils in very dangerous times, and even built very populous and rich cities. The first founder of Marseille <note>original: "Meſſalia"; Plutarch records that the founder of the city of Marseille was a Greek merchant</note> was a merchant and founder of a principal city in France. Thales, and Hippocrates the Mathematician <note>likely Hippocrates of Chios, a 5th-century BC geometer who, according to tradition, turned to study after being a merchant</note>, both illustrious men who through their philosophy and study achieved great fame throughout the world, first practiced commerce. # Of the Principle and Origin

<margin>Cicero in Book 1 of *On Duties* [De Officiis]: Commerce, if it is small, is to be considered mean; if it is large and abundant, bringing many things from everywhere and distributing them to many without vanity, it is not to be greatly blamed. <note>original: "Cice.in.l. 1. de officijs. mercatura si tenuis est sordida putada est, si magna & copiosa multa vndiq; asportas, multis sine vanitate impertiens. nō est admodū vituperanda."</note></margin>
...to the Hebrews, he took a great quantity of oil to sell, whereby he might save on the cost of the journey <note>A common historical anecdote of the era suggested that ancient philosophers like Thales or Plato traded goods to fund their travels for wisdom.</note>. Also Solon, the reformer of the Athenians and a man of noble spirit, considered it wise counsel to follow trade to earn a living, having become poor because his parents had spent almost all their income on magnificences (which were, perhaps, unnecessary). Afterward, in truth, once the primary goal of merchants became gold and silver, rather than the knowledge and news of peoples and cities (a thing which, according to reason, is highly valued), the art justly came to be held in low regard, and its practice became shameful to illustrious men. Because being a merchant no longer meant being a man desirous of the good of his country as before, but rather a lover of his own money and greedy for that of others: a vice that has always been an affront to men of good intellect. In this state trade stands at present, as the common judgment of the people clearly proves. The discourse and matter of this chapter, although it seems plain and clearly stated in common terms, is drawn from many ancient doctors: from Saint Thomas <note>referring to the *Secunda Secundae* of the *Summa Theologiae*</note>, from the Philosopher <note>The standard Renaissance title for Aristotle</note> in the 5th book of his *Ethics* and the first of his *Politics*, and from canon and civil law <term>Digest</term> <note>original: "ff. de contrahenda emptione," referring to the section of Roman law concerning the contracting of purchases</note>, as appears in the citations and texts placed in the margin. And since so many have treated of it, it is only right that we know what standing and place this state usually holds among the virtues and vices.

->### The Art of the Merchant<-

...indifferent things, which considered in themselves have no part of good or evil—such as walking, talking, going to the countryside, or dressing oneself. These in themselves suggest neither virtue nor vice; rather, if they are performed for a good end, they will be good, and if for a bad one, they will be evil and vicious. But among these things, which are (so to speak) in the neutral middle, there are some that lean—at least in appearance—more toward one extreme than the other. Some have a greater disposition toward rectitude and justice than toward sin and guilt. Keeping silent, eating little, and dressing plainly are qualities that serve <term>honesty<note>In this historical context, "honesty" (honestidad) refers to moral integrity, modesty, and living in a way that earns social respect.</note></term> more than distraction and lack of restraint. Conversely, there are other actions that, although they may not be inherently evil, appear to be so, and have the reputation and public opinion for it—such as walking elegantly, dressing expensively, or eating luxuriously.

Of this number and condition, says the <term>Angelic Doctor<note>A common title for St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval philosopher and theologian whose writings on the ethics of trade were authoritative in the 16th century.</note></term>, is this trade and way of life. That is to say, it has a "bad face," and according to some, even worse deeds. What gives it such a bad reputation is the convenience and opportunity it provides for breeding and increasing many vices, particularly <term>avarice<note>Greed or the excessive desire for wealth.</note></term>, toward which it seems to be directed as its ultimate goal and target.

For it cannot be denied (as Aristotle says) that the common intent of the merchant is to increase his traded capital. This is a desire which, as Solon says—who had experienced it firsthand—is without rule, measure, or end. Although, as the philosopher <note>Aristotle.</note> says in that passage, riches and the desire for them ought to have a limit, since they are nothing more than an instrument for life. Life is so brief, yet wealth is so pleasing to all, that it serves as an argument that effectively tempts the merchant with greed; it is a rare and difficult thing for him not to be overcome by it. Because through the practice of trade, a thousand means for gain and profit are discovered and offered to him at every moment, and most of them are dangerous and "sticky" <note>original: "pegajosos"; the author implies these opportunities for profit are morally corrupting and hard to clean oneself of once touched.</note>. It would require a greater virtue than that which merchants typically profess or possess to remain upright and not fall when these occasions arise. For this cause, it is suspected that, either through malice or weakness, they fall.

In this <term>Opuscule<note>A minor work or small treatise.</note></term>, I did not wish to be a preacher, but a doctor; not an eloquent and elegant rhetorician, but a **moral theologian**, clear and brief. ### The Art of the Merchant

[This is what] the glorious <term>Doctor<note>Likely a reference to St. Augustine or St. John Chrysostom, Church Fathers frequently cited in 16th-century Spanish manuals regarding the morality of trade.</note></term> says—let those merchants hear this whose greed is so disordered that if any loss befalls them, whether by sea or by land, they often speak words that are even blasphemous. Their life is such that, though they are Christians, they give cause for the <term>Gentiles<note>In this context, 'Gentiles' and 'infidels' refers to non-Christians, specifically Muslim or Jewish trading partners, who might judge Christianity by the dishonest behavior of Catholic merchants.</note></term> and infidels to blaspheme the name of the Lord. For, as if mocking the Gospel law and its perfection, the Gentiles say to one another: "Look at the customs of these Catholics." Thus, let Christians amend and correct themselves, and let them not be merchants.

But you will say to me: "I provide the <term>Republic<note>Original: 'republica'. In the 16th century, this referred to the 'Commonwealth' or the organized body politic and the common good of the city.</note></term> with many provisions, and if I gain something by selling for more than I bought, it is as a stipend and salary for my labor, according to what is written in the Gospel: *the laborer is worthy of his hire* <note>original: 'digno es el obrero de su jornal.' A reference to the Latin Vulgate, Luke 10:7: 'dignus est enim operarius mercede sua.'</note>. If I lie and swear, those are my own vices and sins; they belong to the man, not to the art, which could very well be practiced without lying or swearing if I so willed. This admonishes and persuades me: not that I should stop being a merchant, but that I should stop being a liar and a perjurer. If you command me to leave this office, tell me in which you would have me occupy myself? What office is there in the Republic that a wicked man cannot use poorly? Does the farmer not perhaps swear or blaspheme when either a cloud does not appear or the sun does not appear at its proper times?"

In this way he continues giving examples in many other matters; and so he remains, satisfied that since they will not leave the art, they should at least practice it with rectitude and justice, not mixing so many evils into an art that is not bad in itself. And so I also remain, and am especially content because I doubt that those of this city could stop being [merchants], since it is so necessary and profitable for them to be so for so many kingdoms. One thing only I would dare to say—and it should be said briefly, and even advised to whoever wishes to be advised—that one should not be a merchant in everything, but only in one kind—

### ¶ CHAPTER IV. ON THE END AND INTENTION
### that the Merchant should have in his dealings.

<margin>Aristotle, *Politics* 1; St. Thomas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 77. There is a double exchange: one is natural, for things necessary for life; the other is for business.</margin>
<image-desc>Decorative drop cap initial 'E' featuring a central circular landscape/architectural scene surrounded by intricate floral and scrollwork patterns.</image-desc>Selling and buying is done in one of two ways (namely): either for the provision of the family, or to gain something by buying and selling. I say that we either buy to spend and consume it, or to profit by selling. For the household, one buys wheat, barley, wine, oil, tapestries, silks, and linens. All this and other things in this vein are usually bought to be used by the person, the wife, children, and servants, for the provisioning of their estates, or for the <term>vintages<note>The seasonal gathering of grapes for winemaking.</note></term>, harvest, or reaping.

<margin>Since it is indeed double: one is the discipline of the household, the other is the pursuit of money. The former is indeed necessary; the latter is deservedly condemned. <note>original Latin: 'Cū vero fit duplex altera disciplina rei familiaris altera pecuniaria...'</note></margin>This buying or selling is a business so lawful that it is natural, like honoring our elders. For we are no less obliged to sustain the minors who are under our care and obedience than to give honor to our superiors. And for one to sell what he has in excess, or what he fancies, to buy with the price what he needs for his sustenance, is an obligation and most lawful. But this (though it is buying and selling) is not being a merchant, but rather a <term>civilized man<note>original: 'hombre político.' In the 16th century, this referred to a person who participates properly in the 'polis' or organized community life, fulfilling their social duties.</note></term>, and one careful in what is just. There is another kind of sale, which is to buy some clothing—such as <term>fardels<note>original: 'fardos.' Large bundles or bales of cloth.</note></term>—or <term>pipes<note>original: 'pipas.' Large casks used for transporting wine or oil.</note></term> of wine or oil, to carry them to other parts, or waiting for other times to resell them for more than they cost. To understand and live by this (as the law says) is to be a merchant. And for such a person, we seek some good purpose so that he may act well; for the other [the head of household], it is not necessary to seek one, as he already has it within his nature.

# To have the Merchant.

## D

...tians to gain true happiness in their trade, which they are obliged to do even if they were not members of the Church, being guided only by <term>natural light<note>A philosophical concept referring to human reason and the innate ability to discern moral truths without the aid of divine revelation.</note></term>. It says that just as in all human offices and practices it is necessary for men to have their goals, so too merchants must have in their diligence and labor some good intent that moves them in their operations. 

This must be the **common good** and the advancement of the **public state**, aiming to provide for their neighbors, through their industry, the necessary provisions. For it is established and verified among men of good judgment that our primary works are always directed toward and performed for the general good of all, and in them the growth and comfort of the <term>commonwealth<note>Original: *republica*. In the 16th century, this term referred to the "public thing" or the collective well-being of the community, rather than a specific form of government.</note></term> is sought. And since among human institutions and arts trade holds such a primary place, it is in accordance with reason that the merchant should aim in it, first and foremost, at public and universal utility. 

The **second goal** should be to favor the poor with their profit, maintaining a certain order and arrangement in their <term>pious works<note>Acts of charity or religious devotion, such as giving alms or supporting the Church.</note></term>, helping first the poorest and those closest in blood, or in similarity of good character, as ordered by the **natural law** itself, written by divine providence in our hearts. 

The **third and lowest goal** should be to sustain the expenses of his household with his trade and <term>profits<note>Original: *interesses*. While this can mean "interest" in a modern sense, here it refers more broadly to the financial returns or gains from business dealings.</note></term>. It is right for each of these levels to be valued according to its dignity and worth; but the evil is that common people, given over to the delights of sensuality, furiously pervert this order and quality, which is most worthy of being kept with great diligence. And they pay more attention to the last (which is the lowest) than to the first and second, which are so sovereign. And not only do they prefer it with great madness, but they follow this alone and aim for this alone, totally forgetting the others, as if they were creatures lacking knowledge, formed for the service of their bel- <note>The word is completed by the catchword "tre" on the next page, forming *vientre*, meaning "belly" or "appetite."</note>

# On the intention that [the merchant] should have

## D

...among us, or as if the luster and apparent prosperity of this life were the true human happiness that we seek. **Plutarch**—a <term>Gentile<note>A term used by the author to refer to Plutarch as a non-Christian, Greco-Roman philosopher whose wisdom is nonetheless respected.</note></term> man—says this of those merchants who only intend to gain through their <term>art of earning a living<note>Original: *arte de comer*. While literally "the art of eating," it refers to the business of providing for one's basic needs.</note></term>. If he said this of those with a good intent, what do we think he would say of those who no longer seek mere sustenance through trade, but rather riches and treasures, as many do today? This is a corrupt and deadly intention.

Certainly, he would call it an **unspeakable vice**, unworthy of even being named among people. For truly, it is against all reason in a trade so common to the <term>commonwealth<note>Original: *republica*. This refers to the public interest and the shared social order of the community.</note></term>, such as merchandise is, to seek either solely or principally one’s private profit; how much worse is it to seek one’s own extreme vanity and pomp to the harm and grievance of all.

Wherein it is much to be noted that it is not the same to want to earn a living as it is to want to grow rich; for the first will is good and upright, while the other is vicious and pernicious. The appetite to sustain oneself and one’s family is natural, but the desire for riches is abominable. The great distance between one intent and the other is clearly known and understood: he who seeks to maintain himself, as soon as he achieves this, is at peace, not involving himself from then on in more business than is sufficient for him to draw a moderate interest.

But he who has as his target the hoarding and increasing of his wealth is never satisfied, no matter how much he achieves. This is because money has no limit, nor is the desire (as **Solomon** says) ever satiated when it is employed in such things. And in this, it is clearly seen that modern traders do not hold any of the three good ends—not even maintaining themselves—as their principal goal. Instead, they seek only to grow rich (a thing they can never fully achieve). Even when they have enough to live well, they do not retire nor set their lives in order; rather, seeing the possibilities before them, they conceive great ambitions for greater assets. Then, they hurl themselves into larger shipments and engulf themselves, entering that **labyrinth** of exchanges, usury, <term>annuities<note>Original: *censos*. A common 16th-century financial instrument where a person received a lump sum in exchange for an annual payment, often used to navigate religious prohibitions against usury.</note></term>, and taxes, where they live more restlessly than...

## CHAPTER V. ON CERTAIN USEFUL AND NECESSARY INSTRUCTIONS.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring intricate floral and vine-like ornamentation within a square border.</image-desc>

**BEFORE** we enter into the specific means that must be taken, I wish to give these gentlemen some good advice; instructions of such a kind that, if they are taken and followed, even if they do not gain a great estate, they will gain by them (in my opinion) a great reputation and a good standing among the people. Furthermore, they will avoid many expenses that are damaging to the purse and not very honorable to the person.

The first piece of advice is that they should not keep a large or costly house, whether in its buildings, its servants, its furnishings, or its jewelry. This is because, since they gain everything by selling to the citizens, if the people see them spending excessively, they immediately suspect that they have been greatly cheated. In this matter, the merchants bear great blame...

# Some useful instructions

...for, because they spend their <term>wealth<note>Original: *hazienda*. In this context, it refers to one's estate, assets, or property.</note></term> on vanities, they fall into the great hatred of the people, a thing that weighs heavily upon them. For people cannot endure with a good spirit the sight of others triumphing with their wealth. Even to **Publicola** <note>Publius Valerius Publicola (died 503 BC), a legendary leader of the Roman Republic known for his modesty and for being a "friend of the people."</note>, a Roman captain so beneficial to his homeland that he had delivered it from fundamental ruin, the Romans (despite holding him in the highest reputation) could not help but murmur in public and in secret upon seeing him increase the service and administration of his house with a little more pomp and splendor, falsely thinking it had not been well-acquired. How much more will they blaspheme with spite and rage against the **merchant**, whose display they know for certain came out of their own purses and estates. Thus, in living modestly, he avoids expense, saves money, and makes himself well-liked and trusted.

Likewise, they should be restrained in their speech and of few words, considering that if they speak much—as they always speak in favor of their own advantage <note>Original: *en derecho de su dedo*. Likewise, they should abhor swearing and accustom themselves never to do it. Considering that if they do not hold it in great abhorrence, as their own interest always moves them, they will swear at every moment. And as the matters they deal with are most often uncertain and doubtful, they will think they are telling the truth, and yet they will lie. ...about what is certain and true: by the second or third month they have oaths so much on the tip of their tongue that they swear without noticing whether what they affirm or deny is a lie or the truth. # Some useful instructions

...[every] day Mass, especially having such great convenience in this cathedral <note>Original: *yglesia mayor*.
