# Some useful instructions

...liberty, and even authority. And it is this: given that [the confessor] holds an opinion and defends it, he should not bind the penitent <note>A "penitent" is a person confessing their sins to a priest and seeking absolution.</note> by it if the penitent does not wish to be bound, nor follow it; and if the path the penitent follows is probable <note>In 16th-century "moral theology," a "probable" opinion was one supported by logic and the authority of respected scholars, even if it wasn't the only or most popular view. This allowed for flexibility in complex business cases.</note>, and has its reasons, foundations, and authors. It is enough for the confessor to advise him on what he holds to be most certain, or what pleases him more; but if it displeases the penitent, and what he does can be done and is approved by many approved authors, it would be great stubbornness and arrogance for the confessor to condemn it or refuse to absolve him unless he desists from it.

When there are good opinions among the learned on both sides of a contract, everyone is free to follow whichever they choose. I understand the same, in substance, when a business matter is proposed to a theologian outside of confession. If there are opinions for both sides, and either one can be done and followed without danger (even if the theologian has chosen one of them as more probable), he must not bind the one who asks to his own view, but rather tell him plainly his opinion while advising him that doing the contrary is not a sin. This is because there are many <term>Doctors<note>Original: *doctores*. These are recognized experts in Church law and theology whose writings carry official weight.</note></term> who hold it to be lawful. 

I consider this advice to be very important in the business of merchants, which commonly involves interest <note>Profit or financial gain.</note>. And I do not know why, if someone asks me if he can make a profit in a certain way—with many grave and learned authors conceding the profit to him—I should take it away from him or forbid it solely because I am of the contrary opinion. Of these cases, there are a hundred thousand in <term>moral theology<note>The study of how to apply religious and ethical principles to specific human actions and dilemmas.</note></term>. It should suffice for the theologian that he has, and ought to have, the license and authority to give his judgment; but he must not give it as an inviolable rule and law if, as I say, the matter is in itself merely a matter of opinion, and there is an equal or nearly equal probability to the contrary. "Equal" is understood to mean when, in public schools and universities, the disciples of their authors hold, read, and defend that view. 

I was moved to say this because I see that interest moves man so much that at times, even thinking something is forbidden, he seeks and pursues it; and it could happen that in some business matter it seems...

# Some useful instructions

...it seemed to me and to other more learned individuals that one could not, nor should one, charge interest <note>The original Spanish *interessar* refers to the complex moral and legal issue of usury or earning a profit from a loan, which was heavily regulated by the Church.</note>, while there were others of no less reputation to whom it seemed that one could. And if [the confessor] were to resolutely condemn and forbid it, and the merchant—believing me to be moved by his own greed—should still desire and obtain it, he would sin mortally in doing so. This would be because of what his own conscience dictates to him, and even more so because of my own foolishness and arrogance. In my judgment, it is a great pity for someone to sin while earning what they could have earned with merit, or at least without sin. For this reason, the confessor and theologian must not be so enamored of their own concepts as to consider all others invalid; rather, they must be discreet. They must discern between what is evidence and what is merely opinion or probability, and not value anything more than what it truly is, even if their own personal preference inclines and moves them toward it.

All that I have said must be left to the judgment of the confessor and theologian who is well-read and knows when it is permissible to follow an opinion and when it is not (because it has become an error). It must not be left to the greed and blind judgment of the merchant who is ignorant of letters. In this, the merchants will realize how much it is in their own interest to choose a prudent, wise, and independent <note>The author uses *libre* (free), meaning a confessor who is not beholden to the merchant's money or his own rigid biases.</note> confessor. This is so necessary that it will be useful to explain to them more specifically what kind of confessor they should choose and what qualities he must possess. This is especially true since there are cases specifically referred to the good knowledge and prudence of the confessor—cases of such a nature that they should not be resolved outside of confession.

We say that the truth should not always be told; there are some truths that cannot be dealt with except when administering the sacrament <note>This refers to the Sacrament of Penance (Confession), where the seal of the confessional provides absolute privacy for sensitive financial or legal admissions.</note>. This is just like the laws themselves, which for many crimes—such as punches, insults, or knife wounds—do not assign a specific penalty or express how they are to be punished. In these criminal cases, it is very important to have an experienced, wise, and impartial judge. How much more important will it be in the discretionary business of the soul to have a confessor whose decision leaves a man feeling secure?

Some traders and people of status say: "My confessor tells me I can do it, so I am not obliged to do more." Certainly, in doubtful cases, it is enough to follow the confessor, provided he is of the appropriate sort. But if you deliberately choose him—not because he is the one you need, but because he is the one who delights and pleases you most—or if he truly lacks the required qualities, you do not fulfill your duty by following his opinion. Do not secure your conscience with such weak guarantees. Because to speak plainly, to confess to someone who is not sufficient for your state of life is not to confess fruitfully. Nor can one remain secure whose own conscience tells them how poorly they are fulfilling their duty.

# Some useful instructions

...[not] one who possesses a scattered, loose, and smooth tongue, seeking the delight of the ears more than the benefit of the soul. Nor is it required that he be a profoundly learned scholar (for such men are very rare), as it would then be necessary to travel twenty or thirty leagues from one's town to go to confession many times. What is necessary is that he possesses moderate learning along with a great knowledge of practice <note>original: "praxis"</note>. Because the law governing all these contracts is contained within very few rules; but they are so universal, and the subject matter so broad, that they are applied in two thousand ways. For this reason, it is of the utmost importance to understand the practical reality of business. 

Moral theology <note>The branch of theology focused on how a Christian should act in daily life.</note> is, in reality, moral philosophy, for which—according to Aristotle—experience is of great benefit. So much so that he says that one who lacks it, such as a youth, is not fit even to be a disciple, much less a teacher. This science is like law and medicine, where theory alone is not enough unless accompanied by practice. Thus we see that after having studied for four years in Salamanca <note>The University of Salamanca was the intellectual center of the Spanish Empire and the birthplace of the School of Salamanca, which pioneered early economic theory.</note>, those who intend to excel in their faculty go to the Chancelleries <note>term: Chancelleries — High courts of appeal in Spain where lawyers and judges gained practical legal experience.</note> for a couple of years to learn the practice. And once one has studied medicine, he spends no few days as a practitioner <note>original: "practicāte"</note> visiting the sick in the company of some physician who has already grown old. 

Thus, the merchant should not take as a confessor someone who possesses only book-learning, even if it is great, for he would not dare entrust his bodily illness to a clever youth who had just finished studying medicine, nor would he entrust his lawsuit to a new lawyer. For people of high status, it seems to me that more learning and less experience are necessary. Because they have greater and more serious business, the practice of which, in truth, is discussed extensively in the schools themselves. And as Socrates argues in the dialogue of Plato regarding the science of governing, it seems we all emerge as masters from our mothers' wombs <note>A sarcastic reference to the common belief that everyone is naturally qualified to rule or offer political opinions.</note>. But the dealings of merchants and money-changers are very subtle <note>original: "delgados"</note>, and in the category of business, they are like the "insoluble" or "reflexive" arts...

...to aggrandize and ennoble his own homeland, and he strives to transfer to it all the wealth and treasure that he can seize and strip from this one; and those from here do the same when they are there. Furthermore, since everyone so loves and takes pleasure in the customs, uses, rites, and dress in which they were raised: wherever they go, they wish to graft and plant them, and they preach and persuade others to adopt them. And as the common people <note>original: "vulgo" — the masses or general public, often characterized by elite writers of this era as fickle or easily led astray.</note> are so fickle and fond of novelty, they immediately imitate and receive them. These customs are often inherently harmful and corrupt; and if they are not, they at least do not suit this land as they did their own. And so it is provided in what concerns the Indies <note>The "Indies" refers to the Spanish territories in the Americas.</note> by the law of the kingdom in these words:

> We command that no foreigner may trade in the Indies, nor may any foreigner, nor *Morisco* <note>original: "morisco" — a person of Muslim descent who had converted to Christianity, often subject to legal restrictions in the Spanish Empire.</note>, nor muleteer <note>original: "harriero" — someone who transports goods by pack animals.</note> buy gold or silver, in bars or in ingots, under penalty of forfeiture and perpetual exile.

Because when outsiders conduct trade, there is neither lasting wealth in the kingdom nor good ancient customs. Of these damages and evils, Spain, Seville, and the Indies are eyewitnesses. For this reason, the philosophers feel it is very necessary to disqualify foreigners from trade, just as they are justly disqualified in all places from government and the administration of justice; and to grant it instead to the natives, appointing, as I say, some specific individuals by their own hand. 

This would be (if any city were to do it) a busy and laborious business (I confess), but it would simultaneously be so profitable that the great benefit would be the pay and reward for the small amount of labor. The commonweal <note>The "republica" or organized political community.</note> itself could give to two or four men the money with which to bring what is necessary, designating a certain amount for their commission <note>original: "fatoria" — an agency fee or commission paid to a factor or commercial agent.</note>. And if not giving them the capital, but rather having them provide it, the commonweal could grant them a moderate profit that would be light and easy for everyone. This especially could and should be done by the republics of Peru and New Spain <note>Modern-day Mexico and central/northern Spanish colonies in the Americas.</note>, and it would prevent such notable harm as they suffer every day. # On the Authority of the Commonwealth in Price-Setting

<margin>Digest, Book 1, regarding the office of the urban prefect. <note>original: "L. 1. ff. de officio praefe. urb." — A reference to the *Corpus Juris Civilis*, the foundation of Western law, detailing the duties of the Roman official responsible for maintaining order and regulating markets in the city.</note></margin>

Because it is the office of the commonwealth <term>commonwealth: "republica" — the state or the organized political community acting for the public good</term> to appraise and give value to all things that serve human life. These things do not have a fixed value of their own; or if they do, it is neither just nor appropriate to follow or consider what they are worth in their own essence, but rather how they can serve and benefit man, for whose sake they were produced and are preserved. This appears clearly through examples. To gold and silver—merely a bit of congealed earth—the commonwealth gave so much status and value that it made them the measure and price of all things. Conversely, a horse or an ox, if one looks at its nature and essence, is worth as much as its weight in gold because it is a living being and exceeds the metal beyond comparison; yet it does not have such high esteem, and it would be nonsense to hold it so. For a thing must not be valued...

<margin>Our need is the cause and measure of human exchanges. <note>original: "indigentia nostra est causa & mesura humanarum commutationum."</note> Saint Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica*, Second part of the Second part, Question 77, article 2, reply 3.</margin>
...at more than what it contributes to our sustenance. Aristotle says admirably, in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, that what gives value and price to all earthly things is our necessity. If we had no need of them, we would neither buy nor appraise them. This is the measure and weight of their value. They are not valued at more than they serve, and those things are held in higher regard which are more necessary and more beneficial. And the fact that men do not make use of the same things in every place causes that which some hold in high regard to be held by others in low regard. The silks and brocades that we value so much are trodden upon by the Ethiopians; the hides and skins of which they make so much account, we despise. This is because they do not wear silk, nor do we wear raw leather. In no place, in no nation, was a thing ever appraised according to its nature, but rather by our necessity and use. Even in metals, and in currency itself, the gold, silver, stones, and pearls—which are the height of all the Orient and Occident of this Old World—did not have such a reputation in any province or kingdom of the New World (which we call the Indies), and in many of them, they have none even to this day. # On the Authority of the Commonwealth in Price-Setting 33

...the highest status [gold] reached during their pagan times <note>original: "gentilidad" — referring to the pre-Christian era of the Indigenous peoples</note> was in Peru and New Spain; and it amounted to nothing more than being a jewel or finery, like a plume of feathers here: not a price for things, nor currency. In Florida, which is as large as all of Europe, they hold gold and silver in such low regard that they disdain to take it in their hands just as we do with dirt: copper and iron are, among them, the highest wealth. And they desire one pound of copper more than four of gold. They say that with the former they work and cultivate the land that sustains them and produces fruit. Certainly, there is not, nor have I read of a people (in this regard) more wise.

A notable story, and worthy of perpetual memory, is that which occurred in the year [15]56 to the New Spain fleet that was lost there. After the ships had run aground by the force of the water and wind, and the treasure had been removed and spread across the beach (which amounted to eight hundred thousand ducats <term>ducats: "ducados" — high-value coins used for international trade</term>), the Spaniards gave of them and offered the Indians as much as they wanted, both to appease them and for provisions. The Indians laughed at this to an extreme. They would approach a sack with a knife—without anyone opposing them—that contained one or two thousand ducats, and opening it, they emptied the reals <term>reals: "reales" — the standard silver Spanish coin</term> onto the ground as if they were dust; and with only the hemp and linen from the bundles, they went away so happy that they fled with it through their sands and wilderness like deer, thinking that our men would come after them to take it away. Our men also laughed quite a bit at this.

And what is more to be admired is that they left it all there on the beach and traveled by land to Mexico: where, having arrived, they gave word to the Viceroy Don Luis de Velasco <note>Luis de Velasco (1511–1564) was the second Viceroy of New Spain, known for his attempts to protect Indigenous rights.</note>. Saint Augustine also alludes sharply and delicately to this purpose in his book *The City of God*, where he says that our whim and thought differ so much from nature that, although a mouse is worth more in itself for being a living animal than much wheat, there is no one who would not prefer a little wheat in his granary <term>granary: "troxa" — a storehouse for grain</term> over many mice. And since price should not follow the dignity and natural being of creatures, but rather the benefit and convenience we derive from them, there is no one better suited to make this appraisal than the commonwealth <term>commonwealth: "republica" — referring to the state or organized society</term> and its prince, who is the head of all. And it is even good reason that, if it was within his jurisdiction and office to choose two or three metals and make them the price for the rest, it should also be his right to apply and divide their value to clothing—letting this be worth so much and this provision worth more or less—and that sales and contracts be made with such and such conditions. And if these are not met, let such sales be null, of no value or effect; it is just that subordinates observe these, since princes establish them with such consideration for their own good. ### E 2

...to sell each thing for what it is worth. This is a natural dictate of reason that teaches all nations without the need for any teacher <note>original: "doctor"</note> or positive law <note>Man-made laws enacted by a government, as opposed to natural or divine law</note>. However, nature does not set or designate what the **just price** <note>term: <term>Just Price</term> (Latin: *iustum pretium*) — a theological and legal theory that prices should reflect a fair value rather than whatever the market will bear</note> of each thing should be. Nature created and produced these things, but it did not assign them a value. For in truth, nature did not create them to be sold or signed away to others; rather, it created them so that they might serve everyone collectively, as we declared in the second chapter. Our malice made things private property, and our necessity made them for sale. Buying and selling was a human ingenuity, as was the invention of men to make gold and silver the price for everything else. 

Therefore, if nature does not dictate how much things must be worth—how many reals or how many ducats <note>Standard currency of the era; the ducat was a high-value gold coin</note>—to whom would it more reasonably belong to provide for this, it being so necessary, than to the **commonwealth**? Its duty is to supplement through its ordinances what is lacking in nature. For public power is nature's vicar <note>A representative or deputy acting on behalf of a higher authority</note>, divinely given to the peoples so that they may use it to order what is most convenient for their good government according to the times. 

And just as natural law (from which civil law is derived) is divine law that flows from God and was engraved in our hearts, for this reason, the wise say that the secular power and jurisdiction which establishes these pragmatic decrees <note>original: "pragmaticas" — specific royal or state ordinances</note> also comes from heaven by way of natural law. Therefore, it is very just that the state assesses and sets the price <note>term: <term>taffa</term> — a legally fixed price set by authorities, often to ensure staples like bread remained affordable</note> for provisions and other saleable goods. It is necessary to have a set price, and since nature has not provided one, the state must. 

Furthermore, even the "headless" common people <note>original: "vulgo sin cabeça" — referring to the collective but unorganized public or the market as a whole</note> are capable of valuing merchandise in such a way that others are obliged to follow it. This is the "accidental price" introduced by time and the people, and one is required in conscience to sell at the current public value. # On the Authority of the Commonwealth in Price-Setting

...the commonwealth, in whom resides all the power and authority of all its citizens. How much more appropriate will it be for this commonwealth to set prices for things, and how much more binding will those prices be for everyone—no matter how exempt they might otherwise be—than any price set by an individual? And so it is certain that the **legal price** <note>A price fixed by law or decree, as opposed to a "natural" price determined by market fluctuation</note> carries greater force and virtue; it binds everyone to a single point, marking a certain limit that no one may exceed. This ought to be considered by those who blindly and maliciously persuade themselves that it is within their own corrupt judgment to set the prices of their own wares. They should know that if a single person has the authority to value their goods, the whole community joined together has a much greater right. For the community is the **commonwealth** <note>term: <term>Republica</term> — In this period, this does not mean a "republic" in the modern sense, but the "commonwealth" or the body politic including the prince and the people</note>, its prince, and its head. Thus, their pernicious lie is refuted, and our profitable truth is proven.

This reasoning is also very effective: buying and selling are acts of **commutative justice** <note>term: <term>Commutative Justice</term> — The branch of justice concerned with fairness in exchange and contracts, ensuring that what is given is equal in value to what is received</note>, a virtue that consists of maintaining equality in contracts. That is to say, one gives as much as one receives—not in physical substance (for in a purchase, the things exchanged are of very different natures), but in value and price. 

For example, a horse that is worth one hundred **ducats** <note>A high-value gold coin used throughout Europe</note>; in terms of the sale, the hundred ducats and the horse are equal. Commutative justice is maintained by giving the hundred and taking the horse, with both parties consenting. Now, if in a purchase that which is sold must be equal to that which is given for it, who could possibly equalize or adjust one hundred ducats to a horse, or to a **Black man** <note>term: <term>Negro</term> — In the context of the 16th century, this refers to an enslaved person. The author includes them in this economic list while simultaneously categorizing them as a 'rational creature' (human), highlighting the legalistic view of the era where people were weighed in the same scales as animals and gold</note>? These things are so different and disparate: one is a **rational creature** <note>A human being, capable of reason</note>, the other a **sensible creature** <note>An animal, capable of feeling but not higher reasoning</note>, and the other a bit of earth <note>Refers to the metal (gold/silver) used in coins</note>. 

Certainly, a public power was necessary—one much greater than that of any individual—to do this. Thus, two things are clear: first, that it belongs to the public power to value goods for sale whenever it seems appropriate; and second, that everyone is obligated to follow this set price. For all must buy and sell with justice, which is an equality—that is, that the item given matches the price received. And once the price has been regulated...

In other matters, such as brocades, fine fabrics, jewels, and other finery, such price regulation is not so required. ...being so clear and lengthy, I leave them aside. This authority is delegated—and must be delegated—both by common and royal law to the **faithful executors** <note>term: <term>Fieles Ejecutores</term> — Municipal officials tasked with inspecting markets, verifying weights and measures, and enforcing price ceilings</note>, as appears in the ordinances of Seville. It is not without reason that the laws are so strict that the governor, and not the merchant, should set the prices. Because everyone is a friend to their own interest, and especially since the aim and desire of these men is to grow rich—and their greed is great—they will for these reasons raise the price quite unreasonably if it is left in their hands. Thus, it is just and very necessary that those things which most serve for life and are most consumed should be valued by the commonwealth. Others may be left to the passage of time <note>This refers to market-driven pricing or the "natural price" determined by supply and demand over time</note>.

<margin>Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 5, Chapter 7</margin>
From all of which it follows that the **just price** we are tracking is of two kinds (as the Philosopher <note>A standard reference to Aristotle</note> says in the fifth book of the *Ethics*): one is **legal**, which the commonwealth establishes and marks, and the other is **natural** or **accidental**, which is introduced by use and is what something is currently worth in the squares or in the shops. Between these prices there is a difference and distinction very much worth knowing. When there is a **fixed price** <note>term: <term>tassa</term> — A legally mandated price ceiling for a specific good</note>, the seller cannot take even a single **ceutí** <note>A small copper coin of very low value originally minted in Ceuta</note> more; and if he takes it, he must restore it; and if it is a significant amount, he commits a mortal sin in taking it. Thus, if he exceeded the fixed price by a lot, he will have sinned in the excess; and if by a little—though he might not sin mortally because the theft is small—it is always necessary to restore it. Although he may well take less than what is set, and the merchant may give it to him, unless the **decree** <note>term: <term>pragmática</term> — A royal edict or law issued by the monarch without the formal involvement of the parliament</note> expressly says otherwise. Thus, in good conscience, these cannot be bought for less—especially annuities or bonds that are well-secured and regularly paid. # On the considerations for prices

Gentlemen: rather, in keeping the **fixed price** <term>taſſa</term> inviolable consists their profit—or would consist—as well as the benefit of the residents. For if they once determined not to sell the merchandise for more than the set price, they would not pay for it in the place where they bring it from, except for an amount that would allow them some interest. And by not paying [higher prices]: it is certain that the others would lower their prices. Thus, everyone would buy cheaply, and everyone would profit.

Let us give an example in the price-fixing of the **black people of Cape Verde** <note>This refers to the enslaved West Africans brought to the Americas through the *asiento* system</note>: which His Majesty established in the year [15]60, that they should be worth in the Indies—in the island of Hispaniola, one hundred ducats; in **New Spain** <note>Modern-day Mexico</note>, one hundred and twenty; in Peru, one hundred and fifty. If this had been executed with rigor and had remained (as it began), and the Sevillians did not pay more than fifty or fifty-five in Cape Verde for a black person—so that, comparing the costs and the risk, they would gain and profit something—and they did not rush to offer excessive prices (as they indiscreetly do), I am sure that the Portuguese <note>At this time, the Portuguese held the monopoly on the slave trade from the African coast</note> would lower their prices in order to sell; for they are not going to keep them (as the saying goes) "wrapped in a pastry" <note>original: *en empanada* — a Spanish idiom meaning to hide something away or keep it salted away without use</note>.

So, in keeping the fixed price, everyone would benefit: both the merchants and the miners. The merchants would have obtained the black people at low prices, as they did at the beginning; those in the Indies could have bought in greater quantity and would have extracted more silver; also, the **royal fifths** <term>quintos</term> <note>The *quinto real*, a 20% tax paid to the Spanish Crown on all mineral profits</note> of His Majesty would have been greater. For the traders, because of their returns which they would have in cash; for the **Spanish settlers** <term>Indianos</term> <note>original: *Indianos* — Spaniards who lived in or had returned from the Americas, often having made their fortune there</note>, because of the prosperity of their mines: the law would have suited everyone very well if it had persevered as it began and had been strengthened by use and custom.

The opposite follows, and has followed, from having repealed it. Since they [the enslaved] are so expensive, there is no man there in the Indies who buys except very few—far fewer than he needs—because to obtain them at their current value, a fortune is necessary. The same can and should be understood regarding the price settings <note>original: *poſturas*</note> that the city imposes here on small items: wine, meat, and fish. The root and fundamental reason for this doctrine is that of the two things essential to any **commonwealth** <term>republica</term>—namely, laws that are kept, and a judge or head who ensures they are fulfilled—the most profitable and substantial law among all those that have existed or could exist, even for the civic life of a city, was and always is the divine law. Likewise, the most necessary forum and court is that of the conscience and penance <note>referring to the Sacrament of Confession</note>.

Of this, there is manifest proof and demonstration: in places where this is lacking—as in ancient paganism and present-day infidelity—despite the many laws that existed in Rome (whether brought from the Areopagus of Athens or established in the Senate), people lived and continue to live so errantly. The nature and being of any law is to be a rule and measure with which we level and regulate our works: from which we will understand that to lack divine law is to lack the most certain, straight, equal, and infallible rule, without which all other human rules are crooked and knotted, not smooth or consistent. # Of the considerations
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

...is received and maintained with great ease throughout all of Christendom: that no person, regardless of how sublime their status may be, is shown as much reverence nor held in as much subjection as the confessor when he exercises and administers his office, because he is currently exercising the office of God, which is to forgive sins. For this reason, our Redeemer <note>Referring to Jesus Christ</note>, understanding that His church and faith were to spread through all peoples and nations, instituted for the government of all the ecclesiastical power and jurisdiction that resides in prelates and confessors, knowing that human power by itself is not enough for everyone. He established the superior power, by which the inferior—which is the secular <note>Non-religious or civil authority</note>—is aided, so that it may moderate, with its help, all insolence and outrage. Because confession subjects and humbles the subjects. 

One of the great responsibilities that the confessor has is to make the penitent <term>penitente: a person seeking the sacrament of confession to repent for their sins</term> understand how much it matters to our salvation to obey (as the Gospel says) the vassals to their princes, to pay them their tributes and taxes <note>original: "pechos" — a specific type of direct tax paid by commoners to the Spanish Crown</note>, to respond simply to their judge who proceeds and questions according to the law, and to declare to them how these authorities stand in the place of God. Regarding physical government, the confessor must require them to keep their statutes, ordinances, price controls, and regulations. These are things that, if the confessor did not preach and show them, the people would not value. 

Because the common people do not feel nor understand the virtue and obligation of civil laws except in confession; nor do they value them in conscience (setting aside the legal penalty) any more than the value the confessor places on them, and according to how they see him ask and proceed regarding them in the administration of his sacrament. Rather, in my opinion, if prices were raised or lowered according to the times, not one, but many great effects would follow and be achieved. 

The first is that, through this careful change and variety, the people and common folk would understand how great an obligation they have to keep that which their elders provided and commanded with such diligence, solicitude, and care. The second is that they would have a more justified cause to punish offenders. For as necessary as it is for other general laws established in the **Cortes** <note>The representative assemblies or parliaments of the Spanish kingdoms</note> to be durable—as Aristotle says in the second book of his *Politics*, chapter 6 <note>original: "enel segundo de sus Politicas.c.6."</note>—and as prejudicial as it is to change them every three years (an alteration and change very painful and harmful to the people), it is just as profitable for these specific price controls to be temporary in the city. 

And one of the principal reasons the King entrusts them to individual governors is because they must be so variable and changeable that every week (if necessary) they may be altered and changed. Conversely, when the price does not vary, no matter how much the times vary and change, subordinates either think the **pragmatic** <term>pragmática: a type of royal edict or law issued by the monarch</term> has already been abolished, or, if it is enforced, many maliciously suspect that they let it stand merely to have an occasion to collect **monetary fines**. And finally, nothing is kept well because it is not renewed. 

And so, two thousand scruples and two thousand inconveniences are incurred to avoid (as they say) just one. For, speaking strictly, as long as the price-setting stands and is punished and enforced, it binds the subjects in **conscience**, unless it is clearly unjust; and even then, it is right to first petition against it and advise the **councilors** <term>regidores: members of a municipal council who managed the city's administration</term> of the new events and causes that exist, so that it may be removed, repealed, or changed. And until this fulfillment is met, it is not just for every individual, because it seems unjust to them (in which they might easily be mistaken), to trespass and break it. Of this we spoke at length regarding the **edict on grain**.

AT length we have treated in the preceding chapter the legal price, how much obligation there is to follow it, and how necessary it is to make restitution for whatever is charged in excess, however small it may be. This is because such a price consists of an indivisible point, without any range <term>latitud: a technical term in Scholastic economics referring to the "latitude" or allowable range within which a price can fluctuate and still be considered "just."</term> for more or for less. This, given that it has been explained at length, rarely applies to the merchants of the steps <term>mercaderes de gradas: elite merchants who conducted business on the steps of the Seville Cathedral, then the center of global trade</term> or to those in the Indies who are called "merchants of Castile" <note>In the Spanish colonies, goods and traders arriving from the mainland (Castile) were distinguished from local products and traders.</note> (although those over there certainly ought to be bound by it continually, since the value of clothing in the shops depends radically on their sales, as we shall see below). Thus, the obligation that most concerns them is to observe the just price, which we call "natural" or "accidental" with its range. We shall treat this in this chapter, as it is the most general and universal among them.

This just price is that which runs in cash publicly, and is used this week and this hour, as they say, in the marketplace—provided there is no force or deceit involved. This is true even though it is more variable (as experience teaches) than the wind. That which yesterday was worth fifty ducats <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe and the Spanish Empire.</note> (such as cochineal <note>A precious red dye produced from insects in Mexico; it was a highly volatile and valuable commodity.</note>) is worth thirty today, either because a great deal arrived from Mexico, or because news arrived from Florence that there was no passage to Turkey, or for two thousand other occasions that we all know, and some of which will be written here. I said "provided there is no deceit," because there can be deceit in this matter in one of two ways: either in the merchandise, if it is tainted, or in the merchant, who practices his craft with deceit by forming a monopoly <term>monipodio: a secret agreement or conspiracy among sellers to fix prices or restrict supply.</term> with his associates and companions so that the price does not drop. And if it is not a defect in substance, it may be in quantity, such as if the *arroba* <term>arroba: a traditional Spanish unit of weight, approximately 25 pounds or 11.5 kilograms</term> is small, or the *vara* <term>vara: a traditional unit of length, roughly equivalent to a yard or 33 inches</term> is not just, nor marked; false weights and scales, deceptions and tricks (which according to Wisdom <note>A reference to the biblical Book of Proverbs 11:1: "A false balance is an abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is his delight."</note>) God hates most highly. In these things and in any others whatsoever that are sold while having defects—such as houses, estates, sown fields, or town rents—firstly, one cannot, nor ought one to charge as much as if it lacked the defect. And if one does charge that much, he must restore the difference; whether he knows of the defect or is ignorant of it, although one is worse than the other. If he knew of the defect it had, he sinned in selling it as good; if he was invincibly ignorant of it, he shall be excused from the sin, but not from the obligation of returning [the excess]. This is because to sell it lawfully, the price must be diminished from the set price, or from the current market rate, by the difference between "bad" and "good," or by how much less it is worth due to the defect. It is certain and evident: that if ten is the just value of well-conditioned goods, it must be worth less if it is flawed; and that it will be unjust to charge as much for the one as for the other. This rule is so general and true that it has no exception whatsoever, but rather it must be kept inviolably, even when there might be a set rate <note>original: "tassa." A legally fixed price for a commodity.</note> for the reasons mentioned before. That is to say, all price settings are understood to apply when the merchandise is well-conditioned; otherwise, it is left to natural judgment and a good conscience to ensure it is worth as much less as it is more ruined.

Regarding the accidental price <term>accidental price: the market value of an item based on its specific condition or current circumstances, rather than its stable, intrinsic value</term> of which we now treat, it is also verified that it is not the same—nor has it ever entered into the understanding of men—that good cloth and bad cloth should be worth the same price, even if they are of the same species. In conclusion: sellers are obliged to lower the price as much as the flaw in the goods is greater. 

But many times this will not suffice for the sale to be licit; other efforts and fulfillments are necessary to be able to exit the deal without damage to the conscience. And to know when, I say first, that either the defect of the goods is clear and manifest, or it is hidden and concealed. If it is apparent—such as if the horse is one-eyed, or the enslaved man <note>original: "negro." The text uses the example of an enslaved person as "merchandise," reflecting the legal and social realities of the 16th-century Spanish empire where this was a standard commercial example in moral theology.</note> is lame—it then suffices to follow the first rule: which is to show the buyer what is being sold. If an agreement is reached, one should charge less by the amount that the defect is valued, without even needing to point it out or declare it to him. Because it is presumed that if the defect is obvious, he will have seen it, and thus he accepts it as is; so by reducing the price, no grievance or injury is done to him. 

If the fault is hidden, the seller cannot sell it without making it known and revealing it. Because a sale must be a free act for both parties, and the intention and will of the buyer is to purchase well-conditioned goods, not defective ones; consequently, the seller does not have the right to receive money for his own property that is so lacking. Saint Ambrose <note>A 4th-century Bishop and Doctor of the Church whose writings on ethics and justice heavily influenced later Spanish economic thought.</note> says that in all human contracts, fidelity and truth are very beautiful things, and justice and plainness are very pleasing. But in buying and selling, these are not only beauties, but such pure necessity and substance that if the merchant does not reveal the hidden defects of his goods, even if the sale is concluded, it is void because of the deceit. 

We must conduct all our business with prudent simplicity and simple truth. This teaching must be observed especially and most strictly if the defect is harmful and prejudicial to the buyer, or at least if the goods are useless for his purpose. Our own loss and damage must not be compensated for or undone through the loss of our neighbor.

To this principle many grievances are reduced—those which our great greed makes us believe are either non-existent or very slight when they affect a third party, yet when they affect our own persons or estates, they seem so great that we would not want them for anything. This is common in such protestations, and therefore, whoever does not wish to deceive their own soul should not rely on this practice nor follow it.

However, one could not do this if the shepherd brought the same herbs to sell specifically as healthful and medicinal plants and did not know their true worth. In that case, the buyer would be obligated to tell him if he wished to purchase them. Likewise, if a stone is sold that—beyond its common price based on its clarity, radiance, and size—has some particular virtue for the kidneys <note>original: "hijada," referring to the flank or kidney area, often associated with "kidney stones" or "jade" in early modern medicine</note>, or for the blood, or for the sight, provided it is a virtue that others of its same species and nature do not usually possess, there is no great cause for concern in keeping silent when buying it. It is enough to give for it what it is commonly worth. All this has been said in explanation of that specific point: that there should be no deceit in the sale. Such deceit occurs primarily in the sale of cloth. We have spoken of this until now, but beyond this, there is usually another deception (namely) when merchants conspire not to lower their prices below a certain amount. We Castilians call this a **monopoly** <term>monipodio: a term derived from Greek roots used in Spanish law to describe price-fixing or illegal collusion among merchants</term>, an abominable vice, hateful to all kinds of people because it is highly prejudicial, tyrannical, and harmful, and as such, it is condemned by all laws.

<margin>Code [of Justinian] on Monopolies, sole law.</margin> <note>original: "C. de monipodijs. l. vnica." refers to the Roman legal code's specific title against price-fixing.</note>

First, in the Code under the heading "On Monopolies," such acts are forbidden under heavy penalties, and it is commanded that all their goods be confiscated and they be perpetually exiled. There, various ways of forming these monopolies are recounted and numbered. One is among merchants regarding some kind of cloth. Another is among officials <note>In this context, "officials" refers to skilled craftsmen or tradesmen.</note>, such as among masons and stonemasons. If, wishing to carry out a construction project or some long work, they should agree among themselves not to do it except for a certain price. Also, if after a project has begun, the craftsman should displease the council <note>cabildo: a municipal or ecclesiastical administrative body</note>, and while seeking another, the first craftsman should bribe them so that no one else would take the job. The law commands that all these be punished as persons who are harmful to the republic. ### and of monopolies.

on this point, one law, whose literal tenor and sentence is this:
Merchants establish agreements and price ceilings among themselves, making oaths and brotherhoods <note>original: "cofradias," which in this context refers to guilds or professional associations that acted as cartels</note> to help one another, setting a price among themselves for how much they should sell a yard <note>original: "vara," a traditional Spanish unit of length approximately 33 inches</note> of cloth, and likewise for weights, measures, and every other thing. Likewise, the artisans establish fixed rates among themselves for the price they charge for each of the things they produce in their trades. Furthermore, they make agreements that no one else may work in their trades except those who live in their companies. And they even set a limit in another way: that they shall not teach their trades except to the descendants of their own lineage. And because certain evils follow from this, we therefore forbid such brotherhoods, agreements, and price ceilings (like these) or any others similar to them, from being established without the knowledge and grant of the King. And all those who establish them shall lose everything they own to the King and shall be cast out of the land forever.

And even in conscience, this business contains such manifest injustice that, without much discourse, it is understood to be a type of force and violence they commit against those who shop. By conspiring among themselves, they consequently compel others—who cannot avoid shopping—to give them whatever they ask. Thus, they are obligated to restore <note>original: "restituyr," a theological requirement to return ill-gotten gains to the victim to receive absolution</note> everything that it is morally believed the item would have been worth less, or how much the price would have dropped, had they not set their own. This is not obscure to understand or to assess, considering the course of the fair or the sale, and whether there was much or little cloth, or many or few merchants. What I have exemplified in this contract, I understand to apply to all others expressed in the royal law we have referred to. And I am of the opinion that, in detestation and punishment of their guilt, the assessment should be carried out strictly, which would be a very just penalty <note>original: "justo peccado," likely a play on words suggesting the punishment fits the "sin" of the crime</note>. The same is understood for those who buy, if they conspire together not to pay more. For example, if a fleet of foreigners or locals arrived at a port, and the people of that land were to set—

<margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 78, article 2, reply 5; [Canon law] chapter "Per vestras," [Title] on donations between husband and wife; Cajetan on St. Thomas; Silvester [Prierias], entry "Societas" [partnership].</margin>...to provide clothing, one has need of the company and favor of another, either to create it or to continue it, especially the merchant who trades outside the city. <margin>Cicero [defines] partnership: "A gathering of two or more people contracted for the use of conveniences and more abundant profit." # On Partnerships

<margin>
It is against the laws of partnership to accept the convenience and profit but flee from the loss. <note>original Latin: "Contra leges societatis est sit comodũ, & lucrũ per cipere, dam nũ vero essu gere."</note> See the Digest, [title] "On the partnership," laws "if they were not" and "in the beginning." Also the Digest, [title] "On the rules of law," law "by nature," stating that he who contributes more should profit more. See the Code, [title] "On procurators," law "he who [receives] a stipend," and the Digest, "On the partnership," law "with two." Also Papinian and the law "likewise if it is added," and the law "corrected." </margin>

Against the laws [is any contract] that does not expose one to both loss and gain. The law states, against every good rule of partnership, that it is [wrong] to desire the gain and the **convenience** <note>original Latin: *sit commodum*</note> and profit without the danger of loss and harm. To do the opposite is such a **disguised usury** <note>a way of hiding an illegal, interest-bearing loan under the appearance of a legitimate business partnership</note> that it is not considered an investment, unless it is exposed to this risk or danger. In such a way that if someone invests ten thousand ducats but does not run the risk except for six thousand of them—because the other partners take upon themselves the risk of the remaining four thousand—his investment is not the full amount, but only the six thousand. The other four thousand were essentially like a loan to the company.

And much depends on investigating how much each person contributes. Because the **second hinge** upon which the equity and justice of the partnership turns is that each person should take a share of the profit or loss according to what they contributed **pro-rata** <note>original Spanish: *sueldo arrata*, meaning in proportion to their share</note>, unless the partnership were so general that it encompassed everything: the assets and the estate they currently possess, and that which they hope to have. In that case, it is not necessary to have regard for what they contribute at present, since they are obligated to contribute everything they might earn. For this reason, even if the current investments are unequal, it can be established from the beginning that the profit shall be equal, since the obligation they both take upon themselves is equal: to put into the partnership everything they may have. 

But if it is not a total partnership, but rather a partial one as is customary, one must take into account what each person risks for gain or loss. If the total capital were twenty thousand, a person who "invested" ten thousand in the manner described above [without full risk] should not earn half the profit, but only as if they had contributed six thousand, since they only risked six. 

Furthermore, one should not consider only money as a contribution, but also the labor and effort, which are usually valued and appraised. And if gold is—as they say—what gold is worth, then he who invests his care, sweat, and industry invests gold, for his labor is worth gold. Indeed, these [contributions of labor] <unclear>become</unclear> so great and of such a kind that, as the laws clearly state, such a person should receive a greater interest than the one who provided the entire financial capital. Thus, those who travel to the **Indies** <note>the Spanish colonies in the Americas</note> commonly contribute no money, or very little, yet earn much. And so that he may know how everything is to be valued and appraised, I say that he who invests ten thousand <term>ducats</term> <note>a gold coin used throughout Europe; a very substantial sum in the 16th century</note> does not invest them as if he were throwing them into a well. Rather, he puts the ten thousand at risk and provides the material with which profit can be earned and trade conducted. 

I say he "puts them at risk" because he places them in a position to be either lost or won, and in a long-term partnership, this risk is worth as much as the capital itself. This is because the money is not only risked on one voyage, but on many; and there is danger not only on the road, but in the merchandise itself—which may diminish or rot—and also in the debts of those to whom credit is extended, who often go bankrupt or flee without paying. 

The risk of ten thousand ducats in a partnership, as is common at these <term>Steps</term> <note>original: "estas gradas." This refers to the *Gradas de la Catedral de Sevilla*, the steps of the Seville Cathedral, which served as the city’s informal merchant exchange and the heart of trade with the Americas</note> for trade with the Indies, is the same as the ten thousand themselves. But if the danger the partner faced, his diligence, and his negotiation over the course of four years were valued at twelve thousand, then he contributes more to the partnership than the one who put in the ten thousand ducats. 

This is especially true because, at the time of the division of assets, the one who put in the money takes his principal out first and only then has a claim to the profit. However, the one who contributed his labor loses it entirely if there is no profit, for he is not paid for his work separately; his only payment is his share of the increase. For this reason, the money of the one and the toil of the other must all be compared and weighed, and if they are equal in value, they should share the profits equally. It seems to me that it will appear extremely novel to many that I have placed (as I have done) such high value on a man’s ingenuity, planning, and care...

...in a long-term trade, he should value [the labor] more than the capital. But I do not believe I am mistaken; rather, it is those who think there is nothing of greater value than silver who are deceived. On the contrary, I find among all wise men—both philosophers and theologians—that they do not attribute profit and interest to the money used in trade, but to the wit and industry with which one negotiates. Even experience teaches us that some earn much and grow wealthy with little capital, while others, even with much, lose and become poor. 

<margin>Justinian, on partnerships: the diligence of one of the partners often provides as much as the capital contributed by others. Law on partnerships, Digest, *pro socio*; Code, same title.</margin>

Secondly, the law, which prudently weighed this business and recognizes the dignity and essence of human nature, intended for these things to be held in high account. Justinian says: we all know, and no one doubts, that two people can form a partnership even if only one provides the money, provided the other manages and negotiates it. This is because often the industry and wit of one is as beneficial as the money of the other, and sometimes more so. Money alone never earns anything; and if it ever does earn on its own, as in usury, its gain is against nature—a nefarious gain <note>original: "ganancia nephanda"; a term used for "unspeakable" or wicked profit, typically referring to the sin of usury where money breeds money without labor or risk</note>. But only diligence earns licitly and often enriches a man. 

I will provide a case and a specific example determined by the law itself, 
<margin><unclear>see</unclear></margin>
through which it may be understood that good diligence multiplies and earns more than gold or silver; and consequently, that what the laws themselves say is very much in accordance with reason: that it is not rare for the one who contributed less capital to take more [of the profit], if he contributed more labor. 

<margin>Institutes, as cited above, and the law on partnerships in the Code.</margin>

This was decided and debated in the <term>Institutes</term> <note>The *Institutiones*, a 6th-century textbook of Roman law commissioned by Emperor Justinian</note> between Mucius and Servius Sulpicius <note>Quintus Mucius Scaevola and Servius Sulpicius Rufus, two famous Roman jurists whose differing opinions on whether partnership shares could be unequal were a cornerstone of legal education</note>. Such a person should earn two-thirds of the profit. Because, in reality, he contributed four hundred ducats: three hundred in labor and care, and one hundred in money. Many other conditions are usually included in contracts, such as the requirement that all <term>commissions</term> <note>original: "encomiendas"; goods or tasks entrusted to a merchant by third parties for a fee</note> be shared and that one partner not take them from the other regarding any additional items sent. These are just conditions, provided they follow the moderation mentioned above, so that they do not wrong a partner when seeing him in necessity; rather, if this is asked of him, the profit on the other side should be such that he is compensated. Likewise, a condition may state that a partner cannot hold capital or trade outside the partnership so that he insists upon and cares better for the service and profit of the company; this is licit with the same <term>grain of salt</term> <note>original: "grano de sal"; used here to mean "with the proper qualification" or "with common sense"</note>. 

Finally, when a partnership is formed between people who are not constrained by necessity, any conditions whatsoever can be drawn up and set down, even if they are somewhat unjust in themselves, provided the parties know and understand them. This is because there is no grievance or use of force where there is free will and no ne[cessity]...

It should be noted that no one ventures to lose more than what they put in. For **greed** brings with it foolishness and blindness, and for the world to lack greedy people would be like the sky lacking the sun, which is impossible.

...being <note>The text begins mid-word: "do," completing "siendo" (being) from the previous page.</note> equally subject to the hardships of legal seizures, reprimands <note>original: "sobaruadas"; literally a sharp pull on a horse's reins, used here to mean a sudden, harsh legal or social check.</note>, public shames, and jail fees <note>original: "carcelaxe"; fees that prisoners were required to pay for their own stay in jail.</note>, it is only right that, in compensation for their dishonor, they should equally enjoy any remissions and extensions of payment. For this right is not founded on the accidental outcome or specific fact, but on the obligation they undertook, or the risk of suffering to which they were exposed.

However, if they are bound in unequal degrees, or if only one of them bound himself—as commonly happens in the partnerships that people of this city <note>Referring to Seville, the main port for trade with the New World.</note> have with those in the Indies <note>the Americas</note>, where in the purchase of clothing, only those in Seville bind their persons, and if they go bankrupt they cannot compel the <term>Indiano</term> <note>original: "Indiano"; a Spaniard living or trading in the Indies.</note> to do more than provide an accounting so that those here may be paid from whatever share is available—then according to law, such a free partner should not enjoy the twenty or thirty percent remission <note>A common settlement in 16th-century bankruptcy where creditors would forgive a portion of the debt to recover at least some of the principal.</note> granted to the one who was imprisoned and shamed. This is true even if the debts for which he suffers arose and proceeded from the partnership. This is because these remissions and extensions are given liberally and mercifully by creditors to their debtors, moved by compassion for their misery and oppression. And the other partners are not their debtors at the moment the creditors cannot lay hands on them. Thus, making these donations to the debtors—I mean to the persons, not to the estates, nor to the partnerships; and among the persons, not to those who remain standing, but to the fallen so they may rise and pay—makes our resolution very certain and clear.

# On Selling and Buying for Cash. 99. #

...ways a man wrongs and is wronged in buying and selling. When its **just price** <note>The "just price" (*justo precio*) is a foundational concept in scholastic economics, arguing that every item has an inherent objective value based on common estimation rather than just what someone is willing to pay.</note> is given, there is no complaint from either party, but in various degrees one tends to depart from this middle ground and equity. Sometimes less is given than what it is worth; other times more is taken than it was worth. Let us suppose that a jewel is justly valued at twenty **ducats** <note>A high-value gold coin used throughout Europe during this period.</note>; this justice can be violated in many ways. What a transgression it would be to buy it for 16, or for twelve, or for eight, or for four; likewise, at the other extreme, to take twenty-four or thirty for it. 

In whatever way one exceeds or falls short, and does not reach the price we have designated, the sale is **unjust**. But the Emperors <note>Referring to the Roman Emperors Diocletian and Maximian, mentioned on the previous page.</note> did not wish—and they had good reason—for every injustice and injury to be litigated, nor for a complaint to be brought before their judges, except when the injury was **more than half of the just price**. This occurs when more than half of its value is added to the price of the goods. 

For example, a horse is well worth one hundred ducats; it would be wrong to take one hundred and twenty-five for it, but if someone were deceived by those twenty-five, he could only complain to God alone. This is because earthly judges do not involve themselves in such minor damages. And likewise, if they took one hundred and fifty, they would not provide him relief either; but if he gave five more (that is, one hundred and fifty-five), they would compel him by justice to return the fifty-five in excess, or to undo the **contract**, returning the horse to the first owner. 

To deceive someone in more than half of the just price is: for what is worth ten, to take sixteen or more; for what is worth fifty, seventy-six; for what is worth one hundred, one hundred and sixty. The same applies downwards when selling for less than it is valued: buying for eighteen what is estimated at forty; obtaining for thirty what is worth sixty-five. In such a way that if the excess or deficit is smaller, the contract will be illicit in **natural and divine law** <note>Laws believed to be inherent to human nature or decreed by God, binding the conscience even if the state does not punish the act.</note>, but **civil law** <note>The man-made laws of the state or kingdom.</note>—even though it views this poorly and would wish that everything always be given for what it is worth—did not want it to be tre-

This is the legitimate sense of this imperial statute: namely, that one may **contest a lawsuit in a judicial court** <note>original: "conteſtar lite in foro iudicial"</note> whether they are a seller who sold for less than half the value, or a buyer who was charged more than half of what it was worth.

This is because, at the very least when selling for less, one cannot give "double less" than what it is worth, as that would be giving the item away for more than free. 

Three reasons moved the **Roman Senate** to overlook all the minor grievances committed in these dealings. The first was seeing that they could not prohibit or hinder it, no matter how much they tried. Such is human greed and so great is malice—with so little truth and no charity—that they clearly concluded that despite any rigor they might impose to ensure dealings were always conducted with the utmost equity and sincerity, there would still regularly be (among such an innumerable common crowd as exists across the whole world, for whom these laws were established) one hundred thousand people who would deceive one another in such profitable business. And they did not wish to oppose the torrent, nor command what was not going to be kept or fulfilled, nor was it possible to punish every **transgressor**. Instead, they condescended and wisely treated the human condition and corruption...

# On selling and buying for cash. #

...most people by not punishing them. Just as the law does not punish someone who deceives by selling for more than the **just price** <term>Just price: In Spanish "justo precio," the moral and legal standard for a fair price based on common market estimation rather than individual greed.</term>, provided the excess does not exceed half the value, or someone who bought an item cheaper than its worth. **Civil law** permits this, yet **divine law** leaves no vice without punishment. According to divine law, it is highly illicit to fail to maintain the equality of justice in sales, and one is obligated to restore whatever excess was taken.

However, it is worth knowing in what matters this constitution and rule apply, and how this "half of the just price" is to be measured and determined. Regarding the first point, I say that this does not apply to merchandise or provisions for which the commonwealth <note>original: "republica"</note> sets a **fixed rate** <term>Fixed rate: In Spanish "tassa," a government-mandated price for essential goods like bread or grain to prevent price-gouging during shortages.</term>. In these cases, no matter how small the overcharge, if the aggrieved party complains, they will be heard and the transgressor of the **royal decree** <term>Royal decree: In Spanish "pragmatica," a law or statute issued by the monarch.</term> will be punished. In these instances, all the reasons and causes mentioned above cease to apply, because the exact value of the item is known. It would be a contempt of jurisdiction and royal authority if one could charge as much as half again over the legally fixed rate.

This rule was only created for goods <note>original: "ropa," which in this period referred generally to commodities or merchandise.</note> where the **natural price** <term>Natural price: "precio natural," the price determined by market forces and common estimation when no government price-fixing exists.</term> prevails according to the variable course of time: houses, estates, slaves, jewels, tapestries, and silks. And in these, the "half" is not, and should not be, calculated from the lowest price, but from the highest and supreme price, which we call **rigorous** <term>Rigorous price: "precio riguroso." Moralists of this era divided the fair market price into three tiers: the "pious" (lowest/cheapest), the "moderate" (average), and the "rigorous" (the highest price a fair seller could ask).</term>.

For example <note>original: "V. g." for "Verbi gratia"</note>: a slave is worth ninety, ninety-five, or at the very most, one hundred. The law is not broken by charging one hundred and fifty, despite the fact that the fifty extra units charged are more than half of ninety (which is the lowest of the three prices). This is because the calculation must not be measured by the lowest price, but by the highest; the law would, however, be broken if the slave were sold for one hundred and fifty-five. By this example and those preceding, one can judge and apply this law to any matter.

Note that it should not be taken into account whether the seller acquired the item for that same price or not, or if he himself was previously deceived. This is something that some simple-minded people tend to argue, though it does nothing for their legal standing. One must only look at the pure and simple value of the goods, regardless of what they cost the seller or what they might have...

...sale, even if it is for cash (since because of it I lose my profit, or I am deprived of the hope I had for greater interest), I may charge him more than what is usually given for it. However, he should not charge the full value he expects it to reach at that future time, but rather half [the difference] less. This is because one must subtract the costs he saves, the danger that the goods might be stolen, or that the price might drop, or the quantity shrink, or the oil spoil—risks from which he is now freed. Although, in truth, I believe this case will never occur in a cash transaction. For if the buyer has cash on hand, he will not be so foolish as to want to purchase for more than the current value. But in the end, this is justice.

### CHAPTER XII. CONCERNING THE JUST PRICE IN PUBLIC AUCTIONS. And how income from real estate should be distributed. ###

<margin>x</margin>
The greatest difficulty in this matter concerns purchases and sales in public auctions <term>almonedas: public sales or auctions, often conducted by a town crier, where goods were sold to the highest bidder</term>, where goods are often sold for more or less than their value. There is a great doubt as to whether it will be necessary to adjust the price to the "just price" <term>just price: the moral and legal concept that a good has a fair value based on common estimation rather than individual greed</term> after the auction is finalized, or if the parties will remain secure with the result, whether it be lower or higher. On one hand, it seems that the price at which the auction closed is the just price according to the rigor of commutative justice <term>commutative justice: the ethical principle requiring that the value of what is given in an exchange must equal the value received</term>. This is because the just price is the public price the goods have today; and nothing can be more public than a public auction. For this reason, it seems that one can buy and sell for whatever price the bidding ends at. Furthermore, we know well that the just price is heavily influenced by the *manner* of selling; that which is worth ten today in one type of sale might be worth seven on the same day and in the same town in a different type of sale.

# Concerning selling and buying for cash #

...type of selling. For example, a yard of brocade may be worth ten ducats <note>The ducat was a gold coin used throughout Europe; in Spain, it was a high-value currency often used in significant commercial transactions.</note> in the shops, yet in a bargain sale <term>barata: a type of quick or "fire sale" where goods are sold below market value, often to raise cash quickly or liquidate stock</term> it might be given for seven. This sale by auction <term>almoneda: a public auction, often conducted by a town crier</term> is distinct from all others; it is neither a bargain sale, nor like those in the Street of the Franks <note>original: "cal de Francos"; likely referring to the Calle de Francos, a famous commercial street in Seville known for its high-end shops and specific trade customs.</note>. Both of those modes are private, whereas the auction is public. Therefore, it has its own conditions, and this one is characteristic of it (as experience shows): namely, that the item is sold for whatever may be found for it—sometimes for more, or commonly for less, than what it would be worth otherwise.

Furthermore, when two bidders compete to outdo one another, they voluntarily raise the price, giving as much as they do simply to get their way. Since they are the true masters of their own money, who can or should deprive the seller of what others, through their own persistence, wish to give him?

Likewise, if an item is sold for less, no injury is done to the seller, provided there is no one else willing to give more. Just as in bargain sales, or during the plundering <note>original: "sacos"; refers to the "sacking" or forced liquidation of goods in a city during war or crisis.</note> of cities, that which would be of the highest value outside of those circumstances is worth very little.

Lastly, this argument carries great weight: in the auctions of the deceased, conducted under the authority of justice and by a public notary <note>original: "escriuano publico"</note>, the final proceeds are delivered to the guardian of the minors <note>original: "tutor delos menores"</note> to be accounted for, and he is obliged to give an account of them in due time. If a piece were ever sold for more than double its worth, it is certain that the guardian is not obligated in conscience to return the excess; indeed, if he did return it, he would have to pay the minor back out of his own personal estate. This would be quite a severe burden. Therefore, it appears that the sale was just, since nothing needs to be returned.

And so, it is concluded that the final bid <term>remate: the conclusion of an auction where the item is "knocked down" to the highest bidder</term> constitutes the just price in an auction. Just as in private sales, when two people agree freely, understanding what each thing is worth and without being compelled by necessity, they create a just value; so too is it lawfully purchased for whatever price is agreed upon in the auction—especially a free auction, where it is within the will of the seller to allow the final bid to be accepted, for this is to consent to the <meta>catchword: bidding,</meta>

# Concerning selling and buying for cash #

...to close the sale <note>The word "mate" is the conclusion of *remate*, the final strike of the auctioneer's hammer.</note> is to reach a free agreement with the buyer. On the other hand, it happens that the civil law <term>derecho civil: the body of law derived from Roman law used to govern private disputes</term> hears those who complain of having been wronged or deceived in public auctions <term>almoneda: a public auction, often conducted by a town crier</term> (as is evident in things given for life in an auction) where, after the sales are finalized, they often claim the prices are too heavily burdened; and the judges grant them relief. They would not do this if the sale were truly just in conscience. For the laws tolerate and pass over many unjust and illicit things, and it cannot be said that a price is so high that it is allowed by secular law but forbidden by divine law.

In this question, there are some clear truths and others that are quite obscure. Among the clear ones, the first is that if the clothing or merchandise has some hidden defect, and is faulty in its kind or nature, the sale is illicit no matter how much it is sold for in a public auction. Because in this regard, all methods of selling are the same: in all of them, the hidden flaw of what is being sold must be discovered and manifested. Concerning this, the rules we established in the eighth chapter must also be observed, for the reasons stated there. The second is that when there are bribes, conspiracies <term>monipodios: illicit agreements or combinations between merchants to fix prices or drive out competition</term>, or as Cicero <note>original: "Ciceron"; Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC), the Roman statesman whose works on duties (De Officiis) were foundational for early modern economic ethics.</note> says, someone is "recruited from the sleeve" <note>original: "echa de manga"; a Spanish idiom meaning to secretly or deceptively bring someone in to act as a fake bidder to drive up prices.</note> to bid, or if the auction were intentionally held at such a time that no one would attend or find it except for certain persons, or if those who were present agreed among themselves not to bid against each other: all of this voids the auction and subjects it to a thousand restitutions. In all of these cases, the just price <term>justo precio: the moral and legal concept of a "fair" value, often determined by the common estimation of the community rather than the individual's desire for profit</term> is what the item is truly worth. The person who acquired the goods for less is as much obliged in conscience to pay the difference, as the seller who sold them for more is to return the excess. Because the deceit or trickery made the sale unjust and involuntary on the part of the wronged person. And so, it must be adjusted to justify it, as if the auction had not been finalized. And perhaps if it were done plainly and sincerely, the seller would have given it for slightly less than what it was truly worth. But they are at fault if we oblige them to give everything...

# On selling and buying for cash.

...justice <note>original: "la justicia," referring here to the legal system or the court’s authority.</note> regulates in its own way of selling: but according to the will [of the owner]. On the other hand, it is established that the just price in this sale <note>referring to a public auction.</note> should not be considered to be the price for which the clothing would be sold outside of it (that is), individually or in shops.
