Which is quite absurd and contrary to the common sense of everyone, both the learned and the unlearned. For in that market of a public auction, with sincerity and openness, they think (and wisely so) that they are safe from any restitution <note>the act of returning ill-gotten gains or compensating for a loss to ensure one is not in a state of sin.</note>, even if they have obtained it for less than it was worth. So, on the one hand, it is necessary for there to be a certain rule of justice in the auction by which the just price is known. On the other hand, this just price is not what the clothing is worth in itself; it is necessary to seek a new [standard]. And rightly so, none of the other ways in which clothing is sold should be the standard for the auction, since this way of selling is distinct from the others. And it is right that just as there is one price in the shops, another for a bargain sale <term>barata: a sale of goods at a low price, often to raise quick cash</term>, another in large batches, and another by retail; so should there be another price specific to the auction. And considering, firstly, that this just value we are seeking should be very broad. For we see how variably the same kind of clothing is sold in them. One sword is sold for six ducats <term>ducado: a gold coin of high purity used throughout Europe and the Spanish Empire</term>, and in the same auction another is sold for four that is just as good, and another perhaps for eight; the other being the specific way of selling by the law. It seems to me that the just price of clothing sold in an auction is whatever the justice system and civil law admit and do not condemn. And the law admits everything that is not more than half of the just price, or less <note>this refers to the legal concept of *laesio enormis*, where a contract could be rescinded if the price was less than 50% or more than 150% of the actual value.</note>. So that if a slave is really worth one hundred ducats, a licit price when sold in an auction is anywhere from fifty up to one hundred and fifty.

# On selling and buying for cash.

And if certain rented houses were worth specifically two hundred ducats: they can be auctioned <term>almoneda: a public sale or auction, often of used goods or estates</term> without a guilty conscience <note>original: "sin escrupulo," referring to moral or religious doubt regarding the fairness of a transaction</note>, ranging from one hundred up to three hundred. Secondly, this is proven by seeing that no one usually has a guilty conscience for having bought in an auction at less than the just price, as long as it is not a notable reduction, nor for having sold for a third or fourth part more.

Thirdly, I am persuaded of this by noting that a sale occurs in one of three ways, in which the legitimate just price expands from one to the next. The first is the fixed price of the state <note>original: "tassa dela republica," referring to price controls set by the government for essential goods</note>. And this (as we have declared) is indivisible, without any latitude. The second is the accidental price, which the people and the time create—as the saying goes when someone was selling very dearly: "time sells it to you." This price is already somewhat extended; it has parts: the "pious" <note>the lowest fair price</note>, the "medium," and the "rigorous" <note>the highest fair price</note>; a middle and two extremes. But the extremes are very little distance from the middle. For example, some Jeronymos <note>likely a type of cloth or garment named after the Hieronymite monks, common in 16th-century Spanish commerce</note> are sold for nine, ten, and eleven. The third is that which civil law permits, where the price neither decreases nor exceeds half of the just price. In such a way, the middle of this price is what the clothing is worth in itself. The "pious" price is half as much, and the "rigorous" is half more. I did not give a place among these modes to the bargain sale <term>barata: a quick, often discounted sale, usually to raise cash quickly</term>, because it is not a universal or legitimate sale, but rather a regularized one. And this curiosity is worth knowing: that among these prices, the legal price is the center and midpoint of the accidental and common price; and the entire accidental price together is the midpoint of what the civil law allows. Therefore, if in an auction one cannot nor should not follow what is worth the state-fixed price (since there is none), nor the accidental price...

# On selling and buying for cash.

...for the reasons mentioned above (that is to say) that justice in a public auction <term>almoneda: a public sale or auction, often of used goods or estates</term> must necessarily be wider and broader than in the accidental price <note>accidental price: the variable market price influenced by supply and demand, rather than a price fixed by the state</note>. One cannot restrict the final bid <term>remate: the closing price or final hammer-strike of an auction</term> to a space as narrow as the common price; indeed, almost nothing could be sold securely in an auction if it always had to be sold for exactly what it is otherwise worth. And there remains no other broader standard to follow than that of civil law <note>civil law: here referring to the "law of the Emperor" or Roman-based secular statutes</note>. One cannot lawfully exceed this standard either. For it is against all good reason that secular law should refuse to tolerate a sale because the price is excessive, while divine law—which is far less likely to admit or suffer such things—would allow it. It would be a fine thing to make the King more just than God, or secular law stricter than the law of heaven; or to make the external judge more zealous than the **worm of conscience** <note>original: "gusano dela consciencia," a traditional metaphor for the nagging sting of guilt or moral remorse</note>. Certainly, when the emperor’s law does not tolerate an excess or reduction in price, the law of conscience and reason tolerates it even less.

From all of this, it is inferred that the auction is not so lacking in rules that the buyer and seller should not take heed if they are harming the other party—by buying or selling for more than half, more or less, of the accidental just price <note>This refers to the legal doctrine of *laesio enormis* (huge injury), which allowed a contract to be overturned if the price was less than half or more than double the fair value</note>.

It remains to answer what the guardian <term>tutor: a legal representative for a minor or an orphan</term> shall do when the assets of their minors, or some of them, are sold for more than what is indicated above: whether they should let it pass and remain silent, or whether they must make restitution. I say that in a case where it is most manifest that these limits have been exceeded, they should not make restitution on their own authority. To do so would be to pay the restitution out of their own pocket, rather than at the expense of the minor. Instead, they are obligated to petition the judge regarding the excess and injustice, protesting that they themselves do not accept it. If, despite this, the judge orders them to take charge of that sum or to collect it as the auction was finalized, they have satisfied their conscience. They also fulfill their duty by notifying the injured party that, if they feel aggrieved by the excess, they should petition the judge in a timely manner. The truth is that the guardian should do none of this unless the excess and injury <note>original: "excesso y agrauio"</note> are absolutely certain...

# On selling and buying for cash.

...that year, in conscience <note>original: "cõfciẽcia"; here referring to the moral judgment and integrity of the individuals involved in the contract</note> one must abide by and follow their agreement, and it shall be as the law says regarding those who made the contract. Each of the parties should see what suits them best; as the income is withheld or granted, the price will decrease or increase accordingly, and there will be equality in everything.

But if they came to an agreement so quickly and with such simplicity that they did not speak of the harvest, or the pension <note>pension: in this period, often meaning an annual payment, annuity, or rent</note>, and the rents for that year, one must consider the nature of the property and its manner of yielding rent and fruit <term>fruit: from the legal concept of "fructus," referring to any product or income generated by an asset, such as crops from land or rent from a building</term>.

There are some properties that yield rent every day; others wait for a certain part of the year, and first and last they involve expenses before they provide profit.

Of the first kind are certain houses, a *censo* <term>censo: a common Spanish financial arrangement where a person pays an annual fee or annuity in exchange for capital or the right to use property</term>, and tribute. As for houses, since there is no day or hour in which they do not provide service (unless they are empty), there is no week or month that it does not cost the tenant something to live in them.

Thus, if one pays one hundred ducats <note>ducat: a gold coin used as a standard currency across Europe</note> in rent, these hundred correspond—divided proportionally—to parts of each month and even each day; and this rent is the fruit and income that the house provides.

Likewise, if one has five thousand ducats placed in *censos*, and they yield four hundred a year, a portion of this tribute corresponds to each part of the time.

Finally, all possessions whose fruits and rents do not depend on the weather and rains from heaven are of this kind and condition (as it occurs to me): their rent and fruit is distributed, and must be distributed, through all parts of the year, and if necessary, by the day.

But vineyards, olive groves, and grain fields <note>Spanish: *sementeras*</note> are not always yielding rent or profiting their owner, but only at their specific time and season.

Vineyards in September and October; grain fields in June and August; olives in November, December, and January—in the full fury of winter.

According to this distinction, the doubt is resolved in two points. The first: in possessions of the first kind, the fruits of that year must be distributed, even if no mention was made...

The same applies if one buys or transfers a *censo* <term>censo: a financial arrangement similar to a perpetual annuity or ground rent, where the owner of capital receives an annual payment from the user of a property</term> of six or seven thousand ducats in June, and no third part <note>tercio: one of three annual payments often used in Spanish financial contracts, rather than monthly or quarterly payments</note> had been received; half belongs to the first holder of the *censo*. The reason is clear and evident, because from the moment they agreed and one declared himself satisfied and the property delivered, and the other accepted the price, the first lost the ownership <term>dominio: the legal right to control, use, and enjoy a property</term> he held until then, and the other acquired it.

And it is very consistent with reason and just law that every thing should bear fruit for its owner, unless he is deprived of it by some legitimate and legal cause. Especially since while they are his, they are at his risk if lost; therefore, it is most just that the profit and fruit <term>fruit: from the legal concept of *fructus*, referring to any recurring income or product generated by an asset</term> also be his. For this reason, since the possessions are his until he sells them, he must enjoy their rents and fruits produced until then, and from then onward, they shall begin to yield rent and serve their new owner.

And the sale is understood to be concluded not merely when they reached an agreement, but when each of the parties was satisfied with the deal and considers the possession delivered, holding it as his own; there is no need to sign a deed <term>escritura: a formal legal document or notarized contract</term> or make a physical delivery. But if by chance he did not cultivate or work them himself, but rather had them leased out—as pastures, estates, or orchards—I say by the same token that if he alienated <term>alienate: to legally transfer ownership of a property to another person</term> them before the land yielded its fruit, the entire rent for that year, even if he had already received it, belongs to the one who buys it. Because the rent is paid only for the fruit, the grass, the wool, the wheat, or the olives; and consequently, it must belong to whoever holds the possession at the time of the harvest. That is the critical moment that provides the benefit. Conversely, if he sells the property after the harvest is over, even if he has not yet collected anything, that whole year’s income is his.

Others allege that if they sold as the market dictates, they would often lose even their cost and principal, and that to at least break even, they choose to sell on credit at a higher price; but they claim this "extra" is not taken for the time they wait, but to avoid the damage that would come to them by negotiating in another way. To these two categories, as if they were headings, are reduced all the reasons that merchants usually give for their contracts, and all the excuses they put forward for their excessive interest. How much should be discounted or taken off cannot be reduced to a fixed rule, nor can it be known; rather, having considered all these circumstances, one must judge what would be fair to deduct from what was expected, which will be at least half. The reason for this exception is that if, at the request and insistence of another and for his utility and benefit, the seller deprives himself of the hope and probability he had for his own interest, and in effect ceases to gain profit (by not keeping the goods for when he thought they would be worth more, as they usually are), he may ask for satisfaction for this injury he receives. It is certain that if someone is the cause of me losing what I almost had in hand, they are obligated to compensate me for it in like amount. This profit which I lose at the request of another gives me the right to charge more for the goods <note>original: "ropa," literally "clothing" or "cloth," but used here as a general term for merchandise</note> than what they are currently worth for cash in the marketplace; this excess is not taken as the price of the goods, but as an account for what I cease to earn because of him.

And so that we may speak of this title <term>título: a legal or moral justification for an action</term> universally, it should be noted that it can occur in many ways across various matters. First, regarding money that someone has designated or kept for some investment and another asks to borrow it. Also, if the debtor delays payment with which the creditor intended to purchase something profitable: if he does not pay him, the profit then ceases <note>original: "le ceſſa entonces el interes," referring to *lucrum cessans*, a legal concept where one is compensated for the profit they failed to make because their capital was tied up</note>. And in the same goods, if he keeps them for when they are usually worth more, and another asks him to sell them, whether for cash or on credit. In all these ways of "ceasing profit," and in any others that are true and legitimate, someone else must always be the cause of this cessation for one to justly claim compensation from them.

The same applies to incurred loss <term>daño emergente: an actual loss or expense suffered by the seller due to the transaction</term>. For instance, if while hoping to remedy some damage with the money he has, another person takes it or requests it. # On selling and buying on credit.

...they overlook this point. They only look at whether they stop gaining or lose money. And finding that their profit ceases—even if only time and its natural course are the cause—they want the buyer’s purse to satisfy this loss, even though the buyer is not at fault. And it is certainly true that when selling on credit because they cannot find anyone to buy for cash, they stop gaining with that money for the entire duration of the credit term; however, no one is the cause of this but time itself. Yet, they still want the person buying on credit to compensate them, charging them prices based on what they imagine they would have earned with that money. It is as if the buyer had compelled them to grant credit. Or as if someone else would have bought for cash, and they refused that person at this buyer’s request. Because they do not consider whether the other person is truly the cause of their loss, but only whether they stop receiving interest, they convince themselves that when selling on credit, they can sell for more than the current value, adjusted more or less according to whether the terms are short or long. They also believe that those who buy in advance <note>original: "compran adelantado," referring to the practice of paying for goods before they are produced or delivered</note> can obtain goods for less than the fair price, more or less according to how far ahead of delivery they pay. They claim they are losing that much interest during that time.

The truth is that they themselves seek out these advance purchases so that no one else takes the opportunity from them <note>original: "lance," meaning a favorable business opportunity or a "catch"</note> (as happens in the trade of wool, cochineal <note>A precious red dye produced from insects in the Americas, a major commodity in the Spanish Empire</note>, and many other businesses). In these cases, since there are many buyers and there is profit to be made in the purchase, some rush to settle the deal and pay early. In this, no one is the cause of any loss, nor does anyone prevent them from using that money for another investment in the meantime; it is only their own benefit and greed that they have and pursue in paying in advance. Consequently, they should not subtract anything from the fair price, as no one is forcing them to stop trading in whatever they wish.

And there is even more harm in this than that. For in none of these contracts—whether selling on credit or paying in advance—does any profit truly "cease." Because something only "ceases" <term>lucrum cessans: a legal concept where one is compensated for "lost profit" that would have certainly occurred if not for someone else's actions</term> when it has already begun to exist and then stops or does not go forward. For example, if the construction of a house is not continued, we say it ceases; but before the trenches are even dug, no one says it ceases, but rather that it has not begun. # On buying and selling on credit.

...merchandise <note>original: "ropa," literally clothing or cloth, but used here as a general term for dry goods or stock</note> without having even begun the transaction, where he imagines he would gain if he had sold for cash, profit does not actually cease for him. That profit never began nor had any existence. It is an intolerable thing to say that profit "ceases" before it has even started. And since it is not truly ceasing, the seller still expects the other party to compensate him for whatever amount they imagine they are no longer risking.

The <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucro cessante," the legal and moral claim for income one fails to receive because of a delay or interruption</note>, speaking specifically about merchandise, requires either that there is a certain buyer ready to buy for cash and the seller wishes to sell to them, and that the seller intends to immediately make a profitable investment with the money that buyer would have given. For if the seller did not have such a certain investment ready at hand, no profit was actually ceasing for him, nor could he sell on credit for more than the strict fair price.

But if these circumstances were present and someone were to trouble the seller to provide the goods on credit instead, then he could claim some lost profit. This is a very rare case among merchants who sell in large quantities, for it is a miracle if such large lots are ever bought for cash. 

And also if the seller did not wish to sell at that time, but was instead keeping his merchandise for when it is known it will be worth more—provided that I do not offer or expose my goods for sale, but am instead begged and petitioned to sell—even then, I am obliged to speak the plain truth. That is to say, I must tell the buyer that I am selling only at his petition and request, and that I had no intention of doing so, but rather of keeping the goods, and explaining how and how much I am failing to gain. I say he is obligated to tell him this at the very least so the buyer is not scandalized <note>In this context, to be "scandalized" means to be led into moral error or to be offended by a perceived injustice.</note> or offended when he sees the seller asking and taking so much for the item, and thinks perhaps that he is being overcharged simply because it is on credit.

Let everyone consider how little place either of these has among merchants. First, they do not store, nor would they want to store, their merchandise for a time when it is known it will be worth more; rather, they are ready to sell whenever and as soon as they find a buyer to their satisfaction, and that is why they have the goods in the first place. The only exception is when the other party is the cause—at least through their plea and petition—of my abandoning my intention to keep the goods until a later time, when there is some moral probability they will be worth more.

Furthermore, it is already an established fact that exceeding the <term>just price</term> <note>the fair value of a good, often determined by law or common market estimation</note> is an injustice. The just price is either that which the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "republica"; refers to the state or organized community</note> establishes, or that which the time and its circumstances introduce. If there is a <term>price cap</term> <note>original: "tassa"; a legally fixed price for a commodity</note>, there is no blind man so lacking in sight that he cannot immediately see that breaking it is a crime. For the price cap does not speak only of what is sold for cash, nor does it make a distinction between these ways of selling. Rather, it impartially sets one price for the goods in both cases, as appears most clearly in the <term>royal decrees</term> <note>original: "pragmáticas"; laws or ordinances issued by the monarch</note> regarding wheat, where it says: "whether on credit or for cash, let it not be sold for more than nine." Therefore, if it is a wickedness to break the law when selling for cash, it is the same injustice not to observe it when selling on credit.

And certainly, if these gentlemen merchants were not so fond of, or biased by, their own interest, this single argument I am about to make would be enough to convince them that it is most illicit to ask for or take more on credit than for cash. It is this: no commonwealth ever included this distinction and difference in its price caps and market regulations; rather, it designates a single price, regardless of how it is sold. If the state sets a price for wines, or <term>enslaved people</term> <note>original: "negros"</note>, or houses, or olive groves—things where, because of their high value, one commonly waits for the full payment or a large part of it—it never sets a distinct price for credit versus cash. Because once the price is fixed, one cannot, nor is it convenient to, wait for a time when it might be worth more. And so that my determination may be better understood and proven with more efficacy: it is necessary to explain this justification for waiting. Especially since, if misunderstood, it causes no small amount of harm. Goods are kept until they are worth more in two ways. <meta>catchword: moral</meta>

...and it rises through June, July, and August. Likewise, if the din and bustle of war is already heard—the beating of drums, the unfurling of standards, the waving of banners, the gathering of companies—where it is held as certain that horses or arms will command a high price. 

The second way of waiting is when someone waits in a general state of uncertainty for the price to happen to rise, without knowing exactly when it will do so. This is what some merchants do when their dry goods <note>original: "merceria"; refers to small wares, textiles, or haberdashery.</note> from Flanders, or other cloth, have dropped in value; they do not wish to sell it but rather keep it until the price goes up, not knowing for certain when that will be. At most, they have some notion that when the Indies fleet <note>The Spanish treasure fleet that brought gold, silver, and demand for goods from the Americas.</note> arrives, there will be demand, or when ships begin to be loaded for transport. 

Of these two types of waiting, this latter one gives no authority to charge one iota more than what the item is worth at the time of sale, whether it is sold by the seller's own will or at the request of the merchant <note>The buyer or fellow trader.</note>. Otherwise, all merchants and retail dealers <note>original: "regatones"; often used to describe small-scale resellers or hucksters.</note> could always sell for more than the current price, since they all await such scarcity and market changes. Everyone desires for the price to increase. Furthermore, it would be outrageous if a future event so doubtful (of which there is no certainty) should increase the price of my goods today and make them worth more. There would be no goods that would not be worth more than they are actually worth—which is a manifest contradiction. To take more now, as a certainty, than what a thing is valued at, based on a "perhaps" it will grow (a chance so uncertain that there is just as much chance it might drop), is so far from all equity that anyone can see it. And so, even if there is no fixed price <term>tasa</term> <note>A government-mandated price ceiling on essential goods.</note>, this waiting for the price to rise gives no license to charge more than its common and present value, even when selling by request—how much more so when there is a fixed price. 

The first kind of waiting—or hope—where there is no set price, reasonably gives the right to charge somewhat more than what is valued today. This is because the near-certainty of the future increase actually makes the goods themselves more valuable now, as we suppose. However, where there is a fixed price <term>tasa</term>, this justification has no place. This is because the Pragmatic <note>original: "Pragmatica"; a royal decree or ordinance issued by the Spanish Crown.</note> does not specify a time period for which the price is binding, but rather commands absolutely that it be sold at that rate. In that case, it is clear that there is no probability...

# On buying and selling on credit.
<meta>catchword: moral</meta>

...it will morally be worth more at another time, its price being fixed by law. Someone will say: at least one might wait until the price cap <note>original: "taſſa"; a legally fixed maximum price, commonly imposed by the Spanish crown on essential goods like grain or bread to prevent price gouging.</note> is removed or repealed. I respond that waiting for the law to be annulled is a frivolous hope—it is like keeping clothes until they are eaten by moths. And it is not just that a thing should be worth more now simply because one keeps it until it is ruined. Thus, it must be held resolutely that where there is a price cap, it is not lawful to exceed it by claiming that the goods <note>original: "ropa"; while literally "clothing," in this period it often refers to general merchandise or dry goods.</note> were being kept for when they would be worth more. For such waiting cannot reasonably be justified. 

When the value is within the legal limit but currently worth less than the maximum, as often happens, keeping it in this second manner would grant the right to sell it for more. For example, if wheat in August is worth six reales <term>reales: Spanish silver coins used during the Golden Age</term>, and a merchant kept it until January—when it is held as certain the price will rise to seven, both prices being within the legal limit—one may charge something more than six, provided the title <note>original: "titulo"; a legal or moral grounds for a claim or action.</note> is understood (as we explained in its proper place). In that case, the arguments we have formed do not apply, nor do the disadvantages we inferred. This is provided that the merchant truly has the intention in his heart—that is, the goods are kept specifically for a certain time and occasion—when it is morally certain they will be worth more. 

Therefore, those merchants who have a quantity of stock held back, simply because there is no demand for it, or because it is not worth as much as they would like or what it cost them—and who are truly waiting only for someone to give them as much as they desire—these people cannot use this justification when others come to buy from them. Many do this, telling buyers that they were keeping the goods for when they would be worth more. But this manner of keeping does not give the right to charge more. Because it is a very confused sort of waiting; and if one persists in it, perhaps they will despair, as their goods may not reach the desired price as quickly as they hoped.

# On buying and selling on credit.

...one must pay close attention to the words, tenor, and condition of the rule, for they were not set down without great consideration and examination. This is because this manner of business—breaking up the bolt <note>original: "deſpernando la pieça"; refers to cutting smaller lengths of fabric from a large roll for individual customers.</note>—allows for selling a bit more dearly, due to the many labors the merchant undergoes in his trade, which is profitable and useful to the commonwealth. It is not just for a wholesale seller to charge as much as a retailer, even when selling on credit. 

Furthermore, these shopkeepers are the ones who commonly buy in large batches for their shops; if the primary wholesaler charges them on credit the same price they would sell for at retail, they are left with no profit. And if they do profit, it must be by raising prices at the expense of the citizens. Thus, our consideration must not skip or waver from one type of sale to another, nor should we regulate or base one upon the other, as they are very distinct. Instead, when one is to give credit for a large quantity, to know what to ask, one must look at what is worth in cash and what is usually given for that kind of goods in the same quantity, adding some amount to this price according to what we have indicated and moderated. 

However, the hucksters <note>original: "regatones"; retail sellers who buy wholesale to resell at a small profit, often viewed with some suspicion by moralists.</note> who also sometimes give credit in their shops and keep accounts in their books for certain private neighbors, must not follow this form. This is because they usually sell at the highest price <note>original: "lo ſummo"; the maximum end of the "just price" range.</note> even when being paid in cash, and thus there is nothing more to add. So, the substance of this entire doctrine, if well understood, is that one cannot charge more on credit than the rigorous value the goods have in that specific type and mode of sale—be it in bulk or at retail. In no way is it permitted or tolerated to mix these two types of sales as some do, charging and claiming to charge for a wholesale purchase on credit as much as it would be worth by the yard or by the piece for cash among hucksters. The foundation for proving how false it is to justify such prices is shown very clearly by the reasons that follow. No one gives their money, nor buys now, the "having-been"; rather, they buy the "being." And if one must only look at what the cloth is now—and at present it is not of as high a price as it once was—it certainly should not be sold for what it was worth, but for what it is worth now. ### On buying and selling on credit.

Thus, if the price has decreased for any **merchandise** <note>original: "ropa"; while "ropa" means clothing today, in this era it referred broadly to general goods or textiles.</note>, it must not be sold for what it used to be worth, but for how it is valued now. For the common rise or fall in value is also a risk to which the goods are exposed. And we see that an item’s improvement in itself, or its deterioration, reasonably changes its value. It is not tolerated that spoiled wine should be worth as much, in the same time and town, as that which is well-conditioned; nor whole wheat as much as that which is **weevil-eaten**. And if in these cases one justly sells for less than what it cost because it was spoiled while in my possession, it is even more appropriate to do so if it has decreased in market value. 

For a drop in price is no less a deterioration or change than a physical decay in the material of the goods; indeed, it is often greater. It may happen that a poorly conditioned item is worth more now than a very healthy one was worth before—as in a time of famine, blighted wheat is worth more than the **prime white wheat** <note>original: "candial"; a high-quality, white wheat used for the finest bread.</note> and whole grain was worth previously. But a drop in the common and public price never fails to have its effect, unless it is unjustly blocked by one of these deceptions that we are uncovering. 

For if you would consider it unjust—having paid eight **reales** <note>The *real* was the standard Spanish silver coin of the period.</note> for wheat—to recoup that cost <note>original: "sanear el costo"</note> after it had spoiled in your house (provided the market has not changed), how much more reason do you have to consider it illicit to sell for what it cost you when the merchandise is now worth less than when you bought it? In such a case, the item has lost more value in your possession than it would have lost if it had physically rotted or corrupted. For there is no greater "corruption" than for goods to lose their value, nor any better "growth" than for them to increase in it. 

Furthermore, if you take your past costs and expenses as a certain rule for the <term>just price<note>The "just price" (pretium iustum) was a central economic theory of the time, holding that the moral value of an item was determined by the common market estimation, not the seller's personal expenses.</note></term>, you would be obliged many times to sell for less than what an item is worth. For example, if the wine cost you three and has risen to five, you ought to sell it for three and a half or four—which is a moderate interest—since you use your cost as your gauge. # On Selling and Buying on Credit.

Just as it would be a clear error to sell at the original low cost after the market value has grown, it is also a patent error to sell at that cost once the market has dropped. And if this is a transgression, selling on credit <note>original: "fiado"</note> does not justify it at all, as some imagine; the price should be the same whether selling for cash or on credit. Certainly, if it were lawful to recoup one's costs <note>original: "sanearse"</note> by selling on credit, it would also be lawful when selling for cash. For goods sold on credit are not worth more than those paid for immediately. And I believe it seems an outrage to everyone to sell for more than an item is worth when paid for immediately, even if it originally cost the merchant more. At least no sensible man would buy it <note>original: "mercará"</note>. From this, it should be understood that no one should take it on credit at such a price either. And if there is someone who does buy it, it is not because the item cost the seller that much, but because the buyer is taking it on credit. Thus, this excess over the current price is not really tied (as these people claim) to what it cost the merchant or what he has invested in it, but rather to the act of providing credit. And if any advantage gained under this title is usurious, then selling at more than the current price—simply because it cost the seller more—truly "limps from the same foot" <note>An idiom meaning the argument has the same fundamental flaw.</note>, even if it does not appear so. 

This matter was treated extensively in the exposition of the **Pragmatic on Wheat** <note>original: "pragmática del trigo"; a royal decree regulating the price and sale of grain.</note>. But merchants are so determined to recoup their costs that when they cannot do so even on credit, they attach to the credit sale another burden <note>original: "esclauo"; literally "slave," here referring to a burdensome condition or a secondary obligation tied to a contract.</note> and some further deceptions. This consists of lending a sum of money along with the goods themselves, so that with this "tasty treat," the other person might buy what they perhaps would not have bought, or at least not at such excessive prices. 

But the buyer suffers it all just to make use of the money being lent. This is done not only in the sale of goods, but also, and even more frequently, in the sale of certain **annuities** <note>term: <term>juros</term>; state-issued bonds or perpetual annuities paid by the Spanish Crown, which were often traded at a discount if the government was failing to make payments.</note> that are so poorly paid that there is no one who wants to buy them, yet no one who does not want to sell them. To get people to buy them, they mix them with a loan of two or three thousand **ducats** <note>A high-value gold or silver coin.</note> for two years or more. Thus, with this silver, the buyer "swallows the pill" of the **annuity** <note>term: <term>censo</term>; a type of perpetual rent charge or mortgage-backed investment.</note>. In all of this, there is very clear usury. For so much would not be paid for the goods or the annuity if the money were not also being lent. And the amount paid above what the item is actually worth is not a true price for what is sold, but rather interest for the money lent. Because if the just price is the...

You might argue: "I am not using a loan, but rather seeking to redeem my own losses <note>original: "redemir mi vexacion"; the merchant argues they are just trying to get back what the investment is legally worth.</note>, for I am not taking more than what the tax or tribute is truly worth, even when extending credit."

There are also those who, knowing this doctrine and seeing that their goods are dropping in value in the town, say to themselves: "I want to keep them for when they are worth more." And if in the meantime some naive buyer <note>original: "boçal"; used here to mean someone inexperienced, unrefined, or easily misled in business.</note> comes to buy from them on credit, they foist the goods upon him for as much as they possibly can. They claim they are not charging that price because they are selling on credit, but because they were saving the goods for a time when they would be worth more. It seems to them that this title of "storing the merchandise" is approved by law and is sufficient reason to sell above the just price. 

However, in this case, their "storing" is proven to be a pretense; as soon as someone appears who will take the goods at the price the merchant wants, he offers them up immediately. Furthermore, if he were interested in profit by storing the goods, he could seek that profit while selling for cash. Yet this merchant would not make such a profit except by selling on credit. Furthermore <note>original: "Item"</note> (as was treated extensively above), simply storing goods in a general way <note>original: "en confuso"</note> until they might be worth more does not give one the right to charge more than the current market price. Storing goods requires keeping them for specific times of the year or for certain opportunities when they are usually worth more. For this reason, these people of whom we speak have no right to gain anything from the sale of their goods beyond what they are currently valued at.

There are some who, in order to flee these inconveniences, fall into others that are greater and more tyrannical. One of these is when they set the price of their merchandise by their own authority and whim <note>original: "aluedrio"</note> alone, at excessive prices. When someone comes to buy, they say: "You must give me this much for it, whether you pay me now..."

# On buying and selling on credit.
<meta>catchword: -ry</meta>

...[the] goods and the time, but also the manner of selling them. It is certain that the same type of goods is sold at a bargain sale <note>original: "barata"; a liquidation or discount sale.</note> and in shops; but it has one price on the same day and in the same town at a bargain sale, another in the shop, and another at auction <note>original: "almoneda".</note>. And selling by retail <term>retail (vender por menudo): the sale of goods in small quantities directly to consumers.</term> is a type of sale that increases the price because of the labor and hardships that are experienced in doing so. In such a way that if a yard of velvet is worth three ducats <note>original: "ducados"; a gold coin used as a standard of value.</note> in the Alcaycería <note>original: "Alcayceria"; a marketplace specifically for silk or fine goods, typically regulated.</note>, it is worth that much not only because it is a yard of velvet, but because it is sold with such labor and such risks. And in those three ducats, the velvet is paid for, and the "sweat" <note>meaning the merchant's physical and mental exertion.</note> spent in selling it is compensated. This trade is beneficial to all residents, and it is just that they pay for it. Therefore, if the labor is avoided (as it is saved when selling in large bulk lots), the velvet is worth less. And so, it is an injustice to make one price equal to the other. Reason dictates that since the modes of selling are diverse, the prices should also be unequal. And regarding what we argued about the huckster <term>huckster (regatón): a petty merchant or middleman who buys to resell at a small profit.</term>, when he happens to sell many yards together, we respond that this is "by accident" <note>original Latin: "per accidens"; a philosophical term meaning an incidental or non-essential occurrence.</note>. He may sell in bulk once or twice, and for this reason, he is not obligated to lower his price. Although I believe that, without any obligation, he would be happy to lower it to make cash and move his goods.

However, with all this, it is right to point out that there is a very just reason why a man should most faithfully pay everything that was credited to him once the term is up, even if he has been cheated in the price. Because despite the fact that the seller erred and sinned gravely by overcharging, it is necessary in every way that the buyer fulfills what he signed and agreed to. So much so that, in part, it would be a greater evil not to pay the debt than to have taken the goods—provided the grievance and excess did not exceed half of the fair price <note>This refers to the legal doctrine of *laesio enormis* (enormous injury), which allowed a contract to be rescied if the price was less than half or more than double the "just price."</note>. Because having expensive goods is a private harm, but failing to pay when the time comes is a harm to the whole Commonwealth <note>original: "Republica"; referring to the public good or the organized community.</note>. ## On buying and selling on credit.

...[necessa]ry for governing and preserving themselves that there be credit among men, and that they trust and rely on one another, as money cannot always be found for many business dealings; if these were not carried out in trust, we would live very limited and handicapped lives. Cicero says that there is nothing more necessary to the city and its citizens than paying debts with faithfulness and speed. And not to plainly fulfill one's word and signature is to disturb the entire political order of the people, and to destroy and damage human conversation and trade. There will be no peace, nor quiet, nor justice; even the bread for one's mouth—not to mention clothing—will often be lacking where debts are not paid, or are paid with tricks and delays.

Mainly, the commonwealth <note>original: "republica"; referring to the state or organized community.</note> extremely requires, in order to be well-provided, that men feel and have some favor and satisfaction in their state and trade. It would be intolerable to always go about disgruntled; they would become exasperated and would flee from labor within a few days. And there is nothing more unpleasant than selling and crediting one's clothing and not collecting, or having the payment delayed. Even just this phrase, "they do not pay me for my property," is insufferable, let alone suffering the act itself. 

And since one cannot deal continuously with money in hand, nor avoid credit, it is necessary to pay well so that trade and business may be conducted with some satisfaction and delight. And it is a great pleasure—even if one does not pay immediately—to give credit to a good payer, and even to lower the price by two or three percent of its just value. Here, our adage is truly verified: "The good payer is master of what belongs to others." <note>original: "el buen pagador, es señor de lo ageno."</note> Because in buying and selling, they give him some of it by reducing the price for him. 

On the contrary, dealing with a trickster <note>original: "tramposo"; someone who uses deceits to avoid payment.</note> is most hateful; a man almost feels that he is throwing away what he credits to him, or losing it. Let everyone look at how much they enjoy having their property in secure accounts <term>accounts (ditas): entries in a merchant's ledger representing money owed by customers.</term> and collecting without trouble or importunity; then they will understand how profitable it is to the whole body of the community that everyone should be

And once the agreement is made according to what is commonly expected, even if the price later changes and it is worth more or less due to some accident, it remains binding in conscience. Nor is it necessary to have scruples if one of the parties anticipated the change that was to occur; no matter how much they anticipated it, if they sold or bought according to the common estimation of persons knowledgeable in those dealings, it is a just sale.

Second, the price can be left unsettled, deferring it to the time of delivery. For example, if one hundred ducats were given as an advance for a certain amount of wheat, with the obligation to pay whatever the harvest is worth, and you are obligated to deliver it to me. When done this way, the month and day must be specified, because otherwise it is a litigious and burdensome business, as the price can vary in a thousand ways within the span of a month. Therefore, it will be better to specify "the price as it stands on such a day." But if the contract is made plainly and simply, referring to the entire harvest or an entire month, it is understood to be the price that lasts the longest, or has lasted the longest, during that time. For this is the general and common price that one must always abide by, unless something else is explained in the agreement.

Consistent with this doctrine is the law that the Emperor Charles <note>referring to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (Charles I of Spain), who reigned 1516–1556</note> established regarding wheat when it is bought in advance; it says as follows: We command that whoever buys grain <note>original: "pan"; literally "bread," but used here for grain or wheat crops</note> in advance shall pay for it at the price it holds in the principal town <note>original: "cabeça del lugar"; the administrative or market center of a district</note> where it is bought, fifteen days before or after the feast of Our Lady of September <note>September 8th, the Nativity of the Virgin Mary, a traditional milestone for the harvest season</note>: notwithstanding that they may have bought it at a lower price. The reason and foundation of this rule is that when it is delivered, it begins to belong to the other person, to serve and benefit its owner, and to be at his risk and venture <note>original: "riesgo, y ventura"; the legal concept that the owner bears the risk of loss or the benefit of gain once property is transferred</note>; for which reason it is just that it costs him what it is worth then. # On buying and selling on credit.

In this matter, the same evils always occur: no one buys in advance unless they believe the item will be worth more than it is now, and thus they hurry to strike a deal (which is not in itself a bad strategy). However, the evil—the true usury, which is neither hidden nor disguised—lies in the fact that they subtract a portion of what it is expected to be worth then, simply because they are paying in advance. This is nothing other than lending money to this person and taking, as a benefit for this service, what is subtracted from the future price of the goods. This can in no way be done, nor should it be tolerated, except in cases where the buyer intends to trade with their own money and makes the purchase at the petition and plea of a poor and needy seller. If the seller were not in such a state, they would not conclude or agree to the deal with such a loss. In this, everyone will see how foul and scandalous a business this is: for it only becomes lawful in the same cases and under the same conditions as usury would be.

There is a most refined—and not at all rare—type of sale on these steps <note>referring to the *Gradas* of the Cathedral of Seville, the city's central marketplace for merchants</note>: selling goods delivered here at double or more the just price, to be paid in the Indies <note>the Spanish colonies in the Americas</note>. Wine located in Cazalla <note>Cazalla de la Sierra, a town in Seville famous for its wine and spirits</note> (where it is worth two reales per *arroba* <term>arroba: a traditional unit of volume, approximately 16 liters for wine</term>) will be sold for five, provided it is paid for in the Mainland <note>Tierra Firme, generally the northern coast of South America</note> or in Mexico. The practice <note>original: "praxis"</note> of this business is that some, having their capital in the Indies but not receiving it in time and suffering extreme need, purchase a quantity of goods for resale <note>original: "para barata," implying selling them quickly at a loss to get cash</note> at the price they believe it will be worth there in the Indies, where the payment is settled. And seeing that it is a great cruelty to sell at such outrageous prices, the merchants add—to justify their tyranny—that they are running the risk for that amount on a ship sailing in the fleet. Yet no risk is actually taken on the goods, knowing they are not even going there. Thus, the one who bought them not only loses by buying at such an extreme price but even by selling the goods immediately thereafter so cheaply.

This contract is clearly very illicit. Firstly, because the just price (according to natural dictate and general custom) is the price the goods have where they are delivered: not where they are agreed...

# On Buying and Selling on Credit.

...[accoun]t, or where it is paid. The place of payment is very foreign to the agreement and sale. If woolens <term>estameñas: a type of thin, worsted wool fabric</term> are sold in Segovia, even if the money is dispatched to Seville, they are not sold at the price they are worth in Seville. And when hounscots <term>anascotes: a light woolen cloth typically produced in Flanders</term> in Flanders (even if the payment is sent to the fair at Medina <note>referring to Medina del Campo, the most important center for international trade and finance in 16th-century Spain</note>) are sold according to what they are worth in Brussels or Ghent, not as they are in Medina. 

Therefore, it is unjust that when merchandise or wine is sold here, it is paid for according to its value in New Spain <note>modern-day Mexico</note> simply because the payment is sent there—and sometimes they are even sold more dearly. This is because, in reality, the seller only takes into account the current necessity of the buyer. And thus, the price often exceeds not only double or triple the true and current price, but even the price found in the Indies. 

The excuses they give for such an outrage are quite frivolous. Some say they were planning to ship the goods themselves, and that since they desist from their own trade at the buyer's request, the buyer must satisfy their **lost profit** <term>lucro cessante: a legal and ethical concept where a party is compensated for the potential profits they gave up to fulfill a different agreement</term>. But they know well whether they are telling the truth—that they were actually going to ship the goods, and that they only stopped doing so because of the buyer's importunity and pleading. Or if, instead, they were already prepared to sell and, as soon as the discussion began, they jumped at the chance and offered the deal. 

In fact, it is often the opposite: they had no intention of shipping the goods themselves; they only did so because they lacked someone who would buy them at such a high price here. But even if we grant that they are telling the truth, the price should not be so excessive. Firstly, because the profit they would have had from their shipment is so uncertain, small, and dangerous that, after expenses are deducted, they would not have been left with twenty-five percent clear <term>horros: a term meaning "free and clear," referring to profit after all duties and costs are paid</term>. 

By selling the clothing here and claiming interest under this title of **lost profit**, they should earn even less, because the danger and uncertainty of the sea voyage must be subtracted from the calculation. Furthermore, this title of profit is, by its nature, free of risk. What use, then, is that deceptive tangle of claiming to take upon oneself the danger of a ship? All this shows very clearly that everything they allege in this matter is false. Thus, most only say they take that excess they gain,

# On Buying on Credit

...to ensure <note>The previous page ends with the beginning of the word "asegurar" (to ensure/guarantee)</note>, not because they take the clothing to be loaded, but because of the risk they run on the round trip. However, this is less relevant and justifies their excess even less. First, running a risk does not make an **otherwise illicit** <note>original: "aliis illicito"</note> business licit. Nor is this a reason that will justify the profit made from it. It is certain that the usurer runs a risk when lending, as does the person who provides clothing on credit, and neither one nor the other can claim interest because of it. Thus, selling for so much more than the just price is a crime; running a risk does not make it right. Likewise, facing danger is annexed to and nearly inseparable from all contracts of merchandise. Among these, there is no doubt that many are illicit, where profit is made against justice despite being full of danger; they would all be licit if risk justified them. This makes it manifest that running a risk justifies no contract if it is not just in itself. Third, selling a type of clothing for more than it is worth because it must be carried elsewhere, with the seller guaranteeing the passage, is condemned as usury by the Church in **the Decretals on Usury, Chapters *Naviganti* and *In Civitate*** <note>original: "Extra de usuris. Cap. nauiganti. & cap. in ciuitate." These are specific chapters of Canon Law used to regulate medieval and Renaissance maritime insurance and loans</note>. There it is stated that selling a quantity of pepper, or lending money (which is the same thing), in Genoa at more than the just price, to be paid at the fair where it was being taken, even if it were at the risk of the seller, is usury. How much more detestable it is to sell clothing here at such outrageous prices simply for running the risk of the trip there or back. Moreover, the risk is not even carried on the clothing (which would certainly be more to the point), but on a ship. Because most of the time the clothing does not even go there; and when it does, the clothing itself is not insured, but rather a designated ship. To the extent that if the hull were lost but the merchandise were saved (as often happens), the seller would lose that quantity even if the merchandise came out safe. Thus, I ask, what does the merchandise have to do with including the **hull insurance** <term>seguro del casco: a specific type of maritime insurance covering the physical structure of the ship rather than the cargo</term> in its price? Selling and insuring are very distinct businesses.

->**On insuring the ship.**<-

...to insure the ship. And thus he will insure the goods themselves: it seems that both contracts could be joined. But insuring the ship is so different that it cannot even be mixed. Likewise, so that it may be understood upon how little justice this confused scheme <note>original: "machina" — referring to a complex or artificial legal construction</note> is founded: If you insure the hull, why do you charge so little for the insurance? If someone sells twenty pipes <note>A "pipe" was a large cask used for transporting wine, roughly equivalent to 105–120 gallons</note> of wine, where he charges a hundred ducats more than the just price because of this risk, while the ship is worth four or five thousand ducats—he only takes a hundred for the insurance; yet he would not truly insure the ship for less than four hundred. But in truth, he insures neither the goods—since they do not go—nor the ship, since if it is lost, they do not pay him. They only invented this hoax of "running the risk," imagining that this gave them the power to sell so dearly; but it gives them none, as we proved before. Even if it were certain that risk was enough to justify some profit, it would not justify so much. Because they charge much more than this risk is estimated to be worth. <term>V.g.</term> <note>original: "Verbi gratia" — for example</note> Fifty pipes of wine delivered in Cazalla <note>Cazalla de la Sierra, a town in Seville famous for its wine production</note> were worth fifteen each, totaling seven hundred and fifty ducats; they sell them at thirty, to be paid in New Spain <note>The colonial territory primarily comprising modern-day Mexico</note>. This greatly exceeds what it would cost to insure the pipes on the way there and the silver on the way back. Thus, this entanglement and hoax has no true or firm foundation other than their greed, nor any reasonable excuse except their blind and covetous will.

# On Buying on Credit

...usury in the law in the place cited. Secondly, consider that they do not actually insure the goods <note>original: "ropa" — literally "clothing," but used here as a general term for merchandise or dry goods</note>, nor do they take the danger of the voyage upon themselves—as the goods are not even going there—but rather they insure the hull of a ship (a thing quite foreign to the contract). For this reason, when the goods do not actually make the passage, one cannot charge anything for the risk. In real insurance, however much is paid and however many policies are signed, if the merchandise does not actually go, or the silver does not come, the insurance does not take effect <note>original: "no corre el seguro"</note>, and the price of the premium is returned. So, if the sold merchandise does not go in the fleet, how can one charge interest for insuring it? 

You will say: "I already ran the risk on the hull." I respond that this does not justify the sale price of the goods, because these are transactions <note>original: "negocios"</note> most distinct in both their form and their substance. One is a sale; the other is insurance. In the one, the goods are alienated <note>The legal transfer of ownership</note>; in the other, a ship is insured. Furthermore, it does not matter to the merchant <note>The buyer</note> whether you insure the ship, which is not his, nor is he perhaps even traveling on it. Thus, it is as lawful to sell so dearly for this reason as it would be lawful to sell at the same price while running the risk on the life of a man whom the parties might name. For the ship matters as little to the sale as the life of that other person. 

And it is very important to note that these contracts cannot be reduced to conditional sales. In a conditional sale, the transaction depends on the condition in such a way that, if the condition is not met, the sale is void. For example, if one sold a horse to a youth for a hundred ducats provided that his father approved. Should the father say no, the contract is invalid. But in this case of ours, the sale is absolute, and only the future payment is subject to that risk. Thus, the loss of the ship does not undo the sale, but rather causes the sum of money to be lost. 

For which reason I respond resolutely: one must always sell for what the goods are worth at the place where they are delivered. And if payment is to be made in the Indies, one can only charge above the <term>just price</term> <note>A theological and legal concept (Pretium Iustum) holding that there is a moral limit to how much can be charged for goods based on their common estimation</note> what it would cost to insure the amount for the return trip. # On Buying on Credit

...such that the seller does not require it as a condition that he himself wishes to transport the payment or insure it. Instead, he must leave the other party free, so that if the buyer wishes to pay here <note>Presumably in Spain, at the point of sale</note>, he may transport the funds at his own risk. In that case, it will be a sale on credit <term>fiado: a sale where the buyer takes possession of goods immediately with an agreement to pay at a later date</term>. This circumstance is so necessary that doing the opposite is usury and injustice. This is because, in addition to the just price the seller receives for his merchandise <note>original: "ropa" — literally "clothing," but used here as a general term for dry goods or stock</note>, he imposes that additional burden upon the buyer. 

Furthermore, if by his own motion the buyer says he will pay in the Indies <note>The Spanish colonies in the Americas</note>, the price of the merchandise must first be agreed upon for what it is worth on its own, and separately, what the insurance should cost. This ensures the business is clear and without fraud or deception. The insurance premium must not be bundled into the price of the goods. By joining them—inflating the prices and distributing the cost of the insurance, however small it may be—one would exceed the just price. 

And even then, it is necessary that the seller actually transports that specific sum back from the Indies. If he spends it there to pay off debts or on other things, he cannot charge anything for the risk, as he does not actually run any risk in that case. All of this is in accordance with reason, and is such that conscience itself—if some traders would only listen to it—dictates it. And they say that conscience is the best theologian.

But what shall be said if the merchant is a shipmaster <note>original: "maestro de nao" — the officer in charge of the ship's navigation and commercial management</note> who, although he wants the goods to raise money quickly (even at a loss), has no means to pay if the ship were lost on the way? He clearly states that if the ship does not arrive, he cannot fulfill the debt, and for this reason, he asks the seller to insure the voyage. I say that if he is a shipmaster or a person who truly cannot pay unless the ship arrives safely, and the request comes from his side with the sincerity and plainness mentioned, the seller may charge something more than the return insurance for subjecting his capital to that danger. As for how much this is worth, the merchants know very well if they wish to be moderate. But because it is something that cannot be appraised <note>original: "tassar" — to set a fixed legal or controlled price</note> here, nor do I believe they will moderate themselves, my opinion is that when this business presents itself, it should be placed in

**T**HERE is another kind of sale, included among these three we have mentioned (namely): buying and selling debts, IOUs <term>ditas: informal records of debt or promissory notes</term>, and the transferring of deeds <term>escrituras: formal legal contracts or titles of debt</term> toward the account and payment of what is owed for less than the total amount they contain. This is done very frequently in the Indies <note>The Spanish colonies in the Americas</note> at the departure of the fleet <note>The Spanish Treasure Fleet, which transported goods and bullion between Spain and its colonies</note>. At other times, the deadline has already passed but the IOU remains unpaid, or it is not very secure; to rid himself of lawsuits, danger, and his own risk, the creditor sells it or transfers it to another for less.

In all these cases and others like them, I say two things. The first is that since there is nothing more in the business than paying before the deadline, one cannot give less than what the debt amounts to. The opposite is manifest usury <term>usura manifiesta: the illegal and sinful practice of charging interest on a loan or profiting from the passage of time in a transaction</term>. # On Buying in Advance.

...[collect it] for less, in relation to the debtor himself, the transaction is complete, and it is worth as much as is owed. And thus he cannot obtain it for less, except if the one who sold it to him had clearly cheated him on the price, and to make amends, reduced the amount and declared it so to him. It is true that in some parts outside of Spain, it is practiced much more than among us—though it is now being introduced here—to buy these collections of <term>juros: perpetual or redeemable annuities often paid by the Crown</term>, <term>fincas: properties or revenue streams used as security for a debt</term>, and customs duties for less than what is owed.

And there are people who, when writing, do not dare to condemn a general custom of the fatherland, even if they see clearly (as they say) that it is dissonant with reason, merely to avoid opposing the current. But they should consider that there are nations long given to a vice and infamous for it, in which they do not stop sinning, even if the vice is very ancient. Consequently, the truth should not be silenced or hushed when public duty requires it to be spoken.

For this reason, it seemed appropriate to me to strengthen our doctrine and distinction with new reasons and arguments (namely): that if the debt is sound and very certain, without risk or danger, it is not licit to buy it for less than its value simply to pay it before the deadline.

First, if in this contract the "right" is sold—as <note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), a highly influential Italian theologian and cardinal</note> Gayetano maintains—the right that I have to that money which is to be given to me in its due time: this right really is worth that same money, and not one jot less (as these reasons evidently show). For one, men never morally <note>In this context, "morally" refers to practical, everyday judgment or the consensus of the community</note> distinguish in their business between money and the right to have it, if, as I say, it is secure and settled. Whoever sells houses for three thousand <term>ducados: a gold coin used as a standard of currency across Europe</term> to be paid in one year: when asked for how much he sold them, he responds, "for three thousand." And it is certain that they did not give him anything more than the right to collect them once the year is completed. But this right is morally the same as the three thousand. Second, if we admit that a secure right and "action" <note>the legal standing or power to claim payment</note> is worth less than the total quantity, it would follow that one could not sell on credit for the same rigorous price as one would for cash.

# On Buying and Selling on Credit.

<note original: "Que es contra todos los doctores.">This is against the opinions of all the learned scholars.</note> Secondly, it would mean that goods could be sold <term>on credit: purchasing goods now to pay at a later date</term> for a higher price than if paid in <term>cash: immediate payment in ready money</term>. Both outcomes are quite shameful, and they must necessarily be accepted if the first premise is granted.

Let us suppose that a bale of goods is worth exactly thirty <term>ducats: a gold or silver coin used throughout Europe for trade</term>. If I sell it on credit for thirty, you tell me that the "right" I hold to collect those thirty is worth less than the thirty itself. Therefore, I did not actually sell the bale for what it was worth, since they did not give me anything for it now except for this "right," which you claim is worth less. This is something that does not fit within the <term>judgment of contracting parties: the common understanding or fair evaluation of a deal by those involved</term>.

The second point follows as well. Because if the right to collect thirty is worth less than the cash, it would be necessary for it to be a right to collect thirty-five or forty to make up the difference. Thus, it would be necessary to sell goods at a higher price when selling on credit than when selling for cash, so that the values align and are equalized in both types of <note original: "vendiciones">sales</note>. All of this is a great absurdity. And such is the first point, from which it is inferred—namely—that the right to collect one hundred "sure" units is worth less of itself than the one hundred units themselves. Rather, it should be said that they are the same in common judgment. A firm and secure <note original: "eſcriptura">legal deed or contract</note> for ten thousand is held to be worth ten thousand. They say it is worth that much to me, and they believe they have sold for ten thousand, provided there is <term>moral certainty: a level of certainty that is sufficient for practical action, even if not mathematically proven</term> of collecting the money at its due time without any trouble. And if a fair sale requires giving a <term>just price: the ethically and legally correct value of a good, neither too high nor too low</term>, one cannot value a secure debt of ten thousand at less than ten thousand, if ten thousand (as we have proved) is its just value.

Furthermore, the entire world condemns as a <term>usurer: someone who charges an immoral or illegal rate of interest on a loan</term> anyone who lends with interest. The world would not condemn him if the "right" were worth less than the <note original: "plata">silver</note>. For if I lend silver, and in lending it I alienate it from myself—and the person who receives it becomes its true owner—he gives me nothing in return for it but a "right" to collect it later. This right is worth less, according to what you claim. Well, it is certain that this reduction I make from my silver to the right, the mon- <margin>the money</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the ethics of debt collection and the valuation of credit. It focuses on the distinction between certain and uncertain debts, the morality of bankruptcy, and the obligations of debtors who seek extensions or debt forgiveness.</meta>

# On buying and selling on credit.

Ancient laws state that legal rights are worth less than the physical substance and matter of the thing itself, and that just possession is better than the mere right to it. Master Soto <note>Domingo de Soto (1494–1560), a prominent Spanish Dominican theologian and key figure in the School of Salamanca, known for his work on justice and economics.</note> responds to this doubt with the same distinction: if the debt is entirely certain, secure, and easy to collect—such that there will be no trouble or delay—it is not lawful to pay less than the full sum simply for the sake of disbursing the money before the deadline. However, if any of these conditions are missing, it is certainly permissible to purchase the debt for less. This is provided that the debtor <note>original: "deudor"</note> himself does not buy it, as he is already bound by the original contract and is obligated to pay it all in full.

<margin>Cajetan, 2-2, Question 63, Article 8; Silvester, Response 7, Question 1, Section 2.</margin>

This also applies in cases where a person can do no more, as commonly happens. Those who go bankrupt <note>original: "quiebran"</note> reach an agreement with their creditors <note>original: "acreedores"</note>, paying one part and being released from the other, or being granted extensions <note>original: "esperas"</note>. Regarding this, it should be noted that if a person is able to pay (even with difficulty), faking bankruptcy or hiding their assets <note>original: "hazienda"</note> is a mortal sin. Such a person is obligated to restitute the principal in full, as well as the damages and grievances that the parties suffered because of them. 

If someone goes into hiding and negotiates for a three-year extension, yet they were able to pay (even if it left them poor), provided they did not end up in the poorhouses <note>original: "hospitales"; in this context, charitable institutions for the destitute</note>, they sin by hiding and negotiating. They must compensate, if they are able, for what the creditors could have likely earned with those assets during that long term or space of time that they were forced to give him. This is true regardless of whether the creditors acknowledge in writing that they are forgiving the debt willingly; for it is not true will, but force, if—as I say—the person was able to fulfill the debt but went bankrupt specifically to obtain that pardon. 

But if he failed because he truly could do no more, I say that he may lawfully use the extensions. He is not obligated to any satisfaction <note>original: "satisfacion"; legal or moral restitution</note>, and he may use his capital to trade and earn all that he can. It is enough for him to pay the principal. However, if an agreement was made to forgive some part of the principal, the path he should take is not entirely clear or settled. Nonetheless, the most secure and probable course is that he should eventually fulfill the debt in full.

In reality, it is not a remission <note>original: "remission"; here meaning the forgiveness or cancellation of a debt</note>, nor a donation, nor are they giving him something that lawfully belonged to them. This differs from sales and purchases, where the seller is established as the true master of the price. Therefore, just as someone does not sin who even feignedly goes bankrupt when facing debts caused by and emanating from interest-bearing loans (provided that they pay the principal), so too it is not illicit to pretend that one cannot pay the interest on exchanges and re-exchanges, unless a <term>guarantor</term> <note>original: "fiador"; a person who takes legal responsibility for another's debt.</note> is included in those debts. In such a case, the debtor is obliged not to allow the guarantor to suffer loss for him, if he can avoid it. And if the guarantor should pay, as the Church says: *Concerning guarantors. Chapters "it has come to us" and "the complaint."* <note>original: "Extra de fidei iussoribus. c. pervenist. & .c. conquestus."; These are citations to the Decretals of Gregory IX, a major collection of Canon Law.</note> The debtor must not only pay him as much as he disbursed, but also all the damages incurred by making that payment. For even though the debt with the first creditor was null regarding the interest, it becomes most just toward the guarantor on the day he pays it on the debtor's behalf, since the debtor placed him in that situation. However, if the debtor alone is obligated, the bankruptcy is not such an injustice as the act of breaking the contract might suggest. This is not said so that it should be done, but to warn certain money-changers of the malice and nullity of their dealings.

This is the resolution of this case in conscience; for to write of the variety of laws that have existed until this day in the <term>external forum</term> <note>original: "foro exteriori"; referring to civil or public courts, as opposed to the "internal forum" of confession and conscience.</note> regarding the payment of debts is not our office.
