### CHAPTER XVII. ON THE TRADE of the Indies, and those who trade in them.

Regarding the loading of ships for the **Indies** <note>The Spanish colonies in the Americas.</note> and the sale of those shipments there, there are several notable things to observe. The first concerns those here in Spain who load the ships; they purchase almost all the **clothing and cloth** <note>original: "ropa"; in this period, textiles were the primary export from Spain to the colonies.</note> on credit with long repayment terms, and consequently, at a very high price. This is a matter of concern for the conscience, as it is extremely harmful to the residents who live in those parts, from whose estates everything ultimately flows. Because the retailer over there charges a certain percentage over the costs from here, and according to what it costs him, he asks the private citizens who come to his shops. Thus, everything rests upon what they call "the cost in **Castile**." And since the cloth bought on credit is charged a third more than its fair value, it ends up at an excessive price.

It should be noted that the price is almost never discounted, nor is it sold for a lower percentage, most often because the prices are already inflated. This is because, over there, people commonly do not look at the base cost, but rather at the **timing** of the **fleet’s arrival** <note>original: "flota"; the Spanish treasure fleet system that arrived once or twice a year, causing massive market fluctuations.</note>, the number of ships it brings, and the local state of necessity or abundance. These causes make the percentage markup fall or rise, not the prices that were originally set in the ledgers. Especially since everyone ships on credit, they all appear to be the same and equal over there, where people believe that such must be the value in Spain.

In this way, a yard of velvet that is worth one thousand **maravedis** <note>A Spanish copper coin used as a unit of account; here used to illustrate a price point.</note> in cash would cost two thousand over there if we add a hundred percent markup. But since the merchant buys it on credit for one thousand four hundred, it ends up costing two thousand eight hundred. And if any price is lowered (even when the prices are notoriously inflated), it is only by two or three percent. This cannot fail to be very poorly done in terms of conscience. From this comes the lack of restraint where both the poor and the rich ship goods, and by shipping this way, they destroy both **commonwealths** <note>original: "republicas"; referring to the organized societies of both Spain and the American colonies.</note>: Spain, by making...

...whether it be a cargo of two million or four million in value, it all goes together: including linens, cloths, silks, light fabrics, merchandise from Flanders <note>At this time, Flanders (modern-day Belgium/Netherlands) was a major textile hub within the Spanish Empire.</note>, and all manner of small wares, even including ironwork and wax. In Medina <note>Medina del Campo, the site of the most important financial and commodity fairs in 16th-century Spain.</note> and in other parts of Spain, goods are sold by retail. Even if a large quantity of cloth is sold at once to a merchant, it is sold by the piece. If ten thousand ducats <note>A gold coin used as a standard of value across Europe.</note> worth of goods are dispatched, it consists of various types of clothing, with the price being negotiated for each individual item. They might sell forty bales, each one at a certain price; or thirty pieces of silk at a certain price per yard <note>The original Spanish "vara" was a unit of length approximately 33 inches long.</note>, depending on the weight and fineness. 

Thus, in these regions, although selling a large quantity together means it cannot be paid for immediately—making it necessary to sell on credit—they have a clear and well-known cash price which they follow and maintain in their sales, as we declared above. It is very well known what one bale of Rouen linen <note>A specific type of high-quality linen imported from Rouen, France, which was a staple of the Atlantic trade.</note> is worth if paid for immediately; consequently, it is known what they should charge when selling on credit, and the same applies to forty bales sold on credit. Because even if there are fifty bales, they are appraised one by one, and all at an equal price. The same applies to silks or cloths.

From this, one can gather that in Medina and in Burgos, there is always a cash price that can serve as a rule for credit sales. This is not because they can be paid immediately when selling the large lots they usually handle, but because their style and method of selling is by the piece. It may happen that so many pieces and so many types of clothing are sold that it reaches a great sum, yet each is appraised individually. 

In the Indies <note>The Americas.</note>, everything is done in one single stroke. In a single agreement, eight or ten thousand ducats worth of goods are dispatched. In such a deal, there is no type of clothing that is not included, from the lowest to the highest quality, and it proceeds in this manner: once the fleet <note>The Spanish Treasure Fleet, which arrived in the Americas only once or twice a year, creating a sudden, intense period of trading.</note> arrives, prices are set for the bulk shipments (because they are all commonly dispatched within twenty or thirty days), and they follow the conditions and factors currently prevailing there, which are then taken into consideration.

### On the Trade of the Indies.

...sorting the **bulk shipments** <term>cargazones</term> at the beginning, according to the types and quality of the clothing. I know well that if they were paid for immediately, [the merchants] would give them for less; but I have already responded as **Saint Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential theologian whose views on "just price" and "usury" governed Spanish colonial economic ethics.</note> responds: that this is not because the clothing is not strictly worth that price, but because the merchant would be losing his chance to gain. This [logic] precedes all the tricks that are later devised, and it arises from the simple—and therefore just—estimation that people then have of the clothing. For this reason, it is consistent with reason to judge it as upright and legitimate.

   In one thing, or in two, the merchants in those lands err most gravely and commit **usury**. First: if the **bulk shipments** are set at sixty-five percent and at "three-fours" <note>A credit arrangement where the debt is paid in three installments every four months.</note>, which is the just price at that time; if they ask one of them to provide his clothing on credit at "four-sevens" <note>Four installments every seven months—a much longer extension of credit.</note>, he will raise the price of his **bulk shipment**, due to the delay in time, to eighty percent, and they will even give it to him at that price—or more, if they ask for even longer terms. This is the moth <note>A metaphor for something that slowly consumes or destroys wealth.</note> of all those contractors, and it is what the sacred **Theologians** who are there murmur against and abominate; it is what [the merchants] are obliged to restitute, and where everything we wrote in the previous chapter applies against them. Because they most clearly take interest for the time they wait, and they take into account and respect the prices based on the waiting and delay they grant, which is **palliated usury** <term>usura palliada</term> <note>original: "usura palliada"; This refers to "cloaked" or "disguised" usury, where interest is hidden by inflating the price of goods sold on credit.</note>. Second: if they have begun to give either half or two-thirds in cash, and it is not given to them, they also raise and lower the price according to whether the cash payment increases or decreases—especially in **Mainland South America** <term>tierra firme</term>—when they should take nothing else into account but the percentage, which is the current and just price at that time. In these two vices (although they are both one), a great part of the contracts in those parts sin in **palliated usury**; namely, in that a longer or shorter term, or a larger or smaller cash payment, makes them lower or raise the price of the **bulk shipment**.

<summary>The author explains that while setting prices based on bulk quality is fair, merchants often commit "palliated usury" by inflating prices in exchange for extending credit or for lack of immediate cash.</summary>

-># On the Trade of the Indies.<-

Regarding this "Indian" way of selling in such a literal sense, it should be noted that it is also used here at times: in Seville and Medina <note>Medina del Campo was a major center for trade fairs and international finance in 16th-century Spain.</note>, as well as in Flanders; though it is not so universal. For from a haberdasher’s shop or warehouse, almost an entire **bulk shipment** <term>cargazón</term> is supplied. At least, all the types [of goods] that usually come from the regions where one trades are taken together. For example, from one who trades in Flanders: cloths, **hounscots** <term>anascotes</term> <note>A light, twilled woolen fabric originally from Hondschoote in Flanders.</note>, tapestry, **Holland linens** <term>olandas</term>, copper, haberdashery, or **trinkets** <term>bujerías</term>. From one who trades in France: **Rouen linens** <term>ruanes</term> <note>High-quality linens imported from Rouen, France.</note> and **coarse linens** <term>coletas</term>. And everything is sold for five hundred or a thousand pounds, at 1,700 [maravedis] <note>A small Spanish copper coin used as a unit of account.</note> one with another; which seems to imitate the dispatch of **bulk shipments**. And it is of such a large sum that commonly the total is not paid in cash, but rather a third or fourth part; the rest is on credit.

There is doubt as to what price is just to sell in this kind of sale. I say that when one or two types of clothing are sold, whether in large or small quantities, the rules given in the eleventh chapter must be kept, because there is a cash price that serves as a measure. But when many different items are bundled into so many pounds, sold at such a price "one with another" (where some will turn out expensive and others cheap, because they are valued all together, not each one individually), it does not seem that the cash price can be followed, as there is no such price in that specific type of sale.

But I say, that when there is a cash price in such inventories (because in truth, they are often bought for cash), especially in **Antwerp** <note>The author uses "Envers," the name for Antwerp, which was a global financial hub at the time.</note> and in Medina—provided that it is not a "fire sale" <note>original: "barata" — a sale at a loss to get quick cash.</note>, but sold by merchants who deal in it to earn a profit and interest—this same price must be the one for credit, adding at most sixty or seventy maravedis per pound, which will be the strict price for that cloth; but one must not add more for the terms being longer. In such a way that the price is measured by, or has respect for, the time. I hear it said that there is always a cash price in all these parts, not because the entire sum is paid at once, but because it is known what each pound is worth. But if in some place it were not the custom...

...faithful **agents** <term>factores: commercial representatives who managed business for merchants</term>, selling on the best **credit terms** <term>ditas: outstanding debts or credit accounts</term> and for the most just prices they can. They must understand that since they take a commission—either from the partnership or the commission itself—they are obligated to be most faithful and to ensure the credit and the **merchandise** <term>ropa</term> are as secure as possible.

Likewise, once the terms of payment have expired, they must not be negligent in collecting, nor look the other way because the debtors are their friends—especially when the **fleet** <note>The "Flota de Indias," the organized convoy system that transported wealth and goods between Spain and its American colonies.</note> is about to depart, at which time the owner could be provided for. Though in truth, this is understood with moderation and prudence, as the time permits and circumstances demand.

### CHAPTER XVIII. ON BUYING SILVER
### in bullion, and the tomines.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'S' with floral and scrollwork motifs.</image-desc>
THERE tends to be in those regions, among those with a sensitive conscience, a doubt that is not foolish: whether it is ethical to buy silver bullion that is below the legal standard of purity. This is firstly because it is a general rule that where there is a royal price setting <term>tassa real: a fixed price established by the crown for certain goods or currency</term>, it is not lawful to exceed or fall below it, as it consists of an indivisible standard and lacks adjustable parts. 

Secondly, and most importantly, silver and gold possess no value in themselves other than what the royal institution estimates and values them at. Other things, because we need them naturally and cannot do without them, receive their value from our natural necessity, even without the state assigning them a value. The city [the government] can value anything, but there is this difference: money can be made from whatever material the state happens to desire or choose, and it can be valued at whatever the state wishes; however, other things must be valued according to how they benefit us. 

Thus, such things have their own value without any public regulation or price fixing, and our necessity causes that value to rise and fall. But currency is made valuable only by our will. Therefore, as long as the King—upon whom it depends—does not change it, one cannot lawfully vary it, nor give more or less for it. 

For this reason, there is a justified doubt regarding the buying and selling of these metals, where the law is often broken. In this matter, it should be noted that these metals have their carats <term>quilates: units used here to measure the purity or fineness of the metal</term>, each of which is worth twenty maravedís <term>maravedís: the smallest unit of Spanish currency and account</term>. And given that the value of a mark <term>marco: a unit of weight for precious metals, approximately 230 grams</term> is six ducats <term>ducados: high-value gold coins or units of account</term> in silver, this is understood to be the case only if it has enough carats to reach that standard—and the same applies to gold and its legal purity,

In the sale and purchase of these minted and coined metals, there are some illicit abuses, both in those parts <note>referring to the Spanish Americas</note> and in these <note>referring to Spain</note>. To understand them, and to understand at the same time how harmful and prejudicial they are, one must suppose that among many things highly necessary for good government and the tranquility of the kingdom, one is that the value and standard of the currency—and even its stamp and mark—be durable and as invariable as possible. In this, Spain possesses greater excellence, perhaps, than any other nation: because its valuation lasts and is almost perpetual, as is fitting, and is not changed every *lustre*—that is, every six years—as in other places: a matter of great unrest for the people. 

Here it must be noted that the essence, office, and dignity of money—which in itself is worth nothing—is to be the value and measure of all sellable things. The pound, the *arroba* <term>arroba: a traditional Spanish unit of weight, approximately 25 pounds or 11.5 kilograms</term>, and other weights of this kind measure quantity, but money measures value and price: a most principal office. It is a universal and necessary rule that any measure must be fixed, certain, and permanent. All other things can, and even should, change; but the measure must remain: because through it, as through an immovable sign, we know the extent of the change and variety in other things. We all complain that things have changed much in our time, and we know this because what was worth three twenty years ago, so to speak, is now worth thirty. In this way, through the currency, we understand the difference and the scarcity <term>carestia: high prices or dearness of goods, often used to describe inflation</term>. # On the Trade of the Indies

...nor grasp this variety. Time is necessary, and it makes its distinctions—night and day, afternoon and morning—but the clock by which we know time and its passage must be uniform and very regular. Its moments must always pass at a steady rhythm; otherwise, it will be, as we say, a faulty clock, of no use until it is adjusted. Its adjustment consists in its movements being equal and unchanging, for no other reason than that it is a measure.

Just as much, and even more, is this consistency and perpetuity required in money, which is a measure of great importance. Every day the value of everything else varies; what is expensive today falls tomorrow. And how necessary it is for human coexistence <term>convicto: from the Latin *convictus*, referring here to social interaction and the "living together" of a community</term> and trade that it be so, and that the prices of clothing and provisions change, so that everyone may profit and find satisfaction in selling and buying. Sometimes the sellers benefit from the profit, other times the buyers from the bargain. It is so necessary that the currency neither increase nor decrease, nor be raised or lowered in value, if it were possible, for two hundred years.

There should be one thing in the commonwealth <term>republica: the state or public body</term> that is semi-divine and sacred, which it is not lawful to touch, nor even to speak of changing. Besides the great benefit that the measure and standard in such an important business (as is buying and selling) be perpetual, it is a great disorder to change it. Because lowering or raising the value of currency is to increase or diminish everyone’s wealth <term>hazienda: the total assets, property, or estate of an individual</term>—which in the end is all money—and ultimately it changes everything, making the poor rich and the rich poor.

For this reason, Aristotle says that one of the fixed and durable things that must exist in the commonwealth is that money should continuously maintain the same value and last, if possible, for twenty generations. Thus, great-grandchildren may know what they inherited from their grandfathers, and what they, as good men, added, earned, and left to their parents. In this way, stirred by a just emulation, they strive to go from good to better and "always push the bar forward" <note>original: "echar siempre à delante la barra," a Spanish idiom meaning to excel, outdo oneself, or surpass previous achievements</note>. Firstly, in New Spain <note>Mexico</note>, those who bring silver to the mint charge the merchants twelve and fifteen percent for <term>reales senzillos: "simple" or small one-real coins, as opposed to larger denominations</term> for the trade <note>original: "rescate," the process of purchasing or bartering for goods</note> of cochineal <note>grana cochinilla: a highly prized red dye produced from insects on cacti</term>. They do this for no other reason than that it is the currency that seems good to the Indians and pleases them greatly. Minting these costs no more than minting <term>tostones: silver coins worth four reales</term>, because it is already a law <note>original: "constitucion"</note> that in every mark <note>marco: a unit of weight for silver, roughly 230 grams</note> a certain number of <term>tomines: a small unit of silver weight or currency</term> must be coined.

Thus, there is no foundation for charging this interest other than the merchants' need for small reales to satisfy the Indians, who receive them more willingly than coins of four <note>reales de a cuatro</note>; yet the Indians do not accept them in their own payments for more than thirty-four <note>maravedís</note>. For this reason, I say that the silversmiths or <term>cacaguateros: literally "cocoa-bean sellers," but here referring to small-scale retailers or money changers</term> sin most gravely. It is a most unjust exchange—if they do not wish to call it a sale—to charge one hundred and fifteen for one hundred small reales, to be paid in two months. This is excessive interest: fifteen percent for small change, especially within the same city; three or four percent would be a tolerable profit. But as they see the merchants in such need of them for the purchase of the dye <note>original: "rescate de grana"</note>, they raise the price tyrannically to the clouds. I have even seen it given at twenty-five percent. Although I believe that if they do not make restitution, they will have to descend with their weight and the burden on their conscience to the abyss. For it is not bearable in good conscience to charge for money—nor even for any kind of clothing—more than what it is worth, simply because my neighbor has need of it, especially when it does not cost...

# On the Trade of the Indies

...restricting the seller nor the money changer to more than the law allows.

Here, a most foul and condemned custom has been introduced—one even punished, as we shall see—in the sale and exchange of the <term>coronas: gold coins known as "crowns," likely referring to the gold escudo</term> that are sold for twelve <term>reales: a silver unit of currency</term>, though their legal value is only ten [reales] and ten <term>maravedís: the smallest Spanish unit of currency</term> <note>original: "diez, y diez marauedis," referring to the official valuation of 10 reales and 10 maravedís</note>. They give as a reason or excuse: first, that buyers profit and gain interest in other kingdoms due to the fineness of Spanish gold; and that it is beneficial to carry a large amount of money on a journey in a small volume; and that even the silversmiths in Seville profit while acquiring them for those same twelve reales. 

To the first point, one could say it is foolishness and simplicity to think there is more gold in a crown than ten [reales] and ten [maravedís], given that His Majesty places such a multitude of skillful, faithful, and most diligent officials in the <term>Casa de la Moneda: the Royal Mint</term> to refine, weigh, alloy, mix, and distribute the gold and silver that they would, as they say, "split a hair from a head" right down the middle <note>The author uses this idiom to emphasize the extreme precision of the mint officials</note>. And if the silversmiths profit, it is not because there is more gold than stated, but because they cast the entire crown into their pieces as if it were pure gold, when it is actually an alloy. When a crown is weighed, it weighs more than ten reales because it contains an alloy, but it contains no more gold than ten reales and ten maravedís. And the silversmith 
<margin>†</margin> treats the metal and gold together as if it were all gold, and thus this reasoning is of no value, nor does it give any right to charge more. 

But whatever the case may be, I say that once a coin is minted and valued—and not being a rare or highly precious coin at this time—one must only account for its legal price. To scrutinize whether it is worth more or has more metal is a curiosity that is not permitted to the common people. # On Cornering the Market.

[...ne]cessity of wine, or of oil. For this reason, I say that they are obligated, as soon as a shortage begins to be felt, to begin bringing out the goods <term>ropa: while literally "clothing," in this economic context it refers to general merchandise or dry goods</term> they have stored, and to sell them, so that by everyone bringing them out there may be abundance, and the rise in price may be prevented. This is a thing most pernicious to the people. They do the opposite: when there is a need, they wait for it to be even greater so they can profit more; thus the price necessarily keeps growing, as they become stubborn about bringing goods out, or very persistent in withholding them. 

The commonwealth <note>republica: referring to the organized community or the state’s regulatory authority</note> ought to exercise its authority, compelling them to sell, for if they had not meddled (where it would have been most just that they did not enter at all), the farmers who harvested the crops or the merchants who brought them would have sold them without such harm and sorrow to the residents. 

What shall we say of many gentlemen, rich farmers, and clergy, who have from their own harvest, planting, or rents a great quantity of wheat stored in lofts <term>encamarado: grain stored in upper rooms or granaries to wait for higher prices</term>, or any other kind of provisions <term>bastimentos: essential food supplies for a community</term>, who, when there is a shortage, wait for it to become extreme in order to sell at excessive prices? Certainly, they sin mortally in this; rather, they ought to begin to sell, and they are obliged—if not immediately at the beginning of the necessity (as those who first bought it are)—at least by the middle of it. And to speak plainly, after thirty or at most forty days of shortage, to withhold it further is cruelty and inhumanity.

Into this kind of crime and charge, the merchants of Castile in the Indies <note>Indias: the Spanish territories in the Americas</note> often fall. First, those of Mexico [City], where it happens that there is no wine in the city, even though there are two or three thousand casks <term>pipas: large barrels used for transporting wine or oil</term> in the warehouses in Veracruz. And the same occurs with many types of goods, both there as well as in Nombre de Dios <note>a major Spanish port in present-day Panama</note> and Lima, all for the purpose that by creating a shortage, the price may grow. They are obliged, since they are merchants and brought those things to sell, to sell them when there is a shortage and demand, especially when they not only do not lose money by selling but actually profit; yet they must not wait to gain everything they desire.

He who might have bought merchandise <term>ropa: while literally "clothing," here it refers to general dry goods or stock</term> so dearly that he cannot break even at its current value, such a person may keep it—even if there is some demand—until it is worth enough to recover his principal investment; but this happens only once in a lifetime <note>original Latin: "semel in vita"</note>. Perhaps they can pace themselves and enjoy a range of prices, but they are obliged to begin selling immediately so that the scarcity does not fail to be met, or grow suddenly like foam or weeds, but rather levels out over the course of time. 

Those who keep non-essential things, as we explained, may keep them as long as they wish and profit from them as much as they lawfully can. By "non-essential," we mean those things which serve merely for indulgence and pure pomp: jewels, rich harnesses, tapestries, and brocades. However, things for eating and dressing—even if they are silks and scarlet cloth <note>Grana: a high-quality cloth dyed with kermes or cochineal, considered a luxury but still a staple of the textile trade</note>—are always necessary to the whole body of the commonwealth <term>republica: the organized community or the state</term>. And thus, one ought not to meddle in these or practice this evil ingenuity of buying them in large quantities to resell them after hoarding them. And if it is done, it is necessary to follow the instruction we set down. Concerning wheat, it is forbidden by the law of the kingdom for there to be forestallers <term>regatones: middlemen who buy up goods before they reach the market to resell them at a higher price</term>, and it was a just prohibition for the reasons expressed; and if it is not forbidden in other goods, it is not because it is not illicit, but because a prince <note>referring to a sovereign ruler</note> does not dare to prohibit the common people from everything that seems wrong to him.

I would very much like the father confessors <note>priests responsible for hearing confessions and providing moral guidance on business ethics</note> to take great notice of this chapter, because there is a great multitude of people who occupy themselves, negotiate, and sin in these trades and profits.

**R**egarding two business dealings, it seemed to me appropriate to treat in the final part of this little work two matters that are very frequent on these steps <note>The "Gradas de Sevilla," the stone steps surrounding the Cathedral where merchants gathered to conduct business</note>, and are very scrupulous and even scandalous. One is the trade <term>grangeria: a business venture or profit-making enterprise, often implying exploitation</term> of Black people from Cape Verde. The other is the "discounts" <term>baratas: a deceptive type of sale used to hide usury, where goods were sold on credit at inflated prices and immediately bought back for cash at a lower price</term> that are so commonly used in this city. In this chapter, we will treat the first; in the one that follows, the second. As for the matter of Black people, I will not speak of, nor touch upon—as it would be to enter a labyrinth—the jurisdiction the King of Portugal holds in those parts over them, nor the laws or edicts <term>pragmaticas: royal decrees with the force of law</term> that he establishes and proclaims regarding the means that must be followed in the trade and sale of them. Instead, I will presuppose what ought to be: that he holds lordship, empire, and authority, according to reason and justice, at least on the coasts. I also presuppose what in fact occurs, according to public report and fame: that in ransoming, taking, and bringing Black people from their land to the Indies, or to here, there are two thousand deceits, a thousand robberies are committed, and a thousand acts of force are perpetrated. But because this business is very long to treat, and we cannot fail to be brief, as we have been until now, it is necessary that we resolve with clarity the law, and then descend to the facts—which are not only crooked but lamentable and miserable. # On the Trade of Black People.

...nations and peoples, no matter how barbaric, regular, or political <term>politicas: organized or civilized societies with established governance</term> they may be—at least among those I have seen and read about so far—it is a general custom without exception that a captive becomes a slave, to be sold and alienated as such. This title <note>In sixteenth-century legal thought, a "title" was a valid legal basis or justification for ownership or action</note> is current and practiced in Guinea more than in other parts, for the reason that the lordships and kingdoms there are very small. They live almost in the ancient manner, where each town has its own lord and its own King; there is no supreme prince over them whom all obey and respect. In this, they differ from the West Indians <note>The indigenous peoples of the Americas</note>, who, though they might have had in each place a natural lord called a *Cacique*—and often two or three in partnership—all these *Caciques* had one who acted as emperor. In New Spain <note>Mexico</note>, this was the King of Mexico, or that of Michoacán, or that of Tlaxcala; in Peru, it was the King of Cusco.

But these Black people do not recognize a single lord, and if they have one in some provinces, they are so barbaric that they are very little subject to them. From both circumstances, it arises that their towns always burn in continuous war, much like in Italy, where there are many lordships and temporal heads, such that it is a marvel if there is ever universal peace throughout the land. From this continuous war and dissension, it follows that many are captured by one side or the other.

Another title is that of public crimes, for there are just laws among them—as there were also among the Indians, which lasted even after they were converted to the Christian religion—stating that he who commits such a crime shall lose his liberty. Our laws say: let him who kills die, or go to the galleys; let him who steals be exiled. Their laws say: let him be made a slave and be sold, and let the price go to the commonwealth <note>original: *republica*</note> or to the injured and aggrieved party. And as they are vicious and barbaric, they commit enormous and detestable crimes for which, according to their laws, they are lawfully captured and sold. There is another title: that parents in extreme necessity have the natural faculty to sell their children for their own relief.

# On the Trade of Black People.

...gave. Because the son is something very much belonging to the father, and received from him his very being and life, it is considered just that he give up or lose his liberty—which is of lesser value—when there is no other way to sustain or maintain the life of the parents. Of this paternal authority and license, the law makes mention. It is a very ancient law, though because of its rigorous reputation, it is not observed, nor was it observed everywhere in ancient times. In Rome, it was abolished by Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome (reigned 715–673 BCE), credited with many of the city's religious and political institutions</note>, the second king of the Romans, and in Athens by Solon <note>An Athenian statesman and lawmaker (c. 638–558 BCE) known for his reforms against political, economic, and moral decline</note>, as Plutarch recounts in his *Lives*; nor, generally—thanks be to God—has such misery ever been seen among the faithful <note>A term used here for Christians</note>. Otherwise, such needs are met through charity. No one until today (as far as I know) has had the need to alienate his children by selling them. But in Guinea this is practiced, and I have seen many arrive from there who, when asked in confession how they came to be there, respond that their parents sold them.

This being supposed, let it be a general conclusion that all those who come by one of these three titles <note>The three traditional justifications were: capture in a "just war," punishment for a crime, or being sold by a father in cases of extreme necessity</note> may be sold, and bought, and carried to any parts, because any of them is sufficient to deprive a man of his liberty—if the title is true. However, the evil is that with these three licit and sufficient titles, infinite feigned or unjust ones are mixed in, for they arrive deceived, violated, forced, and stolen.

Regarding the first title of just war, there is the added complication that many—or almost all—are unjust. Because they are barbarians, they are never moved by reason, but by passion; they neither examine nor take counsel regarding the legal rights they have. Furthermore, because the Portuguese and Castilians <note>Spaniards</note> offer so much for a Black person, even without there being a formal war, they go about hunting one another as if they were deer. The Ethiopians <term>Ethiopians: a term commonly used in the 16th century to refer to all Black Africans, regardless of their specific region</term> themselves are moved by private interest, making war and treating the capture of people as a trade <note>original: "granjeria"</note>. They hunt each other in the mountains where they go for the hunt—which is a very common exercise among them—or to cut wood for their huts. In this way, infinite captives come against all justice.

...their liberty <note>original: "libertad"</note>, lost through their demerits and crimes, is mixed [with other causes]. It happens that if a king becomes angry with someone, or if a person causes him some annoyance—just as among us someone might be banished from the court or lose their influence and favor—there, they instead ensure that they lose their liberty. They make slaves of the individual and their entire family, capturing them with two thousand deceptions and false testimonies. For such a purpose, there is never a lack of a couple of witnesses to support the charges against them. Others are sent along rugged paths, through forests and mountains, where the king's favorites and servants lie in ambush. There, unable to defend themselves, they are captured and taken to some port where the wretched souls are dispatched <note>Meaning "sold and shipped off"</note> without their families perhaps even knowing of it. 

And let no one be shocked that these people treat each other so poorly and sell one another. For they are a barbarous, savage, and wild people; and this is inherent to them: a degree of barbarity, lowliness, and rusticity so great that they treat each other like beasts. It is as the fables say: that savages wound and beat one another. The same was true of the Indians <note>A reference to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas</note>, who even ate each other without even being enemies. 

Regarding the other title—that of parents selling their children in cases of extreme necessity—this is compounded by their bestiality, as they often sell them without any necessity at all. Often it is done out of anger or rage, because of some annoyance or disrespect shown to them. And just as here, in a fit of fury, one might say, "Get out of my house!" or throw them out, there they take the wretched boys and lead them to the market square to be sold. And because the trade is now so vast, there are Portuguese or even other Black people themselves ready in every place to buy them. For there are also traders among them now in this beastly and brutal business, who buy their own countrymen <note>original: "naturales"</note> further inland and bring them to the coasts or the islands to sell them at a higher price. 

And I have seen many arrive in this manner. The Portuguese who trade in Cape Verde, and bring Black people from São Tomé, from Biafra, from the Sape and Wolof peoples <note>The author refers to specific regions and ethnic groups: "Biafera" (Biafra), "çape" (Sape people of Sierra Leone), and "Iolofe" (the Wolof Empire in modern Senegal/Gambia).</note>, and the same Africans <note>original: "Ethiopes"; at the time, this was a general term for all Black people from sub-Saharan Africa.</note> who sell them, are notorious (as we all know) for often acquiring them wrongly and through evil means. For this reason, it is necessary that those here, if they do not wish to share in the sin, should desist and keep away from this contract and sale. 

And this is all the more true in this kind of dealing, because the "merchandise" <note>original: "ropa"; literally "cloth," but here used as a general term for trade goods, specifically the enslaved people themselves.</note> being sold is capable of suffering injury and violence, and a most grave and irrecoverable harm is done to them, for they lose their liberty forever—which has neither value nor price. Even with any other merchandise, though it is inanimate and incapable of feeling injury, if one simply believes it is likely stolen or belongs to another, no one can purchase it except for the sole purpose of returning it to its master. For this reason, we condemn second-hand dealers when they buy what they likely believe to be stolen, and silversmiths if they buy from those they believe are likely thieves. 

How much less appropriate is it, then, to buy Black people from those about whom it is certain that most, or many of them, are wrongly acquired and even more wrongly transported—unless it is for the purpose of freeing them <term>ahorrar: in this legal context, to manumit or grant an enslaved person their freedom</term>. It is a general rule that for a sale and purchase to be licit, it is necessary for me to be certain that what the merchant sells is his own and that he holds it with a just title. At the very least, it is required that there be no rumor to the contrary; and if there is such a rumor, I am obliged not to take anything from him. If a fleet of Bretons <note>Sailors from Brittany, France, who were frequently involved in smuggling and privateering in Spanish waters.</note> were to come to this port, and there were a rumor that a large part of the linens they carried were stolen, no one could buy them, even though there is no doubt that they would have brought some of their own goods mixed in. Thus, as it is said in public (as indeed it is said) that a large part of the Black people taken are held captive against justice, no one can buy them, nor can anyone involve themselves in such a business, under penalty of sin and restitution.

# On the *Baratas* <note>A *barata* (literally "a cheap sale") was a common 16th-century financial maneuver where a person in need of cash bought goods on credit at a high price and immediately sold them for cash at a significant loss to obtain liquidity.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial O with a floral and geometric pattern inside a square frame.</image-desc>

**ANOTHER OCEAN** of fraudulent contracts <term>mohatras: usurious contracts where one buys on credit to sell immediately for cash at a loss</term> are the *baratas* that are used here—a fabric and weave so tangled and so poorly woven that there is no other wit to unweave it than that of Alexander with the blind knot of Corinth <note>The author likely refers to the "Gordian Knot," though he calls it "Corinthian."</note>, which was to break it. And so that we do not become entangled in it ourselves, it will be necessary to state the matter with few words and great clarity. The origin of this business is, and was, the necessity in which many find themselves for money, which cannot be obtained through exchange <term>cambio: a financial transaction involving bills of exchange or currency</term> because the terms are so short when they require very long ones. Fearing that by dealing in exchanges and re-exchanges, from fair to fair, they will lose more than by taking a *barata*, they agree to perform one to obtain the quantity of coin they presently need. The substance of which consists in purchasing a quantity of cloth on credit and selling it immediately for cash, for so much less than what it is worth that the low price invites everyone to buy. Thus, losing twenty-five or thirty percent, they find the money they can make use of for the time being. This is the essence <term>quididad: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing</term> of the trade, and the first kind that existed within it, the most straightforward and secure. I say this to write clearly: for one to perform a *barata*, if moved by just necessity—and I believe it always moves and constrains them, for if they could do otherwise, they would not choose to lose—and if it is done plainly (that is, buying the cloth at its fair price and selling it in public, lowering the price as seems appropriate), it is not a sin. On the part of the one who takes the *barata*, it is clear, for he does no one an injury; rather, he performs a good deed for others while receiving a very bad one for himself. The one for whom there is great scruple in these businesses is the merchant who provides the goods on credit, who ordinarily, because he is selling on credit, charges much more than the item is worth. Seeing the poor man in need, with the rope—as they say—at his throat, he thrusts the spear in up to the butt-end <note>original: *regaton*; meaning he takes the maximum possible advantage of the situation</note>, both in the prices...

# On the Baratas.

There is another type of *barata* <term>barata: a deceptive credit transaction where goods are sold at high prices on credit and then resold for immediate cash at a loss</term>, which they call "infernal": when the same person who gives the clothing on credit takes it back for themselves, and pays in cash twenty-five or thirty percent less than what they sold it for, and many times without the merchandise ever having left their house or shop. And there is no lack of certain brokers <term>corredores: licensed commercial intermediaries or agents</term> who involve themselves in these morally hazardous <note>original: "escrupulosos" — here meaning business that causes moral doubt or risks to the soul</note> and illicit dealings, acting as intermediaries to arrange them. It is a most well-established fact regarding these brokers that every time they mediate on behalf of the one who sins in the contract, harming the other, they also sin mortally and incur the obligation to restore the damage if the principal party does not make restitution. But being on the side of the patient <note>The "patient" refers to the victim or the party in need who is being exploited</note>, doing everything possible for him in both the sale and the purchase, he may do so, just as the needy party themselves might do. These *baratas* are ordinarily done in this manner: the one who is in need says to the broker, "I need a thousand ducats <term>ducado: a gold coin used as a standard of currency</term>, to be paid a year from now or more; find them for me." The broker seeks someone who will provide clothing on credit for that period; and on the other hand, someone who will take it and buy it for cash, with a loss of a certain percentage, and provides the thousand ducats through that lot. This contract is lawful under the conditions mentioned above; but as it is usually done, it is most often unjust and usurious <term>usurario: pertaining to usury, the practice of charging illegal or immoral interest on a loan</term>. It is unjust because of the excessive prices they charge. It is usurious, for one, because this excess is due to the time allowed for credit—a reason that applies to all such cases—and secondly, for a reason specific to those who take the clothing back for themselves. For in effect, putting aside words and masks <note>A metaphor for legal pretenses or deceptive language used to hide the true nature of a loan</note>, it is nothing other than lending them the thousand ducats and charging as much interest as the loss amounts to. They usually claim that since someone else has to buy it, they can buy it themselves, and that they even do him...

# On the Baratas

For in truth, whoever takes [the credit or goods] does not fail to lose credit unless they are very well established in property <term>hazienda: an individual's wealth, estate, or total assets</term>. But certainly, they [the lenders] do not have the same license as others to purchase it back. This is quite clear, for to the common people themselves, without much philosophy but by the light of nature alone, it seems very wrong for the lender to take the goods back, and they hold them in poor regard—while they do not condemn or reprove any others who might buy those same goods. This should be an argument to them that the practice is not lawful for everyone. Such a negotiation is an affront <note>original: "da en rostro" — literally "hits one in the face," meaning it is a shameful or offensive sight</note>; it has a very bad appearance and, perhaps, bad substance as well. I mean that, inside and out, it has nothing healthy or proper about it. 

Also (as we said above), one of the things that validates these *baratas* <term>barata: a predatory credit transaction where goods are sold at high prices on credit and then resold for immediate cash at a loss</term> is when the goods are sold in public, and many people are aware of it, so that more buyers attend and the items can be sold for better prices—and not just known to the broker and the retailer <term>regatón: a petty merchant or reseller, often viewed as a middleman who drives up prices</term>. 

Thus, I say in conclusion that this business is very shameful, because it is generally forbidden for the same person who gives the clothing to take it back. This is especially true when they have not actually delivered the merchandise, but rather everything happens only in words; this is not a true sale, but rather a real and manifest usury, and as such it is condemned. If it should happen that, having sold his clothing, a merchant sees it later in a shop or at an auction <term>almoneda: a public sale or auction of goods</term> exposed for sale—with no secret agreement involved, and without fear of infamy—he may well buy it just like any other person at the price others pay. He will not be at fault, unless he was at fault in the initial sale he made by charging more than it was worth simply because he was selling it on credit. 

Although the best thing is to abandon the practice entirely, due to the great evils mixed within it. These were noticed by the kingdom; and thus His Majesty prohibited it in the Royal Laws, under this form: *Law 22, Title 11, Book 5* <note>The author is citing the "Leyes de Recopilación," the standard legal code of 16th-century Spain</note>: "No merchant, nor silversmith, nor broker, nor other persons who intervene...

-># On the *Baratas*<-

...in extracting, or in taking on credit silver or other merchandise for other persons, and then returning to recover the said silver or merchandise at low prices by paying in ready cash. We command that the said merchants—neither by themselves nor through other intermediaries <note>original: "interpósitas personas" — a legal term for a "straw man" or agent used to hide a principal's identity</note>, directly or indirectly—shall not recover what they have thus given on credit. This is under penalty of forfeiture [of the goods], loss of their official positions, and a further fine of fifty thousand maravedis <term>maravedi: a small copper coin used as the standard unit of account in Spain</term>.

Thirdly, certain brokers <term>corredores: commercial intermediaries or agents who match buyers and sellers for a commission</term> in this business of *baratas* are accustomed to being both the principals and the third parties in the following manner. They arrange with a merchant to take fifty or one hundred bundles of Rouen <note>Rouen, in France, was a major center for linen production; "fardos de Ruan" (Rouen bundles) were a staple of the international textile trade</note> at a certain price per yard <term>vara: a traditional Spanish unit of length, roughly equivalent to 33 inches or a yard</term>, to be paid in one year. This is done with the condition that if, within a month or two, they provide other debtors to the merchant’s satisfaction, they themselves are released from the obligation. 

Then, they seek out persons in need of money who are looking for a *barata* <term>barata: a predatory credit transaction where goods are sold at high prices on credit and then resold for immediate cash at a loss</term>. They arrange with these needy people to give them the goods at a loss of twenty-five or thirty percent. They force these people to become the ones obligated to the original owners of the linens, thus "marrying" the two parties through this path. Meanwhile, they sell the clothing to someone else who wants to buy it for cash, making sure to give it to them with only a fifteen or twenty percent discount. 

In this way, besides their brokerage fee <term>corretage: the commission paid to a broker for facilitating a deal</term>, they gain five or six percent on the whole thing. In every part of this, they sin: namely, in the fee and in the profit. They could not rightfully take a brokerage fee because they handled the business as principals [the buyers], not as third-party intermediaries; and they cannot have the profit because they are not permitted to be principals, but only brokers, as we shall soon see. Thus, by being in the deal as those who they could not be, and by failing to be what they ought to have been, they can gain nothing. 

But they, caring nothing for these true reasons, gain much against all justice. They are persons to whom one must speak with wordplay and ciphers <note>original: "retruecanos y cifras" — implies they use deceptive or coded language to hide their tracks</note>, because they commonly sin through being overly ingenious and sharp. They argue in their own defense that they can do this because they put themselves at risk of loss if the person who paid in cash was not satisfied with those prices.

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral critique of predatory lending practices, specifically focusing on the "mohatra" and the "barata." -># On the *Baratas*<-

The <term>mohatra</term> <note>a fraudulent contract where goods are sold on credit at an inflated price only to be bought back immediately for cash at a lower price, effectively creating a high-interest loan that circumvented usury laws</note> is quite tangled and diabolical. Firstly, these individuals are forbidden from buying any of the clothing they trade for the purpose of resale; they may only buy for their own household use. This is due to the many great inconveniences and harms that experience shows follow otherwise. Secondly, they rarely run any risk in such contracts. Before they even come to an agreement with the first parties, they already have someone lined up to take the <term>barata</term> <note>a predatory credit transaction involving the exchange of goods for quick cash</note> and someone to pay for it in cash, with the prices already set. If they do not have this, they take such people at such a timing that they never lose, always gain, and remain secure. 

Furthermore, while the <term>corredor</term> <note>a commercial broker or intermediary</note> should always act in favor of the "fallen" <note>the debtor or the person in financial distress</note> for these baratas to be handled lawfully, in this case, the broker acts in favor of the one selling on credit for more than the goods are worth. He acts on the seller's behalf, and he himself has even become a principal party to it, since he bought and took the clothing on credit. And so, as a man with a personal interest in the matter, he eats the very entrails of the one making the barata, making him believe heaven is an onion <note>original: "haziendole entender del cielo cebolla" — a Spanish idiom meaning to deceive someone with absurd lies or to pull the wool over their eyes</note>. In the end, it is an abominable mixture and conjunction: to be the third party and the principal, to be the judge and the accuser, to be a party to the deal and the witness. It is something so patently illicit that the civil laws themselves forbid it with these words:

> We command and forbid that no broker of the exchange <note>original: "corredor de lonja" — the lonja was the commercial hub where merchants gathered</note>, nor of livestock, nor of other merchandise—whether movable goods or real estate—shall dare to buy for themselves any estates, livestock, or merchandise, nor any other movable or fixed goods whatsoever that are given to them to sell. This applies regardless of whether the price is low or high, whether they buy for themselves or through intermediaries <note>original: "interpósitas personas"</note>, under penalty of losing their office and a further fine of fifty thousand <term>maravedis</term> <note>a traditional Spanish unit of account</note>.

There is another fourth kind of barata, and there will be another four thousand if merchants and brokers take the fancy. This consists of giving money or clothing to be paid in the Indies <note>the Spanish colonies in the Americas</note>, with the principal person obligating himself and providing a guarantor that if it is not paid there, it will be paid here. And the one who gives it says that he runs the risk of the voyage on some ship where the recipient is traveling. This is a laughable trick they have invented, which is properly an infernal exchange, according to—

### CHAPTER XXII. ON THE PASSAGE FROM EUROPE TO THE EAST AND WEST INDIES.

IN THIS last chapter, it would be lawful, and perhaps profitable, to examine the conscience a little regarding this passage so dangerous, from Europe to the Indies, and yet so little feared. We should examine if it were safe in conscience to cross indifferently, out of mere whim and greed, or if some urgent causes were necessary to justify this so patently risking of one's life. For it is not such a settled matter, this embarking by the thousands in every fleet, that it would be an ostentation of wit to show it to be many times—at the very least—great temerity <note>reckless boldness</note>, since they are moved to put themselves in such great danger without any grave or honest reason. I well know that concerning both things—that is, going in person, and negotiating in distinct parts two thousand leagues across the sea—**Saint Ambrose** <note>A 4th-century Bishop of Milan and Doctor of the Church who wrote extensively on the dangers of the sea and the greed of merchants</note> would preach great things in this church if, just as he was Archbishop of Milan, he were Archbishop of Seville. If he saw this river <note>The Guadalquivir River in Seville, which held the monopoly on trade with the New World</note> so full of ships, this wharf, this coming and going of fleets for the Indies and returning from there; and if he heard, as we hear every day, the grim losses and shipwrecks of property and people, where they perish and drown two hundred at a time. He could not fail to give us clearly to understand, with effective reasons, that our boldness is unheard of. For since the creation of the world until now, men never sailed as far as the Spaniards sail. And if we do not [frighten ourselves...]

...it would frighten the ears, at the very least shut the eyes, and cover the mouths of those who, on these steps <note>Likely referring to the steps of the Cathedral of Seville, a famous gathering place for merchants and traders known as "Las Gradas"</note>, so continually fill the air with cries and mourning for their maritime disasters. According to the judgment of the Holy Doctor <note>Referring to Saint Ambrose, cited below</note>, it is the height of madness for men to "plow the sea," since God formed them from the earth as animals meant to live on land, and set the waters to one side—which previously covered the earth—in order to provide them with their natural habitation. "Be ashamed," says Isaiah, "for the sea speaks to Sidon" <note>Isaiah 23:4; Sidon was an ancient Phoenician port city</note>—a city which the same text affirms is home to many merchants and great trade. And the sea rebukes them for plunging so far into its dangers. This is the voice and complaint of this element, says Saint Ambrose, as if it were already weary of suffering them, for it ought not to suffer or sustain anything but its own fish.

Divine Wisdom itself wonders at navigation; and even being Solomon, he does not know how they escape such danger <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:18–19, where the "way of a ship in the midst of the sea" is one of the four things the wise king finds too wonderful to understand</note>. And so great is the thoughtlessness of some that they expose themselves to it for the slightest causes and motives—being all the more daring and reprehensible in their navigation than Leander in his crossing or Icarus in his flight, according to the fables of the poets. For, in reality and truth, is not the Atlantic Ocean, which separates the Indies from Europe, greater and more dangerous than the Strait of the Hellespont <note>The narrow strait in northwestern Turkey now known as the Dardanelles</note> that divides Sestos from Abydos?

Certainly, they deservedly suffer all their misfortunes, especially the merchants of this city <note>Presumably Seville</note>, who dispatch <term>naos</term> <note>large, multi-decked sailing ships or carracks</note> and <term>urcas</term> <note>heavy, broad-bottomed cargo vessels or hulks</note> with the greatest barbarity. And let no one find the term harsh, for it is very mild if one looks at the deed. They dispatch ships and caravels—mere tiny hulls, first of all—alone across an ocean so vast, proud, and fearsome; through gulfs so long and wide that in ancient times merely to name them was terrifying. Second, they do so in the heart of winter during November, December, and January—a time so rigid and tempestuous that one does not even travel by land due to storms of rain and ice. There is no distinction more celebrated or notorious in history than the "time for sailing" and the "time for wintering."

To hear a conclusion without its proof is like someone watching a dance without hearing the music: they cannot discern if the dancer moves their feet in rhythm. Many authors reproach Aristotle because he reported the maxims of Plato—which are his conclusions—while remaining silent about the proofs on which he based them. Thus they seem like dreams, which perhaps they would not seem if we heard Plato's motives and understandings; just as Seneca and Saint Augustine, who were his more faithful and devoted disciples, explain and apply them in some matters. <meta>This page transitions from the general relationship between civil and natural law to a specific case study: the regulation of wheat prices. It argues that the state has a moral and practical obligation to set price ceilings on essential goods to prevent exploitation during shortages.</meta>

# On the Decree regarding Wheat.

Provisions and clothing must be priced according to law, for being necessary in the commonwealth <note>original: "republica," referring to the state or community at large</note>, they are constantly consumed; their sale and purchase is the most common among neighbors. Therefore, if there were no fixed price <term>tassa</term> <note>A government-mandated price ceiling or valuation intended to prevent price gouging.</note>, people could deceive or be deceived almost every hour, giving or taking more or less than what a thing is worth. And so, because such common trade should be safe and clear to everyone, it is right that there should be a fixed price, so that all may know what they must give and what they may ask. It is a great satisfaction for people to know exactly what the things they buy or sell every day are worth, and a great displeasure to have to continually inform themselves anew of their just value. 

How much better this reasoning applies to wheat, being the provision that is most consumed, most continually purchased, and most frequently sold. For this reason, it is very necessary for the peace of the whole town that its value be publicly appraised. And even if the exact amount to be given is not specified, a limit should be set that may never be exceeded without Royal license and authority. It is a relief to know that one must not charge more than nine *reales* <note>A Spanish silver coin used as a standard currency unit.</note> and above, but from there downwards, whatever the parties might agree upon.

The other reason, which is the foundation of the law I mentioned and the motive of princes—namely, that things necessary for human coexistence <note>original: "conuicto humano," referring to the social living together of people</note> should be appraised by the governor so that the price does not increase due to their necessity—has particular force regarding bread, which is the most necessary provision of all. For with only bread and water, they say one can sustain not just man, but his physical life. Thus, we saw by experience how quickly and rapidly the price of wheat rose when there began to be a shortage, back when there was no fixed price. The prices to which it then climbed were excessive. For if any kind of clothing, whose value is left to the discretion of the sellers, is known to increase in price as much as it can, how much more so will it be with necessary provisions, knowing that the residents cannot avoid buying them, no matter how expensive they may be.

## Chapter Two, in which the Royal Decrees concerning the sale of Wheat are related.

-> § Summary of the fourth chapter. § <-

<margin>1</margin> *All the royal decrees <term>pragmaticas</term> <note>A "Pragmática" was a high-level royal edict that had the force of law without needing the formal consent of the Cortes (parliament).</note> that have been made in these kingdoms from the time of the Catholic Monarchs until now concerning the sale of wheat, both in grain and as dough, are related.*

<margin>2</margin> *¶ How in all the decrees it is ordered to sell at the same price, whether the wheat is given on credit or sold for cash. From this, a universal rule for other contracts is gathered: that a thing should be sold for the same price on credit as for cash.* <note>This was a significant moral ruling intended to prevent hidden interest (usury) being added to the price of goods sold on credit.</note>

<margin>3</margin> *¶ That baked bread must be sold according to the value of the grain, adding the costs of milling and kneading, and a moderate profit. Judges are obliged to appraise and designate this.*

<margin>4</margin> *¶ That the royal decree on wheat, and the appraisal of the governors regarding kneaded bread, binds in conscience not only the common people, but all ecclesiastics, clergy, and members of religious orders, even if they are otherwise exempt.* <note>In this period, the clergy often had their own legal jurisdiction (fuero), but the author argues that moral obligation to follow price laws applies to everyone.</note>

<margin>5</margin> *¶ If in any commonwealth the judge should be negligent in publicly appraising the bread, it cannot for that reason be sold for more than what the law commonly says (that is to say) what it is worth in grain, adding the costs and a moderate interest.*

All these ordinances are so clear that they do not demand an explanation, but only a reading, and to be kept exactly as they sound. For there is not a word in them that, in the place where it is fitted, could produce two meanings. Nor is there any ignorant person who, reading them, would not easily understand what is truly commanded, ordered, or forbidden. ## On the Royal Edict concerning Bread.

The first point established and indicated in all these royal edicts <term>pragmaticas</term> <note>A *pragmática* was a form of royal decree issued by the Spanish monarch that carried the force of law without needing the formal approval of the parliament (*Cortes*).</note> is a single price for wheat, whether it is paid for in cash or on credit. From this, one can infer how obvious the legislators consider it to be that goods are not worth more when sold on credit than when sold for cash. Nor is the granting of credit a sufficient reason to increase the price. If it were, it would certainly have been explained in a matter so universal. For it would be a most general injury if wheat were worth more when sold on credit, thus depriving everyone of their interest.

But in so many Kings setting the price of wheat with such careful counsel, as the business required, at the same price—whether it is bought on credit or paid for at the moment—and in not disagreeing at all on this point (even though they may differ on other points within these same edicts), it is clearly shown to be natural law. To this law, positive laws <note>Positive laws are man-made statutes enacted by a government, which, according to the legal philosophy of the time, should ideally align with "Natural Law"—a system of ethics believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason.</note> cannot contradict, but must rather serve: that goods must have the same esteem and value whether paid for later or paid for immediately. In this, merchants will see how they act against both natural and civil law. And consequently, they act outside of the rule and against the rule (since laws are the rule of human acts) by selling more expensively the longer the payment is delayed, and generally by charging more for credit than if they were paid in the present.

Regarding the sale of baked bread, two notable things are ordained. First, that it be sold at a price that recovers the cost of the wheat, as well as the costs of milling and kneading, along with a moderate profit. This is found in the edict of His Majesty, dated in the year 1558. Second, that this moderate profit be set by the judges in their districts, according to the edict of the year 1568.

On this point, there has been great confusion these past years in some cities of these Kingdoms for many causes. One is that in some of them, I believe this original edict has not yet arrived, and the town councils <note>The original Spanish *consultados* refers to the governing bodies or legal advisors of the cities.</note> speak of it only by hearsay. <margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae*, 1a 2ae, question 96, article 1. *Digest, on laws*: laws ought to be established regarding those things which occur most frequently, not those which happen by chance or unexpectedly. Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 5, chapter 20: common cases are to be prescribed by laws; particular and rarely occurring ones are to be left aside. Book 1 of the *Rhetoric*, chapter 1; and Book 2 of the *Politics*, title 6.</margin>...is obliged to observe it, even if he loses money by doing so. Because the law looks only to what commonly happens in that matter; and being founded on this universality, it binds even those for whom, in their particular case, the universal reasoning does not apply. In this way, if the price cap <term>tassa</term> allows for a moderate profit above the public cost of wheat and the common expenses of milling and kneading, it binds everyone to observe it—even the individual who, due to various accidents, finds that the cost to him is higher. This is because no law can account for every particular case that occurs, but only those which are likely to happen most of the time. Aristotle says in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, as does the Jurist <note>Likely a reference to the Roman legal authorities in the *Digest*.</note>, that the law is established as a universal rule for that which happens to almost the entire community. And if it should occasionally fail in a rare instance, it does not for that reason cease to be just and binding.

It is a most necessary statute that weapons should not be carried at night, as they are commonly used for ill during such hours. Wisdom says that night and wine never persuade one toward moderation and temperance. And there is no doubt that there would be some who would use them very well, even if it were very dark. But the legislator should not fix his eyes upon what these few and rare individuals might do, but rather on what the multitude of the common people <term>vulgo</term> is accustomed to do, and intervene with his authority and power against the enormous crimes committed with weapons at night. Once established, the law binds in the external forum <note>The jurisdiction of civil and ecclesiastical courts over public actions, as opposed to the internal forum of the soul or conscience.</note> and includes even the very peaceful, for whom the reasoning used to establish the law does not specifically apply.

# On the Royal Edict concerning Wheat.

...the flesh weakens with fasting, whereby the spirit, relieved of such a heavy burden, might gain some strength. A person who not only does not grow weak but actually grows fat by not eating supper—as happens with some—is still obliged to fast, even though the universal intent of the law is not fulfilled in them. And if this is a certain truth even regarding laws of temperance—which are primarily directed toward the personal well-being of the one who obeys them—how much more true must it be for laws of justice? These laws look more toward the common good <term>bien común: the collective welfare and stability of society</term> than to the individual, and this is particularly true of this law concerning the price cap <term>taſſa: a government-mandated maximum price for essential goods</term>. In this case, the primary concern is not the profit of the seller, but rather the availability of cheap provisions <term>baſtimento</term> throughout the kingdom. Therefore, one will be obliged to sell within the price cap, even if it cost them more to acquire the grain.

This doctrine is most effectively confirmed by considering what great confusion would follow in the commonwealth <term>republica</term> otherwise—that is, if the law did not encompass those for whom the lawmaker's motive does not apply. This is because such an examination—of whether or not the motive applies—would necessarily be left to each individual's own judgment. And if left to the individuals, who would not truly think themselves excused? Who would not use such a shield to break the law when their appetite demanded it or their self-interest moved them? 

Even though people know this resolution of ours is certain, and held generally by all the doctors <note>referring to "Doctors" of the Church or learned legal scholars</note>, they still struggle to restrain themselves from offering this frivolous excuse in confession <note>confessors were often the ones who had to decide if a merchant had committed a sin by overcharging</note>: that "it cost me more." What would happen if this were a true excuse? Thus, even though this matter must be repeated later and explained extensively, let this much be determined here: that the price cap, being just, requires observance from those for whom, at various times, the wheat or baked bread <term>pan amaſſado</term> costs more.

# On the Edict concerning Wheat.

...baked bread <term>pan cozido: bread already baked and ready for consumption, as opposed to raw grain</term>, should be priced only slightly higher than the value of the grain, after costs are deducted. The King mandates this for everyone. He only commissions the judges to tax the profit that [the bakers] should receive for their labor. However, if the judges do not do so, it remains at the discretion of a prudent man to determine what would be a fair interest. Even if the King had not established this himself, it seems quite exorbitant to charge sixteen [reales] for prepared bread <term>amaſſado: refers to the processed dough or bread</term> when the grain is worth nine. There is no reason or foundation in such a trade to earn so much. For there is no risk—or very little—in such times of scarcity, nor is the sale delayed, nor is the merchant's capital tied up for a longer time by selling it as bread. Because he has hardly brought it out to the marketplace when it is already sold. These are the reasons that usually grant a right to some interest; thus, I believe that even without a positive law <note>A "positive law" is a man-made statute, as opposed to "natural law" which is seen as inherent to morality</note>, excessive interest on baked bread would be illicit in itself, and even more so when it is prohibited by law with such rigor and so expressly.

In this matter, as it conforms to reason, it appears that the law did no more than explain what was already part of natural equity <term>equidad natural: the principle of justice that exists independently of written laws</term>, as is evident in the sale of flour. Regarding flour, the law orders that one may only charge more than the price of the wheat by what the milling <term>molienda</term> costs in each province. The exception is baked bread: because there is labor involved in kneading and baking it, and it is sold in small portions <note>Selling "por menudo" (retail/by the piece) typically allowed for higher margins than wholesale</note>—which are sufficient reasons to earn a profit—the law reasonably grants some interest. But this interest must be in the moderate quantity dictated by these same reasons, since the labor of both [kneading and baking] is small. Furthermore, if any price were permitted for bread, what benefit would come from the price cap <term>taſſa</term> on grain? It would be poorly said, as the laws themselves confess. For no one would sell grain if they could gain so much more by turning it into bread. From this I conclude that even if the governors in some areas proclaim that people may sell bread for whatever price they can, any profit that greatly exceeds the value of the grain is not licit. ...[obligation], it was a permission of the evil done therein, not an approval. Judges then leave the matter to the individual consciences of private citizens according to the natural law <term>ley natural: universal moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature</term> which dictates and teaches: that if grain is worth nine, then once prepared <term>amaſſado: refers here to the processed dough or bread</term>, it should be worth fourteen at most, allowing two and a half *reales* <note>The real was a silver coin used in Spain for centuries</note> for costs, and the remainder as a reasonable interest in such circumstances. Natural light <note>The "light of reason" or innate human understanding</note> dictates this because there is so little difference between the one and the other. If the price control <term>taſſa: a government-mandated price cap</term> on grain were lifted, one could profit from the prepared bread—not because of the act of kneading it, but because of the increased value of the wheat itself. However, while the price control remains in force, the trade of kneading it offers little profit according to natural law. To preserve the legal price of grain is to tie the feet of the greedy; it is to remove their shackles regarding the prepared bread [only to keep them bound by the grain price]. Because grain and baked bread are so nearly the same thing in terms of selling them, the price of one can exceed the other by very little. It is like when a hunter holds a hawk by its jesses <note>original: "piguelas" — the leather straps attached to a bird of prey's legs</note>; no matter how much it flutters, it can fly very little. Thus, according to natural law (from which no one is exempt), the price of baked bread is so tied to the value of the grain that the bread must be sold just as the wheat is sold, with only a moderate interest added.

# Chapter three: regarding how no lay or ecclesiastical persons may sell baked bread for themselves or through a third party, but only the bakers; and at what prices it must be sold in the cities and places exempt from this price control and edict.

->§ Summary of the Third Chapter. ❧<-

<margin>1</margin>
**THAT** no member of the Clergy <term>Eccleſiaſtico: a person belonging to the church</term> may sell baked bread, either by themselves or through a third party; nor may any layperson <term>ſeglar: a person not in holy orders; a member of the general public</term>, except for the bakers, who hold this as their official trade. And how necessary it is for the people that this mandate and prohibition be observed.

*¶ That no one may be a retailer in wheat, buying it to resell it, except for the muleteers and carriers, along with the others whom the law exempts.*

This constitution <note>A term used here for a specific legal decree or statute</note> binds everyone, as it concerns a matter that is primary and very necessary to the entire commonwealth. Thus, to ensure there is bread available both as grain and baked, it is necessary to prohibit the sale of baked goods by those who do not hold the official trade.
