And whatever the just price of a thing may be, the commonwealth <note>original: "republica"</note> must define it and grant it.

And it is very much worth noting regarding this, that the price is not set conditionally—that is, if such-and-such persons sell or buy it—but rather it absolutely values and fixes it at a certain amount, without having any respect for the sellers, whether they be these people or those. Therefore, whoever takes more than the fixed price for it commits an injustice, taking more than the just price. And consequently, he sins and must make restitution, whether he be a layman or a clergyman. <margin>
...[laws regarding goods that] were taken out of the kingdom, and others of that sort, bind clerics equally with laypeople.
<note>original Latin: "extrahebantur ab regno atque aliae idgenus ex aequo clericos cum secularibus obligant"</note>
</margin>

<unclear>...most bound</unclear> are the foreigners to sell their wheat at the fixed price <term>tassa: a legally mandated price ceiling intended to prevent inflation during shortages</term>, unless the prince himself exempts them. Therefore, if (as these people say) the clergy are as exempt as foreigners, it follows that they are obliged to observe the royal decree <term>pragmatica: a sovereign's edict that has the force of law</term>, just as those from outside are perfectly obliged to do. And if foreigners were ever exempted, there were sufficient reasons: in those cases, the law looked not so much at the foreigners' own profit, but at the benefit of the native citizens. None of these reasons apply to the Ecclesiastics, as is evident. Thus, it was not just to exempt them. 

On the contrary, the opposite of what they argue follows. Namely, that if they are no less exempt than foreigners, then their wheat—which by its nature ought to be sold at the fixed price—would indeed be sold at that price if it were not specifically exempted. Because that wheat was truly subject to the law, it was necessary for the King to grant a special privilege to exempt it. It follows then that the wheat of the Ecclesiastics must follow the royal decree, since the King did not exempt it. And in truth, there was no reason to exempt it; rather, there are many reasons that invite them to sell it in times of necessity, even for less than the price charged by laypeople.

Likewise, it should be noted that no one can lawfully be a middleman <term>regatón: a person who buys goods specifically to resell them at a higher price; a "regrater"</term> in wheat. This means buying it to resell it, except for those whom the royal decree specifically licenses to do so. This decree of the Emperor was most necessary because, in any kind of provisions <term>bastimentos: essential food supplies or staples</term>, these middlemen are harmful because they act as second-hand sellers. The original owner, such as the farmers, earns a profit—and it is just they should earn it—by selling to the middlemen. Then the middlemen also earn a profit by reselling it. Thus, the price of the goods <note>original: "ropa"; while usually meaning "clothing," in this period it often referred to general merchandise or "dry goods"</note> in the town increases by exactly the amount of their profit margin. The original farmer would be content to sell directly to private individuals for the same price he gives the middleman; and thus the price of provisions would be lower by as much as the middlemen increase it by inserting themselves. This is because the citizens necessarily obtain the goods at a price that is higher the more sales and hands it passes through...

### On the Royal Edict regarding Wheat.

The same law also addresses what comes from abroad. Regarding the <term>bread: specifically "pan," which in this period refers broadly to grain and the wheat used for basic sustenance</term> that comes from outside these kingdoms by sea, if those who brought it were forced to observe the aforementioned <term>price cap: "tasas," the government-mandated maximum price for grain</term>, they might cease to bring it at all. This would result in a great shortage and harm to many of our coasts and ports. Therefore, it is our will that regarding the said grain that comes from outside these kingdoms by sea, the said price cap shall not apply.

However, it is worth knowing at what price those whom the law has privileged or liberated ought to sell. I am moved to clarify this by seeing how many misunderstand and even more poorly use this privilege. Because the law says that in these places they may sell freely "as they are able," and says the same for wheat coming from abroad by sea, some wrongly conclude that they may set the price at their own whim without any restriction. They believe that each person may sell it for as much as they can negotiate, saying that the King gives them the power to sell "as they are able." 

But they must know that the phrase *as they are able* is understood to mean as they are able *licitly* <note>meaning "lawfully" or "within the bounds of moral and legal permission"</note>. For the law always understands that what "can" be done is that which can be done with justice. That which is done in fact, but not by right, is called "impossible" by the law, even though it physically occurs. For this reason, there is a common adage among theologians and jurists:

> <note>original: "Id poſſumus , quod iure poſſumus."</note> *We can do that which we can do by right.*

Thus, when we are often asked if certain things can be done, we answer "no," even though it is true they *could* be done against the law. No one "can" kill a citizen without being their judge. Yet there is no doubt that (as the proverb says) he who despises his own life is master of another's. Generally, men are secure in the knowledge that they will not be killed insofar as they understand that no one wants to die, knowing that he who kills where there is justice, dies himself. Therefore, even though the <term>royal edict: "pragmatica," a decree with the force of law</term> says they may sell "as they are able," the field is not left entirely to their own whims, nor can they sell without measure or standard. That phrase *as they are able* is understood to be in accordance with justice and the law. And the natural law still remains for them to obey and keep: for...

### On the Royal Edict regarding Wheat.

It commands that it always be sold for its **just price**. And in this mat-
ter of selling, there is also a universal and
famous maxim: **A thing is worth as much as it can be sold for.** <note>original Latin: "Res tanti valet, quanti vendi potest"</note> But this is understood as for how
much it can be sold *with justice*, not for as much as
the seller might be able to extract. What the King did was not re-
strict them to his **set price cap** <term>set price cap: "tassa positiva," a specific price fixed by the government</term>; but he did not exempt them from the **market price** <term>market price: "precio accidental," the fluctuating value determined by current supply and demand</term>,
which is what natural law obliges them to follow in such cases.
This reason proves this again with efficacy (be-
cause in cases of profit, great energy and persuasive force
is necessary to restrain a man). I ask those
who, upon hearing these words, "Sell for as much as you are able,"
believe and persuade themselves that they can take as much as they desire:
Did the King leave them more free in his edict than if
he had never promulgated it? They cannot be more permitted
to sell than they would be if no price cap had been established.
And it is certain that if there were none, they could not sell for
whatever they fancied. We well know that there are two prices: one
that time and its circumstances create (which we call **accidental**)
and another designated by the state. And where it is not designated,
the first one runs and is obligatory.

The same rule must be followed in these examples as is
followed by the **velvet makers** <term>velvet makers: "terciopeleros," artisans of luxury fabrics whose goods were not price-controlled</term>, since for velvets there is no
price cap at all. And we see that they, and universally all
traders, observe and must observe the common price that
the times have introduced. Thus also are these
privileged persons required to sell—not at the price cap, which no
longer binds them, but at the **market price** that is current in the city, town,
or village. This is a true resolution and very much in accordance with reason.
For it is not just for anyone to think that natural law leaves the
value of such a necessary **staple** <term>staple: "bastimento," referring here to essential food supplies like grain</term> to the corrupt appetite
of their greed. The King can exempt them from his edict,
but natural law and reason bind them again to general equity.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the moral and legal constraints on wheat pricing. ### On the Royal Edict regarding Wheat.

Namely, that everything be sold for its common current price now in the town. Civil law (which in this matter is certainly natural) states very prudently that the price of things should not be set by the personal affection of the owner, but by the dispassionate judgment of many. This is the price that the community introduces through the act of buying and selling.

But some will ask: what will this **accidental price** <term>accidental price: "precio accidental," the market value determined by supply, demand, and local conditions rather than by decree</term> be that binds everyone? When the royal and **just legal price** <term>just legal price: the "tasa," or government-mandated price cap</term> is active in the town, it does not seem there would be any other to follow.

I respond that in excepted places, such as Cadiz and the ports on the contrary, nothing but the **accidental price** will run, according to which everyone must sell. In such a way that if in Cadiz it is traded at ten, whoever comes from elsewhere anew, whether by sea or by land, cannot charge twelve—no matter how much the law says, "sell for as much as you can." Because truly, according to justice, he cannot take more than ten. For there at least there is no reason to claim license or exemption, since only the **common price** created by the times runs. For if it is worth less, that price is no longer the legal one, but the accidental one. 

It is like the rope on a bull: it stops him precisely when he is bellowing and the rope is taut. But when it lies loose, stretched out on the ground, the bull is not restrained by it <note>The author uses this metaphor to explain that the law is a "ceiling." The Royal Edict does not help the seller at that time any more than if it did not exist. And if it did not exist: he would be obligated to sell at the **current price**. 

Furthermore, it is established that in such a case, a local neighbor is as free from the Edict to sell the wheat of his own harvest up to nine as the foreigner is. And it is also certain that the neighbor would sin if, while it was worth six, he sold it for nine, even though the justice system would not punish him. Therefore, in the same way, he who sells wheat brought from outside by sea for that much or more sins when the local wheat is worth less than the price cap. And if the earthly judge does not punish him, the heavenly one will: and his own conscience will condemn him, and he will remain obligated to make **restitution** <term>restitution: "restituir," the theological requirement to return excess profits gained through unjust pricing</term> for however much he took in excess.

In this case, it will necessarily be worth more. The question is asked: at what price can it be licitly sold? I say that it should be sold at whatever price the foreign wheat has begun to be traded for in public. 

The basis for this is that whoever is not bound by the Royal price cap (either because of the place where he sells, or because the goods he sells are excepted) is instead bound by the **accidental price** that exists in his exempt and free mode of selling. He is obligated to observe this price, because it is then his own proper standard. From this it follows that, if there is no other foreign wheat present whose example he can follow, or through whose sale the accidental price can be known, he may set his wheat at whatever price seems right to him. However, he must carefully avoid being barbaric and cruel. He would be so if, once the value is left to his own determination, he asks for outrageous prices. Tho." referring to St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential 13th-century theologian</note> notes elsewhere when treating the **just price** <note>original: "precio justo"</note>)—or believing that in that small excess God is not offended nor the neighbor harmed, would not sin mortally, nor be obliged to return such an excess." Regarding the first words mentioned from his first conclusion, I say they are not well stated. Because while it is true that one sins mortally by exceeding the cap significantly (which obliges one to restitution) and sometimes sins **venially** <note>venial sin: in Catholic teaching, a lesser sin that does not result in complete separation from God's grace, unlike a mortal sin</note> by exceeding it slightly (as we shall declare), it would be proper to explain the case of significant excess without using that specific word ["notably"], which among Spaniards sounds like something massive or excessive. One does not need such a massive excess to commit a mortal sin by breaking the law. Secondly, one must add that even when the excess is small, it is still necessary to restore it. Finally, neither the one nor the other is sound doctrine. Because, as I will explain almost immediately, one sins mortally by exceeding the set price even by a little.

Regarding the first point, it should be known that everything taken beyond the just price—especially where there is a legal price cap—is to steal it. And just as and when one sins by stealing, one sins by selling for more than the law allows. Since this is so true, one can see how imprudently a certain "universal rule" was pronounced and written, which is almost never verified in practice. Such a rule is not true, nor does it apply, except in the rare case where someone sells only once for slightly more than the fixed price with a simple mind, without intending to do so again. This is a very rare intention and will among people who deal in selling wheat or any other kind of merchandise; for what they gain once, they desire and intend to gain every time they sell.

The core of this Conclusion is false doctrine: it should in no way be held, much less followed. This applies both to what he asserts—that one may charge everything it cost him—as well as to the reasoning provided: namely, that it suffices to act lawfully by believing one can do so in good conscience. As he says, Saint Thomas and Cajetan teach this. But let no one believe that Saint Thomas or Cajetan ever gave such a nonsensical reason. And in the passages he cites, they say nothing that could even be an occasion for such a wild error—that for a thing to be lawful, it suffices to think that it is.

Regarding this matter, it should be noted that the **just value** <term>just value: the morally and legally upright price of a good, often determined by common market estimation or law</term> must not be regulated by what it cost the seller, once a price has been fixed, but rather by what it is currently worth. Having cost a low or high price does not increase or decrease the just price of any cloth. This is even more evident when there is a price ceiling in the city, which removes a thousand doubts, a thousand licenses, and determinations...

This is something that no one is ignorant of being very false and against all good reason. Justice requires that he who bought dearly, or was cheated, should not cheat; but rather sell for what the item is worth. This is so that he does not commit the same crime in selling that was committed by the other in buying. This is clearly proven by the very example he provides.

For this reason, a righteous heart and good faith are often enough to excuse certain deeds in a temperate man—deeds that were harmful to no one and were beneficial to him. But justice directs a man toward his neighbor; and thus, it primarily considers the injury that is done externally, even if the mind of the person who committed the injury is not entirely corrupt.

Therefore, this fiction that this author imposes upon them never even crossed these doctors' minds in a dream. # Concerning the Decree on Wheat.

More briefly, I say two things. The first is that even if in a certain case—whether by taking from another, selling, or buying at more than the just price—ignorance of the law or of the fact <note>The legal distinction between *ignorantia iuris* (not knowing the law) and *ignorantia facti* (not knowing the specific circumstances).</note> might excuse one from sin (which even then rarely happens), it never excuses one from making restitution as soon as they realize they have overcharged. Thus, ignorance (if it were reasonable) may free a person from guilt, but not from the duty of restitution. It would be quite a fine thing if, simply because I believe I can take whatever I please, I were allowed to keep it! Sin may sometimes find an excuse in ignorance; but as for the property <note>original: "hazienda," referring here to assets or wealth.</note> that you have in your possession and now know belongs to someone else: what ignorance can excuse you from returning it, once you know it is not yours? 

When I usurp what belongs to another, I do two things. First, I offend God, whose law I break; and second, I remain obligated to return the item. From the first part, which concerns God, a just ignorance excuses me; but from the second, I am not excused. And from this comes what we were saying a little while ago regarding the virtues of temperance and justice. For in temperance—which concerns only the individual man—believing that some act is likely permissible sometimes provides an excuse. But in justice—which concerns one’s neighbor—it might free me from sin, but not from the duty to satisfy him <note>Meaning to make amends or provide compensation to the wronged party.</note>. 

It is just as if I were to take a silver pitcher from someone else’s house, truly thinking it was my own; I remain obligated to return it once I know it was not. In this same way, if someone believed that because their wheat cost them more than what the Decree <term>tasa: the official price ceiling or fixed rate set by the crown</term> allows, it was permissible for them to violate the law by selling at higher prices, it might be that they did not sin in doing so (though there is still great doubt about this, as we shall soon see), but in no way could they keep the surplus they received. This is true even if it had been done in good faith and with a sincere heart. This doctrine is very well known even among common people. Such people often return whatever they realize they have profited illicitly in past contracts or sales...

Some argue that this Decree is insufficient because it sets a universal price throughout all of Castile and Andalusia, even though the expenses and the cost of wheat in those regions are so unequal. However, they do not consider the ingenuity and the manner in which the law was ordained. Specifically, it was determined by considering how much a fanega <term>hanega</term> <note>A Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly 55.5 liters, used primarily for grain.</note> might cost a farmer <term>labrador</term> <note>The *labrador* was a small-scale independent farmer or tenant who worked the land.</note> in any location. They found that, though it might cost more in some parts and less in others, in no place would the cost exceed eight reales. Thus, by selling at nine, all farmers and the townspeople would profit. From that point downward, the law left the freedom and space to sell for more or less, according to the condition of the land and the state of the weather. 

If the law had strictly set a fixed price for every fanega (in the same way that wine prices are set for each individual city), it would have been impossible to designate a general price, nor one that could last across so many provinces. It would have been necessary to set a distinct price in Castile and another in Toledo; one in Extremadura and another in Andalusia. But by determining one maximum that could not be exceeded, but which could be lowered according to the time and place, it was well understood that in no province would the cost exceed eight, and thus it was commanded that in no province should it be sold for more than nine.

If in some province or an entire kingdom it commonly cost the farmer more than eight reales per fanega, such that almost no profit remained for them, one might doubt whether such people were obligated to observe the law. ## Chapter Seven: On the Virtue
### of Equity <term>Epichia</term> <note>From the Greek 'epieikeia', this refers to the principle of fairness or 'equity'—interpreting the spirit of a law when a literal application would be unjust.</note>.

->❧ Summary of Chapter Seven. ❧<-

1. Equity is a virtue that teaches how to supply what the law lacks, or what could not be provided or established by law.
2. ¶ *There are two types of laws: some that are directed immediately toward the private good of each person, such as the laws of fasting and annual confession; others toward the public and common utility, such as the Royal Decree <term>Pragmatica</term> against carrying weapons, and many others.*
3. ¶ *When following a law results in neither a direct benefit nor a harm contrary to the good intended by the law, it is necessary that it be observed. Thus, it is enough that the law does not cause the opposite of what was intended for it to remain binding. But if the opposite occurs, the law can be broken with the legislator's permission, if it can be obtained; if it cannot, then that is precisely when Equity applies.*
4. ¶ *The proverb that says, "where the reason for the law ceases, the law itself ceases" <note>original: "do cessa la razon de la ley cessa ella." This is a translation of the Latin legal maxim: 'Cessante ratione legis, cessat ipsa lex'.</note>, is understood to apply when its reason ceases in general. If the reason is lacking only in a particular case for one person or another, the law still binds everyone.*

The rule is that **when the reason for the law fails, its obligation ceases** <note>This is a standard legal maxim: *Cessante causa legis, cessat lex*.</note>. The virtue is <term>equity</term> <note>original: "epichia", from the Greek *epieikeia*. It refers to the principle of fairness that looks at the heart of the law rather than just the literal words.</note>, a part of justice which, just as it teaches us to obey our superiors, also teaches us not to be so tied to the literal words of their precepts that we do not occasionally do the opposite—acting as wise and law-abiding men to preserve that same universal good which the legislator intended. <term>Equity</term> is a virtue that demands great prudence, and even perfect obedience, a spirit that is very submissive and well-inclined toward virtue. 

As Aristotle says, <term>equity</term> is the master of the laws themselves; it is a teacher that amends and corrects them at the proper time, supplying what they lack (and if they lack anything, it is because it is impossible for a law to provide for every specific circumstance). What the laws command is always just, but what <term>equity</term> shows is *more* just. One is good, and the other is better. 

How much wisdom, then, will be necessary to understand without error when the law is failing? And how can it be appropriately and correctly supplemented? It is easy for a person to be deceived by their own private and vehement desires, which lead them to believe that what is actually the dissolution and destruction of political and legal discipline is "equity." Few possess this virtue, and even fewer exercise it perfectly. From this comes the fact that many understand it poorly. For certainly, while many things can be achieved through speculation and scholastic study, those matters belonging to prudence and moral virtue are not well understood except through continuous practice. 

For this reason, I decided to explain briefly and clearly the nature and office of <term>equity</term>, so that it may be known how much it is *against* <term>equity</term> to sell for more than the publicly established price ceiling <term>tassa</term> <note>The 'tasa' was the government-mandated maximum price for grain to ensure the poor could afford bread.</note>, and how poorly those people grasp the concept when they say this is lawful if the goods cost the seller more than the legal price.

One of the required conditions that the law demands is to be universal, directed toward the public utility. Consequently, it must command what is commonly beneficial to all. To command what is largely harmful would be blindness or tyranny rather than a just law. And there are things so generally suitable that they are never harmful, such as honoring parents in the proper time and place, and loving God above all things. Not lying, nor swearing falsely, not committing adultery, nor stealing. No business transaction can present itself where it would be lawful to lie, nor where it would be fitting to commit adultery or cause some injury—not even to protect the reputation of one’s neighbor, nor to preserve one's own life. It is never lawful to break laws that command such things, nor does <term>equity</term> <note>original: "epichia". As noted previously, this is the principle of looking at the spirit of the law rather than the letter.</note> have a place in them. These are, for the most part, the natural laws, where perfect prudence and wisdom consist in always fulfilling and practicing them.

However, a law cannot suit everyone so perfectly in every instance that occasionally (though rarely) its utility does not cease; in fact, a very great harm may come from keeping it.

It is a universal law for all peoples that a man should be faithful to those who trust him, returning what was given to him for safekeeping. This is almost always necessary, and otherwise, no small evils would result. Human society would be undone. The trust that is necessary for people to have in one another would be disturbed. This, then, demonstrates the virtue of <term>equity</term> <note>original: *epichia*. This is a transliteration of the Greek *epieikeia*, the principle of applying the "spirit" of the law when the "letter" would lead to injustice.</note> (that is to say) when it is appropriate and proper to do the opposite of what the written text says for just causes, while still observing and following the fundamental justice of the law. Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> provides a most fitting example: if a city were under siege and the governor ordered that the gates not be opened under penalty of death without his permission, and the next day the guards saw from the walls some of their own soldiers retreating from a skirmish and they were able to safely shelter them by opening the gate (ensuring that no enemies slipped in with them), they could and should open it in such a crisis, despite the captain’s previous proclamation. This applies if the necessity is so urgent that it does not allow for going to ask for permission; because by following the order strictly, a great evil would occur. It would truly go against the governor's primary intent, which was to preserve the citizens and soldiers, all of whom would undoubtedly perish if his command were strictly observed.

In ancient times, this was a hotly debated question among philosophers, both the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note> and the Stoics: whether it was lawful for a captain, in certain cases, not to follow the instructions he received for his campaign from his prince or his general. Cicero discusses this in his book *On Duties* <note>original: *lib. de offijs* (De Officiis).</note>, as does Aulus Gellius in his *Attic Nights* <note>original: *noches Aticas* (Noctes Atticae).</note>. On the contrary, there are some subordinates of such free-spirited minds that they never wish to be bound by the instructions of their prince, changing them almost at their own whim.

Returning to our purpose, to easily and clearly demonstrate this admirable virtue, it must be understood that there are two types of laws: some ordered primarily and immediately for the benefit of each individual, others for the **common good**. And the private good—even if shared by many or by everyone individually—is very distinct from the common good. For example <note>original: *V.g.*, abbreviation for *verbi gratia*</note>, it is a private good for a neighbor to have a good wife, obedient children, and sufficient property. The public good is the peace and tranquility of all. It is that everyone may peacefully possess their estate, and that justice is administered so equally that everyone feels secure from harm and injury in their homes. # Regarding the Ordinance on Wheat.

...and to the whole community harm. Just as if the laity were wealthy and well-married, but poorly governed. For this reason, as human well-being and happiness—according to **Aristotle**—is sought and attained primarily through the observance of laws, and laws aspire to this (namely) that men live a happy life. This human good is twofold: one is individual, the other universal. Thus, some laws are ordered immediately toward the individual benefit of each person, such as the law of **fasting** and annual **confession**. In these, the primary intent is for each person to perform penance and be reconciled with God, from whom they hope for eternal life. Others are ordered toward **public utility**. They are established to such an extent that sometimes they must result in harm to some individuals, such as **penal laws** that punish crimes, or public price controls on **provisions** <note>original: *bastimentos*; refers to food supplies and basic necessities</note> or merchandise.

Having established this distinction in order to know when it would be appropriate to do the opposite of what the law requires without error (certainly a difficult undertaking), given the great authority of the law and the obedience owed to a legitimate prince, I set forth two true and universal rules, which the **Scholastics** <note>Medieval theologians and philosophers who used logic to reconcile faith and reason</note> call "Conclusions." The first: when observing the law (even if no specific good follows from it, at least no harm follows), it is binding within its own category, and it is not lawful to violate it. For example <note>original: *V. g.*, abbreviation for the Latin *Verbi gratia*</note>, in laws of the first type—made for the benefit of individuals, such as fasting—if no bodily harm follows from it, even if one does not lose weight (which is the legislator's intent), but rather grows fat from skipping supper or finds such abstinence healthy for the body, one is still obliged to fast. And in those ordered toward the common good, as in the example from **Saint Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas, a highly influential philosopher whose work shaped the legal and moral theories discussed here</note>: if not opening the gates causes no harm to the neighbors, one is obliged not to open them—since it was commanded that they remain closed—even if it seems that doing so no longer matters much.

<summary>The author distinguishes between laws meant for personal spiritual benefit and those meant for public order, arguing that laws remain binding even when their specific purpose seems irrelevant, provided no harm is caused by obeying.</summary>

## Regarding the Pragmatic Ordinance on Wheat

Reason is effective, and the obligation is manifest. For if obedience is owed to a superior and observance to his precepts, what could be more consistent with equity than to keep the law when no inconvenience follows from doing so, even if no immediate benefit follows from it? Sufficient good is achieved and performed simply because one obeys.

Thus, this is almost a natural instinct, and there is no one to whom it does not seem wrong to go against the tenor of the law when no great evil follows from keeping it. When keeping it is very prejudicial <note>harmful or damaging to one's interests</note>, this alone compels a man to consult whether it binds him. For when people see no grave damage in obeying it, they all hold themselves bound to its obedience. So, to know if a law is binding, one must not look at whether its observance is profitable in its kind, but rather if it is harmful. And as long as no such harm follows (of the kind we shall explain), the conscience is required to obey, even if the specific goal intended by the law is not achieved by fulfilling it.

I said "each in its kind." As in those laws ordered toward the comfort of individuals, one must weigh with prudence and without passion whether fulfilling it notably harms them. If it should cause harm then, and in no other way, it would excuse the person, and they could make use of <term>epikeia</term> <note>original: *epichia*; a legal principle allowing for the "spirit" of the law to be followed instead of the "letter" when the literal application would be unjust or harmful</note>. In those laws directed immediately toward the common good, if by keeping the law the opposite occurs—a common evil contrary to the intended good—it does not bind. An example is given by the **Angelic Doctor** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a hugely influential theologian</note>, speaking on this matter regarding **Aristotle**. In a city besieged by enemies, where there were many pilgrims, it was commanded under pain of death that no pilgrims should go up onto the walls, because they were not trusted, the leaders most prudently fearing some act of treason. The enemies suddenly launched an assault with ladders. And those who found themselves inside and closest to the walls were the pilgrims.

<summary>The author explains that laws are naturally binding unless their observance causes significant harm, introducing the concept of "epikeia" to interpret the spirit of the law over its literal word. He uses the example of a besieged city to show how the common good can supersede specific legal prohibitions.</summary>

## Regarding the Pragmatic Ordinance on Wheat

...pilgrims. Who, in the absence of those above, defended the city faithfully and courageously, throwing down those who were already climbing and their ladders. <note>This likely refers to a historical or hypothetical example where foreigners defended a city in an emergency, perhaps violating a law that forbid them from bearing arms or being on the walls, yet their actions saved the community.</note> It was an act of prudence and equity then to act against the literal wording of the law, though not against its intent, which was to safeguard the city. Thus, as <term>Cajetan</term> <note>original: *Gayetano*; Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), an influential Dominican theologian known for his commentaries on Thomas Aquinas</note> says, <term>epikeia</term> <note>original: *epichia*; the legal principle of interpreting a law according to its spirit and the "common good" rather than its strict literal text in exceptional circumstances</note> takes place when following the literal text results in the opposite of what was intended when establishing it. One must be mindful that laws made for the good of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: *republica*; the state or the public interest</note> must be observed, even if they harm certain individuals. For in these laws, the concern is not so much for what is good for those individuals as for what is good for the community. Nevertheless, it can also happen—though very rarely or almost never—that there is little or no common harm, yet the harm to the individual is so extremely grave that reason and prudence must and can arbitrate the matter.

For this reason, it is most illicit to exceed the <term>price ceilings</term> <note>original: *tassas*; government-fixed maximum prices</note> of clothing or provisions, whether because they cost the seller more or because he earns little by observing them. Nor would the legislator, if he were present and knew that this person was losing money by keeping the price ceiling, grant him a dispensation without himself being in error. Rather, he would tell him (and with much reason) that if he lost money now, he would gain it at another time or in another sale he might make. Because laws ordained for public utility must be kept, provided that their observance is not pernicious to the community itself. And even then, once the law has been received, it is highly proper to consult the legislator, entreating him to lift and annul it, if he is nearby and the case allows for such a consultation.

As <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> says: human law is not to be kept when it is harmful in its kind (as we have declared), but one must turn to the prince for a remedy, if the new circumstance permits delay. # Regarding the pragmatic ordinance on wheat.

...against natural law to observe such **positive laws** <note>Laws created by human authorities, as opposed to natural or divine law.</note>. Therefore, in such cases, one should not keep to the letter of the law, but rather use <term>epikeia</term> <note>original: *epichia*; the principle that a law should not be applied strictly when doing so would violate its intended spirit or the common good</note>, following not so much the literal wording as the intention of the legislator.

From this follows the true understanding and explanation of the first rule: that when the fundamental reason for a law ceases, the law itself ceases. This is understood to apply not when the reason fails for a single individual, but for everyone universally—in such a way that it is harmful for all to observe it, as seen in the examples we have mentioned. It is then that this excellent virtue of which we have spoken is exercised, with the moderation and submission already explained—that is, by asking for permission from the prince who established it, if the necessity allows for the time. But if time does not permit, because the situation requires a most immediate remedy, and the harm is obvious and certain, it is lawful to use <term>epikeia</term>.

Indeed, the resulting harm could be such that it would not only be lawful, but an obligation, to go against the legal text. However, if the harm is not certain but doubtful, one should either request a dispensation or follow the letter of the law until the matter is further investigated. From this, it will be clearly seen how many conditions are required to prudently and lawfully break a law on one’s own authority. And how much those err who, in the most trivial matters and for non-urgent causes, at every step claim <term>epikeia</term> when it is not truly <term>epikeia</term>, but rather actual dissoluteness and inner passion, which blinds the understanding and makes the heart rebellious. Both of these rules, and especially the second, are understood on their own merit, provided there is no scandal; for if there is scandal, many lawful things should rightly be left undone so as not to cause it.

## § Summary of Chapter Eight. §

1 *How Captains or Governors should behave in putting into execution the mandates of their princes, according to the judgment of the ancient philosophers.*
2 ¶ *If what is commanded is clearly harmful to the commonwealth* <note>original: *republica*; referring to the state or the public good</note> *or the army, it must not be executed; if it is not harmful, even if it is not beneficial, it must be observed.*

---

Up to this point we have treated, according to our profession, what can and should be done in conscience. But what shall we say of those who are not only accountable to God, but also have regard, according to their status, for the world: the lieutenants of certain princes, whether in war or in peace? These princes desire their instructions to be followed so strictly that, if they are not obeyed, they immediately become suspicious, grow exasperated, and consider themselves poorly served. And even if the Viceroy <note>The highest-ranking colonial or regional official representing the King</note> shows most clearly through his letters that great inconveniences follow in the province where they preside if such decrees are put into effect, the princes do not admit them and respond as Pilate did: *What I have written, I have written* <note>original: "Quod scripsi, scripsi" (John 19:22)</note>. How will this minister use legal prudence and zeal—he who puts himself at risk of losing his status and livelihood—if, knowing the temperament of his superior, he were to look after the good of the land by suspending many decrees harmful to the people? There are other princes who, as Ovid <note>The Roman poet Publius Ovidius Naso</note> says, look at the outcome; and if what their Governor or Captain did succeeds well, even if it was contrary to their precepts, they consider him prudent, although in reality he may have been reckless or erratic. And just as disobeying an Assistant or a Magistrate <term>Corregidor; a local administrative and judicial official representing the Crown</term> is to offend the King—whose person they represent and whose office they exercise—so too does His Divine Majesty hold and judge as His own offense any disobedience toward those who represent Him in their rank and order. He punishes such acts as severely as if one of His own divine precepts were broken.

...well, when [authority] commands something merely secular and profane, if it is necessary for the government of the people, it binds in conscience. For instance, if it were to forbid the carrying of arms to a foreign kingdom, or that residents should not abandon some fortress, town, or castle, or that a certain type of clothing be sold at a specific price, along with two thousand other matters of this kind. Before these were commanded, they were indifferent <note>original: *indiferentes*; meaning actions that are morally neutral until a law defines them</note>, and one could do the opposite; but once the law is promulgated, where they are commanded or forbidden, it is necessary in conscience to observe them. 

And the reason is evident. If the prince is to be obeyed because he holds authority to govern and protect the commonwealth <note>original: *republica*; referring to the state or public welfare rather than a specific form of government</note>, and it is often necessary for this end to establish certain political and human rules that neither God nor nature commanded, the vassals will be obliged to obey him even in these and to live according to what he shows them. 

And sometimes these matters are so necessary for the tranquil and quiet state of the Kingdom that he not only has the authority to command them, but also the obligation, and he would sin by not commanding them, as the common necessity requires. Therefore, how consistent with reason it is that the vassal be obliged to obey what the prince, in conscience, could not fail to command. 

We have a clear example in this regulated price of wheat <term>tasa del trigo|a government-imposed price ceiling intended to prevent inflation and ensure the poor could afford bread</term> that we are discussing: before it was established, it was no offense to God to sell at twelve reales; yet the King would not have failed to err if, being able to provide for the universal good of his kingdoms through the pragmatic ordinance <term>pragmatica|a royal decree with the force of law</term>, he had overlooked and permitted [unregulated prices]. 

In such a way that what is commanded in this law was not a divine or natural precept, but after being commanded, it is necessary to observe it by the force and virtue placed in it by the <unclear>jurisdiction</unclear> of the King who established it. And so that everyone may see how completely this author contradicts himself in this writing of his: he says on one hand that to notably exceed the regulated price is a mortal sin; on the other, that to violate a positive law <term>positive law|laws enacted by human legislators for specific societies</term> where no divine or natural precept is broken...

## Regarding the pragmatic ordinance on wheat

...God is not offended. The truth being that the pragmatic ordinance <term>pragmatica: a royal decree issued by the monarch to address specific administrative or economic matters</term> regarding wheat is one of these laws. That is to say, among those that do not contain within themselves, nor command, things that are divine or belonging to natural law. If [the author being criticized] had spoken the truth in this second point, he would have erred in the first; but it is the opposite: he was correct in the first, and in this last point he errs most gravely. For one must not look at whether what the commonwealth <note>original: *republica*; the state or public body</note> commands is from divine or natural law, but rather if he who commands is a legitimate prince and has the jurisdiction to command, and if he commands what is very suitable for the political state of the people. And it is a wonder if these lords <note>referring to sovereign rulers</note> intervene, except in such matters—that is, in those which were previously indifferent <note>original: *indiferentes*; actions that are morally neutral until a law is made</note> in themselves, and which time and opportunity make necessary.

If it suits the tranquility of the city to prohibit some kind of weapon, why would the residents not be obligated to keep what is commanded for their quiet and preservation? On the contrary, it is so far from what this author dreamed that Aristotle, in the fifth book of the *Ethics*, and Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a hugely influential philosopher and theologian</note>, commenting there, and all others who explain him, say: That it properly belongs to the civil power to establish that which is not established by God or by nature. Because for this purpose [God] left this power to men: namely, so that they may newly ordain what is appropriate according to the time, which the natural law could not provide from the beginning, because the events and concurrent cases are temporal, and the laws that were to be perpetual could not deal with them. 

But an excellent and sufficient means was provided, namely: that there should be authority in the commonwealth to establish the laws that the time, events, or the condition of the people might demand. From this it follows that, just as he who transgresses what God commanded offends Him, so too does he offend Him proportionally who does the opposite of what the prince newly provides in particular. Furthermore, what is of natural law...

...natural law, it is universal to all, such as seeking the preservation and perpetuity of one's being, and loving and obeying one's parents—things that benefit everyone and seem right to everyone. Beyond these, there are many other things suitable for one nation or one kingdom, yet very harmful and intolerable to another, either because the constellation of the heavens, the quality of the earth, the site of the city, or the dealings of the people are different. These specific matters are properly what **Positive Laws** <term>positive law: man-made laws established by a government for a specific society, as opposed to natural laws believed to be inherent to all humans</term> command and order, or forbid and prohibit.

So that, to speak clearly, **positive law** commands that which is not already covered by natural law; such things are left to secular power. For the particular, external, and temporal government of a kingdom, while a rule may be very fitting for the present time, it was not necessary for natural and divine law to ordain it for all time. From this follows a remarkable distinction that **Aristotle** and **Saint Thomas** make between what belongs to civil law and what belongs to natural law. That which is of natural law is good or bad in its very nature; but that which is of positive law—which they call **political justice** <note>original: *justo politico*; the standard of justice created by a state's specific legislation</note>—is not good or bad except because it is commanded or forbidden.

<margin>Legal justice is indifferent <note>original: *indiferens*; morally neutral</note> before it is established by law. See *Ethics*, book 5, chapter 7. See Saint Thomas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 60, article 5: Here positive law has a place where, as far as natural law is concerned, it makes no difference whether it is done one way or another.</margin>

In such a way that before it was commanded, one could very well refrain from doing it; or before it was forbidden, it could be lawfully carried out. For example, it is prohibited to carry weapons after the curfew bell <note>original: *en dando la queda*; the ringing of the bell to signal the end of the day when people should be off the streets</note>; before this was promulgated, one could easily carry them at any hour of the night. Thus, if any obedience is owed to the princes and governors of the commonwealth (and a great deal is owed to them, as we have proven), it is owed to them properly and particularly in those things that are not already settled by divine or natural law.

Because such matters are precisely those which God and nature committed to the jurisdiction and authority of the prince. From this it is most clearly gathered how false and rash it was to say that there was no obligation in conscience to obey civil laws, unless they resulted in a violation [of natural law]...

It is now a celebrated fact, in everyone’s mouth, that among laws some are preceptive <term>preceptive law: a law that mandates a specific moral or religious duty, binding the individual's conscience to obey regardless of punishment</term> and others are penal <term>penal law: a law focused on the punishment or fine for an act, rather than the moral command itself</term>. This doctrine is not only false, but quite harmful. This is because most preceptive laws that are important to good government assign the most severe penalties to those who break them. # On the Wheat Ordinance

...ordained with the counsel of prudent men. And Aristotle defines it thus: that law is a common consensus of the city which, in writing, commands how each thing is to be done. In this way, all laws are truly preceptive <term>preceptive: from "precept," meaning a law that directly commands or forbids an action</term> and authoritative. However, sometimes they command judges to punish certain crimes, and at other times they command all subjects what they must do or avoid. Thus, they are rightly called "preceptive" when they command or forbid some action of ours, and "penal" <term>penal: laws that focus primarily on the punishment for a crime rather than the moral instruction</term> when they only command judges to punish certain crimes, specifying the penalty they must carry out. In such a way, for a law to be penal, it is necessary that it neither commands nor forbids any action to the private subjects, but only to the judges, showing them how they must punish wrongdoers. Laws take these titles of "preceptive" or "penal" based on what is primary within them.

And regarding two things that are commonly found in them—which are commanding and punishing—the primary thing is to show the subjects some good work, or that they should abstain from an evil one. The first thing that a prince in any community ought to intend is to show the people what they must follow and what they must flee. Saint Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas, the influential medieval theologian.</note> says in Question 12, and Saint Isidore in his *Etymologies*, and Aristotle in the *Politics*, that the supreme end of a king is to make his subjects virtuous. To this end, he must direct all the laws he establishes. 

<margin>It is the task of the legislator to make good citizens. It is the task of a good prince to render his citizens good. <note>original Latin: *Legislatoris est facere bonos ciues. Boni principis bonos redere ciues.*</note></margin>

And virtue generally consists in fleeing from evil and putting good into practice. For this reason, the primary purpose of laws, whether eternal or temporal, is to forbid the bad and command the good. The rest—which is the reward designated for the good and the punishment for the bad—are taken as means by which people are encouraged toward the former: either through the hope and desire for a reward they set their hands to virtue, or through the fear of punishment they turn away from vice. # On the Wheat Ordinance

...penal laws, containing nothing within themselves but pure punishment for offenders. It is true that among these, although they are penal, some are virtually preceptive. For through the severity of the penalty, the legislator makes it understood that he intends for no one to do that which is punished with such rigor.

As if it were proclaimed in an army: "His Majesty commands that any soldier who, during these eight days, goes over to the enemy's field shall die." This appears to be a merely penal law, yet it is actually preceptive, for it commands that no soldier go across. It would be better proclaimed in these words: "His Majesty commands that no soldier go to the enemy's field during these eight days, under penalty of death." In this, there is already the form and appearance of a precept. But at times this is not scrutinized, and it is enough for the prince to patently explain his will.

Someone might say now: "In this way, all laws are formally or virtually preceptive." There would be no harm in granting that. However, I respond that among these formally penal laws, some punish crimes that are in themselves against natural or divine law, such as those concerning murderers, sodomites <note>original: "someticos," an archaic variant of "sodomitas"</note>, thieves, and traitors. Others penalize acts that are otherwise licit <term>licit: legally or morally permitted</term> in themselves.

As when a General commands that any soldier who leaves the defenses <note>original: "estacada," referring to the stockade or palisade marking the boundary of a military camp</note> be punished. An act that, before the proclamation, was permitted enough, but being forbidden by law, it is now illicit. Such laws can only be called penal in form and preceptive in essence, since through them the King virtually prohibits some evil that was not prohibited before. The others, which punish sins that are already against other better and greater laws, do not need to forbid what is already forbidden by nature. It is enough that they serve to punish the crimes.

In the former case, the penalty shows that what they punish is a "wrongdoing," for without the penalty, it was neither a "wrongdoing" nor was it held as such. For a soldier to leave the camp is licit as long as it is not forbidden to him. And to proclaim that he will be punished for it is to let him know that [it is forbidden]...

# BOOK FOUR
## On Exchanges <note>In this period, "cambios" (exchanges) referred to the business of money-changing and the use of bills of exchange, which were the primary methods for international banking and credit.</note>
### PROLOGUE.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' at the start of the prologue, featuring ornate floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

To treat this matter of **exchanges** appropriately, it is necessary, in my judgment, to provide as much clarity and resolution in the business as the subject itself is obscure and confused. So numerous are the notices and the ingenious and subtle tricks of these **dealers** <term>dealers: "tratantes" in the original, referring to merchants and bankers who specialized in high-level financial transactions</term>, and so tangled are their webs and plots, that understanding them without practice requires greater capacity than actually practicing them—let alone explaining them and putting them into distinct and clear terms. In my opinion, this art is today at a higher level of refinement and precision than ever before. So much so that, while in other businesses continuous practice alone suffices to become skilled, in this particular case, the aid of **nature** <note>original: "naturaleza," here meaning innate talent or intellectual sharp-wittedness</note> is necessary. And let the exchanger be neither slow nor dull-witted, lest more profits slip past him than fish escape a fisherman's net when he pulls it in with laziness and slackness.

This practice is very widespread (as we shall see in the third and fourth chapters). It embraces from the **East** to the **West** and reaches both poles; and it cannot but be a great labor to narrow down and gather—as we intend in this short work—something so vast. For certainly, although we must strive with all our might to be brief, the subject itself demands that we be expansive. Because besides the **trade** having much to deal with and investigate, it is a business frequented by many who earn their living in it like gentlemen, or at least without outward stigma. It is not like **usury** <note>The practice of lending money at interest, which was often condemned by the Church as a sin. To everyone, "exchanging" sounds like a business...

...ennobles a person without any impairment or dishonor. Thus it is necessary to write of it fully, as a trade that affects so many, and where so much is at stake in getting it right or wrong. The third, because they are commonly so clever and sharp-witted that they understand everything we say in ciphers and abbreviations without difficulty when they wish to. And to be compendious and brief (as the subject matter permits), I have decided to use this device and plan: namely, to write extensively about everything regarding this trade currently practiced in these kingdoms, and to trim away either what other nations use or what was used among us and has since been abandoned. ...as we explained at length in the small work on merchants, in the second chapter. At that time, there were no purchases or sales, nor had money been invented, nor was there a mint. Whoever wanted my horse gave me some of his sheep; whoever wanted my wheat gave his wine or oil. Everything was **barter**. After gold and silver existed, the human race began to buy and sell and practice all the other businesses that have been introduced and multiplied. Though, in truth, as all were derived from exchange and barter, all are in some way barters. For buying some houses for three thousand ducats—even granting it be a perfect sale—does not stop being a kind of barter, where the houses are bartered for the money. But in the end, everyone distinguishes, and rightly so, between these two contracts: **barter** and **sale**. 

They call "bartering" the giving of one piece of clothing for another without money intervening in the price. This was a method of negotiating so insufficient that they found it necessary to seek another more adequate one, for which reason they gave value and esteem to gold and silver and made them the price of all salable things. And money having been invented in the beginning for this sole effect—to serve as the value for everything else—men, with their ancient greed as time passed, came to revoke and revive the ancient way of negotiating, even with money, which was bartering. They barter one for another, and without there being clothing or any item to buy, they negotiate and profit with money alone, bartering it and taking interest in doing so. 

All nations today call this **exchange** <note>original: "cambio"; refers to the professional business of currency exchange and banking</note>, though the word itself is Latin. # On the antiquity and origin of exchanges.

...is **barter**, not because it is not so, but because, although it is, it is used with so little sincerity and such a mixture of **usury**: that in the very contract of exchange, the least part of it is exchange, and the principal and total part is an interest-bearing loan and usury. # On the antiquity and origin of exchanges.

...from some neighbor. This necessity invented the **real exchange** <note>original: "cambio real." The author refers to "true" or "actual" exchange, distinguished from usurious or fraudulent financial contracts.</note>, which is to trade two currencies of the same or different value, solely because they are located in different places. Beyond the specific and accidental causes of this necessity—such as a person not having brought their funds with them, or having already spent them—other general and common factors concur in many places.

The primary factor is the inability to move currency from one province to another, either because the metal is different, the price is unequal, or, if everything is uniform, because the passage of currency is prohibited under penalties that people do not wish to risk facing. First, metals do not hold the same value in all kingdoms and provinces; instead, they differ according to whether the gold is of a higher grade and the silver finer, or whether it is more expedient for the land and its prosperity.

Some gold is of a low carat, and some is of many. That of <term>Tepusque</term> <note>A low-grade alloy of gold and copper used as a common currency in early colonial Mexico.</note> is of the lowest grade. That of the **mines** <note>referring to "oro de minas," or high-purity gold</note> is excellent. Thus, a <term>peso de Tepusque</term> is worth eight <term>reales</term>, and one from the mines is worth thirteen. Between these (as is evident), there can be trade and exchange, given their unequal value.

It also happens that a province or land is abundant in one metal and poor in another; consequently, the currency that circulates in one part does not circulate or is not accepted in another. Merchants from both sides are thus forced not to remove the currency from either territory, but rather to give it to a person who has credit abroad, so that they may make use of it where it is needed.

Even the same metal, in the same quantity and the same shape, is worth more in one kingdom than in another. This difference and inequality is beneficial and prudent, as it prevents the money from being taken abroad—which is a most powerful and useful "inability"—ensuring that the kingdom always keeps it and remains wealthy. For one of the primary requirements for the prosperity and happiness of a kingdom is to continually possess within itself a great quantity of money and an abundance of gold and silver, which are, in substance, all...

Therefore, someone who does not want to lose money (if it is worth more elsewhere), or risk it being seized on the road, or losing it if the ship sinks or runs aground, or having it discovered by the law, is forced—having need of it outside the city or the kingdom—to give it in exchange to someone who will return it to him where he desires. # On the antiquity and origin of exchanges.

[...offers] very attractive opportunities that topple a man—who by nature, even without occasion, is already inflamed and fallen in matters of self-interest. And the fact that everyone says money-changers are usurers is an evident argument that they are. For the voice and common judgment of the people, they say, is the voice and judgment of God <note>This refers to the proverb *Vox populi, vox Dei*.</note>, which cannot be false. And their being usurers perfectly proves the great danger and opportunity of the craft to become so, as almost no one escapes it. Both things—namely, the danger and the weakness, the excessive greed of men, and the notorious reputation for falling into these vices—are more than sufficient cause to declare and condemn it as illicit. 

Being a usurer is evil in itself and is condemned because it cannot be done well; but being a money-changer is forbidden not because the craft is not good, but because it is never practiced well. From this it follows that to give [money] once or twice at exchange, due to circumstances that arose, is not a matter of <term>scruple<gloss>an issue of conscience</gloss></term>; but the grave issue is to treat it as a <term>livelihood<gloss>granjería</gloss></term>. 

They say this trade is necessary to the <term>commonwealth<gloss>república</gloss></term>, and this is indeed true. It is certainly a benefit and convenience to have money-changers. However, public women <note>A common early modern euphemism for prostitutes.</note> are also necessary in a city; for if they were absent, grave evils and scandals would follow (as Saint Augustine says) <note>Referring to Augustine's *De Ordine*, where he argues that removing prostitutes would disturb the social order with greater lusts, comparing them to a necessary sewer in a palace.</note>. Yet, serving the commonwealth does not excuse them from sin. This reason—that the craft is necessary—proves that princes ought to permit it, as they do; but it does not exempt the practitioners from guilt and usury if they commit them. 

Secondly, I say it is the craft itself that serves the commonwealth, not the deceptions, lies, and thefts that are mixed into the craft. These instead harm, rob, and devour the property of the citizens themselves. 

If anyone desires my own opinion outside of this very secure and plain definition and judgment: first, I hold for certain that neither I nor anyone else can give a better opinion, nor any other different one, that would not be very dangerous to the person who takes and follows it. The first type of exchange or trade of money is what the <term>Latin speakers<gloss>scholars writing in Latin</gloss></term> call "menudo" [small change]; we can call it **manual**. This involves swapping one coin for another of a different material or a different value: <term>crowns<gloss>coronas, gold coins</gloss></term> for <term>reals<gloss>reales, silver coins</gloss></term>, <term>tostones<gloss>silver coins worth four reals</gloss></term> for small change, or <term>doubloons<gloss>doblones, heavy gold coins</gloss></term> for <term>ducats<gloss>ducados, gold coins often used for accounting</gloss></term>. I say that as long as it is a moderate amount, according to what the <term>royal decrees<gloss>pragmáticas reales</gloss></term> set—especially if there is not a great abundance of that specific currency currently in the city—there is no reason for a guilty conscience. This is especially true when it is held as a profession, as there are some people who deal in this and go to the effort and expense of collecting coins of various values and metals. It is only just that they earn something, if only as a salary and stipend for their labor and service. Even if one does not hold this as a profession, but is asked in the moment to exchange a ducat, earning something from it is neither a great sin nor a small one, if, as I say, the interest is low.

# ...or the sale of crowns.

The value of currency is a highly scrupulous business <note>In this context, "scrupulous" refers to a matter of conscience or moral anxiety regarding sin.</note>. They exchange the <term>crown<gloss>corona, a gold coin</gloss></term> for twelve <term>reals<gloss>reales, silver coins</gloss></term>, even though its legal value is only ten and ten <note>likely meaning ten reals and ten maravedís</note>. These are partly artificial and invented, and partly natural. Naturally, it possesses great virtue and strength; princes and great lords eat it dissolved and added to a pottage in their old age, as a substance of great essence and activity. It also gladdens the heart through a "hidden property," along with other singular effects known to the physicians whose specific study this is. It also has artificial uses, such as serving for ostentation, equipment, display, and celebration—especially when a large quantity is gathered. Silver also has some particular operations, both of one kind and the other, natural and artificial. Secondly, it should be noted that when these metals are made into money, and are valued and minted, the primary intent is for them to be the price and value of everything else; however, this valuation does not fail to take into account their natural being and properties. Certainly, in giving thirty ducats for a <term>mark of gold<gloss>marco, a unit of weight equal to about 230 grams</gloss></term>, and eleven reals for a ducat, one pays for everything the metal can serve for and provide, especially that which it causes according to its nature.

## On Manual Exchange

Although more account is taken of money's primary office and service—which is to serve as a fixed price—it can well be said that its effects are not so entirely valued and paid for that, in certain particular cases, one might not charge something more than the law allows. However, it is very important to know what such a case would be, and when it is licit to exceed the legal price. I say that a <term>doubloon<gloss>doblón, a high-value gold coin</gloss></term>, or any other type of money, can be considered simply as a doubloon already minted; as such, it is worth only twenty-two <term>reals<gloss>reales, the standard silver currency</gloss></term>, just as a <term>ducat<gloss>ducado</gloss></term> is worth eleven reals, and a <term>crown<gloss>corona</gloss></term> is worth ten and ten <note>This likely refers to 10 reals and 10 maravedís.</note>. This consideration is the primary one when coins are used as money with which one may sell and negotiate. 

But money can also be considered as a metal that possesses certain singular properties. (I say singular, because common properties are certainly already accounted for in the initial valuation.) Because of these particular properties, one may at times charge something more. A gold doubloon may be so shiny and clean that it glows like a pearl or a precious stone, and consequently possesses a particular virtue and power to gladden the sight and the heart of the sick, just as is said of coral. Likewise, if it is a "piece of ten" or a "piece of twenty" <note>Referring to large denomination gold coins worth 10 or 20 doubloons.</note>, it is suited by its size and beauty for a royal display <note>A ceremonial collection or "apparatus" of coins used to show wealth or status.</note>, especially when there are many of them.

<margin>
Cajetan, *On Exchanges*, chapter 6. Medina, *On Restitution*, folio 148. <note>original: "Caie. de cābys. c.6. Methina de re ffo.148." These refer to the influential theologians Thomas Cajetan and Juan de Medina.</note>
</margin>

Supposing this right, I say, coming to the facts, that for a doubloon one may safely charge twenty-three reals today—one real more than the law prescribes. This is because they are not commonly sought as currency for negotiating and trading, but rather for these particular effects they can produce. Furthermore, the fact that they are no longer being minted makes them highly prized and held as something very rare. However, with crowns and any other lower currency, it is highly illicit to exchange or sell them for more than their legal rate. This is because they are never sought except as money to be spent and used; nor, in the contracts and business of merchants, is any account taken of the natural or artificial effects of the metal, nor is it just that there should be. Thus, in conclusion, I say that generally among merchants, it is never licit to charge more for money than the law allows. This is because they always treat, give, and receive it as money. Neither crowns nor reals are worth more than their fixed rate between any persons, nor does anyone seek them except as money to be spent; there is no shortage of their gold, nor is the minted coin so beautiful or rare that it should be given a higher value. Therefore, decisively, every good law and all <term>doctors<gloss>learned scholars of law and theology</gloss></term> condemn such an exchange. I also dealt with this at length in my previous <term>opuscule<gloss>a small scholarly work or treatise</gloss></term>, where we proved the same point through various arguments, especially concerning the exchange of "singles" <note>small denomination silver coins</note> used in <term>New Spain<gloss>colonial Mexico</gloss></term> for the purchase of <term>cochineal<gloss>a highly valuable red dye produced from crushed insects</gloss></term>, which I will not repeat here to avoid being tedious.

# On Manual Exchange.

<margin>Soto, *On Justice and Law*, Book 7, Question 5, Article 3, regarding the contract of sale and things through exchange; and Book 3, on the title "on the words of the law" <note>original: "de præscrip. verb. ff." referring to the Digest of Roman Law</note></margin>...a <term>ducat<gloss>a gold coin used throughout Europe</gloss></term> among us is worth eleven reals, while in Rome it is worth thirteen.
A <term>real<gloss>a standard silver coin</gloss></term> is worth thirty-four <note>meaning 34 maravedís, the smallest unit of account</note> here; in Gran Canaria, it is worth thirty-eight. The question now is whether it would be licit to exchange one hundred reals in Seville for one hundred in Gran Canaria, where they would already amount to a difference of four hundred maravedís. The ducat in New Spain <note>colonial Mexico</note> is worth six reals, and in Old Spain, eleven. Is it a fair barter to trade one hundred from here for one hundred from there, or vice versa? And what we illustrate with these regions can be applied to all others where coins have different estimation and value.

This question, and others of this sort that we will go on summarizing, are those that were discussed in times past. For when there was not so much ingenuity among merchants, nor such vast capital, one of the principal contracts was this: exchanging. That is, bartering the ducats and reals of this place for those of other kingdoms where they might be worth more or less. And the theologians who wrote then treated very at length <note>original: "ad longum"</note> of its injustice. 

The resolution of this is, first, that it is not licit to barter coins of different prices and names without there being a compensation in the quantity of one of them. For example, bartering <term>Tepusque pesos<gloss>pesos de Tepusque, silver coins alloyed with copper used in Mexico</gloss></term> in Mexico for ducats in Seville (which is a coin of a different kind), nor ducats from here for <term>mining pesos<gloss>pesos de minas, high-purity silver coins</gloss></term> from there, unless the barter is adjusted by giving more—either more pesos for ducats, or more ducats for pesos. And the injustice is clear if this were not done. Because the excess on one side being so great, the barter would be very unequal, and consequently unjust. 

Likewise, coins of the same kind and name, if they have different values, cannot be exchanged [one-for-one], such as the ducats of Seville for those of Rome. For in an exchange of two thousand ducats, the difference would amount to four thousand reals. We are speaking precisely regarding <term>manual exchange<gloss>cambio manual, the physical, hand-to-hand swapping of one currency for another</gloss></term>, for other circumstances may occur that permit it to be done, and even require and justify it, as in fact it is done. Let us offer a clearer example: it would not be lawful to exchange one thousand <term>ducats<gloss>a high-value gold coin</gloss></term> from <term>New Spain<gloss>colonial Mexico</gloss></term> for one thousand of those from here, nor vice versa. For even if they are all called ducats, they have different prices, whether this diversity arises because the metal of one is of lower or inferior quality, and the other is high, clean, and pure; or because, though the metal is the same, it is valued more in one place than in another; or for any other causes that may occur. In short, as the values differ, it is necessary to equalize them by adding more to one side so that the <term>barter<gloss>direct exchange of goods or currency</gloss></term> reaches a just balance. However, I do not wish to dwell any longer on transactions that are no longer conducted, or are very rare, as that would only serve to obscure the matter.

Secondly, it should be noted that this negotiation of "royal exchanges" <note>original: *cambios reales*—a term referring to large-scale financial transfers, often involving bills of exchange</note> was, at its start, very straightforward and beneficial. It arose because someone might have a need for money at the fair in Medina for merchandise, or in Flanders to acquire haberdashery or books cheaply; not wishing or not being able to carry the physical coins there, they would deliver them here to someone who would return the sum to them there safely, giving that person a certain amount for their labor. I am of the mind that, in the beginning, the exchangers took charge of great sums and actually transported them. Later, becoming so interested in the profit, they sought to establish credit so that, without the cost of transport, they could find the money to pay back what they had received in Seville or elsewhere. 

This was a simple and licit way of contracting. Although when it was done then—and even now, if it were done this way—it was not properly an "exchange," but rather a gentlemanly transport and passage, and the exchanger was a sort of noble-like <term>muleteer<gloss>someone who transports goods by pack animal</gloss></term>. It was a way to carry a great sum of money without the labor, which, because of the great ease with which it was done (namely, through <term>letters of exchange<gloss>early versions of checks or bank transfers</gloss></term> and certificates), I imagine came to be called a "royal exchange."
