# On manual exchange.

...urn them. Their letters of credit carry so much trust and security. And a merchant’s <term>bill of exchange<gloss>cedula de cambio</gloss></term> is of greater certainty and force—and always has been—than twenty public legal deeds. In whatever way it may have been, it is lawful to profit from transporting the currency, or for providing it where it is requested, whether within the kingdom or abroad, and whether one actually incurs costs in transporting it or does so without costs through one's credit and a command that it be returned. The only thing considered is the obligation one takes to deliver the funds in that specific place. The less it costs the provider to do so through letters of credit, the better and more secure it is for the one who gave him the money. And this applies not only to those who do this as a profession, but to everyone, of whatever status or condition they may be. A merchant may well take two thousand <term>ducats<gloss>a high-value gold coin</gloss></term> here and deliver them in <term>Medina<gloss>Medina del Campo, a major financial center and site of trade fairs in Spain</term>, and take some profit for it.

From this, many infer that there is no certain rule in this transaction to discern and designate who should profit and who is responsible for the <term>transport fee<gloss>portazgo</gloss></term>; rather, it is a matter of luck as to who is asked for the exchange, and that person gains. If this is so, our proverb was never truer: "it is better to be the one God helps," for the one who wakes early is the loser. <note>The author is playfully inverting the common proverb "God helps those who wake early" to suggest that in the exchange market, being the proactive seeker can sometimes lead to a worse deal than being the one approached by chance.</note> For example: if two men were to go to the <term>steps<gloss>gradas—the exterior steps of the Seville Cathedral, which served as the city's informal financial exchange</gloss></term>, and the one who had money here needed it in Medina, while the other had it there and needed it here (or will have it by the set deadline), either of them may profit from the other, and whoever profits will be understood as the carrier for the other. 

If the person who has funds in Medina requested money via exchange from the one who had it in Seville—where he expected to lose—he will instead gain interest, and it will be understood as having brought the funds from Medina to here. Many hold this case and doctrine to be true, and it may be so; however, I would not approve of this last merchant encounter we imagined if it were practiced today. Because if I truly give the money immediately, I cannot claim any transport fee on my part, as I brought it neither by letters of credit nor by <term>beasts of burden<gloss>azemilas</gloss></term>. Among merchants, and those who earn their living trading, there are currently three types of people and three types of wealthy businesses, all dependent on one another, such that the second is born from the first and is founded upon it, and the third proceeds from both. The first is of merchants who deal in clothing <note>The "cloth trade" was a primary driver of the early modern economy.</note> of all kinds; the second, money-changers, who negotiate with only currency; the last, bankers, who are like depositaries for the other two, keeping their money, gold, and silver, providing accounts of it, and against whom they draw their debts. All three, as I describe and relate them, are so closely linked that one cannot even understand the latter without the first. For this reason, I determined to paint a picture of commerce so that the art of exchange may be understood.

## On Manual Exchange.

...all the bulk of the cloth, and from where all the wealth of the world comes. In such a way, that any of those from <term>the Steps<gloss>gradas</gloss></term> <note>The ‘Gradas’ refers to the stone steps surrounding the Cathedral of Seville, which served as the city's informal stock exchange and commercial hub before the construction of the Lonja (the current General Archive of the Indies).</note> (of whom we are particularly speaking) has need of having money in all places, either to buy, or to pay, or to collect, because they owe and are owed in all of them. And this trade being so universal was the primary reason why there were <term>money changers<gloss>cambiadores</gloss></term>. As they require <term>reales<gloss>reales</gloss></term> <note>The primary silver currency of the Spanish Empire.</note> in so many places where they could not, or it did not suit them to transport their own, they—or their <term>agents<gloss>factores</gloss></term> in their name—exchanged them with the residents or the merchants of those cities who also needed them in Seville. And seeing the great necessity of those from here, or those from there, when they came to this land, they began to take an interest and to ask for two or three percent. This profit awakened the spirits of many to take up changing as a business and a trade.

In such a way that what was done accidentally or accessorily before, between merchants alone, began to be a particular and principal negotiation for some. Because besides the great greed that moved them, they found opportunity through the continuous necessity in which the foreign merchants found themselves, as persons who did not have their own currency with them. And this having been its beginning and origin, it has grown so much and increased so that, if the trade of merchants is great and general, as I explained, that of the money changers is greater, bulkier, and more profitable—if only it were not more dangerous or harmful to the conscience <note>A reference to the theological concerns regarding usury; at the time, charging interest for the use of money was a complex moral and legal issue that could lead to excommunication or spiritual peril.</note>. Just as the same merchants trade in all parts, so do the money changers, who are always at their heels, trading throughout all of Christendom. Those of Seville exchange with Burgos, and with the <term>Court<gloss>Corte</gloss></term> <note>The traveling royal court of the Spanish monarch, which was the political and financial center of the empire.</note>, and at all the fairs, to Valencia, to Barcelona, to Lisbon, to Flanders, to France, and to Italy. And speaking to the brokers, who know what is happening in all things and even in every corner, they themselves ask for exchange, either feigning that they are in need or stating their good intentions clearly. The merchants who find themselves with silver are happy to give it to them with some interest until the <term>fair<gloss>feria</gloss></term>, where they must make their payments, because the bills of exchange they have given are not being accepted. They have other specific schemes as well. ### ...in the exchanges of these times.

...it is probable that in the upcoming fair of Antwerp <note>original: "Enuers"</note> there will be very little money, and many who demand it. Whoever received the warning gives all he can in Seville via exchange for that place; and if he does not have the funds, he himself takes them, even with interest, for Medina del Campo or for other parts around here, destined for Flanders. He does this because in the return on the investment he expects to earn much more. Having sent word to Lisbon, they provide in his name the largest amount possible, and it is remitted to him here; in two or three months, he has placed in Flanders some fifty or one hundred thousand <term>ducats<gloss>ducados</gloss></term> <note>A gold coin used as a standard for international trade across Europe.</note>. 

Where, once the fair arrives, if not a single <term>blanca<gloss>blanca</gloss></term> <note>A small Spanish copper coin of very low value; the author uses this phrase idiomatically to mean "not a single penny."</note> appears in the land, the exchange rates go through the roof. And opening their purses, they take from him at twenty or twenty-five percent for Seville and Lisbon. In such a way that, even though he lost money in the initial exchanges he made to gather the sum there, in the exchanges he makes there now—or another makes in his name—he gains no small advantage. 

It seemed so necessary to the merchants and money changers that this trade of theirs be universal, and that their businesses extend throughout the whole world, that to be able to practice it more conveniently—seeing that money in various kingdoms had not only different names, but different values (which caused some deception, or at least some confusion or difficulty)—they agreed that among themselves money should have the same value everywhere. They did this by taking no account of, nor caring for, the real and common estimation of the kingdoms. 

This was an ingenious means, and putting it into execution required great courage: to give money a price and value in all lands distinct from that which the <term>commonwealth<gloss>republica</gloss></term> <note>The author uses the term "republica" to refer to the state or the organized community and its official laws regarding legal tender.</note> sets. Thus in Rome, the money changers take no account of how many <term>carlini<gloss>carlines</gloss></term> <note>A silver coin used in Italy, particularly in Naples and Rome.</note> a ducat is worth, nor in Flanders do they concern themselves with the types and diversity of currency used there (which are many), nor in France, nor in Portugal. Especially in Flanders, they made a valuation in the year [15]27 that was to last perpetually, no matter how much the state changed its price and coinage, even a hundred times a year. THE INTERESTS and advantages in exchanges are commonly as follows. Perpetually from outside the kingdom (unless it be from the Indies), one profits in Seville, and conversely, from Seville to any other part, one loses. This is because Seville exceeds all others in money and wealth. From Rome to Seville, fifteen or twenty percent is gained; from here to there, eight or ten is lost. From Flanders to here, they profit eight and nine; on the return, five and six are lost. This, in truth, varies and changes in so many ways that at times (though rarely) the exchanges are made "free" <note>original: "horros"</note>, equal for equal. # On the Fairs of Spain

...if there is much [money], the rate decreases; if little, it increases. If there is a large quantity on the **steps** <term><gloss>gradas</gloss><note>The 'gradas' refers to the stone steps of the Cathedral of Seville, which served as the city’s primary financial and commercial exchange before the Lonja was built.</note></term>, the one who gives the money loses; if in Flanders there is an abundance of gold and silver, the one who takes it gains. The number of people seeking an <term>exchange<gloss>cambio</gloss></term> also contributes to this same increase and decrease. This is the reason why rates remain so high during the fair.

That which is most constantly heard regarding this contract, especially in the exchanges of Spain, is this name: **fairs** <term><gloss>ferias</gloss></term>. This is because almost all exchanges made abroad are remitted to them, paid at them, and finally taken at them. The fair is the beginning, the conclusion, and the final settlement of all payments. For this reason, it seemed necessary to me to describe the facts here for those who seek to know only the law. There are four fairs, whose origin followed the etymology of the name. **Feria** signifies something free, exempt, and released; and as that which is sold in those places at such times is free from the **sales tax** <term><gloss>alcauala</gloss><note>The 'alcabala' was a heavy tax on commercial transactions in Castile, often reaching 10%.</note></term>, which is not paid, they called the market and the season a "feria." Since the *alcabala* is such a general tribute on sales and purchases, the Kings of Castile very liberally granted certain times when their subjects could sell freely and exempt, without paying it. This was a great favor. And they designated four in succession, like the **four seasons** <term><gloss>quatro temporas</gloss><note>The author compares the four fair cycles to the 'Ember Days' or 'Temporas' of the liturgical calendar.</note></term> of which we speak: two were designated in **Medina del Campo** by Lord **Hernando, King of Aragon**, when he was only Infante of Castile and its governor on behalf of King **Don Juan**, his nephew. The other was in **Villalón**, and the last in **Rioseco**, which is recorded in <note>original: "l. 9. ti. 20. lei. 7." referring to the legal code Book 9, Title 20, Law 7.</note>. Those of Medina are currently the principal ones. They are usually celebrated once in May and the other in October. To these and the others, people flock from all over Spain, both sellers and merchants—some to sell, others to buy—knowing that there must necessarily be a great frequency of both, and a great abundance of every kind of cloth.

# On the Fairs of Spain

...them to all parts. And the origin of their becoming so universal was that everyone went to buy at the fair—to buy cheaply and without **tax** <term><gloss>pecho</gloss><note>A general term for taxes or tributes paid by commoners.</note></term>—so much so that they even waited for the fairs to provide for the household and for what was to be spent within it. For this reason, all those who had to go gave their money in **exchange** <term><gloss>cambio</gloss></term> for the fairs so as not to carry it with them; and conversely, for the same reason and cause—that is, because the business of buying was so common there—there were always many in need of money, which they took as loans to be paid back each in their own lands.

And as the **money changers** <term><gloss>cambiadores</gloss></term> are closely linked with them, their business in these fairs is to go there with a great quantity of funds, setting up a **bank** <term><gloss>banco</gloss></term>, or—as is more general—providing exchange without one. And since he who is in need always has a great need at such a juncture, rather than a moderate one, and finds he has come from abroad to conclude his business, he considers it a **matter of losing face** <note>original: "caso de menos valer"</note> to return without having settled his affairs, and thus he pays whatever interest is required.

Likewise, those abroad who took funds from the first group we mentioned remit their **bills of exchange** <term><gloss>letras</gloss></term> to the fair, where they again have a need to take credit to make their payments. This is because they rarely send actual cash for the payment. His Majesty also takes a great sum when he is in need. Thus, the principal business of the fair is now exchanges and payments, not **tax-free** <term><gloss>francas</gloss></term> purchases and sales, although there is still a good portion of the latter.

These fairs, especially those of **Medina** <note>Medina del Campo was the primary financial center of the Spanish Empire, where international payments were cleared.</note>, which are the primary ones, are moved forward or postponed as His Majesty pleases; sometimes they are delayed so that, in the meantime, the **fleet** <term><gloss>flota</gloss><note>The Spanish treasure fleet bringing silver from the Americas.</note></term> may arrive and there may be an abundance of money, or to gather and deliver the sum that must be paid.

To these fairs, people of all nations come from Seville, Lisbon, Burgos, Barcelona, Flanders, and Florence, either to pay insurance, or to take or give exchanges; ultimately, it is a forge of **promissory notes** <term><gloss>cedulas</gloss></term>, such that one almost never sees a blank page, but only letters. This is certainly a **noble** <note>original: "ahidalgado"; suggesting a status or style of business associated with the gentry rather than common laborers.</note> business for merchants. This is especially true as the bankers serve them so freely, although they seek great interest through this apparent generosity—if they are diligent and lucky.

Since everyone places their silver there, the bankers hold a massive sum with which they make great investments. They corner all the silver from a fleet, and all the gold, along with other things of this sort, so that in two or three months, if things go well, they sometimes earn three or four thousand **escudos** <term><gloss>escudos</gloss><note>A high-value gold coin.</note></term>. They also involve themselves in giving and taking on **exchange** <term><gloss>cambio</gloss></term> and commissions. Indeed, a banker in this republic encompasses a whole world and embraces more than the Ocean, although sometimes he grips so poorly that he loses everything.

Those of the fairs operate in much the same way, except that they are motivated by interest. First, two or three individuals stand as guarantors for those who receive the money from people wishing to consign it to their bank; they pay the bills sent to them and keep accounts for those trading and operating through their bank. When the fair ends, each person pays them **generously** <note>original: "caballerosamente," literally "like a gentleman."</note> for their labor (which cannot be denied to be very great, from transferring entries to balancing accounts), according to whether their business has been much or little. ## ¶ CHAPTER V. ON THE FOUNDATION AND
## *Justice of Exchanges.*

Having established this practice, it remains—returning to the first point, which is **exchanges** <term><gloss>cambios</gloss><note>Referring to "bills of exchange," a method of transferring money between different currencies or locations.</note></term>—to inquire how they can be justified in conscience; if not all (for there is great laxity, corruption, and license), at least some of them. We must examine which are licit and which are illicit. There are three principal points to address. First, what reason and foundation exists for the justice of this contract: what title and cause is sufficient to justify earning a profit through exchange. Second, if it is possible to gain some interest, in which exchanges is interest permissible, and in which is it not. Third, specifically whether those exchanges made on the **steps** <note>original: "gradas"; likely referring to the *Gradas de Sevilla*, the steps of the Seville Cathedral where merchants and bankers gathered to conduct business before the construction of a formal exchange building.</note> are safe in conscience. For as we shall see, they possess particular difficulty and even a bad appearance. And all three of these points are so obscure that it is necessary, in investigating and deciding them, to adopt the style and manner of proceeding used by philosophers and **theologians** <term><gloss>theologo</gloss></term>...

### On Exchanges.

Wise men <note>original: "gos" [sabios]</note>, when they track something hidden, subtle, and sublime, first say what it is not—and they say it a thousand times—before saying what it is. If they search for the nature of the **soul** <term><gloss>alma</gloss></term>, which is invisible, a pure spirit that is neither seen nor felt, not being corporeal, they proceed by saying and proving that the soul is not heaven, nor earth, nor any of the elements, nor composed of them. Having concluded it is none of these, they finally hit upon what it must be: namely, a simple, incorruptible, intellectual substance. **Theologians** <term><gloss>Theologos</gloss></term> do the same when they ask who **God** <term><gloss>Dios</gloss></term> is; for it is better known what He is not, than what He is. I intend to do the same in this matter—not because of its excellence or majesty, for it has none, but because of its obscurity and even its disorder. First, we shall say what cannot be held or defended; afterwards, perhaps, we shall arrive at what can be said and done. This is because many reasons that some think are favorable to these dealings are no more founded in justice than they are in the canons of medicine <note>A metaphor suggesting these arguments are completely irrelevant to the legal or moral reality of the situation.</note>.

Among all the theologians who until now have desired to find some good reasons to justify this trade, only three are found. Of these, we shall see that two are merely apparent—not real or substantial. Even if they sometimes apply to a case, they do not do so consistently. Some say that whoever gives an exchange may gain from it because they trade their **present money** for **absent money**. They give it in **Seville** <note>A major economic hub and port for the Spanish Empire.</note> now for that which is in **Medina** <note>Likely referring to Medina del Campo, the site of Spain's most important financial fairs.</note>, or which is to be there. Let us not dwell now on whether one already has it in Medina or must seek it out. It is clear, say these most learned masters, that present money is worth more than absent money. That which one already holds is secure; the absent is subject to two thousand dangers, for it may be that they do not pay, or they defer the payment. In short, as they say, "a bird in the hand is worth more than a vulture flying" <note>original: "mas vale paxaro en mano, q̃ buytre bolãdo." A variation of the English proverb "A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush."</note>. For this reason, whoever gives their money in Seville for that of Medina or **Lisbon** <note>Translated from the catchword "Lisboa" at the bottom of the page.</note>...

# On the Foundation and Justice

...Lisbon, one might pay one percent, and the other's currency is worth that much less because it is in **Medina** <note>Medina del Campo, home to the most important financial fairs in 16th-century Spain.</note>, so far away. Many doctors <note>Legal and theological scholars.</note> follow this path: but in my opinion, although the reasoning is true, it is not good, nor is it relevant to the matter. It is true, speaking generally, that money in the box is worth more than waiting for it. Though for many, it is certainly better to have it absent, because in its absence it earns for them; thus they send it away from themselves, and almost never keep a large quantity of cash together with them. Upon its arrival, they employ it and reinvest it <note>original: "la tornan à cargar"</note>, or send it to the trade fairs. For merchants, **present money** <term><gloss>dınero prefente</gloss> — cash on hand</term> is not worth more than **absent money** <term><gloss>dınero aufente</gloss> — funds held elsewhere or yet to be received</term>; rather, it is the reverse: absent money is worth more than present.

But even assuming this were true, exchanges are not based on it, nor was this rule ever kept or observed, as appears for many reasons. First, if the business went this way, the one who gives in exchange <note>The lender or purchaser of a bill of exchange.</note> would always have to gain, since he has the money and gives it presently, while the other obligates himself to pay it elsewhere; yet we see the opposite most of the time—that he loses. If a merchant has money here and gives it in exchange for **Flanders**, he loses six or seven percent. If he gave a thousand **ducats** <note>A gold coin used as a standard currency across Europe.</note> in cash in **Seville**, they do not return a thousand to him in **Antwerp** <note>original: "Enuers"</note>, but nine hundred and twenty, more or less. The common practice is to return less to him. 

<margin>Cajetan, *Treatise on Exchanges*, chapter 7.</margin>The same occurs if he gives them for **Rome**. He will not, in short, give them in exchange to any part outside the kingdom without losing on it, despite providing the money presently. Likewise, if he gives them for some trade fair in Spain, sometimes he loses, and other times he gains. From this it is evidently clear that this reason—namely, that present money is worth more than absent money—is not a firm foundation upon which exchanges rest, nor did they ever rest upon it. Because even in the beginning, when this negotiation was in its sincerity and purity, the one who gave in exchange always lost, paying a certain amount so that they would place the funds where he requested, as we shall soon see. Furthermore, if this reason...

# On Exchanges

If the fact that money is "absent" <note>In this context, "absent" refers to funds that the borrower or exchanger does not currently possess or that are located in a different city.</note> could justify exchanges, then pure usury <term>vsura — the practice of lending money at interest, which was then considered a sin</term> would be justified as well. This is because whenever someone takes a loan or an exchange, the money with which they must pay is absent. It is certainly "absent" when one does not have it, and perhaps does not even know from where it might come—which is a greater absence—especially since many times when a person receives an exchange, they do not have the funds available, but must seek them out through new exchanges. Thus, the money is no more "absent" than when taking a simple loan. Yet, despite all this absence, usury remains most illicit; therefore, absence cannot justify the exchange either. There are others who say that the foundation lies in the interest being like a salary <note>A fee paid for the service of moving money.</note> which they receive for carrying the coin. They argue that if I have a need for a thousand **ducats** <note>A gold coin used as a standard currency across Europe.</note> in **Flanders**, it would cost me a great deal to transport them there; if another person provides them to me there, they reasonably earn, and may earn something of what it would have cost me to carry them, especially by freeing me from the risk involved in the journey. For by transferring them through an exchange, I do not venture to lose them on the road.

Regarding this opinion, it should be considered that in ancient times the business began in this way, as we said in Chapter 3. Whoever had a need for money in **Burgos** or in **Barcelona** gave it here to someone whose credit would ensure they were given the money there; this was, in truth, like carrying it themselves, and they gave a certain amount for it. This was a very licit and reasonable thing. Today, however, this trade has grown, and human ingenuity and greed have altered it in such a way that no trace of the original practice remains. Everything is so new that if modern exchange and what is done within it were compared to the old way, they would be further apart than heaven is from the abyss. I would be happy if the original way were kept, as it is less prone to scruples, and if this machine or "chimera" <note>The author uses "chimera" to describe the complex, artificial, and perhaps monstrous nature of modern financial systems.</note> of business could be built on such a good foundation. But I will show most clearly that the money changers have already played a trick <note>original: "cãtonada" — a colloquialism for a deception or a "cornering" trick.</note> on this form of exchange, and that no account is taken—

## On the Foundation and Justice

...[nothing to do] with tolls, nor with paying them, nor satisfying them, nor is interest taken for this reason. In exchanges, whether outside the kingdom or within it. Firstly, from **Flanders** to **Seville**, money is commonly exchanged at seven or eight percent profit. If one gives a thousand **ducats** <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe as a trade currency.</note> in **Ghent**, they will be given one thousand and seventy in **Seville**, more or less, depending on how the **market** <term>lonja — a merchant's exchange or marketplace where financial transactions were negotiated</term> is moving. Let us suppose a case where one has two thousand ducats in **Antwerp** and wants them in **Seville**, and he offers them and goes looking for someone to give them to, or someone to take them. If it were true that interest is a salary for the transport, the one who takes them there and gives them here—who is, in reality, the one who brings them—ought to receive his share, especially when they were offered to him. Yet, it is the opposite. Even if I ask him to deliver them to me in Seville, he earns seven percent, or eight, or nine; and from Rome to here twelve or thirteen, no matter how much I might need to move them to Seville and request the transfer. Whereby it appears clear that profit is not made in the exchange for moving or carrying the money, since many times the one who moves it loses, and the other gains interest. Furthermore, within the kingdom, from Seville to **Medina** <note>Referring to Medina del Campo, a major center for trade fairs and finance in Spain.</note>, the market rate fluctuates so much that sometimes the one who gives loses, and other times the one who receives loses, whether they have planned ahead or not. This is the point upon which these **doctors** <note>The "Doctors" or Scholastic theologians who debated the morality of financial contracts.</note> emphasize, as we have stated: at other times it is exchanged **for free** <term>horro — an exchange made without any profit or loss, literally "freed" or "clean"</term>. This is something that could not be done in any way if interest were charged for carrying or transferring it. Since there is always a transfer—either real or imaginary (as these people say)—there would always have to be interest, yet we see that there is none. Fourthly, if this opinion is true, I do not know why everyone raises a **scruple** <term>escrupulo — a moral or religious doubt regarding the sinfulness of an action</term> regarding the exchanges made within the kingdom, since it would be most lawful to gain something for carrying money from one city to another, even if it were nearby, let alone if it were distant and remote. Thus, there would be nothing to doubt, nor to have scruples about, in these exchanges to Medina and **Burgos**, since it is a certain thing to earn something for carrying money there. And we see that everyone doubts and has scruples, and with good reason. And one cannot respond that they have scruples simply because the interest is high,

# Concerning exchanges.

...for compared to this calculation, it is little. For a fair transport fee from here to **Medina** <note>Medina del Campo, the most important financial center in 16th-century Spain due to its major trade fairs.</note> would be four percent, and to **Burgos** five, since to **Salamanca** they are appraised at three; yet it is very rare that four percent is given from **Seville** to Medina, or vice versa, by a bill of exchange at sight. From which it appears clear that profit is not made in the exchange for the sake of transport. Finally, in this it shines forth how no account is taken of the toll nowadays; for the road from Medina or from **Rome** to here is always the same, and the costs are always the same, and the danger the same, whereby if the reason for the interest were the transport, a single rate of transport would have to be carried continuously, as we see on other roads. For to Salamanca, it perpetually carries the ordinary rate of three percent. The same is true for the freightage of ships, which, unless there is some particular circumstance, have a single price. At least they increase little by little over two or three years, like all things that twenty years ago were worth less. 

But these exchanges vary and change from moment to moment; sometimes profit is made from Seville to Medina—I mean, all those who give money profit—whether they anticipate the need and plead, or are themselves pleaded with; at other times they lose, no matter how they act; at other times neither one nor the other makes a profit. This is an evident argument that tolls are not taken into account, for exchanges are made "free" <term>horros — exempt from the usual fees or interest</term>, and "par for par" <term>tanto por tanto — an equal exchange of value without any additional charge or profit</term>, without any gain at all. 

Likewise <note>original: "Item"</note>, we see clearly that the abundance or scarcity of money in a city—whether here, or in **Venice**, or **Naples**—causes the exchange rate to rise or fall; and if the price were charged for transport, the interest would not change based on there being little or much money: for having much wine in **Cazalla** <note>Cazalla de la Sierra, a town near Seville famous for its wine production.</note> does not cause the muleteer teams <term>arrias — the strings of pack animals or the cost of their transport</term> to be expensive or cheap. All these reasons show most manifestly that nowadays no account is taken of the passage of currency from one kingdom to another. In times past, I confess this was its principle and justice, but now the water flows through other pipes <note>A metaphor suggesting that the mechanism or "plumbing" of the economy has changed and follows new rules.</note>, and it cannot be governed by this measure.

# On the foundation and justice

...granted. Would to God it were regulated; then it would proceed in order and harmony. And if anyone should persist in basing themselves on this reason, very few of the exchanges that are made fit into that mold <note>original: "çanja," literally a trench or foundation ditch</note>, and if he were to reject all those that do not fit, he would have to condemn them all.

The third reason that others believe to be the foundation is the **differing estimation of money**. And to understand this (because it is a very good point), one must note that the value and price of money are not the same as its "estimation" <note>In 16th-century economics, "estimation" refers to the subjective value or purchasing power of money based on its abundance or scarcity in a specific location.</note>. A very clear example of this is that in the **Indies** <note>The Spanish Americas.</note>, money has the same value as it does here (namely, one **real** <term>real: a silver coin</term> is thirty-four **maravedís** <term>maravedís: the smallest unit of account in Spain</term>). A **peso de minas** <term>peso de minas: a high-quality gold coin minted from refined ore</term> is worth thirteen reales, and it is worth the same in **Spain**; but although the value and price are the same, the estimation is very different in both places. For it is estimated much less in the Indies than in Spain. The quality of the land and its disposition are such that, upon entering it, a man develops a heart so generous in this regard that he values a dozen reales no more than one would value a single maravedí here, so to speak. After the Indies, where it is held in least regard is in **Seville**, as it is the city that receives all the good things from there; then the other parts of Spain. It is highly estimated in **Flanders**, in **Rome**, in **Germany**, and in **England**.

This estimation and appraisal is caused, firstly, by having a great abundance or a great scarcity of these metals; and since they are born and harvested in those parts, they are held in little regard. For even men, according to the proverb, are not commonly honored or esteemed in their own homeland. In accordance with this, there is the story of the **Augustinian** friars and soldiers whom His Majesty recently sent from **New Spain** <note>Colonial Mexico.</note> to **China**, where the rivers produce much **gold**. They told the Indians—who are already quite weary of it—how little they cared to extract it. The Indians responded that it was safe there in the rivers for whenever they might want it. # on exchanges.

...[it is because there is] much to buy and sell, although the first cause is the principal one. We see that in the **Indies** <note>The Spanish Americas.</note> there is much to buy, and things are bought at excessive prices, as they are goods carried from so far away; yet even so, money is esteemed less there because the abundance [of silver] is so great that it outweighs this other cause. We will perceive this same distinction between price and estimation clearly by what is usually said of a miser: that he "holds his **real** at thirty-four" <note>A silver **real** was legally worth thirty-four **maravedís**; the author implies the miser values the coin more than its legal worth.</note>. Thus there are kingdoms and provinces where—for these reasons I have mentioned, and for others that may concur (and indeed do concur) which I have not grasped or do not occur to me—money is worth and is esteemed much more than it is here, while retaining the exact same price in both places. [Spain] more than in Peru. What I have said is evident and appears clearly if we turn our eyes toward this business. Never in exchanges are such great interests <note>In this context, "interests" refers to the profit or premium earned on the exchange of currency.</note> charged as in those made in places where it is evident that money is highly valued. The most advantageous ones are those between Flanders and Rome and here [in Spain], where it is well known that money is held in higher regard than in other parts. This is a good sign that the money changers and the exchange markets keep an eye on this diverse estimation. 

Secondly, from Seville to Medina and to Lisbon, or to any other place, what causes the market to fall or rise is the abundance or scarcity of silver. If there is much, the exchanges are low; if there is little, they rise; and it is clear that abundance or lack causes it to be valued highly or held cheaply. From this it follows that if money was valued more in Seville at this juncture than it was a month ago—perhaps due to some specific account <note>original: "cuento," referring to a financial report or specific set of circumstances</note>—it was enough to change the market and increase it; and when it becomes abundant, the value will fall. Thus, this same estimation is the foundation upon which these businesses always lean and are based. 

Certainly, these two reasons seem clear and effective to me, showing plainly how central to this trade is the holding of money more in one place than in another. Thus we see it in practice, that when the money changer knows that in some province or city there is to be a great shortage <note>original: "estrechura," literally a "tightness" or liquidity crisis</note>, he seeks to gather a large amount of capital there in advance.

# Diverse valuation of money

[If a]nyone persists that this is not the foundation, I will not argue much with them; but they remain obligated to discover the true and proper one, or at least another that is better and more proportionate. In these obscure and tangled matters, I am not so stubborn or tenacious in my opinion and judgment that I believe in it as if it were the Gospel <note>original: "euangelio"</note>. This which I have explained seemed to me the most similar to the practice and use of the art <note>The "art" here refers to the professional practice of banking and currency exchange.</note>, especially since we are not tracing now the nature and justice of one exchange, nor of two, nor of any specific type in particular—neither those outside the kingdom nor those within—but generally of all, and for everyone in common. I certainly see no root more universal, nor one that fits so well. I know well that at times the necessity of one person and the tyranny of another cause great interest <note>In this context, "interest" refers to the premium or profit earned; the author acknowledges that while greed can drive prices, it shouldn't be the basis for a general theory of fair trade.</note> to be charged, but it is not right that this should be taken as a rule when discussing all cases in common.

It remains to be proven that this suffices to justify the profit attained in exchanges. We have already said that to exchange, in plain Spanish, was to barter <note>original: "trocar," meaning to swap or trade one thing for another</note>, and for a barter to be lawful, the first and principal requirement is that it be equal; one thing must be worth as much as the other, for if it were worth less, it would be an injustice and a grievance. We also know that the same kind of clothing, without being changed itself, is priced higher in one province than in another. An *arroba* <term>arroba: a traditional Spanish unit of weight (approximately 25 pounds) or volume (approximately 4 gallons)</term> of wine is priced much higher, beyond comparison, in the Indies <note>The "Indies" refers to the Spanish colonies in the Americas.</note> than in Spain, and one of oil more in Flanders than in Castile; so much so that they are equal: one pipe <note>A "pipe" was a large cask used for shipping wine or spirits.</note> of wine in Mexico and ten in Jerez, and they could be bartered and exchanged lawfully—giving one in New Spain <note>Mexico</note> for ten in Cazalla. And within the same kingdom, a basket of *gordal* <note>A variety of large, "fat" olives.</note> olives in Valladolid can be exchanged for four in Manzanilla, and these would be just exchanges and barters, and there would be equality in them. In this same way it happens with coins: because they are valued more in one part than in another, they come to be equal, even though the quantity is different—ninety-three...

...in Flanders with a hundred in Seville, not because the ducat <note>A gold coin used across Europe.</note> is of a different fineness or a different value, but because the land itself (as they say) causes one to make more of money. We are accustomed to saying, "I would rather have one real <note>A silver coin; at the time, one real was worth 34 maravedís.</note> here than two elsewhere": not because one is not worth thirty-four here, and two sixty-eight, but because the thirty-four are valued more here than the sixty-eight are elsewhere. Thus, just as the advantage that the Indies <note>The Spanish Americas.</note> hold over these kingdoms in the abundance of gold and silver is great, seventy ducats at Court <note>The Spanish Royal Court, the center of political and economic life.</note> are of equal esteem and reputation as one hundred in Lima, or ninety in Veracruz; and even if I were to point out a greater discrepancy, I believe I would not be mistaken. The same applies from these lands to Rome: one hundred in Burgos would be roughly equal to ninety-four in Rome. In this way, exchanging the hundred for the ninety-four is an equal exchange, even if it were possible to deliver those ninety-four in Italy that very same night, without delay or passage of time. And in fact, people would often want it so—those who send funds for certain dispensations <note>Official exemptions from Church law.</note> or to obtain certain benefices <note>Ecclesiastical offices that provided an income.</note>. On the day they hand over the money here, they would wish, if it were possible, for the letter of exchange to take no more than a few hours. And they lose ten, and sometimes fourteen percent.

Someone might say that in these things where we used the examples of olives and wine in equal quantities, the barter is unequal because the value is truly distinct. For in these parts, a barrel of olives is worth four times less than in the Villa Rica <note>Villa Rica de la Vera Cruz, the first Spanish town founded in Mexico.</note>. However, the currency—silver and gold—has the same value and fineness <term>fineness (ley): the proportion of precious metal in a coin, which determined its legal value</term> in these kingdoms, and indeed in all of them, regarding exchange. Therefore, these are not suitable examples, or they do not follow the same reasoning. Regarding this, it is very important to note that just as in salable goods there is substance and value—as in wheat there is its nature and its price—so often that which is of a better nature (such as a horse, which is a living, feeling thing) is worth less—

# Of Exchanges

<meta>catchword: dry</meta>

...[just as we see] that a diamond (an inanimate thing) <note>The OCR "nos que" likely completes the word "Senos" or "Séanos," meaning "Let us see" or "Let us take the example."</note> behaves, so in money there are two factors: one is its value and fineness <term>ley: the legally mandated purity or standard of precious metal in a coin</term>, which is its substance and nature in being money; and the other is its esteem <note>In this context, "esteem" refers to the market value or purchasing power, which can fluctuate regardless of the metal content.</note>. In such a way that what is extrinsic and variable in other things is essential and natural in money, while esteem is accidental. And although in some things price and esteem go hand-in-hand, in most they are separate. What is of little price is highly esteemed by everyone, either for being rare or for other reasons that may coincide. 

Especially in money, these two are divorced. Regarding exchange, the primary consideration must be the universal esteem held for the money, not its fineness. Just as with goods for sale <term>venal things: items produced or held specifically for trade or sale</term>, the price does not follow their nature, nor are they valued according to their inherent dignity, but rather according to the necessity we have for them and the purpose they serve. Thus, in the actual exchange of currencies, one should not notice the value (which is its nature) as much as the esteem that is placed upon that value. And we clearly see that although metals have the same price in many nations, they are esteemed unequally. 

So, while in other things barter <term>trueque: the direct exchange of goods without using money</term> is justified by the price—which in those cases is extrinsic and accidental—in currencies, it is justified by esteem, which is also outside its nature and variable. In this regard, the examples are very fitting. Namely, just as the trade of goods for sale does not follow their nature or quantity, but their price (which is accidental), so the exchange of money does not look at the fineness or the quantity of value (which is its nature), but rather the esteem that the people place upon that quantity. From all of this, it is gathered that it is so necessary for exchange to be conducted in diverse places that this condition is essential to it. If this condition is lacking—that is, if it is done in the same place, giving and collecting the money in the very same town—it will either be "petty exchange" <term>cambio menudo: small-scale currency swapping, such as changing a large gold coin for smaller silver or copper ones</term>, involving almost no profit, or if it is "large-scale exchange," it will be...

He concludes that for a legitimate exchange to occur with significant profit, it must involve different geographical locations.</summary>

->for outside the kingdom.<-

dry or fraudulent <note>The author refers to "dry exchange" (cambio seco), a common 16th-century financial workaround where a loan was disguised as a foreign currency exchange to bypass laws against usury.</note>. Three things are essential to exchange: namely, that the esteem of money be unequal, but that this inequality be equalized by an unequal quantity. This necessarily requires a diversity of locations. For example, one hundred ducats in Seville and ninety-five in Antwerp <note>original: Enuers</note> are equal in esteem, because they are unequal in quantity. The unequal quantity equalizes the different reputation of money held in these places. And if exchange is founded on this diverse general esteem (a thing that cannot exist within a single town), it is most necessary that it be given in one place and paid in another. This provides sufficient cause and just reason for interest; if this is missing, it cannot be anything but usury <term>usury: the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was heavily regulated or prohibited by Church law if it lacked a justification like "risk" or "distance."</term>. For this is the difference between exchange and usury: exchange profits through the distance and difference of locations where money is esteemed differently. Usury, without traveling these paths, profits solely from the necessity of the person asking for it. All of this must be repeated and explained more extensively in the remainder of this little work, as the foundation of this building and the base of this column we are raising; for almost nothing remains but to apply this doctrine and common rule to each specific type of exchange.

Thus, our theologians, speaking in absolute terms, say that exchanges made outside the realm are lawful. However, it is necessary to understand that this is not a universal rule for all other places. # for [trade] outside the kingdom.

it is in substance to trade with oneself. This is a very repugnant thing. Every contract demands two parties. No one contracts with himself alone, nor is justice maintained [in such a case]. And in this business, for it to be what it is—real usury (which is to give the money here, and to receive it back here, as is done in effect)—two parties are very clear and distinct. But if it is an exchange that consists of paying in another place, there is only one, namely, the agent <term>agent: translated from the Spanish "factor," a business representative who acts on behalf of a merchant in a distant city or trade fair</term> there. This agent, regarding the negotiation, is the same person as the one who gave the money for exchange. No one there replaces or represents the person who received it, and it was absolutely necessary that there were such a person. Just as in the giving of money, two are needed here—one to give and one to receive—so in the payment there must be two there: one to pay and another to collect. And just as one person alone cannot perform a true exchange here, there being no one to take it, so too there is no true payment there.

Concerning this, it should be noted that as it is so clearly illicit, some money changers of good conscience avoid it. For this reason, among those who receive an exchange, those who have no correspondents <term>correspondent: translated from "responsal," a person in a foreign market who takes responsibility for a debt or credit</term> at the fairs, nor credit in them, need a friend to have his agent answer for them, taking on exchange the amount they draw in the bill. This third party, being requested here, takes one percent, or one and a half, for appointing a correspondent. And there is great doubt whether this interest <note>the author uses "interes" here to mean a service fee or commission, but cautions that if it masks a loan, it may be usurious</note> is lawful. 

Regarding this, I say that whoever receives the bill at the fair, or in any other place, and pays it justly, takes some interest, provided it is small, since it is a type of agency fee <term>agency fee: translated from "factorage," the commission paid to an agent for managing business affairs at a fair</term>, and any agent takes some commission <term>commission: translated from "encomienda," a payment for a specific service or task performed by an agent</term> for his labor. This being so well-verified and customary, there is no moral objection. Whether the interest that this third party takes is the same that the partner whom he appoints was to take at the fair, is also without objection. Since the agent can safely take it there, it does not matter if the amount he is to take is agreed upon with the one in Seville, both being partners. This is done so that there is only one interest, not two. This interest they can, if they wish, later divide between themselves. Also, another type—

One may certainly profit something for providing such a guarantee, provided it is a very moderate amount. But if there is nothing more to it than letters of request, praying that he do it, it is not decent to sell even words of courtesy.

Firstly, if a true exchange is a true swap, how can you swap your money in Madrid with that of someone in Ghent, if he has nothing there, as you well know? It is not an exchange, nor can it be, where two things are lacking that are to be changed and swapped in different places. And since there is nothing but one thing in this contract—which is your money that you give in Madrid—there cannot be an exchange between the two. Thus they call this <term>dry exchange: translated from "cambio seco," a fictional exchange used to hide a high-interest loan that never actually involves foreign currency or travel</term>, because it is done "in the dry" and without real substance; it is usury not even thinly veiled, without a cloak or mantle to cover it, save for that single word and name of "exchange."

What difference is there between this business and usury, except only for the refusal to give it its proper name? In the natural order of things, the one is as much a loan, and as bad, as the other.

### On Exchanges

It is well established that drawing a bill on a fictitious person, or on someone who will not correspond or accept it, is common practice. It is astonishing how much this vice clouds the understanding of these <term>exchangers: individuals who traded in currencies and bills of exchange, often functioning as early bankers</term>, that they persuade themselves they are somewhat remedying the evil by sending the <term>letter: a bill of exchange, the standard document for transferring money between cities</term> to their own <term>factor: a business agent or representative who handled affairs for a merchant in a distant market</term> so that he may re-exchange it, especially with new interest. This is so clearly a greater crime and a greater harm: a crime because he goes about defaming his own signature, and a harm because these interests on re-exchanges cost him more than if he had simply borrowed the money with <term>usury: the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was heavily regulated and often condemned by the Church during this period</term> from the beginning. 

The third thing, which is to demand two percent for the <term>commission and brokerage: "encomienda y fatoraje," the fees paid to agents for their services</term>, is to "throw it to the wind," as they say <note>original: "echarlo como dizen á doze," a Spanish idiom implying negligence or excessive rates</note>; it is to not want wealth, but only this life, which is brief and fleeting, and in the next (which is eternal) to choose, almost on purpose, infinite misery. For if to grow rich and store up treasures there, it is necessary here to take care not to steal the property of others, one can only guess what it will be to go about thus draining and consuming <note>original: "chupando y comiendo," literally "sucking and eating"</note> wealth with such pacts and conditions. 

This is what concerns the <term>dry exchanges: "cambios secos," fictitious transactions where no money actually moves to another city; they were used to bypass laws against usury</term> that they say are celebrated outside the kingdom, when they are not even truly celebrated within it. All of them are unjust and usurious. This is because the first thing required by the equity of this business is that it be a true transaction, not one feigned with mere words. Indeed, the exchanger is not only obliged to avoid the first <note>original: "embuſte," meaning a trick or fraud</note>, which is to keep the <term>note: "cedula," the physical document of the debt</term> in the cash box; and the second, which is to send it to someone to re-exchange it; and the third, which is to demand interest for naming a correspondent; but he is also obliged whenever he probably understands that he has no money there, nor will have any. This is especially true when the person he designates is not there, or if they are, they will not or usually do not respond. If the person here intends nothing more than to make use of the money in that <term>interim: the period between the issuance of the bill and its supposed maturity</term>, he is obliged not to make such a contract, because it is usurious. I do not say, nor do I command, that he who gives at exchange must always know for certain that he actually has money where...

It is clear that if he understands the other party has neither coin nor credit, he sees plainly with his own eyes that it is a mere loan. 

And this condition is so necessary that if, after having simply and plainly made an exchange and sent the <term>letters: "letras," bills of exchange used to transfer money between cities</term>, he discovers it was a mockery to give them—because there was no such man to pay them, and the borrower only intended to collect his rents at that time or wait for the <term>fleet: the Spanish Treasure Fleet that brought silver and goods from the Americas</term> to arrive—he is obliged to undo the contract and take no interest by reason of the exchange. This is because the exchange was null; there was no true barter, nor things to be exchanged. 

It is true that in such a case, he may keep a large portion of the funds, not because of the exchange—since it lacked the substance and nature of one—but because of what the other party, through deceit and <term>dissimulation: the concealment of one's thoughts or feelings; here, hiding the lack of funds</term>, caused him to lose during those months. In that time, he could have made a profitable exchange. All of this is an explanation and declaration of the first property required for this business (namely) that it be true and real, not imagined; that it walks on its own feet upon the ground, and is not something flying in the wind or represented merely in the mind's fantasy.

The second requirement is that it be without deceit or coercion, because for contracts to be legitimate, they must be free and voluntary. To the extent that if one were to compel another through illicit means to buy—even if he sold it to him at a <term>just price: "justo precio," the morally and legally acceptable market value of a good</term>—he would be sinning because of the clear force he applied. Deceit and force strip a person of their freedom and will in the business they conduct. This is because the wise do not judge that a deceived person acts voluntarily, for if they knew of the deception, they would not have acted. 

Force is even worse than deceit. It is a much greater evil to compel someone to do what they did not want to do than to deceive them so that they do it of their own will. And this vice and regrettable defect is very common and widespread among these traders.

It is a type of deceit and violence to seize and gather to oneself all the money available in the city in order to force merchants to take loans at high interest. An even greater iniquity is to then constrain them to take and settle payments in places where the profits are higher—or even if they are not, where the lender needs them and the merchant does not have them available. 

If cornering the market on clothing, and especially on <note>original: "bastimentos," food supplies and essential goods</note> provisions—which occurs when one or two people buy up an entire type of good, or the majority of what is in the town, to resell it at higher prices—is a common harm to the <note>original: "republica," referring to the common good or the community as a whole</note> commonwealth (as we explained in the first <note>original: "Opusculo," a small treatise or work</note> Treatise), how much more so is it to corner all the money? That is, to gather all or a large part of what exists into one's own hand through trickery to compel merchants to take it as a <term>change: "cambio," a financial transaction involving bills of exchange and currency conversion</term> at whatever rate the lender wishes. The more a thing is necessary for human life, the greater the crime to seek...

# On Exchanges

...[to increase] its scarcity or reduction, but rather the reverse. Everyone (each in their own degree and rank) is so obligated to seek the common good: some by not hindering it, others by preserving it, and others by increasing it. And since money is so very necessary among temporal goods for human interaction, no one can ignore how much harm is done by those who restrict, diminish, or hide it. 

This is a much greater evil than raising the price of wheat. Regarding wheat, <term>hucksters: "regatones," small-scale retailers often accused of price-gouging</term> or <term>resellers: "revendientes"</term> are justly prohibited by <term>positive law: "ley positiva," man-made statutes as opposed to natural or divine law</term> so that they do not drive up the price; however, for money, it seems such actions are prohibited by natural law itself. 

Such are these exchangers, who collect money to make it more expensive—not according to any law, but by manipulating its necessity and perceived value—so that their interest profits increase beyond all measure. Furthermore, a <term>monopoly: "monipodio," an illicit agreement or conspiracy among merchants to fix prices and stifle competition</term> (an abhorrent and harmful vice) is not as constant among any other kind of merchants as it is among these exchangers. 

They make such a habit of this that, just as the <note>original: "consulado"</note> merchant guild meets to discuss the dispatch of a fleet, or as members of a religious brotherhood meet to arrange a procession, these men—or the wealthiest among them—meet with just as much freedom at every fair, and even outside the fairs in many places, to agree on "how the market will go" and what price they will set. And since they have the money in their power and see themselves as masters of the field, they take from it whatever they want, setting prices according to their own whim and greed. They do not even act according to their own better judgment, for they set prices so outrageously that their own reason shows them the exorbitance and excess, were it not that their depraved appetite blinds them. 

If it is necessary for judges to value and set a price for any kind of clothing or goods required for human life, and not leave it to the corrupt will of the traders, how much more is this required in the exchange? For here, one deals with, barters, and trades the most necessary "merchandise" <note>original: "ropa," literally "clothing," but here used metaphorically for essential commodities</note> that exists among men: money, without which one cannot live in a civil and comfortable manner. Certainly, judges with a commission from His Majesty should set the interest rates for the exchanges at every fe- <note>This catchword "fe-" indicates the next page begins with "feria" (fair).</note>

### On Exchanges

...to exchange, he must perform the exchange according to the petition and will of the recipient, as requested for the location where the exchanger usually issues bills of exchange <note>A "bill of exchange" (letra) allowed a person to pay money in one city and receive it in another, avoiding the risk of transporting physical gold.</note>. Nor is it necessary for the exchanger to conduct his business in all places, or for him to have correspondents everywhere; but at the very least, they should not deny service to those places where they usually operate. I am not saying he is obligated to always grant it. For if one person asks for an exchange to a place where more profit is made, and another for where there is less interest, he may well grant it to the first. 

But to use this leverage when he sees people in need, demanding they take bills for the locations where the profits are highest—either for the current outward journey or for the subsequent return—this is the evil. The money exchanger is to money what the merchant is to cloth. By right, the merchant cannot and should not compel the buyer to pay in one specific type of currency or another, so long as he is paid in good, current coin. And if, beyond paying him what the item is worth, the merchant were to demand payment in gold, or in silver, or in something that—to put it simply—required extra effort or labor to find, it would be an injustice. 

In the same way, the exchanger should not constrain the requester to take a bill for whatever location the exchanger prefers, provided the person is asking for a place where the exchanger usually provides service. To compel or constrain them to this is illicit. And when they use this trickery, they understand it very well—perhaps even better than I could explain it here. 

I added especially that if it were probable that the exchanger had no funds in that particular kingdom, it is so poorly done to make the client exchange there that one would not be far off in calling it a <term>dry exchange: "cambio seco," a fraudulent transaction where no money is actually transferred abroad, used as a cover for a usurious loan</term>. A person who does not live by this trade, but who happens to offer an exchange by chance, clearly must do so at his own convenience and for the locations where he needs funds, since that is why he does it. Some will say that those in this profession must exchange for their own profit; this is true. But there is a difference: for professional exchangers, an exchange to any location is useful, though more so in one place than another. It is not just to always insist upon [the most profitable route]...

IN THESE exchanges <note>The term *cambios* here refers to bills of exchange—financial instruments used to move credit between cities without the risk of transporting physical gold or silver.</note> that are made within the kingdom, there is first a great moral hesitation [scruple] as to whether they may be made at all; and second, even granting that they can be made, there are great evils in the manner in which they are conducted. for the fairs of Spain.

the principal city of this land is today [Seville], by reason of the West Indies <note>The Americas, which at this time were the source of immense Spanish wealth.</note>: of all of which it is the port and the gateway for all, the richest without exaggeration that exists in all the world. Secondly, I also consider and observe—to dare to speak at such length and to declare the matter—that this diverse valuation of money, which is the foundation of the equity and justice of this business, must not be considered only between one province and another, but joined with, and even principally between, two **universities** <term>universities</term> <note>In this context, *universidades* refers to merchant guilds or professional corporations, not academic institutions.</note> or consulates of merchants. This is a very well-known, universal, and permanent property. But the Consulate of Burgos and the merchants of Medina come at times, despite all this, to be more flush and prosperous with money than those of the city of Seville. And on the contrary, **the steps** <term>the steps</term> <note>Original: *las gradas*. This refers to the steps of the Cathedral of Seville, which served as the city's open-air financial exchange and trade floor before a dedicated building was constructed.</note> are abundant while those there are narrow and squeezed; and other times they walk as equals and run neck-and-neck. Regarding which, if I am not mistaken, consideration can and should licitly be given in the exchanges, making them according to this different or equal valuation that exists between the merchant guilds according to the time, and not only with the prosperity and poverty of an entire kingdom. This shows with evidence that the usage and practice, which is neither refuted nor rebuked, is true: namely, that sometimes interest is gained from Seville to Medina, other times they lose, and other times they break even.

# For the fairs of Spain.

Because [exchanges] will always be conducted outside the Kingdom if we restrict the definition of the Kingdom so much. If one understands a single lordship of a supreme Prince—*Spain* and the *Indies* being one principality—money can, and usually does, pass freely from one part to another. There is no doubt that there can be most lawful <term>exchanges</term> <note>original: "cambios." These were bills of exchange, financial contracts that allowed merchants to pay money in one location and receive it in another, often involving different currencies or a fee for the service.</note> from here to there; and no one will reproach them for being within a Kingdom, especially in places where there is such unequal valuation.

In this, it is clearly evident that the reasoning used by many is frivolous. They claim that a profit is taken only because money cannot be moved from one place to another. Yet, since it can indeed be moved, and nothing else is done but moving it, there can be very real exchanges. These can yield no small profit (as we shall see). Furthermore, even if the same Prince possessed *Spain*, *France*, and *Italy*—as he did in ancient times and now possesses *Spain*, *Flanders*, and *Naples*—and money were moved from one part to another, one could lawfully exchange from *Madrid* to *Paris*, just as one exchanges from *Cordoba* to *Ghent*; and these would be exchanges within the Kingdom. Finally, the <term>Papal decree</term> <note>original: "decretal Pontifical." A reference to canon law rulings on banking and usury, likely the decretal 'Navarrus' which was central to these 16th-century economic debates.</note> regarding exchanges makes no distinction between those inside the Kingdom and those outside; it does not even name them or use such terms, nor does it approve some and condemn others. It speaks of all in general, and in all cases—whether they are made for <term>fairs</term> <note>Large, seasonal international markets where merchants gathered to settle debts and trade bills of exchange.</note> or other places—it approves those that are real and just, and condemns those that are <term>dry</term> <note>original: "secos." 'Dry exchange' was a term for a fraudulent loan designed to look like a bill of exchange to bypass usury laws; no actual travel or currency exchange took place.</note> and outrageous.

For all these reasons, I believe it is certain that, speaking of <term>natural law</term> <note>A system of ethics based on human reason and the perceived order of nature, considered universal regardless of local government laws.</note>, and excluding <term>positive law</term> <note>Specific statutes or decrees enacted by a monarch or government.</note> (which, for good reasons, may provide what is most convenient for the commerce of its subjects and vassals), there is no distinction regarding the justification of exchanges within the Kingdom versus those outside. But speaking of what is just in itself, I say: they may be granted, provided that no further interest is taken. If a <term>notified letter</term> <note>original: "cedula leyda." Effective proof of this truth is what we have already said, and what all wise men confess: that in sales <term>on credit</term> <note>original: "al fiado." Buying items now to pay later, usually at a higher price.</note>, one cannot nor should not sell for more than what, in all rigor, the goods are worth <term>for cash</term> <note>original: "de contado." Immediate payment in physical currency.</note>. And just as there are two types of sales—one on credit, others for cash—it can be said that there are two types of exchanges: some to be paid immediately, others on credit. Thus, by granting them on credit, no more interest can be taken than is taken at the most for a notified note. Because if with merchandise, which is somewhat fertile by nature and which, if kept, gives hope its value will grow, it is not licit to sell it more dearly for delaying the payment, how much less appropriate is it to profit more from exchange for giving some time, the matter of this trade being money...

it, which always retains the same law, and is inherently sterile so that it does not bear fruit. <note>A common medieval and Renaissance economic theory, derived from Aristotle, holding that money is "sterile" (barren) and should not naturally breed more money through interest.</note> Much less certainly can one take into account the extension of the term in currency exchange than in sales. Furthermore, just as a sale must look to the present price, so too must the exchange follow the current valuation of the money that exists in both places where it is being exchanged. One must look at the inequality that exists in this regard now, in the place where the money is given and in the place where it is drawn; and if there is little difference, little interest can be taken, even if it is believed there will be much at the time of payment. For this reason, one cannot in any way charge more for a <term>bill at sight</term> <note>original: "letra vista." A bill of exchange payable immediately upon being presented.</note> than for one at a specified term. For even in a bill at sight, one must not consider for the interest the valuation that will exist when the document arrives, but rather the valuation that exists now, if it can be known.

They usually respond to this with one of those titles of <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucro cessante." A legal concept allowing compensation for profits that were not realized due to a delay.</note> and <term>incurred loss</term> <note>original: "daño emergente." Compensation for an actual loss or expense incurred.</note> (namely) that they cease to earn during the time they are waiting. They argue that if they were paid at the immediate fair, they would not lack someone to whom they could give money in exchange for a profit, and thus they lose out, as is evident, by giving it for the fair that follows afterward. 

But I have already responded many times to this objection, especially in the treatise on merchants and in the one on <term>usury</term>, <note>original: "usuris." The practice of charging excessive or illegal interest.</note> and I have shown that in none of these traders do these titles have a place, nor is there in them lost profit or incurred loss. This is because, just as the duty of some is to buy and sell, so that of others is to exchange—sometimes by bill at sight, other times at a certain term. Therefore, no profit ceases for him, nor does he lose anything, even if, according to his great greed, the contrary seems true to him. Nor can he—since he is currently practicing his trade, even with profit—take more interest for an <term>interim fair</term> <note>original: "feria intercalada." An unofficial or secondary trading period between major fairs.</note> than if it were not so. Whoever wishes to see this point discussed more distinctly and clearly, let him see the cited passages. ->para las ferias de España.<-

to profit. He ceases to profit, who, having the profit almost certain in one instance and close in the other, gives it up for some respect; and if he gives it up at the request of the other party, it is just that his loss be satisfied. But merely not profiting gives no one the right to charge more interest. And certainly, regarding these money changers, when they exchange across two or three fairs <note>The "ferias" or trade fairs of Spain (like those in Medina del Campo) were the primary locations for large-scale financial transactions and settling bills of exchange.</note>, it could be said that they do not profit in the second or third with the money they gave in the first; but not that they *cease* to profit, the profit being so doubtful that perhaps they would have lost it, or else so remote and distant.

It can hardly be said that he desists from profiting from this moment. For how does he desist, when he is actually persisting in his trade and office? He ceases to profit who removes his money from an investment that he already intended to make, and employs it in another contract of a distinct kind. As if, wanting to invest it in must <note>original: "mosto"; unfermented grape juice. Investing in the wine harvest was a common form of agricultural speculation.</note>, at my instance he abandoned his intent and lent it to me. But for him who exchanges at this fair—who, even by exchanging on credit for two or three fairs, is conducting his business—no profit ceases, nor does he abandon any. 

They will still say that at least he loses that opportunity, and perhaps he would have profited. I confess it, but losing this so distant venture—especially when his art <note>The "art" refers to the professional practice and expertise of the banker or merchant.</note> requires him to exchange sometimes at the next fair, other times at an intervening one—gives no right to charge interest in this exchange that he now celebrates at such a long term. For it would be to make certain and present a profit that is so dangerous and future. 

In such a way, it is a universal and infallible rule that because the terms in the exchange are longer, it is not lawful for the interest to be higher. And so it must be given for an extended time, just as for a <term>bill at sight</term> <note>A bill of exchange payable immediately upon being presented to the recipient.</note>. By this, they will understand how much better it is for them always to exchange (even if they gain little) at the shortest terms they can, for that little will result in more profit, being safe in conscience, than much earned otherwise. For (as Wisdom says) it is better to gain and have little serving God, than much in his disgrace. Truly, whoever negotiates in this way will gain temporal wealth with security, and will secure eternal wealth in his very work.

The first is from fair to fair, where both fairs take place within the same town; the other is from one town to another, such as from Naples to Genoa, or from Córdoba to Coimbra.
