# For the fairs of Spain.

...exchanges, which are often made from one fair to another. Because when money is valued and held in equal regard in both places, there is no advantage of one over the other. And since one hundred here is equal to one hundred there, taking interest would be a form of inequality—making what is equal, unequal. One cannot truly believe, nor even feign another title <note>In this context, a "title" is a legal or moral justification for taking a profit.</note> to profit, except for the exchanger waiting for that short duration of time while the other party makes use of the money in the interim; this is a quite insufficient reason.

For this reason, commonly one cannot and should not trade or exchange except "free and clear" <note>original: "horro," meaning an exchange without added fees or obligations</note>, "tit-for-tat" <note>original: "taz a raz," an idiom for an even or equal exchange</note>, equal for equal. This is because they lack the "cause and reason" that gives one the right to profit from money alone: which is the unequal valuation <term>valuation (estimacion): the fluctuating market value of a currency in different regions based on supply and demand</term> of it in different places.

These two vices are very frequent in both types of exchanges: in those made within Spain at the fairs, and in those involving Flanders or Italy. The first vice is that if a fair passes in the interim before the payment is due, the lenders profit more than they would have at the more immediate fair. This is a most blatant and proven sin, even if the exchange were not specifically from fair to fair. Because, as we have already said, it is always generally prohibited in all exchanges to take into account the passage of time and delay.

The second vice, particularly in these fair-related exchanges—even if they are for the next upcoming fair—is that interest is constantly charged. This interest should only be charged rarely and in small amounts, because in almost all these fairs, the reputation and value of gold and silver are equal. It is true that it is not very evident to everyone today that this last type of interest we condemn is illicit, although certainly, for the peace of one's conscience, it has no security. The safe and probable course is not to use them, but rather to exchange from a fair to a town where no fair is currently being held, or at a time when there is not to be one, or conversely from other places to a fair. In this way, what we primarily prohibit here is that an exchange be made from one fair to another fair in a different town when both are held at the same time. In this manner, the valuation will always be different...

-># On exchanges.<-
<meta>catchword: dry</meta>

...of the money, there will be an advantage and excess from one to the other, and one could gain interest. But this so-commonly used abuse that exists in exchanging from one fair to another cannot fail to be extremely dangerous, for being so suspicious and very close to clear usury.

In the other first way of exchanging from fair to fair within the same town, there is so much evil that it is frightening how, being most illicit, it is used so much. They are all **dry** <term>dry exchange (cambio seco): a deceptive financial transaction where a bill of exchange is issued without any intention of actually transferring funds to another location, serving only to hide a high-interest loan</term>, feigned, and pure usuries, taking interest solely for the duration of the time that the lender waits. The profit of the exchange, as we have seen, is based on one currency being worth more than another, even though both are of the same standard <note>original: "ley," referring to the purity and weight of the metal in the coins</note>. And for this to take place, the first thing required—according to the word of all the doctors <note>The "doctors" are the Scholastic theologians and jurists of the School of Salamanca who defined early economic ethics.</note>—is that there be different locations. For in one and the same town, the valuation of some ducats <term>ducat: a gold coin used as a standard for international trade and accounting</term> cannot be distinct from others, especially and mostly when one delivery and the other are made during the time of the fair, where everything is equal.

Thus, from Medina to Medina—unless it is from Rioseco to Medina del Campo <note>Medina del Campo and Medina de Rioseco were the sites of the major trade fairs in Castile.</note>—it is usury, not exchange, to trade with interest. An example and manifest proof of this is that if, in this city, one thousand ducats are given with interest to be paid here in four months, everyone without exception proclaims it as usury and an infamous business. I do not know why it should not be the same thing when the money is given in Medina to be paid in five months in that same Medina? Unless it is that Medina, Antwerp <note>original: "Enuers"</note>, Venice, and the other places where many fairs are held, have more privilege to do evil than Seville. Furthermore, it is necessary that there be a different valuation present in both places in order to be able to make a profit. For it is impossible in a single town for there to be an unequal universal reputation (as is required), since a particular individual's reputation is irrelevant and should not be considered. In addition to this, if everyone judges them to be **dry exchanges**—and as such the Apostolic See <note>The central government of the Catholic Church in Rome.</note> declares and condemns them in its decretal—when a bill is drawn on another town but the letter is not actually valid there, how much more clearly will it be a **dry exchange**...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 37 regarding "dry exchange." ->### for the fairs of Spain.<-

...**dry** from the fair of Antwerp to another in Antwerp, since not only does the bill of exchange <note>original: "letra," referring to the *letra de cambio* or bill of exchange, the standard financial instrument of the era</note> not go to another town, but no other place is even named. For this reason, all these exchanges are actually loans, and they are as evil as the interest charged on them. This is because one cannot gain more interest from one fair to another within the same location than one could by exchanging or lending from Seville to Seville, or from Lisbon to Lisbon, or from Barcelona to Barcelona. And despite these profits being pure usuries—without any mixture of good, nor anything that sounds righteous except for that name of "exchange" which they impose upon it, or rather, which they falsely attribute to it—they are the primary and largest transactions among money changers, and the bulk of their trade.

In this manner, many merchants, and all the Knights, Counts, Dukes, Princes, and Lords take loans from the May fair to the October fair—either of the same year or the one following—and often from the May fair to the next May fair. This is a more blatant iniquity and absurdity, as it is obvious they intend nothing more than to make use of the money during that time until their rents arrive from other parts or they collect their debts. Regarding the currency, there is no disparity in value, only a consistent abundance and prosperity, or penury and lack. Likewise, if the labor of transport <note>original: "porte," the cost of physically moving money, which was often used to justify exchange fees</note> contributes anything to the case—as some think and teach that a toll could exist within the same city—there is none here.

All of this is an explanation of that first point and required condition for exchanges (namely): that it must be a true and real swap, not feigned or apparent like a phantom <term>phantom: the original "estantigua" refers to a spectral procession or a "vision" that appears human but is actually "condensed air," used here as a metaphor for a fake financial contract</term> that looks like a man but is merely thick, condensed air. Of this condition and quality are all those transactions we have mentioned, despite being the largest and most profitable. They appear to be exchanges and are named as such, but it has been proven that they are mere usuries, as all authorities agree.

## CHAPTER IX. ON EXCHANGES
### Concerning the "steps," and other general conditions required in all of them.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter "T" featuring stylized floral motifs and foliage within a rectangular border.</image-desc>

THERE IS ALSO a strong suspicion and great probability that this condition is missing in all, or most, of the exchanges that the <term>merchants of the Indies<gloss>merchants involved in the trade between Spain and the Americas</gloss></term> take on these <term>steps<gloss>the "gradas" or stone steps of the Cathedral in Seville, which served as the city's open-air financial hub before the construction of a dedicated exchange building (the Lonja)</gloss></term> for the <term>fairs<gloss>large-scale seasonal markets, like those in Medina del Campo, where international debts were settled</gloss></term>, though for different reasons than those previously mentioned. And it is nothing new for a business to cease being just through various paths. For evil, there are infinite paths and ways. What makes these exchanges with <term>Indianos<gloss>Spaniards who had lived in or traded with the American colonies (the West Indies)</gloss></term> most suspicious is that they do not actually have money in Medina <note>Medina del Campo, the site of the most important trade fairs in Castile</note> to trade for the money here. Second, it is evident that they do not request these funds except to sustain themselves until the arrival of the <term>fleet<gloss>the annual convoy of ships bringing silver and goods from the Americas</gloss></term>. Third, they must ultimately come to pay them back here, all of which makes it appear to be <term>dry exchange<gloss>a deceptive financial transaction where no actual currency is exchanged between different locations; instead, it is a disguised high-interest loan intended to bypass religious bans on usury</gloss></term>, as the merchant lacks both the actual currency and the goods; nor is there a true exchange, but only from "steps to steps," where the payments must ultimately be made. Certainly, this trade is so common in this city that one fears to oppose the current by condemning it; on the other hand, it has such a poor appearance and truly so little foundation in justice that one does not dare to approve it, or at least to guarantee its safety. What can be done—so that we do not answer for the sins of others, as the saying goes, by yielding more to the corrupt desires of many than defending equity and truth—is to state what is certain in this matter, and in what is doubtful, offer the middle path that seems most probable and correct.

### On Exchanges.

Experts affirm that it is necessary—on pain of the contract being void <note>original: "seco," literally "dry," meaning the contract lacks legal or moral "juice" or validity</note>—that payments be made really and effectively at the place where the <term>bills of exchange<gloss>letras</gloss></term> are drawn. If funds are taken up again as a "re-exchange" in order to make a payment, they must not be taken from the same person—that is, from the <term>agent<gloss>factor; a business representative acting on behalf of a merchant</gloss></term> who is supposed to collect them—as is the common practice. What happens is that once the bill of exchange is received in **Medina** <note>Medina del Campo, the site of the most important financial fairs in 16th-century Spain</note>, the correspondents agree that it be "re-exchanged" by you back to **Seville**. In doing so, they employ the deception of <term>sham sales<gloss>baratas or mohatras; fraudulent contracts designed to circumvent usury laws by selling an item on credit and buying it back immediately for a lower cash price</gloss></term> which we previously discussed. In those cases, the seller "buys" his own cloth without it ever having been delivered; it is a "sale in the wind." In the same way, these merchants exchange and re-exchange the bill without any real payment ever occurring, except in words. All of this is usury, and one is obligated to make restitution for it.

Some may argue that I have left such a vital matter as the <term>exchanges on the steps<gloss>cambios de gradas; financial transactions conducted on the steps of the Seville Cathedral, the city's informal financial district</gloss></term> poorly defined and insufficiently investigated—even though this is the primary motive of this work. I respond that, instead, they should realize from this how scrupulous one must be, and how weak and lacking in moral fiber these transactions are regarding rectitude and justice. Although the primary reason I was moved to write was to address the practices used here in **Seville**, I have been unable to grant them any more validity, clarity, or security. I pray to God that this is due to my own limited knowledge, and not because these transactions lack any inherent logic or are conducted with such great malice. 

They must understand that true theologians are merely interpreters of law and equity, not legislators. They do not justify—nor should they justify—what God condemns. They are like physicians who assist nature; it is impossible for them to heal a patient whom nature and her inherent power have abandoned. Truly, earning money using nothing but money is a business so devoid of justice that great "props" are required just to keep it upright. Is there any business in the world less deserving of profit <note>original: "interes"</note> than exchange? It is a trade in currency alone, which is inherently sterile <note>The Aristotelian and Scholastic view that money does not "breed" or produce value like a crop or livestock; therefore, charging interest was seen as unnatural.</note>—a concept I explained in my <term>treatise on usury<gloss>original: "opusculo de usuris"; a Latin reference to the author's previous writings on the ethics of lending</gloss></term>.

# On the Steps.

And we desire that [our trade] be the most profitable, and that there be—as indeed happens—the greatest and most secure profits. Because of this, justice and **natural law** <term>natural law<gloss>the concept of a universal moral code accessible to human reason</gloss></term> cannot help but seem very narrow to us. We feel this way because we do not want to follow it, nor regulate ourselves by it, nor conform to it; instead, we wish to drag it violently toward our own purpose and intent. And when it cannot be moved by force, we even try to stretch and lengthen it with our own arms, or simply break and shatter it. The <term>money changers<gloss>cambiadores</gloss></term> want to trade, and do trade, with money for money with as much freedom and license as a merchant does with cloth—which can be sold and kept, always seeking a profit—because they claim money is fertile and yields fruit, as we have previously declared <note>In the medieval and early modern view, money was traditionally seen as "barren." To claim money was "fertile" (able to produce more money on its own) was often viewed as a justification for usury.</note>.

Returning to our purpose, I say that if all these circumstances are observed, one may conduct an exchange at a <term>fair<gloss>feria; a large-scale gathering for international trade and the clearing of debts</gloss></term> with the merchants of the **Indies** <note>The Spanish colonies in the Americas</note>. As long as they are settled in person, or someone pays in their name, it is in my opinion a licit business—although this opinion of mine is not founded on the **Rock of Martos** <note>original: "peña de Martus." This refers to a famous landmark in Jaén, Spain; the author is using it idiomatically to say his opinion is not an immovable, absolute dogma.</note>. It is very sobering to know that the merchant only seeks a deferment and the use of the money until the <term>ships<gloss>naos; the treasure fleets or galleons</gloss></term> arrive, and that in the end, through exchanges and re-exchanges, they must come to pay it back here. This is essentially a loan for two or three months. And in truth I believe, according to the doctrine being uncovered, that I did them no small service in not clarifying this business too much; for it is of such a nature that the more they explain it, the worse it appears. The best course would be not to give money on exchange to those who, on these **Steps** <note>The "Gradas" or steps of the Seville Cathedral, where the city's financial and commercial transactions took place before the construction of the Lonja (Exchange building).</note>, are known to have no assets or business at the fairs; and if it is done, it should be very rare. This was said while explaining the first condition required—namely, that the exchange be true and not a sham. Under this vice of "sham" are included all the cases we have related, though not with equal certainty. For the first ones were and are clearly and evidently <term>dry<gloss>secos; a term for usurious contracts that lack a real exchange of currency and exist only as a disguised loan</term></term> and false, existing only in title and name; these latter ones on the **Steps** truly have a "bad face" <note>meaning they look suspicious or lack moral integrity.</note>.

*other two conditions, and a discussion is held on re-exchanges and interest on exchanges.*

The second condition is that there be neither coercion nor deceit in the matter. The third is that there be no injustice in the interest. These are conditions well-justified in themselves. For these qualities—namely coercion, deceit, and injustice—will vitiate and corrupt any contract, no matter how sound it might have been; all the more so with exchange, a contract so **brittle** <note>original: "vedriado"; literally "glazed" or "glass-like." The author suggests that exchange contracts are morally fragile and easily broken or corrupted compared to more straightforward trades.</note> that it has so little strength and sinew of virtue. There are other businesses so inherently just that they can withstand certain circumstances that are not very reasonable, for their minor malice is overcome and undone by the great justice of the main endeavor. But the substance of exchange, in its rectitude and equity, is so delicate that it is necessary to support it with one's arms, dressing it in such circumstances and conditions that its own rectitude keeps it upright; much less should one join it with such evils as deceit or coercion.

Regarding these, it must be noted that under good law, it is neither suffered nor permitted that the interest of the lender should increase in proportion to the need of the borrower. Second, for the <term>money changers<gloss>cambiadores</gloss></term> to set prices and market rates, or to form any **monopoly** <term>monipodio<gloss>a conspiracy or agreement between merchants to fix prices or control a market</gloss></term> in this business, is to bid farewell to heaven. But these two points were already noted in the previous chapter.

Even so, it is a form of **usury** <note>The charging of any interest on a loan, which was traditionally considered a sin in Catholic social teaching.</note> so widespread that there is nothing else in the trade. <header>On the conditions of exchanges</header>

...this business is such that if a <term>bill of exchange<gloss>cedula</gloss></term> is issued to Toledo and no correspondent was found to pay it, or if there was one but he did not accept it, or if he accepted but did not pay on time: they are accustomed in all three of these cases to "re-exchange" it immediately, adding damages and interest, to the place where it was originally sent. In this manner, and under this condition, they <term>exchange<gloss>cambian</gloss></term>—though we would more properly and truthfully say they "commit usury"—with high-ranking gentlemen for three-month terms, knowing full well they will not be paid for an entire year. For this reason, to ensure their own profit, they make their pact and agreement that if the bill is not paid at the appointed time, the merchant may re-exchange it. The merchant then takes the greatest care—namely—to send it every three months to his <term>agent<gloss>factor</gloss></term>, and the agent to return it to him re-exchanged, as if it were some portion of taxes or rents. 

And while the poor <term>heir<gloss>mayorazgo</gloss></term> <note>The heir to an entailed family estate. This is the sole, or at least the greatest, "woodworm" <note>original: "carcoma"; a wood-boring pest that symbolizes how debt silently and steadily hollows out a family's wealth.</note> of the great revenues and the many millions belonging to the lords, who go into debt at this Court for their follies to the tune of fifty or one hundred thousand <term>ducats<gloss>ducados</gloss></term>, which they cannot later pay off even with fifty thousand more. This vice in exchange is pernicious and contains (as we shall see) many evils. In itself, even if it stood alone, it is illicit and usurious; all the more so when accompanied by the many wicked circumstances that surround it.

The first point is that to re-exchange the bill as soon as it is not paid, when no express agreement has preceded it because the failure to pay was not suspected (as sometimes happens), is not to exchange, but to rob. ## On the conditions of exchanges

...their profit is so certain and revolving that it never fails, when it should be quite the opposite—highly subject to faults and shortfalls. This is because the business is conducted solely with <term>currency<gloss>moneda</gloss></term>: a material very unfit for multiplying or being traded by itself without being invested in some type of <term>merchandise<gloss>ropa</gloss></term> <note>Literally "clothing" or "cloth," but used here as a general term for physical commodities. The author is echoing the Aristotelian and Scholastic view that money is "sterile" and should not produce more money through interest alone.</note>. Furthermore, the majority of this trade consists of bills of exchange, credit, and trust; and while this trust is and ought to be great, in the end, it not infrequently fails.

Aside from this: one of the first conditions necessary for a contract is that the parties involved consent to it, even formally and expressly, when they are able. And since in this act of "re-exchanging," the [debtor] party neither consented nor was requested to do so, this second re-exchange—which you carry out over there with your bills—is utterly forced and involuntary. Furthermore, if this re-exchange is to be a true contract, it must necessarily be between two people: one who receives and obligates himself to pay, and another who gives. These are missing here, as there is no one but the <term>money-exchanger<gloss>cambiador</gloss></term> himself, or his <term>agent<gloss>factor</gloss></term>, which amounts to the same thing. The first exchange had multiple parties and could have been a true contract, but this second one lacks them. To these arguments, which are so effective, there is no solution but to clearly confess that these are neither exchanges nor contracts; they simply do it so that their profit does not cease. And thus, the debtor pays them more than they could have perhaps gained through legitimate ventures. But I will soon show how frivolous this excuse is, and how it is entirely tyranny and grievance.

And it is very much to be noted that re-exchanging adds an even greater grievance: they also re-exchange with interest. A bill came from Barcelona to Lisbon, and no man appears to speak for it, or he does not accept it, or he does not pay; it is then re-exchanged back to Barcelona with two or three percent interest. This is something more than cruel and inhuman—it is most unjust, because the lender carries it out against all reason and without any foundation. Firstly, if there is a currency advantage of one or two percent from there to here, how is it that you also find a similar advantage in the opposite direction, from Lisbon to Barcelona, and re-exchange with two and three percent interest? Certainly, you would be strangely deluded if some madman wanted to find a basis for it; but his strangeness and wonder cease as soon as one under- <note>The text ends mid-word with the catchword "entiẽ-", which would complete the sentence "as soon as one understands..." on the following page.</note>

# On the conditions of exchanges.

...it is understood that the business is not conducted by reason. In this very thing they do, they clearly show that they do not take into account in their <term>exchanges<gloss>cambios</gloss></term> the value and reputation of money in those places where and for which they conduct them; rather, they look only to the necessity suffered by the <term>miserable petitioner<gloss>mísero-postulante</gloss></term> <note>This refers to the borrower or debtor who is "petitioning" for credit out of financial desperation.</note>. Instead, your <term>agent<gloss>factor</gloss></term> (with whom I speak as if you are both one and the same) should have to re-exchange at a loss, since he is exchanging from Lisbon, where it is worth less, to Barcelona, where it is currently valued at more.

And they are often even pleased when the <term>bill<gloss>cedula</gloss></term> <note>A bill of exchange or promissory note.</note> arrives and is not paid, considering the interest to be more certain and immediate that way. Indeed, I have seen them not even present the bill, or if presented, ask for payment with such lukewarmness and indifference that they make it understood they will wait, only to catch the debtors off guard through their own neglect and pretense. We see in the trade of <term>merchandise<gloss>mercancía</gloss></term> that when selling on credit, more than twenty days commonly pass after the deadline, and if they are not paid so quickly, they wait, they ask, and they urge, and only after all this do they take legal action. These are the troubles, risks, and dangers that human business and contracts naturally bring with them.

For dealing with men is not the same as negotiating with good angels, who never lie or fail. Certainly, I cannot say with modesty—and for that reason I leave it in silence—how bold this license is which the Exchangers take in making their regular and infallible trade so contrary to justice. In Seville, one might well carry off a thousand, and nine hundred and twenty there are worth as much as a thousand here; but within the same city, it cannot be anything but **usury**, or something very similar to it.

They say it is like a penalty already understood in all exchanges, especially those involving foreigners. For this reason, they ask for a bank or a guarantor to pay them if the payment is not made where the <term>bill is issued<gloss>donde se libra</gloss></term>. I say that this is precisely what we are showing to be **illicit**: namely, the imposition of a penalty so rigid, harsh, and excessive—much more than what is permitted. Especially since this is not an imperial or royal decree, nor is it authorized by law, but only by their own authority (which is none), and by their own will (which is corrupt), and by their own greed (which is exorbitant and blind).

If the penalty were moderate—that is to say, if the <term>correspondent<gloss>correspondiente</gloss></term> <note>The person or bank designated to pay the bill at its destination.</note> failed to pay, and the lender received one-fifth of the interest or something similar there—it would be tolerable and safe in conscience. But that they should pay the entire exchange in full is a desire to practice usury, not exchange. Above all, this tyranny provides them an excuse for the rigor they apply when collecting once the <term>bill of exchange<gloss>letra</gloss></term> is received; and when the deadline arrives, they will not wait fifteen or twenty days. This is because they prefer the bill *not* to be collected, as it is very profitable for them to collect the entire quantity there in **Antwerp** <note>Original: "Enuers".</note>, or in Genoa, or in Florence, or in Rome, where they earn more.

The whole business is **outrageous** <note>Original: "desaforado," meaning lawless or exceeding all reasonable bounds.</note>. # On the conditions of exchanges

...like his companions, the merchants, who must go to collect with some effort. If the person designated <note>The "correspondent" or person intended to pay the bill at its destination.</note> is not there, or does not accept the bill, the merchant cannot "re-exchange" it. Instead, he must return it to the person who sent it, and that person should collect according to this doctrine. This is what we note regarding this abuse: the practice of collecting the exchange in full at the place where it was first made, if it is not paid at the place where it was <term>issued<gloss>donde se libra</gloss></term>.

Until now we have dealt with these <term>re-exchanges<gloss>recambios</gloss></term> <note>A "re-exchange" occurred when a bill was not paid at its destination, and a new bill was issued to return the funds, usually at a much higher cost to the borrower.</note> in cases where they were not agreed upon at the start. But what shall we say if it was specifically agreed upon, and the party consented to it? Certainly, the consent of the one who suffers the loss does not give the other party any more right to it—assuming the act is illicit in itself—any more than a borrower’s consent to his own loss gives a right to a <term>usurer<gloss>usurero</gloss></term>. If someone borrows two thousand <term>escudos<gloss>escudos</gloss></term> <note>A gold coin widely used in the 16th century.</note> with the condition that if he does not pay within three months, the interest will increase, it does not stop being **usury**, even if it was consented to. For there is no difference between these two types of contracts, and thus both are usurious.

Consent might perhaps make the re-exchanges less violent and involuntary, but it does not stop them from being unjust and void. Because consent does not take away the malice from an unjust business. For if it is an injustice to sell on credit for more than the cash price, it is not justified simply because the other person buys of his own will. This is especially true when it is evident (as it is) that the borrower does not consent except very much against his will. Who, unless compelled by pure necessity, would consent to such great losses? Even if at times this "necessity" is brought on by pure vanity. And that the business is illicit in its own right is most manifest, since it is clearly a <term>dry exchange<gloss>cambio seco</gloss></term> <note>A "dry exchange" was a financial trick where a loan was disguised as a foreign currency exchange, even though no money actually left the city, purely to hide interest charges.</note> and a feigned one, there being no real payment involved in it. It would be a very laughable thing if, just because a person wanted it so, a painted man could become a real man. In the same way, it is laughable that, by mere consent, a "dry" exchange could become a real exchange.

Item: to understand how this entire business of exchanges consists of loans and usury, and a pretense only to [gain]...

# On the conditions of exchanges

In this way, whether the exchange rates in the kingdom rise or fall, those rates remain regular and stable. Which is to say, in <note>original: "en buen romance"</note> plain English, it is simply a loan and an agreement for the duration of the time they wait. 

All of this has now been newly condemned as **usury** and declared as such by the <term>Apostolic See<gloss>sede apostólica</gloss></term> <note>The Papacy in Rome.</note>, and ordered under heavy penalties not to be done. Because [the See] commands that no interest be agreed upon at the start of the contract, nor afterward in the event that the bill is not honored. Thus, it forbids the parties from agreeing that the bill be re-exchanged at a specific interest rate, or at whatever the market rate may be over there, if the <term>document<gloss>police</gloss></term> is not fulfilled. And if one cannot re-exchange by agreeing to it beforehand, how much less can they do so without a prior agreement? That would be much worse, for it would be suffering [the loss] by force.

To all these injustices, regarding both re-exchanges and the <term>transfer of notes<gloss>remisiones de cédulas</gloss></term>, these dealers respond that if it were not done this way, there would be infinite defaults, and everyone would dare to ask for money and <term>issue on the wind<gloss>librar en el viento</gloss></term> <note>A phrase meaning to draw a bill of exchange without having funds or credit at the destination; essentially writing a "bad check" or engaging in speculative credit.</note>, knowing that no harm would come to them for it. But as it is currently practiced—where failure to pay is at the borrower's own expense—everyone watches what they do. They also allege that they exchange under this condition accepted by both parties: that it is now like a law of trade, confirmed by the ancient and inviolable custom that has always been held. I refute the first of these excuses: if the exchangers maintained the justice and equity I have described by not re-exchanging, they would be more careful about those with whom they deal...

Consequently, this penalty must not be as much as the changer thinks he could have earned during that time by making other exchanges (for that falls under the other title of "lost profit," which we shall discuss shortly). Furthermore, if a large penalty were set, it would open the door for those same re-exchanges—that is, for those same interest rates—simply by changing the form of the contract or replacing the word "re-exchange" with "penalty." Instead, it must be (as I said) a very small amount, such as a sixth or a fifth of the interest.

Someone might say that this is opening the door to **usury**, because under the name of "penalty," they will set a rate high enough to serve as sufficient interest for the entire delay. It seems to me that we should not fear this. Therefore, the certain thing is to leave it undecided for when it occurs, binding oneself at the start to satisfy all damages and losses that may arise.

First, he does not have to satisfy him for the full amount, for the reasons alleged, but at most half. Second, many times the exchange is made with a loss, other times with a saving. And in those cases, the debtor will not be obligated to anything.

Thus, if he likely understood that he was not to be paid, and yet still made the exchange, he cannot lawfully claim the title of lost profit, nor for this reason may he re-exchange the bill, nor agree to it in this way at the beginning; for they hardly explain it except when they see that it really is not going to be paid. And for the very same reason that they understand it, if they celebrate the contract, they lose the right to the title of lost profit. 

And it is very noteworthy that this title of lost profit is not prohibited in modern <term>canon law<gloss>ley pontifical</gloss></term>. Because it is natural law to pay for the damage a man does to his neighbor. His Holiness does not exempt the one who takes an exchange from this obligation. What he forbids is that it be agreed upon at the beginning or afterward, before the amount [of damage] has occurred; rather, it should be left so that if one party really suffered through the fault of the other, he is satisfied after he has suffered, with the moderations we set out above.

If the <term>money changer<gloss>cambiador</gloss></term> understood and knew through moral conjectures that he was not to be paid there, either because the bill was not to be accepted, or if accepted, not fulfilled, and still made the exchange, thus the fault and the damage that came to him must be attributed to himself. He cannot re-exchange, nor charge the other anything, except to recover what he disbursed, and learn his lesson for another day by not putting himself so deliberately in danger. However, he can and should demand that he be satisfied for the damage and loss he has incurred because of the other party, who by withholding his money, prevented him from making one or several profitable exchanges.

Although, as the law very rightly says, this should not be everything he *could* have gained, nor should it be paid as fully as those who pay themselves by making "perfect re-exchanges" at the debtor's expense. Instead, considering the circumstances occurring in terms of time, place, and persons, one should arbitrate and assign an amount to be restored on top of the original debt. Sometimes this will be a small amount, and sometimes, when everything is well-considered, it will result in nothing at all.

This satisfaction and recompense is so consistent with reason, and so due by right, that even if the money-changer does not ask for it, the one who received the money remains obligated in conscience to pay it. This is understood to apply not only when the money was not given or the <term>bill<gloss>letra</gloss></term> was not accepted, but even when it was collected with great costs, trickery, and significant delays.

But for a delay of fifteen or twenty days, it is extremely rigorous to become annoyed and demand that the money never cease to earn profit for even a single moment. That is a very great cruelty and inhumanity, and no small injustice. There must be <term>civility<gloss>Vrbandad</gloss></term> and good order in business, and a giving of space to the man who is settling his affairs, if one wants God to give him space for penance. 

Thus, it is never lawful to re-exchange the <term>bill of exchange<gloss>librança</gloss></term>, yet it is always lawful for damages and losses suffered due to not paying on time to be paid and satisfied. This is provided the particulars I mentioned are considered: namely, if there was someone ready and certain to give the money to in exchange over there, or if, because of the failure to pay, the creditor incurred expenses to fulfill certain debts he had planned to meet with that money, along with other small matters of this sort. These specific details are easy to notice and weigh in individual cases, but in general, they cannot be fully grasped. And it was found—

# On the conditions of exchanges.

...future, which does not give the money-changers any right in conscience to take it, any more than to a usurer. This is understood with the aforementioned moderation, provided it is not evident from the start that [the payment] is destined to fail. There is another greater injustice in this business, certainly grim and frightening, which is that they not only <term>re-exchange the bill<gloss>recambian la letra</gloss></term> for the principal, but with interest. In plain English <note>original: "en buen romance"; literally "in good Romance," an idiom meaning to speak clearly or plainly.</note>, this is taking usury upon usury—interest condemned by all laws. For example <note>original: "V. g.", abbreviation for the Latin *verbi gratia*.</note>, they gave a thousand <term>ducats<gloss>ducados</gloss></term> <note>A gold coin used for trade throughout Europe.</note> in exchange for Burgos, at two percent, which is one thousand and twenty; if he does not pay them, he re-exchanges the full thousand and twenty, and they keep adding interest to the principal, everything earning profit through their re-exchanges. In such a way that, without being felt, before one realizes it, the debt has grown more than a weed. By this path, they publicly rob estates without [human] punishment, but not without God’s—spiritual and temporal, present and future. Because it is a path of sinning and increasing guilt, making the required <term>restitution<gloss>restitución</gloss></term> <note>The theological obligation to return ill-gotten gains to the victim as a requirement for the forgiveness of sins.</note> even larger; without it, they cannot convert, and without converting, they will pay in the end in body and soul. And even in this life, they enjoy their gains so poorly that, where they least expect it, God ordains that they lose them. And their profit is already so infamous that I rightly excuse myself from showing how ugly and abominable it is, for there is no one who is ignorant of it. And it is such a cruel profit that, although <term>civil law<gloss>derecho civil</gloss></term> tolerates usury, it cannot abide this "usury upon usury"; it abominates and punishes such cruelty with the most severe penalties: one of which is to condemn as infamous whoever commits this vice.

The money-changers themselves (who are not currently very heartless) do not have hands large enough to hold so much interest. In this, a very timely opportunity presents itself to discover the certain rule of what may be earned through changing money, and once discovered, to understand it clearly.

We all know that for an exchange to be licit, one must not have respect for the time by which the payment is delayed. Just as in selling on credit, one must not consider the terms granted, but rather what the merchandise is worth at present. Thus, in an exchange, one must only take into account how the currency is currently valued in the places where it is drawn and where it is sent, and the inequality that exists between them. This is an easy thing to understand by the exchanges that are made in both places. For example <note>original: "V. G.", an abbreviation for the Latin *verbi gratia*.</note>, an exchange is now made from Medina to Seville at a loss of two percent, because this city is more "tight" <note>Meaning a lack of liquid cash or high demand for currency.</note> than the fair itself. Whoever gives one hundred <term>ducats<gloss>ducados</gloss></term> <note>A standard gold coin used in international trade.</note> in Medina, receives ninety-eight in Seville; from which it is concluded that currency is valued more in Seville today than at the fair by two percent, or at most three. By which it is convincingly evidenced that from Seville to Medina, one cannot give an exchange except with a two or three percent advantage, provided it is delivered to the upcoming October fair. Which, if it is...

# On the conditions of the exchanges.

...the truth (as it is) is that one must only weigh and follow the differing or equal value that is currently circulating in both places. And if they charge fourteen [percent], it is because of how long they think the <term>fair<gloss>feria</gloss></term> will be delayed. 

Another reason reveals this same usury. Let the money-changers ask themselves: if they were asked for, and gave, an exchange to Medina <note>Medina del Campo was the most important financial center in 16th-century Spain, famous for its international trade fairs.</note> at <term>sight<gloss>letra viſta</gloss></term> <note>A 'bill at sight' is a payment order that must be paid immediately upon being presented, rather than at a later date.</note> without waiting for the fair, would they take much less interest than they currently do? They cannot help but confess the reduction they would make. By this they will be convinced, even without a scholar's help, that the extra amount they charge is due to the delay. The clear resolution to this tangle is that (just as we say regarding <term>sales<gloss>vendiciõ</gloss></term>) "the cash price is the rule for credit": likewise, in exchanging, the lawful interest for a bill at sight to a certain place is the infallible level for what may justly be earned at that time when exchanging for that place. This applies even if the payment is deferred for six months or until the fair; one should not take into account the value the currency will have at the time of payment, but rather the present value for both parties. And this interest for a bill at sight will be easily known by noting the remittances coming from there, and what is lost when sending money back here. For if there is a loss from there, money will be <term>tighter<gloss>eſtrecho</gloss></term> <note>In this context, 'tight' refers to a lack of liquidity or a scarcity of available cash in the market.</note> there than here; and thus the state of both marketplaces will be known.

Likewise, those exchanges are neither substantial nor real which are made from fair to fair, when both fairs are held within the same place—such as from the May fair to the October fair—if they were given with an advantage <note>The "advantage" refers to an added profit or interest rate built into the exchange.</note> and not <term>free<gloss>horro</gloss></term> <note>The term "horro" implies a transaction free of interest or additional financial burdens.</note>. Beyond these which are "dry" and feigned, there are others that, even if they were real and true, are unjust—as we treat extensively in the discourse of this work—either due to the deceits and <term>monopolies<gloss>monipodios</gloss></term> that are formed, or because of the high interests that are demanded and taken.

We require only three conditions for <term>exchanges<gloss>cambios</gloss></term> of whatever quality and condition they may be. The first is that they possess the being and nature of an exchange, and not only the name and epithet, like a "painted man" who is nothing more than a man in figure and appearance. When this nature is lacking, the exchange is "dry" <note>A "dry exchange" (cambio seco) was a common 16th-century term for a loan disguised as a currency exchange to circumvent laws against usury (charging interest).</note>. The second is that it be without deceit or violence, in which others also sin. The third is that it be moderate and just; that is, that the interest be compassionate, humane, not excessive, nor measured by the necessity of the other party. Because, as all theologians say, for a thing to be good, it is necessary that nothing it requires be missing from it. Thus, it is necessary for the exchange to be licit that it possess all three conditions. If any one of them is missing, it is vitiated and corrupted. For this reason, they affirm that out of every three parts made, two are illicit, vicious, and condemned.

This doctrine and these rules of ours, if compared and contrasted with the dissolution <note>Here, "dissolution" refers to the breakdown of moral standards or the "looseness" of ethical behavior in the marketplace.</note> that exists in trade, I see well will seem narrow or scrupulous. However, if measured against truth and justice, I hold them to be an equal match; and also if one observes and notes what everyone is already whispering. And we well know how true the proverb is: "The public verdict and voice are usually founded on much truth." The injustice and grievances that exist in this business are now so grave that no one is ignorant of them, and so tyrannical that everyone is amazed at how the republic, princes, and kings tolerate it. Furthermore, the truth in this matter is that the trade is in itself lawful <term>licit: legally and morally permissible according to Canon Law</term> if it is done well and no injustice is committed. Thus, if the Church were to involve herself in it, this alone would have to be her decree and determination. Because responding in detail to every individual case as to whether it is just or unjust does not befit the sacred majesty and authority of a council. Firstly, because they are almost infinite; secondly, many of them are doubtful, and the council determines nothing except what is certain, which it draws and gathers from Scripture or from apostolic traditions, or which shines forth in natural law <term>natural law: a system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than the rules of society</term>. Thus, it is not fitting for the council to meddle in this dark forest. In such an exchange, there can be no profit. From this it follows that there must be, at the very least, a difference in valuation. This valuation cannot be common and universal (as is required) within a single town, nor even in those very close by. For this reason, it is necessary that these exchanges be carried out between different locations. And where this is lacking, it cannot be a true exchange <term>cambio real: a financial transaction involving different currencies or locations, often scrutinized to distinguish it from a hidden interest-bearing loan</term>, but rather a petty exchange <note>original: "menudo"</note> or actual loans; and if interest is involved, they will be true usuries. ## Decretal regarding currency exchanges.

...ere it was issued and sought. These [bills] are returned just as they were sent, without being collected. Likewise, [it is condemned] when they provide exchanges to many merchants who have no assets at the fairs <term>fairs: major international trading events, such as those in Medina del Campo, where debts were settled</term>, nor do they intend to take the money for any reason other than to buy time until they can collect elsewhere, or until the fleet arrives. Because the bills of exchange for these people also end up being paid here [at home]. Here are included all those exchanges made with **letters in the wind** <term>letters in the wind: fictitious bills of exchange backed by no real goods or credit, used as a cover for high-interest loans</term> between the exchanger and his agent—sometimes with the permission of the one who drew the money, and other times without it. This is also condemned in another paragraph further below. Because they always end up being paid in the same place where they were written, or in a nearby one, and not where the bill was [supposedly] issued. 

The reasoning upon which this Decretal <term>Decretal: a papal decree that establishes a rule of canon law</term> is based was explained extensively above. And regarding what someone might say: "Why must I lose out because the other person is a scoundrel?" or "What can I gain in case the payment fails?" There we noted that it was very relevant for claiming some interest, in case the bill was not fulfilled, whether the exchanger knew or strongly suspected <note>original: "sospechaua de vehemẽti," from the Latin legal term 'vehementi'</note> from the start that the settlements <note>original: "quitanças," referring to the formal discharge of debts</note> were not going to be fulfilled there. Or if he truly believed they would be collected. For if he knew of the failure to pay, he cannot claim any interest under any of these pretenses <note>original: "colores," meaning legal justifications or appearances</note>, much less the interest of the exchange itself. 

But if he did not know, he may claim—not the interest of the exchange he made (for it is not truly an exchange if it is collected in the same place)—but either the penalty agreed upon between the two, or the damages he incurred due to the failure [of payment]. We shall speak of this below, declaring how this decretal permits one to have this interest, and under what conditions it is licit. However, on this point, I must offer a new warning: that if the one who took the exchange knew his bills would not be fulfilled, he remains liable for damages. But if he issued the bill to a person who usually pays their notes <term>notes: "cedulas," formal written promises to pay a debt</term> (so that just as the giver conducted the business in good faith, the receiver also issued the bill believing his factor <term>factor: a business agent or representative who managed affairs for a merchant in a distant city</term> would fulfill it), then he is much less liable.

# Decretal regarding exchanges.

## All such contracts we declare to be usurious: and we strictly prohibit them from being made in the future.

This encompasses two <term>vices: moral failings or illegal abuses of a system</term>. The first is when, for a higher interest, one performed the exchange from the beginning at longer terms. For example, if for the immediate <term>fair: a seasonal international market where financial settlements occurred</term>, or at four months, the rate is three [percent], but one charges six [percent] for the <term>mediate fair: the second fair in a sequence</term>, or at eight months. The second vice is when, once the exchange has been made for a certain fair or a specific time, it is prolonged without being collected for a new additional interest, moving the first amount to another fair or for more time. And this is precisely what is condemned in this paragraph. For it says that for new interest, the already established deadline is extended. In this, it seems it does not speak of the first abuse—where from the beginning a higher interest is given for a longer term—but rather when a term that was already set is prolonged. This happens in two ways: either by agreeing to it this way at the beginning—*You shall pay at such a deadline, and if not, it will run for your account, with so much more interest for so much more time until you pay.* Within this are enclosed all those abuses and evils of <term>recambios: the practice of "re-exchanging" a bill of exchange back and forth between markets to compound interest and fees</term> which we explained in the tenth chapter. This occurs when the exchanger keeps sending and receiving the other's <term>letter: a bill of exchange</term> with new interests. Because in all of them, the payment is delayed for a new interest, even though it was sometimes agreed at the beginning to give this new interest every so many months that the exchange remained unpaid; however, it does not stop being "new" each time it is added, and it is prohibited in this paragraph.

The second way is when, the payment not being made at the appointed time, the parties or their <term>factors: business agents or representatives</term> negotiate anew: *let it be re-exchanged for you to such a place.* And since the text says that this trickery is used in <term>real exchanges: transactions involving the actual transfer of funds between different locations</term> and condemns it along with the other <term>dry exchanges: purely financial loans disguised as currency exchanges to evade usury laws</term> explained above as usurious, they will understand that...

...in it, I do no more than tell it, and manifest to the people,

those who have taken them before now. Because they

Firstly, because making these <term>dry exchanges: a fraudulent contract that appeared to be a foreign currency exchange but was actually a local loan at high interest</term>, or real ones, more usurious is

nor secular, determines it, it is consequently forbidden.
Secondly, because it was known and understood before now to be evil.
And both the one and the other reason oblige the return of what was wrongly taken.
For which reason, it is not enough for one to abstain now from such profit;
it is necessary to return to its owner what was obtained in such
exchanges, for being ill-gotten.

From all these exchanges that the Pope declares and condemns
here as "dry," they shall draw a general rule: That every
time the money is collected in the same place where
it was given, it is a dry exchange. Because in all these modes that
he relates, he specifies this: that it is collected where it was disbursed.
And this same thing he gives as the reason and cause for it being usurious.
But someone will ask: Why is it usury to collect the exchange in the
same place, since usury is lending, not exchanging?
I respond that every time it is collected so, the exchange is actually
a loan; wherein if any interest is taken, it is clearly usury.
But if it had been an equal exchange, one for one, it would not be
illicit to collect it in the same town. Just as it is not
prohibited to lend without interest, and collect the loan in the
same house, much less in the same city.

And if every dry exchange (which is another universal rule of
all the <term>doctors: highly learned scholars of law and theology</term>, which is also gathered from this same
<term>decretal: a papal decree that forms part of Canon Law</term>) is usury, there follows another teaching no
less common: That he cannot take interest for exchange,
who collects the <term>bill: a "poliça" or formal document used to claim payment</term> in the place where he entered the exchange.

## Decretal regarding the exchanges

Furthermore, in this <term>decretal: a papal decree that provides a ruling on canon law</term>, the Apostolic See speaks of all exchanges in general. It does not distinguish between those made outside the kingdom and those within. As we see, the word "kingdom" does not appear in the entire text, nor does it approve one type more than the other. It deals with all of them universally. And in all of them, it condemns "dry" and truly usurious exchanges, while approving those that are just.

*And to remove, with divine favor, all occasions for sin and the deceptions of usurers, we establish that from now on, no one shall dare to agree at the beginning, or afterward, that they be given some certain interest, even in the case that the payment fails.*

Here begins the second principal part of the decretal, which is almost entirely concerned with <term>positive law: laws established by human authority (like the Church or State) rather than by nature alone</term>. It contains three just, certain, and necessary propositions or statutes; whoever observes them will save themselves from a thousand <term>scruples: moral anxieties or doubts about whether an action is a sin</term> in their financial exchanges.

In this first part, it is forbidden to agree—either at the start or afterward—on a fixed interest rate. This refers to an amount distinct from the first real exchange being conducted at that time. This prohibition applies whether the interest is sought through <term>re-exchange: a secondary transaction used to extend a loan</term>, or as <term>lost profit: compensation for money one could have made elsewhere</term>, or <term>accrued damage: compensation for actual losses suffered</term>, or in any other case, even if the <term>letters: formal financial documents or bills of exchange</term> are not honored.

In this clause, all excessive measures are prohibited—or to put it better, the great greed of certain <term>money changers: individuals who exchanged different currencies, often acting as early bankers</term> is restrained. These individuals wish to profit from money using only money in such a way that it never ceases to produce "fruit" <note>In this context, "fruit" refers to interest or profit generated by capital.</note> for a single moment, month, or day. They tie up their dealings with so many conditions that the contract looks more like a <term>will: a legal document expressing a person's final wishes for their property</term> and testament, where one usually arranges and provides for every possible eventuality—

<term>Positive law</term>: Man-made laws.
<term>Re-exchange</term>: A method of rolling over a debt.
<term>Lost profit</term>: original: "lucro cessante"; compensation for missed opportunities.
<term>Accrued damage</term>: original: "danno emergente"; compensation for direct losses.
<term>Money changers</term>: Early bankers and currency traders.
<term>Will</term>: A legal testament.

It is necessary to know what will be done if your respondent is absent, or if being present they delay the payment until another <term>fair: a periodic gathering for trade where bills of exchange were typically settled</term>, or if they do not pay at all—along with other claims of this tone, such as <term>lost profit: <note>original: "lucro cessante"</note> the profit one fails to make because their capital was tied up</term>, and particularly and principally <term>actual loss: <note>original: "daño emergente"</note> the specific financial damage incurred by the lender due to the borrower's default</term>. They constantly lament these losses, saying they were supposed to make certain payments with that money, and that their credit will "limp" if it is missing. In these declarations (as they call them), though they are more properly described as exactions—not born of prudence and wisdom, but of astuteness and greed—they always try to come away with some new interest. In this way, they argue: "if your representative is absent, mine may <term>re-exchange: a secondary transaction to recover funds when a bill of exchange is not paid at its destination</term> the money," or "if payment is deferred, for every two months a certain amount, such as three percent," and so on with the rest. Regarding all of these, I have already treated extensively which are lawful and unlawful, at least according to <term>natural law: a system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than the rules of society</term>. And above all, I have shown that conducting re-exchanges with the letters of others, and taking interest on them, was in itself very evil—whether the factor is absent or the payment is deferred. And if a re-exchange cannot be agreed upon at the beginning, it can even less be re-exchanged without first having an agreement. It is an even greater injustice to force a re-exchange not consented to by the party involved.

All these evils, and others no less significant, are cut short by this Papal law. Because the money changer, seeing that they cannot secure or agree upon interest at the beginning, nor afterward even if the <term>bill of exchange: <note>original: "poliça"</note> a written order used in international trade that binds one party to pay a fixed sum of money to another party at a predetermined future date</term> is not fulfilled, will look carefully at whom they trade their money with, and will give it to those they know will pay. Their exchanges will be brief and real. They will avoid all these entanglements, into which they voluntarily enter, knowing they must profit whether the payment is made immediately or left unpaid.

For this reason, since the law here only prohibits interest, it is not understood to prohibit a penalty. Regarding the interest that is claimed, sometimes under the title of **lost profit** <note>original: "lucro cessante"</note> or **actual loss** <note>original: "daño emergente"</note>, it is absolutely forbidden here to set any price or rate for it before it actually happens. Such as if one truly ceased to earn a profit, or if one incurred damage from not collecting. For many times there was nothing certain in which to gain even if one had collected, nor does one lose anything even if one does not collect. This very principle is the secure and certain part of natural law: that neither profit nor damage should be compensated except when it truly ceased or was suffered because of me. And since it is not owed except when it is truly incurred, it is with good reason that setting a fixed rate is forbidden until it is actually incurred. # Decretal regarding the exchanges

Whoever was the cause [of a loss] is obligated to pay for it (an obligation of **natural law** <note>Natural law refers to a system of ethics believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, rather than just man-made laws.</note>), from which **His Holiness** <note>referring to the Pope</note> does not exempt him, nor could he even justly exempt him. On the other hand, the amount to be paid can and should be very well appraised. And if the <term>decretal: a papal decree that forms part of Canon Law</term> says that no certain interest should be agreed upon, neither at the beginning nor afterward, this "afterward" is understood to be between the beginning of the exchange and before the damage actually occurs. For example, if the exchange happened yesterday, the law commands that no agreement be made today or tomorrow, and so on for further time, until the event [the loss] actually requires it. And it was necessary to add "nor afterward" to avoid malice, as people would otherwise think of defrauding the law by securing themselves through two contracts—since they could not do it in one—by making the second contract after the exchange had already been celebrated.

Nor should anyone dare to practice <term>Real exchanges: <note>original: "cambios Reales"</note> transactions involving the physical delivery of currency or specific bills of exchange</term> when they are made for <term>fairs: <note>In this era, international banking and debt settlement occurred at specific seasonal trade fairs, such as those in Medina del Campo or Lyon.</note></term> in any way other than for the first upcoming fairs. And when funds are sent to a place outside of a fair, the received use and custom of that place regarding deadlines must be observed, completely discarding that abuse of exchanging for an "intercalated" fair (skipping to the second or third upcoming fair) or for secondary deadlines. Respect should be given to the distance of the place where funds are sent when setting the deadlines. Because if deadlines are set longer than the distance requires, it provides an occasion for <term>usury: the practice of charging excessive or illegal interest on a loan</term>.

## Decretal on exchanges.

# Whoever violates this law of ours should know that they incur the penalties that the sacred Canons <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church authority (Canon Law).</note> impose upon usurers.

This is the second precept, or statute, of this second part, where the Pope commands that the payment terms be short. In this, **His Holiness** cuts short and prunes the great evils of <term>re-exchanges: <note>original: "recambios"; a practice of repeatedly renewing a bill of exchange to extend a loan, often hiding high interest.</note></term> and very costly usury. These could not be prevented by any other means. For to tell one of these merchants who deals in long-term exchanges to earn only as much as if he gave it for a short term is very harsh and "barbaric" language to their ears, even if it is the absolute truth. Because, as we have seen, one could not in good conscience charge more interest by exchanging for an <term>intermediate fair <note>original: "feria mediata"; a fair occurring two cycles away rather than the next immediate one.</note></term> than for an immediate one, nor for long terms than for <term>sight drafts <note>original: "letra vista"; a bill of exchange that is payable immediately upon being presented.</note></term>. And I believe there is no person who observes this. Instead, the more time they understand their money is to be held, the more interest they pretend to claim.

For this reason, it is a most wise method for extirpating these forms of usury to dry up the spring from which they flow, which is long terms. Because by having the power to exchange in this manner, one can humanly expect an amendment of these usuries, just as has been established in <term>selling on credit <note>original: "vender al fiado".</note></term>. And long-term exchanging and long-term credit are so much the same thing that, just as it has been provided in the exchange that terms be short, I believe it will soon be provided that they are not long even in selling. This is because delay is the occasion for usury in a sale just as it is in an exchange. And removing long terms will be to remove the cause and the sin. And because funds are released sometimes for fairs and other times for specific places, it applies in both cases. When it is for a fair, the law commands it be the first one—not the intermediate one, but the upcoming one. And "first" is said to be not only the one that is first to be celebrated once the exchange is agreed upon, but the one that after the reach-

# Decretal on exchanges

...once the letters arrive there. This is a very easy thing to know, according to the current course and circumstances of the mail and the road. If a bill is issued in Seville for Antwerp <note>original: "Enuers"</note> in May, and the fair there is held around Saint John’s Day <note>June 24th</note>, this is not the first fair in respect to this exchange. This is because before the <term>receipt <note>original: "quitança"; a document or bill confirming the settlement of a debt.</note></term> arrives there, the fair will either have already disbanded or be nearing its end. And the Decretal, as is evident, commands that the exchange be made for a fair that is yet to be held when the letters arrive, provided that in sending them, there is no deceit or intentional delay. Nor should it be understood so strictly that if one does not know for certain if it will arrive with plenty of time—even a few days before—one should feel a scruple in committing to the fair that will take place after the letters arrive. Only exchanging for an <term>intercalated fair <note>original: "feria intercalada"; a later, non-consecutive fair used to stretch out the duration of a loan.</note></term> is forbidden. This is the second fair that will be held after the letters arrive, or at least after they could have arrived. In such a way that, as far as time is concerned, they could have traveled and been fulfilled in the preceding fair. Thus, it is now prohibited to exchange for <term>intermediate fairs <note>original: "ferias mediatas"; fairs occurring two cycles away rather than the next immediate one.</note></term>.

When dealing with a place where there is no fair, I would wish that a <term>sight draft <note>original: "letra viſta"; a bill of exchange payable immediately upon being presented to the recipient.</note></term> were always issued. This is as secure in exchanges as selling for cash is in the trade of merchandise. And just as buying on credit in that kind of business is always a suspicious sale of ill repute, so too is giving an exchange for more time than the distance of the place requires—allowing for some extra days or weeks (one need not be a mathematician in this, but a moral philosopher) that serve at least to collect the funds conveniently. But ultimately, the Pontifical law <note>The body of law based on Papal decrees.</note> grants the power to observe the custom already introduced in this matter, and to exchange according to the terms that have been used until now. It is true that even if a bill is given for much longer terms, one cannot (according to natural law, which cannot be abolished) charge more interest than for a sight draft. This is a general rule of exchanges: in such a way that even if one exchanges for the immediate fair, as commanded, it is not permitted to carry more interest than a sight draft would carry.

# Decretal on exchanges

...either because of the suspected delay of the fair, or because of the three months that, according to the common course of things, must pass. And so that this—which is a matter of natural law—might be observed, His Holiness ordered that exchange be conducted at short terms. But even within these short terms, the same natural rule must be followed: that interest should only be as much as could be charged **at sight** <note>original: "a letra viſta"; a bill payable immediately upon presentation to the recipient.</note>, as we have clearly taught in all the preceding sections, particularly in chapter ten.

In such a way that, if from Brussels to Seville one or two months have sometimes been allowed after the arrival of the **bill** <note>original: "poliça"; here referring to the document of exchange.</note>, this is not forbidden. Although he immediately goes on to say that one should strive to exchange continuously at sight, to remove opportunities for **usury** <note>original: "uſurar"; the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender.</note>. For certainly these long terms provide a very great opportunity for it. The substance of this legal paragraph consists in this: that at a fair, exchange should be made at the first available one, with the explanation we gave; but when funds are drawn to places that are not fairs, the old custom may be maintained.

But it is very important to note that, in prohibiting this and in the remainder of the decretal, the **Supreme Pontiff** <note>original: "Sūmo Pōtifice"</note> begins to properly use and exercise his authority and power, which is to make ecclesiastical laws. In these, he forbids what might otherwise have been permissible by itself, or commands the performance of what we were not previously obligated to do. This is what we call a matter of **positive law** <note>original: "derecho poſitiuo"; laws created by human authority, such as the Church or State, rather than inherent natural laws.</note>. These laws must be kept and obeyed for as long as they are not repealed. I say that he begins with this because in the sections above—regarding the condemnation of **dry exchanges** <term>dry exchanges <note>original: "cambios ſecos"; a fraudulent financial arrangement where a loan is disguised as a foreign currency exchange to bypass laws against interest.</note></term>, and illicit pacts and agreements—these are inherently evil, and are condemned by both natural and divine law. But in this clause, which forbids exchanging at an **intercalated fair** <note>original: "feria intercalada"; a later, non-consecutive fair used to artificially extend a loan's duration.</note> or at long terms, His Holiness forbids what could have been done if he had not forbidden it, provided that no extra interest was charged. But he prohibits them with great reason. First, because in effect it leads to wrongdoing by making more profit. Second, because under the guise of what is licit, much that is illicit is covered and hidden.

# Decretal on exchanges

Regarding the penalties imposed on the transgressors of this Decretal—which are certainly fearsome and bring infamy <note>original: "infames"; a legal status of disgrace that stripped an individual of certain civil rights.</note> (as we set out in the fifth book on **usury** <note>original: "vſuris"; the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was strictly regulated or forbidden by the Church.</note>)—it should be noted that they are applied by law to public usurers: those who can be clearly proven to give usury, both relatives and manifest strangers. Now that His Holiness has declared that conducting **dry exchanges** <note>original: "cãbios ſecos"; a fraudulent exchange where no money actually moves between different currencies or locations, used solely to hide an interest-bearing loan.</note> is usury, and by decreeing that they incur the same penalties, money changers will easily fall into them if they do not entirely abstain from such illicit business. This is because they exchange publicly, it is well known, and there are witnesses. Previously, dry exchange was already true usury, but they held it to be "cloaked" usury because of the title of "exchange" they gave it, and because of the fictitious bill sent to the trade fair. Because of this, it seemed to them that they did not easily incur the physical penalties of a public usurer. But from now on, dry exchange is public and manifest usury, subject to the same penalties as if it were openly done under the name of a **loan**. And those who lend at an **intercalated fair** <note>original: "feria intercalada"; an unscheduled or interim trade fair used by lenders to manipulate repayment dates and increase interest.</note> incur the same. It is most just that such harsh penalties be imposed on those so reckless. So that, since the fear of God and hell does not hold them back from evil, the fear of present punishment—physical and shameful—might turn them away. It would be very beneficial if the ecclesiastical judges began to issue certain punishments that the law calls **exemplary**, so that the decretal might be strengthened through practice, and many might learn a lesson from the example of one or two.

We also ordain that all those who conspire or collect all the currency—or the greater part of it—within themselves shall fall under the penalties established by law for **monopolies** <note>original: "monipodios"; a term derived from Greek meaning a conspiracy of merchants to fix prices or control a market.</note>; for it appears they create a monopoly on money.

# Decretal on exchanges

We also condemn this **cursed deception** with very many reasons in the seventh chapter.

This is the tenor and wording of the Decretal, which, although brief, touches upon the whole substance. There are three capital evils in this business. The first is **dry exchanges** <note>original: "cambios secos"; a fraudulent financial transaction where no actual currency is moved between cities, used as a loophole to charge interest on a loan.</note>, and all of these the **Apostolic See** <note>The central government of the Catholic Church in Rome.</note> already condemns, explaining many of them in particular. The second is this very specific accounting of longer or shorter terms, whereby interest increases according to their length. This includes the many evils of re-exchanging bills of exchange <note>original: "recambiar las letras"; a method of rolling over debt by issuing new bills, effectively compounding interest and fees.</note>. All of this the decree declares to be **usurious**. The third is this seizing control of the **market square** <note>original: "alçarse con la plaça"; a term for cornering the market or creating a monopoly to manipulate prices or currency values.</note> and conspiring against the needy—or forcing them into need—by hoarding money for oneself (the source of many grievances and injustices).

Because this is so harmful, the decree prohibits it under heavy penalties. As a remedy for many sins, it ordains that no exchange should be made except at the first **trade fair** <note>original: "feria"; designated international markets where debts were settled and currency exchanged.</note>, or at very short terms as required by the distance of the location, and no longer.

May it please God that they are as diligent in observing it as they have shown themselves to be eager for this Papal law. In which, so that
