IN ACCORDANCE WITH OUR Pastoral office, we apply ourselves diligently to that care, so that we do not delay in applying timely remedies for the salvation of the souls of the Lord’s sheep <note>original: "ouibus" (sheep); a traditional metaphor for the Christian faithful under the care of the Pope.</note>. Since, therefore, it has come to our ears <note>A standard legal opening indicating the Pope has been formally briefed on an issue.</note> that the legitimate use of exchanges <term>cambia: financial transactions involving the trade of currencies or bills of exchange, which were essential for international trade</term>—which necessity and public utility introduced—is frequently so corrupted by the greed for illicit profit that, under its pretext, the wickedness of usury <note>The practice of charging interest on a loan, which the Church historically viewed as a sin against justice and a violation of divine law.</note> is practiced by some. We have decided that the petitions recently made to us concerning these matters must be answered by this decretal <note>A papal decree that has the force of law in the Catholic Church.</note>, which shall be valid forever, so that neither the deceitful might benefit from their fraud—

# Decretal on Exchanges.

...may be supported, nor should ignorance destroy those who are unaware: for in this way we fulfill the office of the Pastor, while we strive by all means to rescue the flock committed to us from the danger of eternal damnation. First, therefore, we condemn all those exchanges which are called "dry" <term>cambia sicca: a deceptive financial transaction where no actual currency is exchanged between different locations; it was used as a legal loophole to disguise a high-interest loan</term>, and are so contrived that the contracting parties pretend to carry out exchanges at certain fairs <term>nundinas: large-scale international trade markets held at set times of the year, which served as the hubs for European banking and debt settlement</term>, or at other places. At these locations, those who receive the money indeed hand over their letters of exchange, but they are not sent; or if they are sent, they are returned empty after the time has passed to the place where they originated. Or even if no such letters are handed over, the money is finally reclaimed with interest in the same place where the contract was celebrated. For between the givers and the receivers, it had been so agreed from the beginning—or certainly such was the intention—that no one would actually make a payment at the fairs or the locations mentioned above upon receiving such letters. Similar to this evil is that practice where money is handed over, whether under the name of a "deposit" or under another name of a fictitious exchange, so that it may later be restored in the same place, or elsewhere, with a profit. Furthermore, even in those exchanges which are called "Real" <note>original: "Realia"; refers to legitimate exchanges involving the actual movement of funds between different currencies or locations for trade purposes.</note>, it is sometimes reported to us that Bankers <term>Campsores: professional money-changers or merchant-bankers who operated in the major financial centers of Europe</term> postpone the set deadline for payment because they have received, or have merely been promised, a profit through a secret or express agreement. All of these practices we declare to be usurious <note>The Church defined "usury" as any profit made directly from a loan; it was considered a grave sin against justice.</note>, and we strictly forbid them from being carried out. Furthermore, to remove the occasions of sin and the frauds of moneylenders <note>original: "fœneratorum"</note> as much as we can with God’s help: we decree that henceforth no one shall dare, whether at the beginning or at another time, to bargain for a certain and determined interest, even in the event of non-payment. Nor shall they conduct Real exchanges except for the first fairs where they are celebrated; or where they are not celebrated, for the first deadlines according to the accepted custom of those places. That abuse of conducting exchanges for second or subsequent fairs or deadlines is utterly rejected. Care must be taken regarding these deadlines, however, so that the distance and proximity of the locations are taken into account.

<summary>In this passage, Pope Pius V formally bans "dry exchanges" and fictitious deposits, identifying them as fraudulent masks for usury. He mandates that all legitimate currency exchanges must correspond to actual trade fairs and establishes rules for payment deadlines to prevent illicit profiting from delays.</summary>

from Seville to the Indies. 61.

### ¶ CHAPTER XIII. ON THE EXCHANGES WHICH
### are used from here to the Indies.

One must make mention of a specific type of exchange <term>Exchange (cambio): a financial contract, often a bill of exchange, where money is provided in one place/currency to be repaid in another</term> that is used in this city for the Indies <term>Indies: the Spanish colonies in the Americas, then referred to as the West Indies</term>. Because it is so singular that it does not fit the common rules and canons of the others, and it is even so deformed and so ugly that it seems like a monster of exchanges, lacking their full shape and appearance. It is a **Chimera** <note>original: "Chimera"; a mythological creature composed of parts from different animals, used here to describe a financial contract that unnaturally blends distinct legal concepts</note> with one part exchange, another part insurance, and another part usury—a mixture both laughable and horrific. 

On these steps <note>The "Steps" (Las Gradas) of the Cathedral of Seville served as the city's informal commercial hub where merchants and bankers gathered to conduct business</note>, exchange is conducted with two kinds of people for the Indies. The first is **passengers**, who are in need and do not have their assets here; they take an exchange to equip themselves for the journey, to be paid there at fifty or sixty percent, and the exchanger carries the risk of a designated ship. The other is with the **ship-masters** to be paid upon their return here, and they are charged eighty or ninety percent, taking on the risk of the ship for both the departure and the return. It happens that ten thousand ducats <term>Ducat: a high-value gold coin used for international trade</term> may be risked on a single hull when the ship itself is not worth two or three thousand. 

When this business is looked at and considered attentively, it is certainly monstrous, having neither feet nor head, nor a place to begin or end. First, if this is indeed an "exchange," what is the point of carrying the risk of the ship? They have not given ships in exchange, but money; nor has the borrower bought the ship with what he was given. Above all, exchange was originally invented and is practiced to save one from dangers <note>The author refers to the traditional purpose of bills of exchange: to avoid the danger of carrying physical gold or silver over long distances</note>, and it is against its nature for the one who gives funds here—to be repaid in another place—to carry the risk. Furthermore, why is sixty percent interest taken? If it is for exchange, it is a most unjust and lawless interest. If it is for insurance, the one taking the exchange is often not even the owner of the ship, but a master or a passenger who has no stake or part in it.

The whole contract is outside of any rule and order. For in merchandise, one would not earn forty percent net <note>original: "horros"; refers to profit free of expenses or "clear" profit</note> after two years, and these people want to earn sixty percent in even less time, without any labor, and with only money. These are two conditions quite contrary to legitimate interest <note>In scholastic economics, "interest" was only justifiable as compensation for loss or risk, not as a profit on money itself</note>. For this reason, all these profits are illicit and bound to be returned <note>original: "aboluerse"; the moral obligation to restore ill-gotten gains to the borrower</note>, as they have neither reason nor cause to be acquired. 

Nor does that trick of taking the danger upon oneself serve as anything more than an awakening to one who sleeps, prompting them to do the evil that many are already suspecting of masters and pilots—although I hold it to be a lie. Namely: that on the return trip, they surreptitiously run the ship onto a shoal or reef, where by losing the hull, they escape wealthy with ten thousand net ducats <term>Ducat (ducado): a high-value gold coin used as a standard of trade across Europe</term> that were insured upon it. 

Item: to give at exchange and make it a condition that they must secure the principal is usury expressly condemned in law. Although, in truth, they do not do this. For the principal they gave is not the ship, but money spent before departure on provisions <term>Provisions (matalotaje): the food, drink, and essential supplies required for a ship's crew and passengers during a voyage</term> and other travel preparations. They only provided it in this imagination, thinking it served their case to take that danger upon themselves so they could take as much as they wanted. As if running a risk were enough to earn or justify the profit, if the business itself is not licit. 

Certainly, they can give no sufficient cause for what they do. What they could say with truth, they dare not say, seeing that they cannot do it, and they do it against all reason. Which is: they charge sixty percent because they see the borrower so needy that he would give a hundred, or sixty-eight for a single real <term>Real: a silver coin; the author is illustrating extreme desperation where someone pays many times the value of a small coin</term>, in exchange for escaping and getting out of his present predicament.

Some are accustomed to allege that they themselves were going to load cargo for the Indies. Others speak conditionally: "if I loaded cargo and ran the risk, the shipment <term>Shipment (cargazon): the total cargo or freight carried by a vessel</term> would be sold at sixty percent profit; and since I forgo loading it myself and give the money to them, and I run the risk, it is almost the same as loading it, and..."

And besides this business being most unjust and usurious, it reaches another level of evil, as it is at times ruinous to many poor people (namely) the sailors, a people for whom one should rightly feel compassion because of the great poverty, labors, and calamities they endure.

And the harm is this: if a <term>shipmaster<note>original: *maestre de nao*; the person responsible for the ship's commercial management and outfitting.</note></term> takes two thousand <term>ducats<note>a gold coin of high value used in international trade.</note></term> on exchange to outfit and provision the vessel, any twenty that he gives to a sailor before departure or during the voyage turns into thirty because of the high interest rates with which he provides it. In this regard, it must be considered that the sailors' wages come from the <term>freight charges<note>original: *fletes*; the fees paid for transporting cargo.</note></term>, which consequently must be paid upon the return trip. However, because they are so poor, they ask for money in <term>Sanlúcar<note>Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the port at the mouth of the Guadalquivir River where the fleets for the Americas were finalized for departure.</note></term> and along the way to buy some small items of clothing, a rough blanket, or some food. The masters, finding themselves <term>penniless<note>original: *sin blanca*; literally "without a blanca," a coin of the smallest possible value.</note></term>, take loans at high interest and give the money to their sailors at the same cost it cost them. This harm, which is great for them given their poverty, was caused by the first person who gave the loan, whose sin is as clear and manifest as that of Judas.

Furthermore, regarding the shipmasters, two points must be noted (of the first, there is no need for me to speak, as everyone talks and blasphemes about it). First, they are often reprehensible because, while having money of their own, they give it to the sailors at high exchange rates, alleging in their wickedness that if they did not have it, they would have had to borrow it elsewhere, and that they are not obligated to have it or, having it, to give it—and that it is reasonable that the interest they would have paid to another should be paid to them. ### from Seville to the Indies.

The brief summary of this is that, just as the other person sins and is damned by making such an exchange, they also sin and are damned by committing the same injustice. This seems so true to me that even those with bleary-eyed understanding <note>The author uses "lagañosos" (bleary-eyed) to mean those who are intellectually or morally dim-witted.</note> can see that this resolution is based on better reason than their dissolute actions. 

Regarding those who actually take funds on <term>exchange<note>original: *cambio*; here referring to a high-interest loan or a maritime contract involving currency exchange rates that masked usury.</note></term>: I say that when the sailors, as often happens, collectively tell the <term>shipmaster<note>original: *maestro*; the officer in charge of the ship's business and crew.</note></term> to take funds on exchange in their name, and he seeks and receives it for their expenses and needs, he takes and distributes it lawfully, in proportion to their wages, as each one desires and requests. 

But if he takes it for his own requirements, and later the sailors happen to ask him for some money, he cannot give it to them with that same exchange rate, but rather at the rate of one real for thirty-four <note>original: *el real por treynta y quatro*; the official exchange rate of 34 maravedís to one silver real. Giving money at this rate means giving it at its face value without adding interest.</note>. 

And the difference and distinction between one case and the other consists in the fact that, in the first, the master does not give the money to the sailors as a loan; rather, he and the sailors form one body and community that receives this exchange—or better said, <term>usury<note>original: *usura*; the practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender.</term> and <term>illicit profit<note>original: *logro*; a term for gain obtained through usury.</note></term>—and being the one to receive it is not a crime. And for this reason, he is exempt from guilt and the duty of <term>restitution<note>original: *restitucion*; the theological requirement to return stolen or unfairly gained money to the rightful owner to receive absolution.</note></term>; however, giving the loan at interest is always evil. 

In the second case, he acts as the principal party, giving the money on exchange to his sailors. And just as the person who gave it to him sinned (though the master did not sin in receiving it), so now the master sins in giving it, while the sailors do not sin in taking it. This is because he commits the same injustice and grievance that was committed against him. 

They say, "It cost me this much, and thus they wronged me." I admit it, but being wronged does not give anyone the right to <margin>Law of danger. *Digest* on nautical interest; and laws 1 and 2, *Code*, same title. <note>These refer to specific sections of Roman Law—the *Digest* and the *Code of Justinian*—concerning *fenus nauticum* or maritime interest.</note></margin> wrong another, nor to undo or compensate for one's own injury through the injury of another. Furthermore, it is common humanity to give some money to the sailors so they may trade, or at least so they can protect themselves from the rain and cold. 

In resolution, I say that those who provide exchange to the shipmasters sin and must make restitution. And for the masters to give it later to the sailors, not having taken...

And in the event that they have received it for their expenses and costs (as I have expressed), giving it later to the sailors with the same interest at which he took it sounds very bad to me, at the very least. All these would be (if they were made) real and true exchanges, without it being necessary to run risk in a ship or caravel, which is a trick of the devil. Instead, one gives the money here and sends the bill of exchange <term>bill of exchange<note>original: *letra*; a document allowing a merchant to pay money in one city and have a correspondent pay the equivalent to a recipient in another city.</note></term>, and receives the funds later; and if they wish to exchange on the return trip, whoever receives a thousand pesos in Mexico can deliver eight hundred and fifty in Spain. They will say that insurance costs less; that is true. This leads to the conclusion that anyone who brought funds by exchange would be quite foolish. They will avoid two thousand illicit acts that they celebrate within Spain. First, it would be a true exchange in this city. # Concerning Bankers

[na]body has investigated the reason or cause why these fees are taken, nor from where this abuse derived or originated.

The practice of this business is that whoever issues a bill <term>bill of exchange<note>A written order to pay a specific sum of money at a future date, used by merchants to settle debts at distant trade fairs without transporting physical gold.</note></term> for a trade fair, since they usually do not have money there with which to pay, they are forced to take it through "exchange" <note>A credit transaction where interest was often hidden in the currency conversion rate to bypass usury laws.</note>. During the fair, the rate for this exchange is high and inflated; to escape that danger, the merchant issues the bill through a bank. Once the letter of credit arrives, the bankers accept it and record it in the bank's books, making the person who brought it a creditor for the full amount plus six per thousand <note>A service fee of 0.6%.</note>. However, the holder cannot withdraw even a single *blanca* <note>original: *blanca*; a copper coin of very small value.</note> in cash; instead, they must go about trading and issuing further bills, and none of the bills they issue are paid until the fair has ended. Thus, if they have spent the entire amount in bills, they have "enjoyed" the use of the full one thousand and six, but we might apply the proverb to them: "much good may it do him." This is because the shopkeepers from whom they buy ask them, before all else <note>original: *ante omnia*</note>, how they intend to pay, or they already know and suspect the situation. Understanding that to get their money out of the bank they must pay their own six per thousand, and because they must wait until the end of the fair to receive it, the shopkeepers take care to compensate for all this by raising their prices. Finally, at the time of payment, the exchange takes its six per thousand from everything that is counted and withdrawn. And so that we may list all the tricks together, I say that these bankers also receive all the money that people wish to deposit in their bank, and they give a certain amount to the person who placed and deposited it there, in this manner: If someone deposited one thousand ducats in the bank, the counting-house <note>original: *caxa*; literally "the chest," referring to the bank’s treasury.</note> opens an account with him, noting in the margin what he withdraws in cash and what he transferred through the bank; when the fair is over, the bank pays him interest on whatever was not withdrawn in cash. Likewise, if those who bring bills of exchange want to be paid immediately, the bank pays them in coin, but with such a loss that it is as if they had given it to him as a high-interest loan. All of these are highly scrupulous <note>In the religious and legal sense of the time, "scrupulous" meant a transaction that burdened the conscience or bordered on the sinful/illegal.</note> dealings, though I should better say, condemned ones. Furthermore, these six per thousand are not always for the banker, but often for the one who carries the bill <term>bill of exchange<note>A document used to transfer money between different markets without moving physical gold.</note></term>, and they make him the creditor for the whole amount, even though he does no work at all. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the "six per thousand" (0.6%) fee charged in banking transactions. The previous page ended mid-sentence, discussing how a guarantor remains liable to pay if another fails, and the text here continues by explaining how these practices flourish in the commercial world.</meta>

# Concerning Bankers

...the use and practice of this business flourishes greatly. These six per thousand <note>A 0.6% commission fee.</note> are not charged, nor even mentioned, in **letters of exchange** <term>letters of exchange<note>A written order used in international trade that allowed a person to receive money in one currency or location after paying it in another.</note></term> that are settled in cash outside the formal exchange markets. They are also generally not applied to those issued for Seville or Rome, where it is not the custom to pay through a bank, but rather in **reales** <term>reales<note>Standard silver coins used in the Spanish Empire.</note></term>. From this, it clearly appears that these six per thousand are given as payment for the bank’s guarantee and its responsibility for the payment <note>Original: *lasto*, referring to the bank fulfilling an obligation on behalf of a debtor.</note>, since they are only established and granted for drafts settled through the bank.

It could also be argued with much probability and likelihood that these fees are given to the person to whom the sum is issued—that is, the one who provided the money—to compensate him for accepting payment through the bank, which is a "crippled" and imperfect form of payment. It would be better for him if he were paid in silver rather than in **certificates** <term>cedulas<note>Written promises to pay; essentially paper credit rather than physical coin.</note></term>. For this very reason, it is certain that the person who brings the letter of exchange is credited in the bank for one thousand and six for every thousand, and he benefits from the whole amount. This is a sufficient legal title <note>A "title" in this context is a moral or legal justification for a transaction.</note> to receive them. 

Since he was legally owed payment in silver **reales**, which would have been more useful and convenient to him than bank drafts and receipts, he may rightly accept five or six per thousand to compensate for the convenience and profit he loses by agreeing to receive the funds in the bank. Following this logic, it is also reasonable that if, once the letter has been accepted at the exchange, the holder should withdraw some amount of money, he should pay that same interest <note>Meaning the commission or fee.</note> of six per thousand to the bank for the amount withdrawn. This is because the bank is disbursing actual silver coins when it is not yet obliged to do so. Furthermore, by receiving the payment in silver, the justification for his receiving the six per thousand—which was the disadvantage of using paper certificates—ceases to exist for that portion. In this case, the fee goes to the banker who fulfills the obligation for the original party and records it in his ledger. Thus, the custom of these dealings is justified regarding the "six per thousand." It is morally permissible to take them—both for the person who accepts payment of his money through a bank, and for the bank itself, if it pays out physical money to such a person.

# Concerning Bankers

...I say it is lawful, provided it is not prohibited by positive law <note>Man-made laws established by a government or church, as opposed to natural law.</note>, which for just causes usually forbids what might otherwise be permissible in itself, because it is being done poorly. Regarding the second point—the bank paying interest to the one who deposits money—all agree that this is usury <note>Original: *logro*, an archaic term for illegal or excessive profit or interest.</note> for the recipient. This is because it is paying for something that does not deserve payment; on the contrary, the depositor should instead pay the bank for the safekeeping of their currency. If they say that the bank benefits and makes much profit because it exchanges currency, none of this gives the depositor the right to take anything from the bank. The industry and ingenuity belong to the banker. And in a matter so evident, it is not necessary to bring many arguments, for that would be like calling witnesses to prove facts that are already notorious and clear.

Regarding the third point—which is deducting a portion from a payment order when a shopkeeper or official wants it in cash, according to the current exchange rate—this is entirely a robbery, and so blatant that it is not even "disguised usury" or "overt usury," but a most manifest theft. And this is no exaggeration; it is the truth. If I were asked what kind of sin this crime is, or to what category it belongs, I cannot see it as anything other than injustice and robbery. It is a selling of currency for more than it is worth, and a failure to pay what is owed. To this man, one hundred **ducats** <term>ducats<note>A gold or silver coin used as a standard unit of account in early modern Europe.</note></term> are owed for the cloth he sold, and the other person, who has credit in your bank, issues a draft for that same amount; to take two away from him because that is the current exchange rate for Seville or Villalón <note>Villalón de Campos, a major fair and financial center in Castile famous for its international trade fairs.</note>—there is no reason to do this other than the desire to do it.

And this question is already an old one between bankers and confessors, dating back to when this practice first began, because its wickedness and injustice were immediately apparent. For they [the confessors] do not even grant absolution to the bankers' apprentices who assist them in such devilry. And they are right, for they are all guilty. Even if they do not share in the stolen goods, they all fall into the category of larceny. Regarding the sins against justice committed in these businesses, I have touched upon all or most of them, I believe, in this short work <note>Original: *opusculo*.</note>, at least according to the style and practice of these kingdoms. Because regarding other types of exchange...

ALTHOUGH I do not know if it would be more profitable to persuade people not to take money at usury <note>The practice of lending money at interest, which was heavily regulated and often condemned by the Church during this period.</note> and in exchanges, than it would be to reproach and weigh how great a wickedness it is to give it. First, to the poor man who asks, there is no one who will lend, because these usurers <term>logreros: profiteers or lenders who sought to "lograr" (gain) illicit profits through the needs of others</term>, who are not at all merciful, only trust those who have credit. There are other convenient means for his remedy: manual labor, learning a trade, or serving someone who will maintain him. ### The harm of exchanges.

He who gets into debt by buying on credit and through exchanges properly fulfills the Latin proverb: *You cannot carry a goat, yet you load yourself with a cow.* <note>original: "no puedes lleuar la cabra, y car gas te vna vaca." A metaphor for someone who, unable to manage a small burden, foolishly takes on a much larger one.</note> For, being unable to sustain himself in his poverty, he takes upon himself a greater burden of debt, by which he truly becomes impoverished. For a man is hardly poor if he simply has nothing; he is poor if he owes. They say that with health one can endure anything; likewise, any necessity is easily suffered as long as one is free of debt. There is no more grievous labor than for a man to hear someone say to him, "pay me," when there are no funds to do so. All the time that one lives without debts, one lives with rest, and I am tempted to say, without poverty.

See what a deranged counsel it is for a poor man to involve himself in usury to find a remedy, where instead he loses himself. And if the poor man is imputed with such great fault, for what shall the rich man be blamed, who never exits the cycle of **exchanges** and **mohatras**? <term>mohatra: A fraudulent contract where a merchant sells goods on credit at a high price and immediately buys them back for a lower cash price, effectively creating a high-interest loan that circumvented religious bans on usury.</term> Certainly, it is a deep madness, an effective desire to ruin oneself, and even a hidden judgment of heaven, which secretly ordains that with his own hands he goes about robbing his own estate, just as he robbed the estates of others. Others die to protect their property; this man truly dies to lose it.

It is a very ancient sentence, a public voice, and a universal opinion that all usurers—both those who are overt and those who are disguised—are nothing but hidden thieves. What then does he intend who never leaves their company, if not to be despoiled? It is a very unjust complaint for a sailor to complain of the sea, especially (as the poets say) if he complains of **Neptune** <note>The Roman god of the sea.</note> who sails for a second time, having already experienced its dangers and tempests. Much more reprehensible are these lords, who so continually complain of the foreigners who "eat them from the feet up" with exchanges and usuries, when they themselves bear the blame for everything by bringing them into their dealings. For, assuming they make use of the foreigner's money, it is not much to take the cloak from one who puts himself at risk of losing even his shirt, and who in reality does not want anything but to end up naked—he who

How can they not fall into the misfortune of the donkey that plows with the ox? <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 22:10. In this context, it is a metaphor for an unequal or unnatural pairing—specifically, a person of modest means trying to keep pace with the financial burdens of the very wealthy.</note> All this—namely, losing oneself without realizing it, and complaining of others once the harm is felt and has no remedy—proceeds from what Saint Ambrose says: that exchange and lending are like the venom of an asp. Which, with a gentle delight caused by its coldness, takes possession of the veins, arteries, and nerves moment by moment without resistance, until reaching the heart, where life ends. <note>Saint Ambrose (c. 340–397) was a Doctor of the Church who wrote extensively against usury, comparing the "interest" on a loan to a snake's bite that isn't felt until the poison has spread.</note>

In this way, he who finds himself in need through his own disorder in spending and borrowing rejoices in his own harm, finding someone who will immediately lend to him, not feeling his wound for the time being. But little by little the debt takes hold of the wretched capital, in such a way that when the deadline arrives, it either takes away the estate—which is his very being and substance—or tears away a large piece of it like a cancer. This little taste of relief, which is escaping the present predicament, prevents them from understanding their ruin until they are entirely lost. 

Merchants are like the silkworm, which entangles and imprisons itself within its own web of business, entering into a greater obligation to escape one, until finding themselves surrounded on all sides by obligations from which they cannot escape except dead in the purse, or most weak and disfigured. And certainly, if they were moderate in their dealings and expenses, they would not lack sufficient means according to their station. Plutarch says: if you wish to always be flush with money, live tightly, because when one constricts oneself, immediately there is a surplus. # The Harm of Financial Exchanges

...[perishable], just so the pomp and display of these things is all mere wind, not substance. Among the ancients, there was once a most solemn temple on the island of Lesbos where those already stripped bare by usury <note>original: "pelados de vsuras"</note> took refuge; however, there is no safer refuge for avoiding jail and imprisonment than moderation and good self-governance. This virtue is a place so sacred that there is no judge so bold as to break or profane it. Manage your estate with prudence; do not trust it all to fortune. Keep one part safe: "one foot in the sea, the other on land." Measure your dealings by your capital; do not stretch your arms further than you can grasp with your strength. Draw the jewels for your house and the expenses for your table from your lawful earnings. Do not spend more than you earn. I will stand as your guarantor: you will not merely be rich in the future, but in the present, for your wealth consists in following this order of life.

For being rich does not consist of having much money (as Boethius says <note>original: "Boccio." Anicia Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524), a philosopher whose works on fortune and wealth were standard educational texts.</note>), but rather that, whether one has much or little, there is a surplus. There are many for whom, according to their perceived needs, a hundred thousand are not enough, and even with a hundred thousand they feel a great lack. On the contrary, if you live in an orderly way, you will have rest even with little—a thing that others seek with great toil and do not achieve. One may well reach prosperity through other paths—via deception and grievances—but a secure and stable prosperity is never reached except through this path I have shown.

And so that you may understand how excellent and admirable it is, notice that the harmony of a house, the modesty of a person, and equity and justice in business are in themselves riches so lovely that they far exceed all gold and silver. All temporal possessions must be justly set aside to acquire these virtues, or once acquired, to preserve them. How much more so if these virtues even serve as a remedy to enrich you bodily, and free you from a thousand usuries and the tightest obligations into which your profanity <note>In this context, "profanity" refers to a lack of religious or moral discipline in worldly affairs, or a devotion to secular vanity.</note> thrusts and places you—taking on great <term>cambios: financial exchanges or bills of credit that often hid high interest rates</term> to satisfy it, where you live

# The Harm of Currency Exchanges

...a corrupt scheme of trade. For if they have the power to remedy it, and yet do not, is it not madness to complain of the money-changer or the cloth-merchant? For considering how great are the sums they provide through exchange or credit, they would be—speaking in human terms—more foolish to give them without interest than the merchants are now mad for allowing them to earn such great usuries <note>In this period, "usury" referred to any interest charged on a loan, which was often condemned by the Church as a sin.</note>. If they had a need for a hundred ducats <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe.</note> a year, it would be inhumanity not to lend them for free; but to complain that, when asking for ten and twenty thousand for their shipments of goods, they are charged interest!

It is, in my judgment, a strange madness, charity being so dead already. Even when it boiled fervently in Christendom, one would not have found anyone who—without the bond of kinship or friendship—would give four or five thousand escudos <note>A unit of currency; the "shield" coin.</note>, two or three times a year, as merchants require and take on exchange—or in clothing, which is itself a species of usury. Let us imagine that foreigners corrected themselves of this vice for which they are noted, lending without interest to the merchants of this city as if they were a *charitable bank* <note>original: "monte pietatis." These were "mounts of piety," institutional pawnbrokers run as charities to offer low-interest loans to the poor.</note>: you, the merchant yourself, would soon judge it an error for them to leave their own country to serve you so profitably in yours, when they could instead benefit their neighbors in their own land.

O blind avarice! Which so enchants with its pretensions that it proclaims it an insult when others do not employ their estates in one’s own service and utility. As if it were a duty for people to travel five hundred leagues <note>A league was roughly 3 miles or 4.8 kilometers.</note> to lend them their capital or provide it on long credit terms. They respond to this by saying they do not grumble about the profits themselves, but about their size and exorbitance. Certainly, I also confess their excess and tyranny when they see their opportunity. But considering the opportunities given to them in Spain, I would sooner dare to exaggerate their malice than to explain our own error. The barbaric way our people trade, and their crazy presumption of being equal to one another—doing what another does even if it costs them their lives—is the lure that calls foreigners to see...

...they come, like birds of prey, to eat their flesh through exchanges and re-exchanges <note>original: "cambios y recambios." We return to imitating the pernicious simplicity of our ancestors. # On Annuities

...to avoid them, if, as I said at the beginning, there were moderation in dealings, neither spending nor charging more than the capital can bear, a small gain would be much, and would yield more profit. What I have expressed as my opinion and sound advice regarding merchants, illustrated or exemplified here, is understood likewise in its degree and proportion across all social classes. Because modesty and temperance were, are, and will always be very useful to everyone, both to prevent grave damages—general and private—and to bring about great benefits in both.

## FINAL CHAPTER, ON ANNUITIES.

<margin>
Innocent IV in the chapter *in civitate*, on usury. Sylvester [Prierias], under the entry "usury," part 2, paragraph 12. Conradus [Summenhart], question 75, on contracts and subsequent ones. [Domingo de] Soto, *On Justice and Law*, book 6, question 5.
</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial letter L featuring stylized floral and vine motifs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>ANNUITIES <term>censos: a financial contract where a person receives a sum of money in exchange for paying a permanent or redeemable annual "pension" or interest, usually secured by real estate</term> AND tributes are a common contract in Spain; and while being lawful and safe, it has been, as they say, unfortunate, always holding such a bad reputation that it would have almost already fallen and ceased if the Apostolic See <note>The Papacy or the central administration of the Catholic Church.</note>, with its authority and approval, had not sustained and supported it. For this reason, I determined to declare how just and lawful it was in its own right—to discuss its equity and justice, and to show the conditions and circumstances that it requires. 

An annuity and tribute, as used among us, is a pension <note>A fixed regular payment.</note> given every year. I say "as it is used," because if we look to the ancient meaning and acceptance of the word, it also signifies the taxes <term>pechos: taxes paid specifically by commoners (those not of noble birth)</term>, sales taxes <term>alcabalas: a significant tax on the sale of goods</term>, and tributes that subjects give to their prince, as is clear from the Gospel text. But now, this word has commonly been reduced or narrowed among us to mean only...

# On Annuities

<header>On Annuities</header>

...during the pension and tribute that one obligates themselves to give to another in particular. This is of two kinds: one is **reservative**, which is very common among ecclesiastics; the other is **consignative**, which is much used by laypeople.

**Reservative** is giving a person a benefit, or a dignity, or some vineyards, olive groves, pastures, or houses, while **reserving** for oneself a certain quantity of the fruits and rents that might arise. We see this every moment in the benefits and prebends of the Church. A canonry, a portion, or a *prestamero* <term>prestamero: a clerical office or title in Spain that allowed the holder to collect specific ecclesiastical revenues</term> is granted, while the person giving it keeps and retains for himself a right and legal action to receive either the third part, or half, or the total gross mass of the fruits, which we call a **pension**. This practice is so widespread that it is rare to find someone who obtains a benefit without it, unless some commutation <note>The legal exchange of one type of payment or obligation for another.</note> was made. I do not wish to say another word about this at present. Firstly, because the subject is vast; and secondly, because it is almost never used except among ecclesiastical persons—people who, for the most part, already know their rights, justice, practice, and style.

The **consignative** annuity is the one the common people celebrate, and the one that holds some suspicion or bad appearance <note>A "bad appearance" refers to the concern that these contracts might be a disguised form of usury, which was morally and legally condemned.</note>, and it is the one we must treat with extreme brevity. Its nature and substance consist in giving a person—secured against certain houses, estates, or other possessions—one thousand ducats, more or less, on the condition that they provide a certain amount of rent every year. This is usually in money, but it could also be in wine, wheat, cochineal (which they call *grana*), or in fruits. For just as I obligate myself to give one hundred ducats, I could be obligated by natural law to give one hundred *fanegas* <term>fanega: a traditional Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly equivalent to 1.5 bushels or 55 liters</term> of wheat.

However, for good reasons and respects, it is prohibited by the law of the kingdom (Title 15, Law 4) to establish annuities to be paid in oil, bread, wine, firewood, charcoal, honey, wax, soap, flax, chickens, bacon, or any other kind of thing that is not money. The reason for forbidding this is that because the price of these things is so variable, sometimes one would pay more than fourteen thousand per thousand <note>original: "quatorze mil el millar." This likely refers to the fluctuating market value relative to the principal of the annuity.</note>, and other times less. Thus, it is better that it be paid in money, which is invariable. Among these annuities, some are **perpetual**, which last...

# On Annuities

<header>On Annuities</header>

...last forever, and are called **irredeemable**, where there is a perpetual obligation to pay them and no freedom to buy them back; others are **redeemable**, which can be removed or exempted, and the person can redeem themselves from them. These in particular were the ones that brought the contract into disrepute as being usurious <note>Specifically, the concern was that these contracts were a way to circumvent the religious prohibition against usury (charging interest on loans).</note>. And this moral concern was not without some basis. For as people saw that one person gave two thousand ducats and received two hundred every year, and after six or seven years, the two thousand were returned to him, it seemed to them a type of interest-bearing loan. And the scandal grew so great that it was not calmed or removed until it was consulted upon by **Urban VI** and **Callixtus III**, Supreme Pontiffs, and they approved it. In this section, I will address three points. First, what is purchased in this annuity? What is actually happening there. Second, concerning those that are perpetual and those that are redeemable. Third, regarding the conditions that are usually requested and expressed in the contracts.

Regarding the first point, so many factors converge in an annuity that their multitude causes confusion and obscures the minds of many unlearned people, who cannot penetrate or even understand what takes place in that contract. One person gives the money; the other designates certain possessions—which, despite all this, remain his own, and he often stays and lives in them—and gives him a certain amount each year. Some think that the houses are bought; others, the leases. But the truth is that neither the houses, nor the farmsteads, nor their rents or fruits are sold, but rather a **right and legal action** <term>right and legal action: *derecho y acción*, a specific legal entitlement to claim a fixed payment from a property's income</term> to collect a specific quantity each year. This appears clear for many reasons.

First, no one doubts that, as the rate is now **fourteen per thousand** <note>This refers to a standard rate of 14 units of currency for every 1,000 units of capital, roughly a 7.14% return.</note>, obtaining a thousand in tribute for fourteen thousand is a licit and just business. And often the possessions upon which they are placed are worth twenty thousand. At the very least, this is common: that they are always worth more. And if placing an annuity on these were to be considered purchasing them, it would be [continued on next page]...

# On Annuities

<header>On Annuities.</header>

[...neither does it conti]nue as an unjust contract, for the just price is never given <note>The author is arguing that if an annuity were a sale of the property, the price paid would be far too low, making the contract illegal under "just price" doctrines.</note>. Because giving fourteen for what is worth twenty is an offense and manifest injustice. Thus, the fact that it is public and well-known that the contract is not blameworthy is evident proof that the properties upon which the annuity is placed are not being purchased. Furthermore, if they were sold, they would not remain in the possession of the first party—because that which is sold is alienated <term>alienated: the legal transfer of ownership to another</term>, and the other person acquires the domain and lordship over it—and we see that houses and estates are not alienated by placing an annuity upon them; they always belong to the person who owned them before. He manages them as he did at first. He leases them out, if they are houses; he cultivates and works them, if they are olive groves. From this it is clearly evident that he does not sell them, nor does the other buy them, as they do not cease to be his.

Furthermore, if I place an annuity on my houses, I can still sell them, unless the contrary is expressed in the deed and agreement. And since I retain the power to do so if it is not otherwise specified, it is a sign that the annuity is not a sale of the property, nor even of its fruits or its rents. This is because often the payment <note>original: "tributo"</note> is more than the rent from the security <term>security: the "hypotheca" or property used to back the agreement</term>; other times it is greater, and other times the property produces nothing at all due to some impediment, yet for all that, the debtor does not cease to pay his annuity every year. 

In conclusion, I say that only a **right** and an **obligation** are purchased—specifically, the obligation the person makes to give a certain amount each year at the designated time, according to what is agreed and practiced. And the real estate <note>original: "bienes rayzes"</note> that is designated serves as a security and a guarantor; if the person fails to pay, the creditor can seize them, sell them, and pay himself what is owed. From this it follows that it is not necessary for the named properties to yield a rent at least equal to the amount of the annuity, or even that they yield or produce anything at all. It is enough that they are certainly and surely worth more than the total sum that was given, because they serve only as a plain and solvent guarantor.

# On Annuities

<header>On Annuities.</header>

[...since it] is bought and sold, it remains to be shown that it is a very licit and clean contract, without any mixture of usury <note>The author is defending annuities against the charge of usury—the sinful practice of charging interest on a loan—which was strictly forbidden by the Church at the time.</note>. And it is certain that, as it is a real sale and purchase, and since one is selling what is salable, it will be a true and just business if the price is not excessive. For to buy what can be sold can certainly be done. And here, as we have shown, one purchases a right to collect a certain amount every year, either in money or in certain fruits of the harvest. This right is salable <term>salable: also referred to as a "venal" right, meaning it is a legal asset that can be traded for money</term>, and it has its own specific value in money, just like all other secular and worldly rights. For even a doubtful right to some estates can be—and usually is—sold while a lawsuit is pending; how much more so a clear and secure right to collect a specific rent every year? 

Furthermore, if someone were to graciously bind their estate to another, or bind themselves to give a certain amount every year as an allowance <note>original: "ayuda de costas," which refers to a stipend or financial assistance for living expenses</note>, no one doubts that they were doing them a favor and gave them something of value and price; yet they truly give them nothing more than a faculty to demand that amount every year. In this, it is clear that the right and faculty to collect a certain amount annually has its own intrinsic value. 

The very root of this point consists in the fact that establishing an annuity is not lending, but buying. And since the purchase involves salable things, it is always licit in itself. It appears clearly to be a sale and not a loan. Because if it were a loan, the one who gave the money could ask for it back whenever it suited him. For lending does not deprive a man of this liberty. But we see the opposite: once the funds are given, he cannot reclaim them <note>original: "repetillos," a legal term from the Latin *repetere*, meaning to legally demand the return of the principal sum</note> as occurs when one buys and sells. 

Beyond these reasons, all positive laws <term>positive laws: man-made laws enacted by authorities (kings or the Church), as opposed to natural or divine law</term>—canonical as well as imperial and royal—approve of this contract, and even frequently command it to be done. Such is the case with the property of minors, which tutors are commanded to invest in annuities. And sometimes the property of the republic <note>The "republic" here refers to the state or the local commonwealth’s public funds</note> is handled this way, so that it may yield rent and bear fruit. Even the Apostolic See <note>The papacy or the central administration of the Roman Catholic Church</note> approves of it, despite abhorring and detesting any form of usury so greatly.

It cites the approval of both secular and canon law, as well as the practical necessity of investing funds for minors and the state.</summary>

In such a way that, even without any law authorizing this contract, it is lawful in its own right, because it is truly a matter of purchase and sale. This shall apply notwithstanding that they may be old and established for a long time, or that they were made in a part or province where it is claimed and alleged that it has been the custom to sell at a lower price. According to this ratio of fourteen thousand per thousand, payments shall be made from now on for what is owed, starting from the day of the publication of this law. And the same shall be understood and observed regarding the *juros* that we have sold until now and shall sell in the future.

# On Annuities

<header>De los censos.</header>

...[so that] it should not be sold for more (as is the case with wheat) nor for less, as is the case with these annuities <term>tributos: here referring to fixed financial obligations or annual payments</term>. In such instances, the commonwealth <term>republica: the state or organized political community</term> can rightly deprive a person of their freedom of contract by appraising their property and ordering them not to give it for less. This is because the disposal of worldly goods <term>temporalidades: secular or material possessions as opposed to spiritual ones</term>, even if they are one's own property, is subject to the laws. Thus we see that laws sometimes annul and invalidate many donations, whether made at the time of death or during life; others they confirm. For this reason, those who consider only the benefit of private individuals are gravely mistaken when judging whether the price cap <term>tassa: a legally fixed price or interest rate limit</term> binds them or not. One must look first and primarily to the common good, and judge the obligation according to that.

The second thing to be noted is that this price cap refers to well-settled annuities <term>censos: financial contracts where capital was exchanged for a guaranteed annual income</term> that are being paid reliably. Both conditions must be met: they must be secured on sound real estate <term>buenas rayzes: literally "good roots," referring to landed property or fixed assets used as collateral</term> and be collected certainly, easily, and promptly. If any of these conditions are missing, the value of the annuity decreases.

This law is often broken with great deceptions and schemes; however, these occur in specific matters of which it is not appropriate to speak for many good reasons. For this cause, it seemed to me unnecessary to write about them, believing that both the subject matter and the schemes themselves will soon cease.

Also, a short while ago, His Holiness published a *motu proprio* <term>motu proprio: a decree issued by the Pope on his own initiative and signed by him personally</term> in which he sets out many conditions that must be observed in these annuities. Most of these serve as a barbican <term>barbacana: a defensive outer wall of a castle, here used metaphorically as a protection</term> to defend against usury <note>The Church was deeply concerned with "usury"—the practice of charging immoral or excessive interest on loans.</note>. It provides the order in which this contract is to be celebrated. The entire *motu proprio* was drafted with great zeal; if it is followed and accepted, it will bring great prestige to this business. However, I do not see it being promoted or discussed among us. For this reason, I have not explained it. I am watching to see where it leads; and I do not know why the prelates <term>prelados: high-ranking church officials, such as bishops or abbots</term> do not preach and proclaim a law so just and necessary...

Second, it is appropriate that they be secured against assets, specifically **landed property** <term>bienes rayzes: literally "rooted goods," meaning real estate or land which cannot be moved or hidden</term>. Their soil and legal status are certain to last **beyond the fourth generation**, and even until the hundredth. Regarding the **redeemable** ones, which are now called temporary, I say that they are worth less, but since there is a law of price <note>A legally fixed interest rate or "tassa."</note> among us, there is no need to dwell on investigating it.

There is one grave doubt in this matter: are **personal** annuities lawful? A personal annuity is placing the annuity upon the person, not upon any particular possessions. And it is a personal annuity when the annuitant <term>censuario: the investor or person receiving the annual payment</term> is satisfied that only the person taking the capital binds themselves, with a general mortgage and obligation of their person and assets, without specifying or singling out any. But it would certainly be, at the very least, great foolishness for one to be satisfied with the person alone, a thing so variable and perishable. Second, it would inevitably serve as a handle for usury and illicit gains <term>logros: profits made through exploitative or illegal lending</term>, from which we must distance ourselves so much. Therefore, it is better for both parties, and more secure, that they not be made. For those who give to the annuity, they will have their investment better established in landed property. For those who receive it, they do not incur the reputation of being vice-ridden.

But concerning the person who buys a possession with that charge already on it, he is not obligated for any longer than it remains in his power: because by reason of that possession alone he incurs the obligation to pay. However, the heirs incur it by reason of the whole inheritance and estate <term>hazienda: the totality of one's property and wealth</term>, which is subject to the real obligations of its master. Certain conditions are usually placed in these contracts, which are partly just, and could be entirely so if **equity** were maintained by both parties. First, that the possessions be clearly worth much more than the amount [of the annuity], so that however much their price and value might drop morally and legally, the amount can still be drawn from them in case the person fails—whether through death or by not paying—which is very much in accordance with reason. And if it were a single possession, no matter how much more it is worth, it is not an imbalance.

Especially if he is bound not to sell them or alienate them. It is a great grievance done to him, to tie up his estate in this way so that he cannot dispose of it for a minor matter. # TREATISE
## ON RENTALS,

### ¶ CHAPTER I. ON THE UGLINESS AND ABOMINATION of the vice of usury.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap letter 'V' featuring ornate floral patterns and vines inside a square border.</image-desc>
ONE OF THE VICES most commonly committed by merchants, bankers, and money-changers in these kingdoms is usury; yet it is the one least understood or noticed. It is committed often, yet recognized rarely. This is because this sin almost always disguises and hides itself—not only with "interest" <note>During this period, "interest" was often used as a legalistic term to justify payments that might otherwise be seen as sinful usury</note> (a makeup that makes it look attractive to men), but with two thousand other costumes and foreign garments that it puts on. It is so abominable and ugly that it does not dare to appear as it truly is; even man, in order to commit it with less disgust, seeks to cover and conceal it. It is, and always was, abominable. No one dares mention it to another, let alone invite them to partake in it. Yet it strives to insert itself into every transaction made. Thus, he who thinks he is far removed from it actually has it deeply incorporated within himself. There is no vice that imitates the devil as much as this one. What thing is more hateful and fearsome for men to see than the devil? Yet there are few among us who do not welcome him a hundred times into our hearts. They loathe him when he is exposed, but when he is dressed in vices, they find him quite pleasant. There is no crime more infamous among people (aside from the unspeakable sin <term>nefando: a legal and theological term for the "sin that cannot be named," usually referring to sodomy, considered the most heinous of crimes</term>) than usury, etc. To say to someone, "be a usurer"...

is to insult him, and he takes it as an injury. But by changing a few words, speaking through circumlocutions of sales and exchanges, there is no crime that merchants throw themselves into more quickly, or commit more often. To a man of good standing, it cannot be tolerated to say "you lie" regarding what he says; yet there are a thousand modes of speaking with which, at every step, this is said and answered to him, and he remains very satisfied and content. It is not tolerated to call a merchant a usurer, but there are a thousand usurious contracts in which, without being told so, he involves himself, celebrates, and carries them out. 

In this way, this vice commonly goes about disguised and hidden behind others. Open and clear usury is for one to lend a thousand <term>ducados: a gold coin used throughout Europe as a standard of trade</term> for four months, with fifty in interest returned. This happens once in a lifetime, and in secret. But giving them under the title of <term>cambio: a bill of exchange or currency transfer</term> for Medina <note>referring to Medina del Campo, the site of the most important financial fairs in 16th-century Spain</note>, while they are to be paid back here, happens at every moment. 

So it is that usury is so abominable that it rarely dares to walk alone; it always goes embedded in businesses and deals that have at least a good name and appearance, so as to enter under that foreign title without being recognized by its own. And my desire to write about the matters and businesses in whose company it usually walks invited me to write first about it. Although this cannot be as brief as the subject requires—which is treated not for its own sake, but so that others might be better understood—it is necessary for two reasons. 

The first is so that once it is perfectly known, it cannot disguise itself so much, nor be palliated <note>palliated: here meaning to cloak or hide the true nature of a sin with legal excuses</note> in other contracts, that it remains unrecognized. The second is so that its gravity and malice may be known; and knowing it, any business where it is encountered may be abandoned and abhorred, even if it offers great temporal interest <note>temporal interest: worldly or monetary profit, as opposed to eternal spiritual gain</note>. It does more spiritual harm to the soul than good to the purse. 

Indeed, in the reality of the truth, it does no good at all, since in the end all usurious gain must be restored <note>restitution: Catholic doctrine required the physical return of ill-gotten gains before a sin could be forgiven in confession</note>, under penalty of the guilt not being forgiven. I must treat of exchanges, <term>censos: annuities or loans secured by property</term>, tributes, sales, and purchases, on credit and in cash; where many times we will say it is "palliated usury." Regarding the second point, that is, hiring and renting, it is to be noted that not all things can be rented, nor can this contract and negotiation take place in all things. There are many things that can be sold and lent, but not rented. Water is not rented, nor wine, oil, vinegar, bread, barley, money, nor many others of this kind that are counted in the law. 

<margin>Certain things are such that their use is the very consumption of the things; however, the use of others is not consumption, just as the use of a house is habitation, not destruction. <note>original Latin: "quædam res ſunt, quarũ vſus eſt ipſa rerũ cõſumptio, aliarũ tamen vſus non eſt conſumpſio, ſic ut vſus domus eſt habitatio non diſsipatio."</note></margin>

Some houses serve as a dwelling, where the person defends himself from heat, rain, winds, and storms, and this for many years if it is well-founded and built, remaining continuously upright. And even after having served for a long time, not only is it not consumed, but it improves—at least in value and price, for it is worth more now than when it was first built. Likewise, a horse is useful for a journey, and if it is well treated, it remains alive and healthy at the end of the day. ### In What It Consists

...is described, is worth money, and is valued by it. A horse is hired from here to the Court, provided it is returned healthy and sound to its owner; the fact that it served for the whole journey is worth something (it is worth whatever the custom dictates). Everyone calls this hire. In this way, he who hires does not purchase the horse—for that remains with its master—but rather its use and service for a certain number of days. And he who leases some houses for a hundred <term>Ducat: A high-value gold or silver coin used throughout Europe.</term> each year does not buy them (as they are sometimes worth four or five thousand). He buys the right to dwell in them for that time, and the use of them—without including the substance and the <term>Shell: Spanish "caxco" (casco), referring to the physical structure or frame of the building.</term>—is valued in the present time at a hundred ducats. 

So, in everything that is leased, we necessarily find two things. One is its nature and substance, such as in houses: the walls, foundations, and roofs, the halls, rooms, upper and lower floors. All of which, even if it is leased, remains intact and complete for its owner, and he may sell or <term>Alienate: To legally transfer the ownership of property to another.</term> it. The other part is the use, the living in them; this belongs to the <term>Lessee: The person who holds the lease; the tenant.</term> <note>In the Spanish of this period, "arrendador" could refer to the tenant, whereas in modern Spanish it refers to the landlord.</note>, and he buys it for so many ducats a year, and he may inhabit it or bring in other neighbors <note>Subtenants or other residents.</note> according to what the law ordains or the deed he made permits. 

There are other things that do not serve unless they are spent and consumed, such as wine, bread, oil, and money. Wine does not begin to serve man except by being consumed. What use are wine and water, if not to be drunk? And as soon as it is drunk, it ceases to be, and can serve no more. Wheat is for eating, and by ceasing to be, it sustains and preserves man in his life. Money, likewise, does not serve except by being spent and paid out. 

From this it is clearly seen how poor a wretched miser is, however rich he may be, for he has nothing to spend. He has much that he could spend, but he guards it so closely that he does not spend it. And to have gold, even if it be a treasure, and not spend it or make use of it, is the same as not having it, because it does not serve nor profit unless it is expended. Thus, to have it and not spend it is, in plain <term>Spanish: The original uses "buen romance," meaning clear, everyday vernacular Spanish as opposed to complex Latin.</term>, not to have it, and to be subject to all the needs of a poor man. ### On Leasing

...the greater is their poverty, just as the greater is their greed. While a hundred <term>Ducats: High-value gold or silver coins.</term> sit in the corner of a chest, they profit nothing; they are not like houses or vineyards which, while remaining still, yield fruit and serve a purpose. It is necessary that they be taken out and <term>Alienated: To transfer ownership to another person.</term> so that they may multiply—by being given, exchanged, or traded. And in whatever of these businesses you engage, you ultimately deprive yourself of them. Such things as these cannot be rented or leased, because no one can make use of them except by becoming the master of them. This is a thing very contrary to a lease, where the first person always remains the master, and while he is the master, I benefit from the thing. How can a hundred ducats be leased, or for how much would they be leased? For in that very instance, they are given to someone so that they may be used. It is necessary that both he who receives them and he who gave them lose them and make them belong to another. They must serve for trading, and they cannot trade without being given as a price, and in giving them, they cease to be mine and begin to belong to others. For this reason, a hundred ducats cannot be rented, nor are they worth more than a hundred.

In houses or estates, there are two things of value and price: one is the use, service, or fruit of them; the other is the substance and <term>Quiddity: A philosophical term referring to the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing.</term> of them. And we commonly see each one sold on its own. It happens a hundred times that someone has his house rented for two hundred <term>Escudos: A gold or silver currency.</term> and sells it—while another is actually living in it—for nine or ten thousand. A <term>Dehesa: A type of Spanish pastureland or estate, often used for grazing.</term> is taken for twenty thousand <term>Maravedis: A small Spanish copper or silver coin.</term> as a <term>Tributo: A fixed annual payment or ground rent.</term>, and it is sold elsewhere for three or four thousand <term>Castellanos: A specific type of high-purity gold coin.</term>. These three thousand are not given for the rent, but for the soil and the <term>Fuero: The legal rights, jurisdiction, or traditional standing of a piece of land.</term> of that estate. Nor are those twenty thousand the value of the lease, but rather that of the entire house, even if it provides no service. Thus we Spaniards are accustomed to saying that there are possessions that rent for little and are worth much, and others conversely that rent for much and are worth little. There are olive groves that are worth twenty thousand ducats and do not rent for six hundred. And a horse is sometimes worth six thousand maravedis and brings in a profit of ten thousand in a year. And consequently, its owner can sell one while keeping the other; he sells the use and the benefit of it—which they call renting—while retaining the ownership of the houses, or vineyards, or orchards. But wine, oil, and wheat have no more than one thing of value, which is their very substance. There is not that distinction between <term>Quiddity: The essential nature or "whatness" of an object.</term> and nature, and service and <term>Usufruct: The legal right to use and enjoy the profits from property belonging to another.</term>. Rather, a thousand <term>Ducats: High-value gold or silver coins.</term> are worth only a thousand ducats, and the use of a thousand ducats is worth those same thousand ducats. Because they are not used except by spending them, and the spending of them is worth a thousand. I would wish that this be primarily taken as the conclusion of this chapter: (namely) that in all things which cannot serve without being consumed, there is no more than one value and price, which is their entire quantity. For which reason they cannot be rented or leased, but only sold or lent. Only those things can be leased which serve or bear fruit while remaining whole and perfect in the power of their master. It will be appropriate for us to treat this contract and its conditions in this chapter, since it is so common in practice and custom everywhere.

Whoever desires to know this in greater detail should consult a **jurist**; we shall write copiously in this chapter on what belongs to our faculty.

From this principle, which we declared in the past—that the leased item always remains with the one who rents it out in regards to its substance and nature, even though another person serves themselves and profits from it—three notable teachings emerge.

The first is that the item stands at the risk of its **master**, whether it be lost, destroyed, or improved. <note>original: "V. g.", abbreviation for the Latin *verbi gratia*, meaning "for example."</note> For example, if I lease a house and it falls—whether because the earth shook, or a lightning bolt struck, or a great storm blew through and knocked it down—the loss belongs to the master, not to the **tenant**. This is because the master was its owner. <note>original: "Itẽ", abbreviation for the Latin *Item*, meaning "likewise" or "furthermore."</note> Likewise, if one held an orchard for rent and the river burst its banks and destroyed it, or if by chance fire broke out and burned it, the loss is for the master. It also increases and grows for him if the property is improved or thrives.

There follows the second point: that when the property is finished or destroyed, the tenant remains free from the <term>rent</term> <note>original: "pensión"; the recurring payment agreed upon in the lease</note> he was paying, and the <term>lease</term> <note>original: "arrendamiento"</note> ceases. Likewise, even if it does not perish entirely, if it is diminished by more than half, it is reasonable that the <term>contract</term> be understood as undone. The law so disposes. Because, as is manifest, the use of the piece—thus destroyed, impaired, or ruined—will no longer be worth as much as it was when whole and perfect, which is what was agreed upon at the beginning.

And then he owes nothing. He does enough in improving the owner's estate, leaving it in better condition at the end.

### ¶ CHAPTER IIII. HOW NECESSARY AND *universal it is among men to lend, and how one must lend without interest or profit.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring ornate scrollwork and figures.</image-desc>

**IT IS A VERY** well-known and celebrated sentiment among philosophers, both Greek and Latin, that there is no man so sufficient unto himself, nor so abundant, that he does not have a need for another in many things. Who was born so fully formed that he does not require others to raise him? Who, once grown, is so wise that they do not need to be taught the arts and instructed in business? Who was ever so rich that they did not ask for something on loan? Rather, I am inclined to say that man by himself is so insufficient that in almost everything he requires another to help him. 

God created **Adam** in a sovereign state, free and exempt from many **burdens and tributes** <note>original: "pechos, y tributos"; while "pechos" were specific taxes paid by commoners in Spain, the author uses it here metaphorically for the physical and social hardships of mortal life</note> that life now brings with it, endowed with all virtues and **knowledge**. <note>original: "sciencias"; in the 16th century, this referred to organized bodies of knowledge or wisdom generally, rather than modern laboratory science</note> And yet, God observed that it was not fitting for him to be alone in paradise, and said: "Let us create a companion for him who may help him," and He created **Eve** to help him. How much less can anyone at present presume—now that we are all subject to hunger, poverty, sickness, sensuality, and death—not to have need of anyone. What does man do, except sleep? (which is not doing, but resting) that is not helped...

...longer grants, but instead he must be helped and favored by another? Whether he dresses, puts on shoes, eats, drinks, learns, works, or rests: things for which he seems sufficient alone, he still requires company—that is to say—someone to cut his clothes, someone to make his shoes, someone to sow, someone to cultivate so that there are foods, and someone to teach him, someone to pay him, and even someone to watch over him. We all depend on one another, and we were born with this law and obligation to help and succor each other. Plato says that man was not born for his own benefit and utility alone: but for himself, and for the good of his **republic** <note>original: "republica"; here referring to the community or commonwealth</note>, for his parents and relatives. And to put it briefly, we were born for the good of all. We cannot live in any other way, let alone endure. From this it is clear upon what right and reason the **charity** <note>original: "charidad"; meaning brotherly love and social duty</note> we owe our neighbors is founded. For setting aside that God commands it of us, the great good and utility we receive from one another obliges us to care for and love each other. It is true that, given that we help each other in all affairs, it is just that in many cases we pay for the labor of the one who is useful to us and serves us. If one requires another to teach him, let him compensate him. If he wishes to live in another’s house, let him rent it. If his neighbor’s horse seems good to him, let him buy it. Because if people served and benefited each other for free and without compensation, it would certainly not be a benefit, but rather our destruction and ruin. For if we occupied ourselves in serving without profit, many in the end would become destitute and poor. But as it is practiced now, he who feels the burden and suffers the labor (as the **law** <note>original: "derecho"; here referring to legal or natural right</note> says) also enjoys the honor and feels the profit; the result is an inequality so harmonious and balanced that everyone is held in their proper weight, and each one sustains and maintains himself in his place. It is also true that not all acts are of this condition. There are some that God willed should be done for free for our neighbors, such as giving **alms** <note>original: "limosna"</note> to the poor, and

-># the loan.<-

<margin><note>original Latin: "Dare mutuo re suam alteri, est actus proprius liberalitatis, et gratiæ, & illud quod liberalitatem tollit, actū ab natura sua auertit, & virtutē iustitiæ vniuersalis corrumpit.
