...lending to the needy. This remained among men, according to natural law, as a way to exercise **liberality** <note>original: "liberalidad"; the virtue of being generous with one's resources</note>, one of the most magnificent and illustrious virtues that exist. Lending is a business that by its very nature demands it be done without interest, although it carries a very great interest attached to it. For if one does not seek interest in temporal things, God gives a reward and eternal prize to those who, out of love for Him, succor their neighbor. Among those whom the Scripture calls blessed and happy, the merciful are named and placed—those who provide for the poor and lend to the needy. They do this, on one hand, for the glory they expect in payment for their merits; on the other, because they imitate in this life their heavenly Father, who does us so much good without claiming anything from us. Thus, lending is an act of mercy and liberality, and both virtues are great enemies of price and payment; it is necessary that they be exercised without these considerations and pretensions.

And because it is very wrong to use a virtue against its nature, it is a grave sin to lend for profit. Instead, each person should lend what they can mercifully and liberally, not seeking temporal **usury** <note>original: "usura"; the practice of charging interest on a loan, which was often considered a sin in this period</note>, but rather the usury of heaven which God promises. One should also remember what we said at the beginning: that another day, or other days will come, when perhaps he himself will be in the same necessity, or an even greater one. But even if this reason and true discourse be granted—showing clearly how great an evil it is to seek interest when lending—there are other more evident and effective reasons that patently uncover its abomination and wickedness. For one sins not only against mercy, but also against justice—a more grave and enormous crime, which brings with it the obligation of **restitution** <note>original: "restitucion"; the legal and moral requirement to return ill-gotten gains to the rightful owner</note>, as we shall see.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section regarding the moral and legal nature of lending. ### Of the types

Resuming that notable distinction from the third chapter: those things fell under **leasing** <note>original: "arrendamiento"</note> which served their purpose without being consumed, where there were two things of value and price. One was the substance and nature—such as houses, vineyards, olive groves, and pastures. The other was the **usufruct** <note>the legal right to use and enjoy the fruits or profits of something belonging to another</note> of it, such as the grapes, the olives, the grass, and the fodder. Because these were distinct, they were usually divided and separated, with the ownership of the possession remaining with its owner, while granting and giving the usufruct to another. And those things which could not be used without being spent and consumed could not, and should not, be rented. This distinction is the basis and foundation of this entire subject, and as such, I would wish it to be understood, internalized, and never forgotten.

Turning now to the second business, that is, the **loan**, I say that it is more general and common. This is because both types can be lent and are lent: those that endure and remain, and those that are spent and consumed. It is common to lend a horse, some clothes, or a house; and one could lend (although it is not common practice) a **field of grain** <note>original: "sementera de pan"</note>. Of the other category, one might lend one hundred **fanegas** <note>a Spanish unit of dry capacity, roughly 1.5 bushels</note> of wheat, one thousand **arrobas** <note>a unit of weight or liquid measure</note> of oil, or two thousand **ducats** <note>gold coins used as currency</note>. The Latins, being richer and more abundant in vocabulary than the Spanish, have different terms and names to designate one type of loan and the other. When those of the first species are lent, such as jewelry or tapestries, they call it a **loan for use** <note>original: "commodatum"</note>; when the second, such as wheat, money, and the like, they call it a **loan for consumption** <note>original: "mutuum"</note>. And although this multitude and abundance of words may not matter much—since with a single term we will touch upon what is necessary for the subject—it matters a great deal whether one lends one thing or another. There are many notable differences between one loan and the other, which we will treat by matching and comparing them both, so that the doctrine may emerge more concisely and clearly.

# Of Lending,
-> M m 3 <-
<meta>catchword: pri-</meta>

<margin>
Digest, on contracts of sale, law 2.
Digest, on commodatum, law 1 & 4.
Aristotle’s Ethics, final book.
Distinction 1, "The law of nature."
In a loan of consumption, the same amount in kind must be returned.

First, whoever received on loan horses, houses, or estates, must return the very same ones that were given to him; the same horse, the same ring, the same clothing, the same houses. We see this put into practice and use, and without anyone saying so—being a **natural law** <note>original: "ley natural"; principles of right and wrong believed to be inherent in human nature rather than created by society</note> that is known without being taught—men take it as an established fact that they must return the same thing that was lent to them. And the **Canon Law** <note>the body of laws and regulations made by ecclesiastical authority, specifically the Catholic Church</note> itself calls it natural law.

This is not the case, however, with things that are consumed in their use; rather, it is enough to return their equivalent of the same kind. If you lend me ten **fanegas** <term>a Spanish unit of dry capacity, approximately 1.5 bushels</term> of wheat, I do not have to return the same grains of wheat you gave me; it is enough that it be ten fanegas of another wheat. If one thousand **ducats** <term>a gold coin used as a currency unit</term> in **reales** <term>a Spanish silver coin</term> are lent, it is enough that I give you another thousand. If the same wheat and money had to be returned, as one returns the same horse or clothes, I do not know why you would lend them, nor how they could have served or benefited me. Wheat generally serves no purpose but to be eaten, and money but to be spent; if you give them to me to eat and expend, how can I return them to you? It is evident that some things must return to the power of their master, and others not—only their equivalents and similar items.

Except, if these were not lent for their proper use, but for some display, pomp, and ceremony. For example, if for certain **nuptial ceremonies** <note>original: "velaciones"; specifically the "veiling" part of a traditional Spanish wedding ceremony</note>, one hundred **doblas** <term>a medieval Spanish gold coin</term> of oil <note>The text says "doblas of oil," which may refer to a specific container or a value of oil measured in coins; it emphasizes that even money, if used for display, must be returned exactly.</note> were given, or a pouch of **crowns** <term>coronas; a type of currency</term> was lent as a pledge in some pawn, the very same ones must be returned, even though they are money. Because, in reality, they were not lent for their own use, but for that appearance, ostentation, and pledge, which is quite accidental to the coins and crowns.

This difference arises from another, which it would be harmful to ignore. And it is that when houses or jewels are lent, I do not become their owner simply because they are lent to me; rather, it is like a **lease** <note>original: "arrendamiento"</note>, where only the use and benefit of them is given to me. It does not differ from renting, except in not carrying a price; in everything else, the lord always remains as much the master...

And since by lending it the owner does not cease to have **lordship** <note>original: "señorio"; legal ownership and right of control</note> over it, it is only just that for him it lives, or is preserved, or dies, or is lost. # On Loans.

...condition <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of special agreements</note> that this [item] be at the risk of the one who asks for it for the time that he possesses it. Once this agreement is accepted, he is obliged to pay for them regardless of the manner in which they perish. The same applies if he agreed to cover any damages or impairments that might occur while in his power—provided there is a reason to impose this condition, which would be based on what was said above. 

The second case is if he uses the item for something other than what he specifically explained when he asked for it. For example, if I lent him an enslaved person <note>The original Spanish uses "negro." In this historical legal context, enslaved individuals were often treated as property in loan contracts.</note> to serve as a groom on horseback, and he instead employs him in carrying heavy hides on his back. Or if I gave him a horse to ride for leisure, and he runs it as a post-horse—a task to which the nag is not accustomed. Or if I lent him houses for him to dwell in, and he turns them into lodgings for soldiers. In short, if he uses the item for any purpose other than the intent I expressed and explained when he asked for it—especially if the damage arose from that use—the payment is then his responsibility. 

<margin>Sylvester Prieras, *Summa Summarum*, "Commodatum," part 8; Digest, "On the action of commodatum," law: *Si ut certo*; *Extravagantes*, single chapter on loans.</margin>

The third case is when the person is at fault for the loss (although not every instance of carelessness or fault is enough to make one liable). One must observe whether the item was lent for the borrower's own utility and profit; if so, even if he has been negligent in its guarding by the smallest degree of fault, he must satisfy the debt in full, not merely according to how reprehensible the fault was. This is because it is only just that any person should take great care of that which belongs to another and has been received for his own benefit and profit; thus, even the slightest neglect obligates him. So the law determines and requires. 

However, if he received it to serve and honor the one who lent it, or for the lender's own profit—such as if someone gives me a fine garment or a jewel to wear for their own festivals—should it be lost, I would not be obliged to pay for it, provided there was no fraud or malice on my part, or if the fault and negligence I had in the matter was not notable. This remains true even if there was some small degree of fault in the loss. 

<margin>Chapter on loans; Digest, book 1, "On actions and obligations," law: *par. Si is vero*.</margin>

Also, if he received a piece of equipment, or anything else, for a specific term and period of time, and he does not return it once the term has ended—especially if it has already been requested and he has delayed in returning it—in whatever manner it is later [lost]...

# On the Types [of Loans]

...is lost, it is just that he pay for it, since he was now holding it against the will of the other, at whose risk it had been until then. <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page regarding a borrower who fails to return an item on time.</note>

All of this we derive as exceptions to that universal rule (namely) that a borrowed item is always at the risk of the lender, provided that if it is returned, or sent with a person considered reputable in the town—or at least among those who knew them to be faithful, safe, and trustworthy—and that person were to abscond with it, the borrower would remain entirely free of liability. In contrast to all this are things that are spent and consumed by using them; by lending these, they are alienated <term>alienated: in legal terms, this means the ownership is transferred from the lender to the borrower</term>, and the person who receives them becomes their owner. Thus, they exist for his benefit and are lost at his own risk and expense. 

For example: if someone lent me a thousand bushels <note>original: "hanegas," a Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly 55 liters</note> of wheat, and it was eaten in my house by weevils <note>original: "gorgojo"</note>; or a thousand *arrobas* <note>A unit of liquid or weight; an arroba of wine is roughly 16 liters</note> of wine, and it turned to vinegar; or a hundred jars of oil, and they broke; or a thousand silver *reales*, and they were stolen from me—I lose everything, not the person who lent them to me. In whatever way or manner they are lost, I remain obligated to satisfy and pay the debt in full. Beyond this, in each of these types of loans, there are several notable points, though they are few and brief.

First, if someone lent me clothes, enslaved persons, horses—finally, things that I must return as the very same items—and I had them together with my own belongings, and we came to such a point that I could not save them all, but rather it was necessary to lose some (as for instance if a storm were raging and it was necessary to throw cargo of weight and volume into the sea, or if thieves surrounded me and asked for "courtesy" <note>This is a cynical reference to thieves demanding a "tribute" or ransom to spare one's life or remaining goods</note> as they usually do). It is often debated among theologians: which item is the person more obligated to protect? 

I respond that in a case where one could not retain or defend both, it is not an injustice to save and protect one's own property and allow the borrowed or entrusted item to be cast into the sea or seized. Even though I must look out for what is lent and entrusted to me, this is not understood to be at the detriment of my own estate and purse. But—

# On Loans

...even if one does not sin against justice in such cases, the item lent to me could be of such price and value, and my own belongings of such little esteem, that I might be obliged by charity to prioritize my neighbor’s property over my own. This is especially true since they were lent to me—a title of possession that adds a greater obligation to look after the items than the law and the common course of love already required. 

However, if the things lent were of the category of money, it has already been said that from the moment they are lent to me, they are at my risk in any event, whether they are lost or stolen by sea or by land, until they are actually paid back. Thus, if I were to send the funds with a messenger or on a ship, and they are lost for any reason, it is at my risk.

Regarding that which is returned in the same kind <term>kind: known in legal terms as *in specie*, meaning returning the same type and quality of goods (like wheat for wheat) rather than the exact same physical objects or their monetary value</term>, and not the same individual item, it should be noted that the same quantity that was given must be returned, even if the price has changed. 

Suppose they lent me two thousand *arrobas* <note>An *arroba* was a Spanish unit of measurement; for wine, it was approximately 16 liters</note> of wine for three or four months, or three bushels <note>original: "hanegas," a dry measure of roughly 55 liters</note> of wheat, when it was cheap—at four *reales* the bushel and three the *arroba*. If at the time of return the wheat happens to be worth a *ducado* <note>A high-value gold coin used at the time</note> and the wine six *reales*, I am still obliged to return the full two thousand *arrobas*. This is because they did not lend me the value (which has fluctuated), but the substance itself, which I must return in the same quantity. 

Conversely, if the price had dropped significantly, no compensation would be necessary. If they were lent to me when they were worth eight, and I return them when they are worth four, it is enough to return the two hundred <note>The author uses "two hundred" here as a illustrative figure for the quantity received</note> that I received. This is because a loan requires such equality and such purity that not a single hair more than what was received should be returned. 

But what should be judged in such a change of value in the event that the wheat or wine is not returned in the same kind, but in money? At what price is it just to pay? At the current price, or the price it had when it was lent? I say that one must distinguish...

# On Annuities
<note>original: "De los censos". In this period, "censos" referred to financial contracts or annuities, often involving the exchange of capital for a yearly return, though the author here applies the logic to commodity loans.</note>

...and to note whether, at the beginning, it was agreed that payment be made in money or not. If there was such an agreement, it is not truly a loan, but a **Real Sale**, which, to be just, requires the price to be set according to what it was worth at the time of delivery, as we showed in the first treatise. However, it could also be agreed that an equal amount of wheat or oil be returned, and if one does not have it, to pay in money. In that case, one must pay according to its value at the time of return, whether it is worth less or more than when it was lent. 

The clear reason for this is that the money is given in place of the wheat or wine that was to be returned. Thus, it is just to pay what it is worth now, so that the other person, with that money, can purchase the goods if they wish. Therefore, the most conscientious <note>original: "sin escrupulo," meaning without moral doubt or hesitation</note> approach is to pay according to its value at the time it was due to be returned, since one gives money instead of the wheat or wine that was owed. But if they agree from the start to return an equal amount [of goods], and if the same material is not returned, that it be paid for at the current value, this is not an illicit agreement. Although it is not a pure loan either, but a conditional sale, or one dependent on the condition that the wheat is not returned. 

But if I lend to you plainly, and by chance at the time of payment you do not have the barley or wine that was received, it is a just law and fair equity <term>equity: (aequitas) the principle of legal fairness used to correct or supplement laws when a strict application would be unfair</term> that it be paid only according to its value at the time it was due to be returned, no matter how much more or less it may be worth. This is so that with that value, the other person can buy, if they wish, the wheat or wine they expected and which the borrower was obligated to deliver.

Regarding the time that is often set for the return of loans, it should be noted that it can be designated in many ways, and no small amount of evil <note>The author likely refers to the "evil" of usury or exploitative contracts designed to profit from price fluctuations</note> can be mixed into it. Three ways occur to me in which the return can be agreed upon regarding time. First, by not setting any specific deadline, but leaving it vague—whenever one party wishes or is able, or the other asks him...

# On Loans
->de prestamo<-

...asks for it. This is as common in small amounts as it is rare in large sums. Very few leave their property thus, so much at the will of another. But when it is done, it is such liberality <note>A term for generosity or the virtuous giving of one's own resources</note> and virtue that there is more to praise in it than to reprove or condemn. 

The second [scenario] is if he were to obligate the borrower not to return it until he asks for it. In this, great injustice can intervene in both types of loans: whether the same thing is returned—such as a **Slave** or a **Horse**—and the lender intends for the other person to maintain or guard them even when they are not needed. And it is much worse in the second type of loan, where the same kind <note>original: "especie," referring to fungible goods like grain or currency</note> is returned—wheat, wine, or money—and the lender intends not to ask for it until it is worth more. This is manifest deceit and no small injury. The safe path is to leave the borrower free to return it when they are able, or for the lender not to ask for it during such scarcity. Doing the opposite is a cruel injustice, requiring the restitution of whatever extra value was gained from the goods <note>original: "ropa," used here in the archaic sense of "commodities" or "merchandise" rather than just clothing</note>.

The third, and most common, is to set a deadline, before which the lender cannot compel the borrower to return it, although the borrower remains free to give it sooner if they wish. This is a contract quite free of suspicion. However, if they obligate the borrower *not* to pay before the deadline either, one must avoid the same inconvenience: that is, not to set a time when it is probably believed that type of goods will be worth more or be of better quality. Because such an advantage and excess would patently be **usurious gain**. All of this, as clearly appears, comes down to this: that no more be returned than what was lent, nor should anyone intend to profit from lending money.

But it is not just to leave in silence that grave doctors <note>Referring to "Doctors of the Church" or high-ranking legal and theological scholars</note> condemn, regarding this point, a contract very commonly used everywhere, and very necessary to be used: which is to lend wheat to laborers <note>original: "labradores," meaning farmers or peasants</note> or bakers, with which

### On the Types of Loans

...they return it at the harvest of the new grain. This is done, first of all, by almost all commonwealths <note>original: "republicas," referring to the organized governing bodies of cities or towns</note>, cities, towns, and villages that maintain common grain deposits for times of necessity. This is a most beneficial practice. In these places, they keep stored in chambers two or three thousand fanegas <term>fanega: a Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly 55 liters or 1.5 bushels</term> from one year to the next. And so that it does not spoil—as it would if it were kept for too long—when they see that the current year’s harvest is prospering for the private farmers, they lend the stored grain to be used, either for baking bread or for sowing. The condition is that in the coming year, the borrowers return it from the new harvest.

The same is also done by certain individuals who keep a quantity locked away, waiting for a time of scarcity. However, they do this not to aid the poor like the commonwealth does, but to impoverish them further by selling it at excessive prices. Very learned men condemn these types of loans. Yet, I would not dare to condemn them so absolutely. This is because there is a necessity for such loans to be made, great utility follows from their being made, and there is no inherent iniquity in the act itself. 

For one thing, the aged wheat <term>original: "trigo anexo," referring to grain from the previous year's harvest</term> that is lent is often better than the new grain for both eating and sowing, and is of greater value. Thus, it appears that no injury is done to the borrower in this arrangement. Furthermore, both parties benefit from it. Therefore, I say that as long as the wheat is simply aged and remains in good condition, the contract is licit <note>legally and morally permissible</note>, and nothing of value is gained in the loan that would constitute usury. This is because the convenience of being able to store the grain longer is merely incidental to the contract, and the aged grain itself possesses other superior advantages.

But if the grain is eaten by weevils <term>gorgojo: a common beetle that infests stored grain</term>, or is full of weeds <note>original: "alpiste," literally birdseed, here implying the presence of inferior seeds or contaminants</note>, or is close to rotting or prone to it, in such a case it is a usurious wickedness to lend it in exchange for new grain. In such an instance, the new grain will clearly be better, and usury is defined by the difference—not between old and new—but between good and bad. In this matter, some Knights and Lords of vassals sin gravely...

## On Loans

...those who compel laborers and bakers <note>original: "panaderas," specifically referring to women who baked and sold bread, a common trade for women at the time</note> to take their wheat, which is nearly spoiled from being stored for too long, and require them to return an equal amount of new grain. They should not, nor can they, distribute such wheat as a loan; it must be through a sale, selling it at low prices. And if they do compel them to pay back that same amount in new grain at whatever price it may then be worth, it is necessary to accept this obligation as partial payment, reducing the price of what the poorly conditioned wheat is actually worth because of this obligation. For example, if it were worth five if paid in cash, they should give it for four and a half to bind the person to return it in wheat.

If anyone has the right to lend such poorly conditioned wheat, it seems to be the commonwealth <note>original: "republica," referring here to the municipal government or town council</note> through its public deposit <term>pósito: a communal grain bank or granary managed by the town to ensure food security for its citizens</term> to its residents, because it all results in their own benefit. After all, the commonwealth keeps and has kept it for their provision. However, I say that it is a business of such poor appearance to lend spoiled grain for an equal amount of new grain that the commonwealth neither should, nor do I believe it can, lawfully do so if it has the revenue—as it commonly does—to buy what is lost from that sum by selling it at low prices. It is not just, under the title of "community," to harass private individuals at every moment if the commonwealth already has sufficient property to remedy these losses. But if it does not (a very rare thing), no one should be scandalized that it is done, nor should they cry out against receiving it this way for the good of their community.

What is lawful for the commonwealth—above any other private person, even if they are the lord of the town—is the power to compel them to take the grain from the deposit as a loan or purchase in whatever condition it may be, making a just restitution <note>original: "refaction," a legal or economic term for a price adjustment or compensation for the diminished value of the goods</note> so that not everything is lost. This is not lawful for these lords who keep thousands of fanegas <term>fanega: a Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly 55 liters or 1.5 bushels</term> stored away in chambers, waiting only for some sterile year <note>a year of crop failure or drought</note>. If the grain spoils for them, let them attribute the loss to their own avarice. In my judgment, they could not with a safe conscience compel even their own vassals...

# How much it may be necessary

...to spend their wheat on them, as the commonwealth <note>original: "republica," referring to the municipal government or local community body</note> does by distributing it among the bakers. For they [private owners] were not keeping it for the good of the community, nor had they obligated themselves to do so; rather, they kept it to earn more from the sale. From this rule, there is no need to except the King—not because he is not exempt, but because he never meddles in such petty dealings <note>original: "grangeria," referring here to small-scale profiteering or commercial management beneath the dignity of the crown</note>, nor is it fitting for his supreme authority. Returning to the beginning of the paragraph, it is a rule so general that a loan must be returned in the same quantity that was received. Even if the measure itself has changed—the <term>fanega: a traditional Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly 1.5 bushels</term> or the <term>arroba: a unit of weight, approximately 25 pounds</term>—it must be paid according to the original, old measure. For example, if until now the fanega held twenty-four <term>almudes: a small dry measure, often one-twelfth of a fanega, though local definitions varied by region</term>, and they increase it to thirty or lower it to twenty, I must return it by neither of those, but at the rate of twenty-four almudes, if that was the measure in which I received it.

And because money has no other measure or quantity except the value and price set by the commonwealth, this is a particular case. Regardless of changes in value and quantity (unlike the other items we discussed), it must be returned according to what it was worth when it was lent to me, in whatever material of gold or silver it is to be paid. Let us take the example of one hundred <term>crowns: (coronas) a type of gold coin</term> which, at the time of the loan, were worth ten <term>reales: the standard silver currency unit</term>. If the value should later rise by law to twelve, I only have to return one thousand and thirty <note>The text specifies 1,030 reales; while 100 multiplied by 10 is 1,000, the "thirty" may reflect contemporary exchange fees or a specific fractional value of the crown at the time</note> reales, which would be the amount lent. To do the opposite is **usury**—that is to say, to receive payment according to the new, higher valuation. And if the value were lower, it would be a theft on the part of the one who received the loan. And it would be much worse if, at the start, it were agreed to return the money at a time when it is known it will be worth more, although this is a very rare case in the kingdoms of Spain, where the same coinage and value remain for many times and ages. In foreign nations, the law and price are very changeable.

Finally, it occurs to me to say that a loan is by its nature an act of mercy and generosity, and it requires that it be done so...

necessarily without interest, for by the very fact that interest is taken, it is not lending it, but renting it. In the preceding chapters, we declared which things could be rented and which could not. From this, it follows that for those things which can be rented, if something is earned when they are lent—provided it is moderate—it is not a mortal sin. However, it will truly be a rental, not a loan, even if they call it such. If someone asks me for a horse on loan for eight days, and I reply that they must give me a dozen <term>reales: Spanish silver coins used from the 14th century</term>, even though it is requested as a loan, it is in effect rented. But a true and pure loan cannot be practiced except nobly <note>original: "ahidalgadamente," implying the generous, disinterested conduct expected of a nobleman or gentleman</note>, without taking profit for it. 

The things that could not be rented were those that were beneficial and served by being consumed, such as money, wine, and oil, among other similar things; these can be sold for a fair price, or lent for free without charge, but not rented. Thus, in lending them, nothing can be taken, because they are not capable of being rented. When this rule is broken and transgressed by taking interest for lending money, gold, and silver—along with the others we always mention—then the sin of usury is committed. In this way, such is the nature of this vice, and it is found (that is to say) in those things that are consumed, perish, and end through their service and use.

# In what it consists

I point out the evil and vice almost with my finger so that it may be loathed, avoided, and fled from, according to the two parts of justice that King David sets forth in the Psalm: *Depart from evil, and follow what is good.* <note>The author refers to Psalm 34:14 (or Psalm 37:27 in some traditions): "Turn from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue it."</note> And although in terms of initial practice, a man first turns away from the sin into which he is born so that he may follow virtue, in terms of understanding, it is the reverse. For first, the good must be proposed to him so that he may love it, and then the evil so that he may loathe it. According to this rule and the instruction of theologians, I have proceeded until now, and I shall continue to proceed.

In these five past chapters, I have discussed how a lease <note>original: "arrendamiento"</note> or a loan <note>original: "prestamo"</note> should be celebrated lawfully and justly, without there being any scruple in it. If I did not explain every single circumstance, or provide every case and consideration that could occur in these matters, it was because my intention is not to write laws for judges to use in sentencing, or for jurists to study. Rather, I intend to provide rules for the Christian to keep in the execution and celebration of these contracts, which are so constant and common among all people. And I believe that regarding what touches the conscience, everything has been addressed, either expressly or virtually.

It remains in the rest of this little work <term>opuscule: a minor or short treatise</term> to treat the evil that is usually done in these contracts, which is neither small nor slight, but great and frequent—especially in the loan, which is usury. This is a vice not only harmful to the soul but infamous to the person. It is a thing of wonder that the ugliness of this crime is so great that, even though it is commonly committed by persons of esteem and reputation in the town—which ought to have turned it into a "gentlemanly sin" <note>original: "peccado ahidalgo," implying a vice that becomes socially acceptable because the upper classes practice it</note>, as they have done with swearing, lying, and fornicating—it has nonetheless never ceased to appear so bad as to be a dishonor. 

We will say three things about it briefly. First, what it consists of. Second, how it is committed many times when we do not think it is. Third, how, for all its abomination and ugliness, it is without even temporal profit. We shall treat this with brevity, given...

# Usury

Though the subject matter is in itself vast and broad, and is usually treated and written about at great length among theologians and jurists, our intent is not to say everything that could be said about it. Rather, we intend to provide only the substance, and to do so with clarity. This is not because it would be wrong to expand upon it, but because those who trade in it have as little will to spend a moment reading and understanding how evil their occupations are as a sick person—whose appetite is already lost and spoiled—usually has a desire for even the finest foods. Thus, as with those who are sick in spirit, it is necessary to give them a little substance, which is a small notice of the truth (for this is their proper food, according to the Gospel), and that must be broken down and dissolved for them.

Twice now I have mentioned that general and very famous distinction regarding goods <note>original: *ropa*; here referring to movable property or commodities</note>, which are the material of all contracts. In the first kind, there are two things, each with its own price and value. For example, houses, whose structure <note>original: *caxco*</note> is worth two or three thousand ducats <term>ducat: a gold coin used as a standard of currency across Europe</term>, more or less, depending on the building, while the living and dwelling in them costs fifty or sixty each year. Of this quality are certain estates, vineyards, orchards, fields <note>original: *sementeras*</note>, horses, slaves, jewels, and ornaments, whose use-fruit <term>usufruct: the legal right to use and profit from property belonging to another</term> is rented out, while the original party remains the owner. There were other things that only had use, and were of no service except by being consumed, such as wine, wheat, money, and gold or silver in bars or coins. In these, and in all things like them, usury is committed in this manner:

<margin>

If some money is lent, or any of the other things mentioned, and some interest is taken for lending it, that which is returned beyond what was given—that excess which was received—is usury. By these very words, St. Ambrose declares it, and St. Thomas defines it. It was also defined by the sacred Council of Agde <note>A church council held in 506 AD which addressed various points of discipline and canon law</note>. If I lend two thousand ducats and they return two thousand one hundred to me, those hundred are the sin and the usury. If I gave ten fanegas <note>original: *hanegas*; a Spanish unit of dry volume, roughly equivalent to 55 liters</note> of wheat and I receive eleven, the eleventh is usury. The labor, the...

## What it consists of

<margin>Usury is where more is received than what is given. <note>original Latin: *Vsura est vbi amplius recipitur, quam quod datur*. A reference to Canon Law: 14. q. 3. & c. plerique.</note></margin>
<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 78, article 1; *De Malo* question 13, article 4; *Quodlibetal Questions* 3, 19; *Opusculum* 73, chapters 1 and 4.</margin>
The difficulty and the core point is now to make understood what reason and cause there is to forbid and prohibit this profit. I will give two reasons, which are in my judgment clear and evident. The first is that to sell what does not exist, or has no price, is clearly an injustice; and a hundred lent ducats <term>ducat: a gold coin used as a standard of currency across Europe</term> are worth no more than a hundred, so the five extra taken are taken for nothing. You did not give me anything of yours that was worth those five, if I return the hundred to you. He who rents out houses lets the tenant stay in them, and I make use of them—a service which, without the house itself, is worth a hundred escudos <term>escudo: a gold or silver coin used in Spain and its colonies</term> a year. But for a man to make use of a thousand ducats either is worth nothing, or is worth only a thousand ducats; the fifty that are added upon the return are given without any "why." To further delimit or "cleanse"—as surgeons say <note>original: *alegrar*; in a medical context, this refers to scraping or cleaning a wound to allow it to heal properly. The author is "cleaning up" the logic of the argument.</note>—this reasoning, I say that in lending a hundred escudos, there are two things: one is the hundred escudos, and the other is the act of lending. Everyone knows well that the money is worth only a hundred; interest cannot be taken for them, since they are already being returned, and the act of lending them is worth nothing.

<margin>In usury, a thing is made one's own from what was not one's own, without a just title. <note>original Latin: *In usura est res facta sua de nõ ſua ſi ne iusto tit.*</note></margin>
It is an act that has no price nor value, which either must not be done at all, or must be done for free; and it is in accordance with reason that it should be worth nothing of itself, because it involves no labor, nor does it consume time, nor does it even involve any movement. In the end, there is nothing in its foundation to give it any value. From this it is gathered that he who gains [from it] gains without cause, and consequently steals it, seizing the property of another against justice. Thus, many Doctors <note>Doctor: a title given to eminent Christian teachers and theologians</note> call usury "theft" and the usurer a "thief." Saint Ambrose and Saint Augustine say that it is the same thing to steal a poor man's clothing by robbing him as it is to steal a rich man's estate by lending to him with usury. And even our Savior himself, if not expressly, then at least almost expressly, calls them such when, casting them out of the temple, he said: "It is written: My house is a house of prayer, but you have made it a den of thieves," calling the usurers "thieves," whom he expelled with the whip and commanded to leave. And because a good opportunity presents itself, I want to point out a curious—

<margin>Usury in itself is unjust against the law of nature because the same thing is sold twice, or that which is not for sale [is sold]. <note>original Latin: *Vsura secundũ ſe eſt iniuſta contra legẽ naturæ quia idẽ bis vẽditur, vel id quod nõ vẽditur eſt*. Citing Aquinas, Opusculum 73, chapter 4.</note></margin>

# Usury

...profitable curiosity. For injustice is often distinguished from usury, and it happens that one may sin against justice without being a usurer. Injustice is to charge more for merchandise than it is worth, but usury is to charge a price for that which has no price nor value. You sell a horse, and it being worth really two hundred escudos <term>escudo: a gold or silver coin used in Spain and its colonies</term>, you take two hundred and twenty; it is an unjust sale, but in the end, you took all of that as the price for something that had a price, even if it was not that much. But if you lend a hundred doblas <term>dobla: a medieval Spanish gold coin of significant value</term>, and they return ten more to you, you take these ten extra for nothing, for that which is worth nothing. 

You will say that you gave me the means with which I might gain; you also gave me the means with which I might lose. For money, without human industry <note>In this context, "industry" refers to human labor, skill, and diligent effort.</note> and so-called "feigned fortune," is indifferent of itself and exposed to danger and risk. Furthermore, I confess you gave me the means to gain, but this "means"—which is the money—was worth no more than the hundred ducats <term>ducat: a gold coin used as a standard of currency across Europe</term> which I am now returning to you; why then do you take ten more? 

If you say that because of what I gained with your hundred, you have no small right to participate in my profit, I ask: if I were to lose—as often happens—with your hundred, would you have been a participant in the loss? It is a thing to be laughed at: that for receiving money from you with which I gained, I must give you ten ducats, but when receiving that with which I lost, you are to lose nothing at all. In this it is clear that you do not share an interest in my profit, since even if I lose, you always gain; and also, that if I gain, I usually gain more. And I am certain that, given how greedy you are, you would not be content with only five if you claimed to gain by this title, but rather you would want a partition, as if it were a partnership <note>The author is pointing out the hypocrisy of the lender: if the lender were truly a partner in the business venture, they would share the risks and the full scale of the rewards, rather than demanding a fixed, guaranteed interest rate.</note>. 

Thus it remains concluded that there is no reason nor cause by which you can take more than what you gave, and consequently you take it for nothing. You can only respond that you receive it because of what you cease to gain <note>original: *dexas de ganar*. This refers to the concept of *lucrum cessans* (lost profit), a legal justification used by some to allow interest if the lender lost other opportunities by lending the money.</note> during the time I am using them; but this title, so common and universal, will be examined...

# What It Consists Of

afterwards, which very rarely takes place, as we shall see.

The second reason has particular force and relevance regarding money, and I believe it will seem so new to many that they will judge it strange; yet it is certain and very true. It is a vice against nature and natural law to make fruitful that which is of itself most sterile, and all the wise men say that there is nothing more sterile than money, which yields no fruit at all. All other things multiply and, as they say, "give birth." If wheat is sown, it multiplies twelve and fifteen times over. And if it cannot be sown or born anew, at the very least there is hope that its value will grow over time and it will be worth more. Wine, oil, and wheat, which are cheap now, will be expensive four months from now; in short, their estimation and price are variable, which is a kind of multiplication. 

But money—this is a frightening matter—no one can profit with it while they hold it as money. It does not bear fruit when sown, nor does its value change with the passing days; it is always subject to one law, and its master never prospers with it while he possesses it as money. To make a living with it, it is necessary to employ it in cloth, in mercery <term>mercery: the trade of a dealer in textiles and fabrics</term>, or in provisions, which can be fertile for him and yield some interest <note>original: *interes*; in this period, the word often referred generally to profit or a return on investment rather than specifically to modern bank interest</note> through their use. If it was spent on wheat at the harvest and cost five reales <term>real: a common silver coin and unit of currency in Spain</term>, and by March or April it is worth eight or nine, it was the wheat, not the money, that immediately caused that profit, which was like its own fruit. 

If he had kept the money in the chest, just as he kept the wheat in the granary, even if he kept it for a year, he would not have gained a single blanca <term>blanca: a Spanish copper coin of very low value</term>. From this, one can clearly see how nothing can be gained with money alone. It is necessary to invest it in some kind of goods <note>The Spanish *ropa* (clothing/cloth) was a primary commodity for trade and investment.</note> so that it may yield profit. For this reason, it is to violate and force nature, as they say, to profit from currency alone. As the usurer does, who profits by lending gold or silver. He makes the money bear fruit and multiply by force—and "force" in this matter is understood as injustice—even though it is by its nature...

# Usury

...a most grave crime; for however blind the <term>pagans</term> <note>original: *gentiles*; referring to non-Christian peoples of antiquity</note> and idolaters were, they understood and detested it. But as little as we need to linger on proving its gravity, so much must we be confounded that the faithful commit this crime, which even among heathens and pagans was always rightly held as infamous. And since everyone knows its gravity, it only remains for me—following always my resolve for brevity—to touch upon how it can be committed. For it is committed not only with money, by lending it, but also if one lends wheat, oil, barley, and everything else that is consumed by use. In all these things the same reason and cause apply: namely, that in them there is only one consideration and one single thing of value, which is their nature and substance. This is not like vineyards, where the soil and the vines have their own value, and the <term>usufruct</term> <note>The legal right to use and enjoy the fruits or profits of another's property without destroying its substance.</note> of it—which is the grape of each year—has another distinct value. Therefore, if an interest is charged for lending the former <note>referring to consumable goods like grain or oil</note>, it is the same sin.

### ¶ CHAPTER VII. REGARDING MANY MATTERS
->*in which there is disguised usury, especially in*<-
->*pledges.*<-

<margin>Everything is considered money that is valued as money. <note>original: *Omne illud est pecunia quod pecunia existimatur.*</note> Aristotle, *Ethics*, Book 3.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial "I" featuring ornate floral and vine motifs within a square frame.</image-desc>
IT IS so contrary to reason to take interest in any loan that is made, and it is so necessary that the loan be given freely and without profit, that one cannot take any thing of value for it, of whatever quality or sort it may be. As Saint Augustine says, and even Saint Jerome adds: not even gifts. Since current practice is quite the opposite, it is not enough to say this in general terms to be understood; rather, one must explain it and express in detail many matters where we do not think usury exists, even when it is very much present.

<header>Matters in which</header>

<margin>
St. Thomas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, Question 78, throughout; Cajetan, Question 3, Distinction 37, Article 6; and *On Evil* [*De Malo*], Question 13, Article 4; *Quodlibetal Questions* 3, Article 19. <note>These are standard citations for the theological works of Thomas Aquinas and the commentator Cardinal Cajetan regarding the morality of interest and usury.</note>

...anything of value in a loan, it clearly follows that not only is money prohibited, but everything that is worth money; for everything is money, and is resolved into money, which is valued by money. Nor does currency have any more evil attached to it than other things, such that one should be forbidden and the others permitted. But this is now difficult for many to discern—namely, which things have value, and are usually worth money—in order to understand which things cannot be acquired through usury. For the universal rule is this: no one can licitly take a price for lending, whether formally or virtually, so that we may encompass all usury, both the blatant and the disguised. The light of natural reason itself teaches this to everyone almost without need for discourse, but not everyone manages to judge with ease, in particular cases, when that which is gained by lending is of value. For this reason, it is necessary to declare it very specifically.

<margin>
If someone, by reason of money lent, requires a gift as if by obligation—whether of the tongue or of service—it is the same as if he expected it from the hand; as seen above in Article 2, Addition 3. <note>original: *Si aliquis ex pecunia mutuata exigat quasi per obligationem munus, ab lingua, vel ab obsequio perinde est ac si expectaret a manu...* This refers to the three types of usurious profit: *munus a manu* (a gift from the hand/money), *munus ab obsequio* (a gift of service), and *munus a lingua* (a gift of the tongue/praise).</note>
</margin>
First, it would be the densest ignorance not to know that all these exterior, sensible, and tangible goods are worth money, as they are so commonly sold. These are what we call <term>movable and real property</term> <note>original: *muebles y rayzes*; referring to personal possessions and land/buildings.</note>: a man’s estate and temporal substance, possessions, <term>annuities</term> <note>original: *juros*; government-funded or private investment bonds that paid annual interest, often a point of moral contention.</note>, rents, provisions, jewelry, precious items, and metals. But no one is ignorant of this, nor is there anyone who does not see that it is most illicit to obtain any of these through usury. Also of value is any personal office or favor in secular and profane matters, such as the service of a servant, or of a procurator, or of a doctor, lawyer, scholar, or intercessor; thus, none of these things can be obtained by agreement through lending. Third, any obligation of justice that a man takes upon himself is <term>venal</term> <note>Capable of being bought or sold; having a financial value.</note>, by which he is bound to another and a right is acquired over him, whether in human or divine matters; and for that very reason, no such obligation can be demanded of anyone for lending to them. <header>...there is disguised usury.</header>

...and the obligation to continue it, if it is to be continued for a long time. Saying Mass is a sacred action, so sublime and excellent that it exceeds all earthly gold. For this reason, one is not permitted to receive or offer any price for it, nor can any price be given that equals its being and worth. The Mass is always said for free by both parties—the celebrant and the petitioner—because the customary alms <note>original: "limosna." In this context, it refers to a Mass stipend—a small donation given to support the priest’s living expenses rather than a payment for the ritual itself.</note> is indeed alms and the sustenance of the minister, not a price. But for the priest to bind himself to celebrate for a long time in a certain church, or in a particular chapel, or for a specific person, living or deceased—this is a very distinct obligation from his Mass or Divine Office <note>The "Divine Office" refers to the official set of daily prayers and psalms recited by clergy.</note>. It is a salable burden that he places upon himself, and he can sell it, and enter into contracts, and haggle over its price, just as is done in the chaplaincies <note>original: "capellanias." These were legal and religious endowments where a donor provided funds or property to support a priest in exchange for specific duties, like praying for the donor's soul.</note>. The Mass itself does not fall under the category of sale; but binding oneself to say many of them, with such restrictions, very well does. A single Mass and the obligation for a single Mass are one and the same, and both are unsalable and must be done for free. However, binding oneself to celebrate many in this manner is a civil obligation—human, not divine or sacred—and consequently, it has a value. And if in celestial matters, which so far exceed all human appraisal, the obligation made to continue them is worth money, it is easy to gather how salable any other inferior matter is. Such as binding oneself to work the land, guard livestock, defend someone in the external forum <note>The "external forum" refers to the public courts of law, whether secular or ecclesiastical.</note>, or teach someone a science. To preach for an entire Lent from a pulpit, or for an entire year in a town—one cannot haggle over or sell a single sermon, but for a learned man to tie himself to a pulpit is something very different from the divine word, and its price can very well be set. Anyone who perceives the foundation will clearly understand all this and much more by reasoning: (that is to say) one must perpetually distinguish between an action and the obligation of its exercise when it is long and lasting, not only in sacred matters...

# Subjects in which...

...but also in secular business. It is a distinct contract to prune a vineyard for a daily wage <note>original: "jornal quotidiano." A daily payment for a day's labor.</note> for one day, or ten, or thirty; versus obliging oneself to prune it for those same thirty days. The latter is of greater price than the former. He who prunes for a whole month, binding himself to do so, deserves more and is owed more than he who works that same month freely, being able to stop whenever he wishes. In the former <note>Referring to the fixed contract of obligation.</note>, there are two things, each with its own value and price. One is the pruning, which is worth one or two reales <note>The silver real was the standard currency of the Spanish Empire.</note> per day. The other is binding oneself to persevere in the work, which is also valued. There is a great difference between working by force or by choice, freely or by obligation. The work done out of obligation exceeds, without comparison, the work done with freedom in merit and value, both before God and people. Because this freedom is worth so much, it makes the obligation to give it up of such high price. Because every time a person binds themselves, they sell as much of that freedom as they have obligated. From this it clearly appears how esteemed any obligation is, and how illicit and condemned it is to impose one on anyone in exchange for lending to them, since any gain obtained from a loan is usurious. We will continue to provide examples of this in the remainder of the chapter.

Thus, one cannot profit from lending, neither money nor anything else of value; for if it has value, it is all "money" according to Aristotle <note>The author refers to Aristotle’s *Ethics* and *Politics*, which were the foundation of medieval and Renaissance economic thought, defining money as a measure of the value of all things.</note> and as we all feel. And things of monetary value (as we have seen) include more than common assets, which are called real estate and movable goods <note>original: "bienes rayzes y muebles." Legal terms for land/buildings versus portable property.</note>. Words, services, and both real and personal obligations also have value. Scholars of lending transactions call interest in the form of money or a physical object (such as clothing or provisions) a "present of the hand" <note>original: "preſente de mano." A tangible gift or bribe.</note>. And to show how freely one must lend, they all say that neither a "present of the mouth" <note>original: "preſente de boca." Intangible favors, such as praise, influence, or verbal promises.</note> nor a service should be sought, much less agreed upon in exchange for the loan, any more than a present of the hand; for it is all the same, since everything has its price and is worth money.

### ...there is cloaked usury.

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], *On the Governance of the Jews*, Opusculum 21, in response to questions.</margin>
First, it is not lawful to lend a sum of money to a prince on the condition that he makes the lender a knight <note>original: *cauallero*</note>, or a commander <note>original: *comẽdador*, referring to a high rank in a military order</note>, or exempts him from some tax <note>original: *pecho*</note> or tribute. This is because one cannot take anything that has monetary value in exchange for a loan, and the nobility or the commandery he asks for is certainly worth money. The same applies if he arranged to have it sold to him at a lower price; forcing a sale as a condition for a loan is usury. 

Neither is it permitted, when a prince seeks a quantity of coin to pay his soldiers, to demand that he take the loan in the form of clothing from one’s shop, which causes many evils. First, forcing him to take merchandise just to move stock quickly is usury. That obligation imposed upon him has a specific value. Second, it is a great injustice because the prices are usually inflated to the extreme. Third, the prince then pays his own debts in that same clothing; the poor knight and the wretched soldier, who have great need not for "Londons" or "veyntenes" <note>Types of imported or high-quality wool cloth; "Londres" refers to London cloth, and "veyntenes" to cloth with 2,000 warp threads</note> but for cash, are forced to sell the fabric immediately and lose nearly half its value. To this, the merchants reply that they do not have the requested sum in coin, but many times they actually do. And if they truly do not have it, they should give all that they have, leaving it to the borrower’s own will to take the rest in cloth. But to make taking the cloth a condition of the deal is clearly usury; and if the borrower does take it, the lender is obliged—since it is being lent or given on credit—to value it at the current market price.

<margin>Canon Law, 14. q. 3. c. *si feneraueris* <note>original Latin: "If you have lent." A reference to the Decretum Gratiani concerning usury.</note> and Silvester, *Summa*, paragraph 6.</margin>
Even worse is what is practiced in this city. If someone needs three or four thousand ducats <note>A gold coin used throughout Europe</note> by exchange <note>term: *cambio* | This refers to a bill of exchange, a common financial instrument used to move money between fairs or cities, often used to disguise interest-bearing loans.</note>, the lenders, seeing the borrower in a tight spot, give him two thousand in silver on the condition that he takes the rest in merchandise. The whole thing is diabolical. It would be acceptable if it were done with the moderation mentioned in the previous case—that is to say, giving the two thousand in a fair Royal Exchange <note>original: *cambio Real*, implying a transaction at the official or market rate</note>, and if the borrower *wants* the rest in cloth (because he thinks he can find a way to sell it), that is fine. If not, let him seek the remainder elsewhere. But the truth is, they do not fail to give the full amount because they lack the money, but because they want to force the borrowers to empty their warehouses of bales of cloth through two thousand deceptions.

->### Subjects in which...<-

...one of which is to buy the goods back from them beforehand—even if they carry or move them—for a third less than the price for which they were given. And even if this trick <note>original: *maraña*</note> is not performed, the first act alone is harmful enough. This is because, in addition to taking the full interest of the exchange, it also obliges them to purchase clothing—something the other party does not need, and instead loses money on. All of this is certainly usury, the destruction of the commonwealth <note>original: *republica*</note>, and a great harm to one's neighbor.

Likewise, it is usury to lend to prelates <note>high-ranking church officials like bishops or abbots</note> on the condition that they grant the lender some benefice <note>original: *beneficio*; an ecclesiastical office that provided a steady income</note>, even if the lender has the qualifications and merits for it. It is forbidden not only to formally arrange this, but even to imply to the prelate that the loan is being made for that reason. Because in truth, this is a contract and an agreement; the only difference is that one is overt and the other is disguised and hidden.

Likewise, it is usury <note>original: *vzura*</note> to lend to someone while obliging them to lend to me in return later. For while it is just that they should be grateful, and in equity they ought to satisfy me by lending to me, their loan must be made as liberally and freely as mine was. Thus, the obligation I impose upon them—being of some value as it is—is rightly judged as usury. In this manner, the other person can and should lend to me, but I cannot *oblige* him to lend to me. To gain this obligation over him is to have profited from the act of lending.

The same applies to lending money to laborers <note>original: *labradores*</note> on the condition that they take one’s estates, pastures <note>original: *dehesas*</note>, or livestock as a rented tribute <note>original: *tributo arrendadas*</note>. This is especially true if the items are given at a higher price, as often happens; but even if they are given at a fair price, it is a sin. Because constraining them and obliging them to take these specific items is an obligation that is worth money, which the lender receives in addition to the loan, and thus it is usury.

In this same pitfall <note>literally "falling on their faces into the same ravine"</note>, some lords of estates and titled knights stumble. They lend quantities of money to their vassals on the condition that the vassals occupy themselves and spend the funds in producing salt, or in bringing in other types of supplies—

Lending them money so that they may produce salt, and even requiring them to produce it—especially if there is a shortage (and certainly there will be a shortage if it is not made, given how necessary it is and how much is consumed)—is a pious and legal act, proper to their jurisdiction and power.

But to treat this as a source of profit <note>original: *granjeria*; referring to mercenary or exploitative gain</note>—especially when the business is not for the benefit of the community but merely to increase the lord's own rents—is usury, even if they paid what the goods were actually worth. When they lower the just price (as commonly happens), injustice is mixed with that usury. Both of these vices, besides being indecent and ugly, bring with them an attached obligation to make restitution <note>The theological requirement to pay back ill-gotten gains to seek forgiveness</note>. This is something these men never do perfectly, for they become obligated and burdened by such a sum that they either cannot pay it out, or simply will not.

# on hidden usury

...cause, even if you gave him his wage. It is necessary either that you lend to them generously, without any agreement or condition, or that, in addition to his labor, you pay him the value of the obligation that you impose and ask of him, and that he be willing to do it. The same applies if you were to demand his word that he will always buy from your shop—clothing, or merchandise, or whatever is sold there—even if you truly gave him a discount, you must not intend to charge him inflated prices. For the nobility of spirit <note>original: "hidalguia," referring to a sense of honor and generosity expected of a gentleman</note> with which a loan should be exercised is great, as it is a heroic work.

What is permitted to do in a loan is to ask for pledges <term>prendas: physical items given as collateral or security for a debt</term> that are worth the amount lent, and a little more—especially if one fears or suspects the person—and to designate when it must be returned. One may set a penalty: that if he should be late or delay the payment and return any longer, he shall lose the pledge (if it was not worth more than the debt), and if it is worth more, that the lender may pay himself from it, returning the remainder. 

By "delay" <term>dilación: a legal delay in payment that exceeds a grace period</term> is understood not one hour, nor one day, nor one week, but fifteen or twenty days, according to how tardiness in debts is commonly held to be a delay. Any other rigor regarding this that exists in some places—holding the pledge as lost, or the penalty incurred, if a single hour passes—shows that there was malice and deceit in the condition. And it is deceit if I see almost clearly that he was not going to be able to pay on time, and this penalty (or what was gained in its execution) was intended as payment for the loan, and we both understood it as such. That he would "forget" on purpose, and I would "pay myself" [with the pledge], is cloaked usury. 

What is permitted is that, plainly and simply, some moderate penalty be set if he should be very late, which serves as spurs to goad him toward payment. If, having been set with this sincerity, he should incur the penalty, the other may safely take it. This penalty is called "just usury" <note>original: "usura juſta." In this historical legal context, "usury" could sometimes refer to any interest or penalty, and "just usury" was a legal fine for late payment rather than predatory interest.</note> by the civil laws, and outside of this there is no other licit kind (namely): when the payment is delayed and the debtor is late, whether he owes it from a loan or through some contract...

And the penalty is so just, and may be taken with such right, that even if it is not explicitly stated, whoever is late is obligated to satisfy (as we shall say) all the damages and losses that the one who sold or lent to him incurs and suffers in credit, honor, and purse because of his delay—provided the debtor could have paid in any way at the proper time. The difference is that if a penalty is expressed and set, even if the other person receives no damage from the delay, the lender may take it. But if it is not explained, the debtor will not be obligated to satisfy it unless the creditor actually suffers. In this way, if the penalty is very moderate, it can be taken even if no harm follows from the delay. But "damage" should not be collected unless it actually occurred. 

However, regarding these penalties and pledges <term>prendas: items of collateral given to secure a debt</term>, there are two notable principles. First, they must be set and received with great sincerity and Christian charity, solely to secure the money or whatever is lent. And they must be executed with much humanity and gentleness when someone is very late in returning it, not at the very moment the deadline is met. For this is already malice, and a misuse of what is good. And when it is executed—if the penalty is that the pledge be sold to pay the debt—it must be sold faithfully for all that it is worth, not under the table <note>original: "de manga," an idiom for a secret or private sale conducted to bypass fair market value</note> nor as a bargain, and all the remainder that amounts to more than the debt must be returned to the debtor. And if a condition is set that the pledge shall be lost entirely or kept by the lender, it is an injustice if it is worth more than the loan. And he must restore everything that it was worth beyond the debt. For this reason, if in any *Mons Pietatis* <term>Mountains of Piety: charitable pawnbroking institutions organized by the Church to provide low-interest loans to the poor</term> or confraternities there should be such a pact or condition, even as a statute, it is usurious; although it may be very old, it is a long-standing evil practice.

# ...there is cloaked usury.
<note>Cloaked or "palliated" usury (*usura palliada*) refers to financial schemes that look like legal contracts but are actually designed to hide the charging of interest, which was restricted by the Church.</note>

<margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, Question 78, Articles 2 and 6.</margin>
<margin>The lender is bound to count the marketable use of the pledge toward the principal. <note>original Latin: "tenetur mutuans cõputare in fortẽ vsum venalẽ pignoris"</note></margin>
...by gathering the fruits, one must count them toward what was lent, discounting them from the principal debt after subtracting the costs incurred for their benefit. Saint Thomas says: the lender must accept the value of the use of the pledge as part of the payment, if it is something marketable. This is so true that the Apostolic See <note>The Papacy or the high governing authority of the Catholic Church.</note> states: If the fruits of the pledge—after subtracting costs—are already worth as much as what was lent, the pledge must be returned without collecting anything further from the loan, since it has already been paid for by the fruits.

<margin>On Use. chapter *plures*, if someone accepted another's possession as a pledge for money given, if by chance he has already received his own back through its fruits, expenses deducted, let him restore the possession to the debtor absolutely. Likewise, the following chapter, *quoniam*. Digest on *solutio matrimonii*, *fructus*. Digest on *petitio hereditatis*, *si a domino*. Code on *fructibus*, etc. Code on *distractione pignorum*, law 1. <note>These margin notes cite various sections of Canon Law and the Justinian Code (the foundation of Civil Law) regarding the legal requirement to return collateral once its profits have covered the debt.</note></margin>
For example: if a horse was pledged for one hundred ducats, and its service is probably worth more than the food and care it receives, the excess value must be discounted from the hundred. The same applies if it is rented out and earns money; everything it earns—minus costs and compensation for the work the renter undergoes—belongs to the one who pledged it. Likewise, if someone gave me houses as collateral and I live in them or rent them out, or vineyards, or olive groves, or fields, and I cultivate, work, and sow them, the rents and fruits that God provides belong to the one who pledged them, after subtracting the expense and labor endured therein. For the lender was not obligated to be the debtor's servant nor to manage his estate for him. And I would not disapprove if, in this valuation of care and diligence to be performed, the status and reputation of the person were considered, appraising their effort "as a gentleman" <note>original: "cauallerosamente." The author suggests that a lender of high social standing should have their administrative labor valued at a higher, more honorable rate.</note>. By this I mean they should be appraised favorably, slightly above their basic value. In truth, the labor of agriculture is so great that it seems to me the farmer buys the fruits of his own land at their fair price, according to the sentence passed upon the first man <note>A reference to the biblical Curse of Adam in Genesis: "By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food."</note>. For not only does the one who digs, prunes, and plows work, but also the master and lord, who even in bed loses sleep over the administration of everything. The former work with the body, the latter with the spirit. Thus, in such a pledge, the greater part will justly belong to the one who lends, since he works and oversees it. # Matters in which there is cloaked usury

...from the pledge, it must be taken and received on account of the principal. The reason and foundation of the rule is that the pledges belong to the one who gives them, and they remain at his risk; if they were to be lost, or destroyed, or die—provided the one who received them was not at fault—they are lost to their owner. Furthermore, in addition to losing them, he would be obliged to pay back what was lent to him. And since he always bears the risk so perfectly and entirely, it is only just that they bear fruit and gain for him. And even if the one who currently holds them collects these profits, he must put them toward the other's account. Otherwise, if the fruit and income from the pledge belonged to the receiver, he would profit greatly from the loan, when he should not profit even a little. For many times the pledge is very profitable. If this permission were given, many would take up the business of lending upon pledges that yielded income, in order to gain the rents for themselves, which would be a most foul contract. Thus, commonly, only sterile things are pledged, such as pieces of gold and silver.

A case occurs to me of some importance where, it seems, this rule is broken, yet in effect, it is observed.

Among princes and kings, it is customary to lend great sums of money. And certain states, cities, towns, and places are pledged, adding at times that if the pledge is not redeemed within a certain number of years, it shall be lost, or sold for the principal amount. In the interim, the one who lent the money carries out and collects all the <term>tributes</term>, <term>taxes</term>, and <term>sales taxes</term> <note>original: "tributos, pechos y alcavalas." Pechos were direct taxes paid by commoners; alcabalas were a ubiquitous Spanish sales tax.</note> without discounting them from the sum. The crown of Castile has pledged to Portugal (according to what they say) the Algarve and Malucha <note>Likely referring to the Algarve region and a territory in North Africa or a specific frontier outpost.</note>, and the revenues are not discounted. On this point there are two things. One is that if that time passes, it remains in his power as if sold for what he lent. This is a condition that—provided the value of the pledge does not greatly exceed the loan—can be well-placed. If five hundred thousand ducats were lent for ten years, and the state is worth four hundred and fifty thousand, the penalty is not unjust in...

# Matters in which there is cloaked usury

But if it were to exceed greatly, it would be unjust, even if the party were to accept it, and it could not be permitted, for it is great cruelty to punish a minor fault with such a severe penalty. And there is also a clear vice of usury in the contract. The second point is the failure to discount the income from the amount they gave. Regarding this, it should be noted that the <term>tributes</term> and <term>taxes</term> <note>original: "tributos y pechos." "Pechos" were direct taxes paid by commoners to the crown.</note> that <term>vassals</term> <note>Subjects who owe allegiance to a lord or king.</note> give to their prince are not given for free, but are well deserved for sufficient causes and titles, as our lord the Emperor <note>Likely Charles V (Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain), whose reign ended shortly before this period; the phrase "who is in glory" indicates he is deceased.</note>—may he be in glory—used to say wisely. This is because of the many obligations that fall upon kings, binding them to preserve and rule them in peace; to maintain and administer justice for them; and to defend, protect, and avenge them against their public and common enemies. Therefore, if the one who receives these territories as a pledge takes them under his care and protection, and governs and rules them according to reason, the tributes, taxes, and honor they give him should be his, as a <term>stipend</term> <note>A fixed payment for services or work performed.</note> for his care and diligence. 

If the former ruler, however, as was customary, should reserve for himself the administration of justice and jurisdiction, and only gave the income as a pledge, receiving those funds and not discounting them from the debt could not escape the charge of usury. But if the lender simultaneously takes on the royal labor and care, it is just that he should enjoy the convenience and profit. Furthermore, this income is used to pay the judges, governors, and officials he appoints. Especially if he maintains a garrison of soldiers, or if there is a coastal cost where <term>galleys</term> <note>Large, oar-powered warships that were extremely expensive to build and maintain.</note> are necessary—which involve great expense—it is just that it all come out of the tributes. This same doctrine was given in general when we were explaining and declaring the rule. Thus, either the rule is not broken, or it is broken only in rare circumstances. That is to say, if the pledged estate yields high income and is very easy to govern, being free from enemies. In such a case, it is necessary to apply a large part of the "fruits" <note>The income or production of the land.</note> toward the principal debt, because to claim it as a "donation" is a mere fantasy.

## tions provided by the law regarding this rule.

<margin>
St. Thomas [Aquinas]: when the thing being pledged belongs to the person who receives the pledge, he may keep the fruits for himself. *Summa Theologica*, Second part of the second part, question 78, article 2.
