<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut drop cap 'T' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral patterns.</image-desc>
THERE are two more apparent exceptions to this rule in Canon Law <note>The body of laws and regulations made by Church authority; in this period, it governed many aspects of daily life, including contracts and loans.</note>, although in reality they are not, even if they appear to be. The first is found in the title on usury, in the chapter *conquaestus* <note>original: "extra de usuris. c. conquestus." A specific chapter in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding the reclamation of usurious interest.</note>, where it is stated: That if someone pledges an estate, the income it yields should be discounted from the debt, except if the lender already held that estate as a rental and the tenant pledged it back to its owner. This is a case that can easily occur, especially regarding ecclesiastical properties and possessions, which are often leased for one, two, or three lives <note>A "lease for lives" was a legal contract where the lease lasted until the death of the last surviving person named in the deed.</note>. For example: I had leased my olive groves for a fixed rent for ten years, and in the fifth or sixth year, the tenant, needing money, borrowed one thousand <term>ducats</term> <note>A gold coin used for trade throughout Europe; in 16th-century Spain, it was a high-value currency.</note> from me, giving the olive groves I myself had leased to him as a pledge. The law grants me that the harvest I gather that year shall be mine, provided the tenant pays no other rent or tribute that year. Now someone might ask: what favor is the law doing me if I receive the harvest in place of what he already owed me this year? This is why I said it was not a true exception, nor was the rule broken. Secondly, it is still a benefit and a service granted to him. This is because usually the <term>tribute</term> or <term>census</term> <note>original: "tributo y censo." A "censo" was a type of perpetual annuity or ground rent common in Spanish law.</note> that one pays for estates is much less than what the land actually yields (otherwise, no one would lease them for such a price). Thus, it is a favor the law grants him if it allows the owner to keep the entire yield during the year or years the groves are pledged. Therefore, the fact that the property is already his gives him the right to take the fruits.

The other exception is very well known in the same title, in the chapter *salubriter* <note>original: "c. salubriter." Another chapter from the Decretals regarding dowries and usury.</note>, which is that if a man provides a <term>dowry</term> <note>Property or money brought by a bride to her husband on their marriage.</note> for his daughter but does not hand over the dowry or a good portion of it immediately, the son-in-law—if he is given possessions as a pledge—may benefit from them and use them without discounting the fruits and increase from the principal debt. ...to understand each other without speaking, and without civil or human obligation, to return a little more than what was received, understanding that it was lent with that hope and respect. And **usury** is such an abominable crime that even explaining it or proposing it in one's mind is foul. **Theologians** say there are two types of usury: one real and exterior, the other spiritual and mental. 

The first is (as we have explained) when one who lends asks for, or gives it to be understood—even if only through signs—that they should receive interest for the loan, whether the amount is specifically named or left in general and vague terms at the discretion and virtue of the borrower. The **interior** type is to do it with outward generosity, but proposing in one's mind to have some gain from it and because of it. Either because one probably suspects that they will give something, or at the very least, one determines within oneself to receive whatever might be given in recompense. 

And both—the asking for it, the proposing of it, and the receiving of it—of whatever quality or condition it may be, whether money, or dignity, or office, or benefit, or favor, as we mentioned above from **Saint Augustine**, all is prohibited. If one were to lend to a Lord in order to obtain, in payment for his service, some office or public charge; or to judges, secretaries, and ministers of justice so that they might favor him in his cause and lawsuit; or to a prelate so that he might give him a <term>canonry</term> <note>A prestigious administrative position within a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> or <term>prebend</term> <note>original: "racion." A fixed portion of a church's revenue granted to a clergyman.</note>. 

In short, everything that is prohibited and forbidden to be extracted by a formal agreement when lending is also forbidden to be received for having lent, even if it was not requested. This is expressly determined in the same title that I have cited, where the **Church** deals principally with usury in the chapter *Consuluit* <note>original: ".c. conſuluit." This refers to a specific section of Canon Law in the Decretals of Gregory IX regarding usurious intent.</note>, where he who lends with such purpose and mind is given over and condemned as a **usurer**, for he would not lend if he did not believe he was to gain some interest for lending. Although this matter of **mental usury** is more extensively and precisely declared in the mediate chapter that follows.

## ¶ CHAPTER IX. ON MANY
## usurious contracts

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'T' within a square frame, decorated with interlaced foliate and floral vine motifs.</image-desc>

**EVERYTHING** that I have said in these chapters, and what I will say in the ones following this, is not what moved me to write, although it is profitable and very important doctrine. Rather, it is what I have not yet said and now wish to say (namely): that not only is there usury in a loan, but in many other very distinct contracts that we do not suspect—in sales, purchases, exchanges, and leases. It is a stain that spreads through all business, whether ecclesiastical or secular, sacred or profane. It is like pride, for there is no vice it does not accompany, nor virtue it does not attack. And it is a fitting comparison, for according to Scripture, there are two heads of all vices: avarice and pride. And there is nowhere that avarice shines more brightly than in the <term>profiteer</term> <note>original: "logrero." A person who makes excessive or unfair profits, specifically through usury or hoarding.</note> and the usurer, since he gains so completely without any legal right or title to gain, and takes interest in a loan even though all interest is repugnant to the nature of lending. Furthermore (as I said in the first chapter), this sin is so foul that it is rarely committed openly; it is so driven by self-interest, and consequently so "sticky," that it is very frequently committed in disguise. For this reason, it is appropriate to read this chapter with the utmost attention as the most substantial part of this <term>opuscule</term> <note>original: "Opusculo." A small book or pamphlet.</note>. There is a distinction that is very well-known, not only among the learned, but also among the unlearned and ignorant—especially merchants—that there are two kinds of usury: one manifest and formal, the other <term>palliated</term> <note>original: "palliada." Derived from the Latin *pallium* (cloak), meaning a hidden, cloaked, or disguised form of usury.</note>, that is, covered and disguised. The patent and manifest kind is the one we have dealt with until now, when it is done under these names: "loan" or "lending." Palliated usury is when the contract is a sale, exchange, lease, tribute, or <term>annuity</term> <note>original: "censo." A financial arrangement where a capital sum is paid in exchange for an annual return; often used as a legal way to circumvent usury laws.</note>, with some loan mixed in...

# usurers.

<term>interest-bearing loan</term> <note>original: "preſtamo intereſſal." The word "pre-" from the previous page combines with "stamo" here.</note>. Usury is then hidden, partly by these words, and partly by that business deal which is of another species or genus. For example: selling on credit for more than the current cash price is disguised usury. In reality, it is a purchase and sale, but it is mixed together because the excess in price is taken for the time one waits for payment. Which is usury, although so covered that—as they say—nothing is visible but the eyes. But once the mask and cloak are removed from the contract, speaking in <term>plain English</term> <note>original: "buen romance." Literally "good Romance/Spanish," an idiom meaning to speak clearly or without pretense.</note>, it is selling him the goods for their fair current price and lending him the money for the designated time, charging him that excess for the waiting. It is a general rule that when a term of payment is awaited, and interest is taken for that waiting, it is usury; and it is a very true rule. Some simple folk give the reason for this as being that it is wrong to sell the time that God created <note>This "selling time" argument was a popular medieval theological concept (gratia temporis), suggesting that since time is a common gift from God to all, no individual has the right to charge for its passage.</note>. But these people should notice that God made all things that are sold, and they do not stop being sold for that reason; thus, this argument does not hold. The true reason is that when it is done this way, a profitable—and consequently usurious—loan is mixed in. If a horse is worth exactly one hundred <term>ducats</term> <note>A gold coin used widely in Europe for trade.</note>, why do you take one hundred and twenty if you sell it on credit? In substance, it is giving it to him for a hundred and taking the ten or twenty for not paying immediately. For if he paid immediately in the present, you would only take a hundred. So, in plain English, it is giving it to him for a hundred and lending him that money for that year, charging him ten for it, which is true usury. But it is not called that, because it is dressed in other clothes; it is named according to how it is dressed, namely: a usurious sale. A sale, because the horse is truly sold and the ownership is transferred to the buyer. Usurious, because great usury is mixed into it. Thus says <term>Pope Alexander III</term> <note>Pope Alexander III (r. 1159–1181) was a significant legislator in the development of Canon Law, particularly regarding the ethics of the marketplace.</note>: that having been asked and consulted whether it was usury to sell on credit for more than the fair price, he responded by condemning as a usurer the merchant who, selling cloth on credit, takes for that credit more than the...

# Of many contracts.

<margin>Whether a merchant should be condemned as a usurer if he sells his goods for a much higher price when a longer delay is granted for payment than if the price were paid to him immediately and on the spot? He is a usurer. Chapter *In Civitate*, in the Decretals regarding usury. <note>original Latin: "An negotiator vſurarius condem nandus sit... c. in ci- vitate extra de vſuris." This refers to Canon Law, specifically the Decretals of Gregory IX.</note></margin>

...than what it is currently worth for cash. This, as the Pope himself says, is so clear and obvious that there is no need for us to dwell long on proving it, as it is so manifestly reproached and condemned in the Holy Gospel. In the first <term>opuscule</term> <note>A small book or treatise; the author is referring to an earlier section of his own work.</note>, in the eleventh chapter, we declared how unjust this act was, but this is the proper place to show how it is also usurious (a matter quite easy to do and understand). This is because if, simply for waiting for payment, one charges five <term>ducats</term> <note>A gold coin used as a standard currency across Europe.</note> more on a <term>bale</term> <note>original: "fardo." A large bundle of merchandise, often cloth.</note> than it was worth on its own, it is easily understood that this interest is fundamentally taken for lending the bale, or its value, for eight months or a year. This practice of taking such close account of the requested deadline—where the price is adjusted more to the delay of payment than to the value of the goods—shows clearly that the merchants themselves calculate that they are giving those eight <note>Likely referring to the interest or the specific value of the goods mentioned in the calculation.</note> as usury for the duration, and that they are profiting from them as if they had given them in <term>exchange</term> <note>A financial transaction involving bills of exchange, which were often used to hide interest-bearing loans.</note>. Thus they ask for more or less, according to how much later or earlier the payment is to be made.

Saint Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent medieval theologian.</note> says these formal words: "Whoever, to wait for payment, sells more expensively than the clothing is worth, clearly commits usury." This is because the delay is a type of loan. Thus, to gain by waiting is to gain virtually by lending, and everything taken in excess is a usurious interest.

And even <term>Sylvester</term> <note>Sylvester Prierias (1456–1523), an influential Dominican theologian and canonist.</note> asks a question: whether someone who sells on credit more expensively than for cash is a <term>public usurer</term> <note>A legal classification for those whose usury was notorious and legally proven, carrying specific civil and religious penalties.</note>. That such a person is a usurer is not doubted, as it is so verified and obvious in the law. But the question is whether he is "public and manifest" among those who incur the penalties of the law against usurers. Both he and <term>Panormitanus</term> <note>Nicolaus de Tudeschis (1386–1445), a famous Benedictine canonist and Archbishop of Palermo.</note> answer: that if it is certain he sells for more on credit than for immediate payment, they hold it as very certain that he is a public usurer of the kind who—as punishment for such a detestable crime—cannot make a will. For even though selling on credit in this way is <term>disguised usury</term> <note>original: "vſura palliada." From the Latin "pallium" (cloak); usury hidden under the appearance of a different type of contract.</note>, it is true usury. And if it is clear and proven that he does it, he is a public usurer. And the same...

# Usurers.

<margin>
St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 78, article 2, reply 7: "If anyone sells more dearly than the just price so that he may wait for the buyer to pay the money, manifest usury is committed because this kind of waiting for the payment has the nature of a loan; therefore, whatever is exacted beyond the just price for such waiting is, as it were, the price of a loan. Similarly, it is usury if anyone buys more cheaply because he pays the money beforehand." <note>original Latin: "S. Tho. 2. 2. q. 78. ar. 2. ad 7. ſi quis carius vendit iuſto precio vt de pecunia ſoluēda expectet emptorẽ... ſimiliter ſi quis emat vilius eo quod pecuniã ante ſoluit."</note>
</margin>
The same law determines that the "palliated" <note>From the Latin *pallium* (cloak); meaning disguised or hidden under a legal facade.</note> and masked usurer incurs the same penalties if he clearly practices it (Chapter *Ad Nostra*). This is something <term>confessors</term> <note>Priests authorized to hear confessions and grant absolution.</note> must be very mindful of, so that they themselves do not remain bound and suspended by improperly absolving and "unbinding" others. For one of the legal penalties of the usurer is that no priest may absolve him unless he first performs manifest penance, repenting of his sin and making <term>restitution</term> <note>The act of returning ill-gotten gains to the original owner.</note>, or giving an order for it (if the necessity of confessing cannot suffer delay) before a notary and witnesses, ensuring that due restitution is made.

Because of this, no confessor—under penalty of being suspended himself—can or should exercise his office with those who have the custom of selling their cloth on credit at higher prices, unless they first restore the overcharge. Indeed, they cannot administer this sacrament, nor that of the Eucharist, to public usurers.

On the contrary, returning to our subject, it is also usury (says the same <term>Angelic Doctor</term> <note>A traditional title for St. Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), the influential Dominican friar and philosopher.</note>) to purchase for less than the just price by anticipating the payment—that is, by paying before the goods are delivered. The seller gives and grants that lower price because the buyer is "lending" him that amount from now until then. For example: if it is probable that in June and July wheat will be worth five <term>reals</term> <note>The *real* was a silver coin used in Spain for centuries.</note>, and Pedro makes an agreement in January with a needy farmer to give him his <term>harvest</term> <note>original: "semetera." Literally the "sowing," referring to the future crop.</note> at four reals, paying him immediately. What reason can be given or invented for losing one real on every <term>hanega</term> <note>A *fanega* (often spelled *hanega* in older texts) is a traditional Spanish unit of dry capacity, roughly equivalent to 1.5 bushels.</note> except for the fact that he was given the money now to make use of it? This is, to speak in plain English, lending it to him until the harvest and taking as interest for the loan everything that the other party reduced out of pure necessity. This is "palliated usury," or usury disguised with the mask of a sale, but not so covered and simulated that it cannot be easily recognized.

</margin>

# On many contracts

Since the sheep farmers <note>Spanish: *ovejeros*; specifically those who raised migratory flocks.</note> are such poor people that they cannot afford the cost of the flock’s grazing without drawing from their shearing profits, necessity and poverty compel them to sell the wool much earlier than the <term>shearing season</term> <note>The annual cutting of the wool, usually in spring, which was the primary source of income for shepherds.</note>. To this purchase and fair come all the wool merchants and cloth weavers from Segovia, Toledo, Burgos, Cuenca, and Salamanca—flocking to Soria, León, and the <term>Maestrazgo</term> <note>A historical region in eastern Spain under the jurisdiction of military orders, known for its pastures.</note>—with great sums of money to provide for the shepherds. They give them one <term>real</term> <note>A silver coin used in Spain for centuries.</note> less per <term>arroba</term> <note>A traditional unit of weight, approximately 25 pounds (11.5 kg).</note> than what the wool is expected to be worth, simply because they give them the money immediately so they may pay for the grass and the <term>dehesas</term> <note>Pasturelands or meadows often rented for seasonal grazing.</note> that they occupy. 

This is the substance of this abuse and vice we are touching upon. Even if other evils are mixed in—which are neither few nor small—they are not relevant to this specific point. I say that if the wool merchants were to negotiate with their money by investing it in some kind of cloth, and the shepherds were to ask them for it and offer the wool that is then being born and growing, the merchants would have some right to take something from the just price. This is because, according to the proverb of the theologians, "goods offered are debased" <note>An adaptation of the Latin legal/theological maxim *Res oblata vilescit*, suggesting that when a seller is desperate to sell, the value naturally drops.</note> and lose some of their value and esteem; furthermore, the merchants would then be desisting from their own pursuits and profits to satisfy the shepherd's request. 

But all these reasons cease here, and against all reason and law, they diminish the price that the goods ought to have. First, the merchants do not intend to invest that money in any other kind of merchandise; rather, they go about scratching together and gathering funds from all sides specifically for this wool, which is a business of great interest <note>Here meaning "profit" or "advantage," but hinting at the sin of interest/usury.</note>. Second, they are not the ones being asked; instead, they seek out the sheep farmers and offer them the money themselves; thus, they have no just title to give them less. If it is illicit to charge more than the merchandise is worth at the time of delivery because of waiting and delaying payment, how can it be, or how could it be, licit to give less simply because one pays before the goods are delivered? And it is not a good response to say that the shepherds agree to it and consent. For it is verified that they do so out of necessity, and against their will, es-

But the evil is that they do not only seek to gain everything, but to suck the blood and sweat of the poor shepherds, who walk through the cold and ice of the night, and the heat and summer sun, grazing their little flocks that produce the fleece. Given this cruelty and injustice, it is common—and frightening—to see such an inhumane business used so frequently among Christians. But it has become such an old habit for men to violate equity and justice in many businesses that what would have amazed people in other times no longer causes wonder.

By this doctrine and rule, usury is revealed and discovered in many types of sales. For if it is usury to pay less than what an item will probably be worth in order to advance the payment, then it must also be reduced to usury to purchase debts for an amount less than their value in order to collect them before they are due, as often happens. The evil in this trade shines and reveals itself so clearly that it is hardly <term>palliated</term> <note>Spanish: *palliada*; meaning disguised or excused through legal loopholes.</note>, but rather open for all to see, especially if the debtor themselves is the one "buying" the debt back at a discount.

### On Various Contracts ###

...and having been given two thousand <term>ducats</term> <note>Spanish: *ducados*; a high-value gold coin used across Europe.</note>, he was not a little happy to earn two hundred in four months. But once the truth was known, he undid the contract like a good Christian, not wanting the interest from such a diabolical trick. Because in point of fact, the usury appears so clear—being formal and express—without the mixture of any other contract to hide it, except for twenty thousand lies told by the broker, signed by the debtor, and ignored by the creditor. These are those names and titles of "sale" and "purchase" which not only do not diminish the guilt, but rather aggravate it before God.

Such also are many <term>baratas</term> <note>Spanish: *baratas*; literally "cheap sales," here referring to fraudulent or discounted transactions used to mask loans.</note> and <term>mohatras</term> <note>Spanish: *mohatras*; a deceptive contract where a merchant "sells" a good on credit at a high price and immediately "buys it back" for a lower cash price, effectively creating a high-interest loan.</note> that are celebrated in these <term>market steps</term> <note>Spanish: *gradas*; refers to the steps of the Cathedral in Seville, which served as a commercial hub and exchange.</note> without truly being celebrated or performed. This includes selling a great quantity of cloth and then immediately buying it back with a fifteen or twenty percent loss. Who has eyes and does not see that, in substance, this is simply lending that sum, and that this is what the other person was asking for and what you are doing? It is only that, because you would not dare to charge such high usury on a direct loan, you think it is more "humane" to charge twenty percent under the guise of a sale, whereas you would not dare take even ten percent if you lent the money formally. If he asked you for a thousand ducats, you would not have the nerve to ask for more than six or seven percent; yet, to be able to profit with less notice, you wrap the business in a larger amount through a sale. In the end, and in conclusion, it is all ill-gotten.

A thousand <term>exchanges</term> <note>Spanish: *cambios*; financial transfers or currency exchanges.</note> do not fail to strike this same note, being given without any actual exchange or barter. These are what they call <term>dry exchanges</term> <note>Spanish: *cambios secos*; a loan disguised as a foreign exchange transaction where no money actually moves to another city.</note>, where between the delivery of money and its return, there is no distance of place, but only a delay of time. There, they do not take four or five percent for the service of exchange, but solely for lending the money—a vice very much attached to the art of exchange. For when looking at the substance (which is what God looks at), it is the same thing to lend a thousand ducats with fifty in usury as it is to give them as an "exchange" with the same interest, if they are ultimately to be paid back right here—no matter how much the letter says they will be paid in <term>Medina</term> <note>Medina del Campo, the site of the most important financial fairs in 16th-century Spain.</note>. This business is a game of <term>sleight of hand</term> <note>Spanish: *passa passa*; a phrase used for magic tricks or street cons.</note> that passes by and ends within...

### CHAPTER X. REGARDING HOW AND HOW MUCH one may gain by lending.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap P featuring floral and scroll motifs.</image-desc>

IT SEEMS TO ME that it will appear to many, upon reading this doctrine, that much severity and rectitude is asked and required in loans, since nothing of value is permitted to be received; and their hearts will sink at the thought of performing such a useless act, from which they are to ask or claim no <term>interest</term> <note>Spanish: *interes*; in this historical context, any profit or increase beyond the principal of a loan.</note>. To this I say two things. The first is that if we were truly men, there is no other human action we ought to perform with greater will. For it is almost in this alone that we show ourselves to be such—namely, in doing good to another without seeking our own profit. It is such an excellent and magnificent thing to do good without regard for one's own utility that the ancients, by way of excellence, called it a "work of kings," and we may call it a divine work proper to God. And if we do not wish to grow so much as to imitate Him in some way, I say the second thing: that we can

->on lending.<-

...we can profit much by lending. First, lending is such a loving act, free of interest, that it makes a man lovable, and it draws and almost convinces the one who receives it to love him. For it cannot be denied that good works are true expressions of love, and to the one who receives them, they are an evident sign of the good will held toward him. And knowing and recognizing this, he must necessarily respond with an affectionate will of his own. For there is nothing more effective in making someone love you than for them to know they are loved. And since, in lending liberally, a man explains and manifests that he loves, he who lends cannot fail to be loved in return, which is a great good. Also, a good deed is of such strength and virtue—especially if it is not a single act—that it softens and levels the enemy, and inclines and attracts the stranger toward friendship. Thus, by lending, one can very easily gain many friends; and since he cannot lack for them, let him take care to lend to good people, so that those he acquires are good. This is one of the most precious and rare things in the world. And it is so characteristic of this act to immediately cause friendship, or at least a pious affection, that it is an inseparable, most proper, and very well-deserved effect.

<margin>St. Thomas: In mutual loans, one can demand recompense only for those things which are not measured by money, such as benevolence and love. <note>Original Latin: "mutuas potest exigere recompensationem tantum eorum quae pecunia non mensuratur benevolentiam amore." Found in the *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 78, article 2, and in Opuscula 53.</note></margin> Truly, he who is not grateful for this benefit deserves not only that he be left to suffer his misery and necessity another day, but that he be stripped of his very status as a man, if such a thing were possible. And if by chance the recipient is not a person who places much value on a good friendship—one whose price and esteem he does not grasp due to his own rusticity and vice—then I say, thirdly, that one can by this means obtain many <term>temporalities</term> <note>Spanish: *temporalidades*; referring to material or worldly benefits, such as political influence or social standing, rather than spiritual ones.</note>. For it is lawful to seek, through the loan, the favor and familiarity of some prince or prelate, so that later, out of love and esteem—not through interest or a contract—he may grant what is sought and desired. This is especially true if the lender is worthy and deserving, through his ability, wit, and letters, of the benefit or dignity he desires. For serving by lending causes love. ...profit, and to acquire something through friendship is not usury, regardless of how they became friends, unless profit is received immediately from the loan itself. It is in this sense and explanation that "mental usury" <note>The sin of lending money with the internal expectation of profit, even if no interest is officially charged or mentioned.</note> must be understood. To hope that the other person is so grateful for the good I do them—convinced of my good works through love, virtue, and benevolence—that they help me however they can, is not bad. As we defined it, "mental" usury occurs when I neither ask for nor imply that I want interest. I lend freely, but knowing by my own conjectures that I would gain something from it (a practice we have already condemned); yet, if received through friendship and benevolence, anything may be lawfully accepted.

It is consistent with reason that if one was pious in lending, the other should be grateful and proper in repayment. Thus, when nothing is asked or implied, if one seeks it as a matter of interest, but something is given out of courtesy, it can be well received. However, it is necessary that everything be clean, sincere, and true—both the hands and the soul. That is to say, the one receives it under this title, plainly understanding that it is given for this mutual bond and no other, and the other responds with similar sincerity. This truth and sincerity are so required from both parties that if I, thinking it came as a gift, were to take it and later discover it was given as interest for the loan (without it being explained or told to me), I am obliged not to take it, or if already taken, to restore it. On the contrary, if they give it to me with good will, but I—as one who is corrupt and greedy—intended it as profit from the loan, I must return it. For it is necessary that we both conform in virtue, so that he may give and I may receive. And virtue in this matter is that he gives it out of friendship, and I receive it as a favor and benefit being done for me. If either party fails or acts with malice, the...

If someone brings a lawsuit against me without having justice on their side, I can redeem my harassment with a loan and ask them to drop the lawsuit or the complaint; but if they truly have justice on their side, I cannot settle the matter through a loan, no matter how much I lend them. And it is just that the person who asks for the loan should compensate and satisfy the lender for both the loss and the missed opportunity.

One can use these two titles <note>These "titles" or legal justifications are the loss incurred and the profit missed.</note>, or either of them, in one of two ways. Either by declaring at the beginning the damage and the amount he fears, and likewise the profit of which he is deprived, if both are absolutely certain, and agreeing with the other party for a set amount, regardless of what happens later.

Consequently, he may take that amount later, even if the actual loss turns out to be less. But if it should turn out to be much greater, there remains no obligation for the other party to give him a single cent <note>original: "blanca," a Spanish coin of very low value.</note> more. The reason for this equal disparity is that by placing himself at risk—that if the loss were greater, he would receive nothing extra—it gives him the right that, if it is less, he may keep the agreed amount. His good fortune in gaining in this case exempts and excuses the other from compensating him if, by misfortune, he should lose more. For this reason, it is fair for both parties. Justice and reason demand that the amount assessed be a middle ground, not an extreme. However, this will rarely take place, or can be safely done, as it requires that the <term>actual loss incurred: *damnum emergens*</term> be indubitable and the <term>lost potential profit: *lucrum cessans*</term> be infallible. This is a very rare condition in human affairs, where the future is so uncertain. Therefore, the common and safe path is to leave the matter, and it should be left, undecided—binding oneself at the start, in general terms, to satisfy whatever damage might come to him and whatever profit he is deprived of. This second method is much safer than the first, as it possesses more plainness and certainty, since the resolution is left until the outcome...

# What Can Be Gained
<meta>catchword: carry</meta>

...concedes without any difficulty, it is a sign that he is willing to endure it all, and that he does not lose it, nor does he suffer at the instance or by the cause of the other. Therefore, those whose profession is to lend or to provide money on exchanges <term>exchanges: the business of currency exchange and bills of credit</term> cannot take advantage of these titles <note>original: "titulos"; here referring to legal justifications for charging interest, such as "lost profit"</note>, nor are these titles truly favorable to them, however much they might imagine or figure them to be. For if his profession is lending, he does not "cease to gain" because of me while exercising his very profession. Suppose someone claims they intended to make an investment where they would earn a thousand doubloons <note>original: "mil doblas"; a high-value gold coin of the era</note>, but did not do so because of me. It is just to keep him free from loss; however, he who does not invest, nor intends to invest, does not "cease to gain." If asked what he would have done with this money, he will answer that, just as he lends it to me now, he would have lent it to another if I had not arrived. They say: "If I did not have this profession, I would trade with my money in another business and would profit, and I cease to do so to serve you and others." It is very much to be noted that this response is quite laughable <note>original: "resible"</note>, for I am not obliged to satisfy another for what he *could* have gained, but only for what he *actually* ceases to gain, having been hindered by my prayers and entreaties. Thus, it is nonsensical logic <note>original: "razon desrazonada"</note> to say, "even though I was not trading, I *could* have traded." To this same tune, a gentleman <note>original: "cauallero"</note> might claim, when he lends: "even though I was not conducting business, I could have conducted business and profited," and thus demand that they also give him some interest for the loan. He certainly *could* have profited if he were a merchant, but he was not one, nor was he going to trade. And consequently, he does not "cease to gain," nor is there any obligation on my part to satisfy him, nor any right on his part to ask for it. So, for two better reasons, they cannot carry usuries <note>original: "vsuras"</note> in loans. The first, because they do not lend having been convinced and drawn in by pleas (which is a necessary condition), but rather of their own will. The other, that they do not actually cease to gain, not being merchants nor traders. And because selling on credit <note>original: "vender al fiado"</note> is a type of loan, as we have declared, he who makes it his profession to sell on credit likewise makes it his profession to lend, and consequently, there is no reason nor cause...

# Regarding how things are to be restored

## ¶ CHAPTER XI. ON HOW THE USURER MUST
## RESTORE ALL THAT HE GAINS.

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' featuring leafy arabesque scrollwork inside a rectangular frame.</image-desc>

<margin>
Decretals, Book on Usury, chapter *consuluit*.
St. Thomas, *Summa Theologica* 22. question 78. article 3. *Quodlibets* 3. question 7. 2. and 22. question 57. article 3. Cajetan, ibid. Alexander [of Hales] 3. part, question 66, member 4. [William of] Auxerre 3. part, treatise 21, question 1. Richard [of Middleton] 4. distinction 15, question 4, article 5. [Duns] Scotus, ibid. question 2, article 3. [Petrus de] Palude, ibid. Adrian, questions on usury. Cajetan, *Quodlibets* 1, question 3. [Domingo de] Soto, *On Justice and Law* book 6, question 1, article 4. Silvester [Prierias], under the word "Usury," 6.
</margin>
Besides usury being a most grave sin, it is of no benefit or delight, and is very infamous. This is not because one does not gain much interest, but because everything must be restored, unless the miserable man wishes to lose himself forever. For this reason, he must lose [his gains], even if it grieves him, in a short time. And so that he may understand how he is to make restitution, and how dangerously one deals with such people, the author sets down here the substance, quantity, and quality of his restitution. All of this must be understood—as we shall continue to point out—in any species or genre of usury, whether formal or palliated <term>palliated usury: interest disguised or "cloaked" within a seemingly legal contract, such as a fake sale</term>, mental or express, tacit or explicit. The first foundation in this matter is that nothing given as interest on a loan, or as an excess in any usurious sale—such as these common sales on credit—or profit from illicit exchange <term>illicit exchange: currency manipulation or bills of exchange that functioned as hidden loans</term>, belongs to him. He acquires neither ownership nor jurisdiction over it; it is all theft, whether it be real estate or movable goods, and as something belonging to another, it must be returned to its owner. 

But in the returning, there is a difference: if they are permanent things, such as houses, estates, or jewels, he must restore the very same items in number, with all the fruits <term>fruits: the profits, rents, or natural produce (like crops) generated by a property</term> that he may have received from them, minus costs. For example: if, for lending a sum of money, they gave him some houses, he must return them along with the rents. And if he has lived in them, he must pay for that stay. If they gave him some estates, and he leased them for tribute <note>original: "tributo"; here referring to a fixed rent or payment from a tenant</note>, he must return all that they have yielded in rent. If he farmed them, he must return everything they have produced. But if he received money—which is most common—and with it he purchased some real estate and possessions, he is not obliged to restore the fruits, because in such a case they are his, not another's <note>This distinction relies on the idea that the "stolen" item was the money itself, not the land later bought with it; therefore, the effort of the usurer in managing the land belongs to him</note>. It happens that when they see themselves rich, they wish to establish estates, buy houses, tributes...

<summary>This chapter outlines the strict requirement for usurers to restore all ill-gotten gains, explaining that interest taken is considered theft and therefore cannot be legally owned. It distinguishes between the restitution of physical property, which must include all generated profits, and profits made from investments of usurious cash.</summary>

### On how he must make restitution

They must compensate for what the other person suffers and ceases to earn, for the victim also presumes to have the wit and industry to do so. 

What shall be said if the usurer no longer possesses the houses or estates that were given to him in usury, such as if he has sold them? I say that whoever acquired them, once the nature of the business is known, is obligated to give them back to their owner and collect the price from the profit-monger <term>profit-monger: the Spanish *logrero* refers specifically to those who seek excessive or illicit gain</term>, just like one who buys from a thief if he later learns to whom the stolen property belongs. This is understood to apply to the possessions or pieces of silver that the usurer acquired immediately as interest from usury. As for those items he bought with the ill-gotten money, that is a real and valid sale; if he sells them, the person who buys them is not obligated to restore them. Regarding the former [items given directly as usury], no one can buy them from him, nor can he sell them; and if he should sell them, the sale is null <note>original: *nulla*</note>, and the profit-monger remains bound to undo the contract if he can, giving what they were worth, even if he had sold them for less. 

And speaking universally, it is so necessary to return this excommunicated interest that if one of these men has gone bankrupt or is imprisoned and has many creditors—some with priority over others—the law commands that if he has any assets known to be acquired through usury, the person who gave them must be paid first. Even if that person is the last [in the list of creditors], he must be preferred in being paid. This is because those goods do not enter into, nor should they be counted as, the estate <term>estate: *hazienda*, the total assets or wealth of the debtor</term> of the one who went bankrupt, nor should they be put into the general pile of assets. From this, it clearly follows that the usurer can at no time dispose of them as something of his own. # THE USURER.

...he must not sell or exchange them, because it is selling property belonging to someone else <note>original: *hazienda agena*; wealth or assets that legally belong to another person due to the injustice of the original transaction</note> without having the permission of the owner. With other things, such as money and movable goods, he may well engage in secure business dealings so that they are not lost; and if they are risky, he should insure them. However, he cannot make donations, nor pay his servants with them, nor provide dowries for his daughters, nor keep his wife elegantly dressed and adorned, nor maintain a lavish lifestyle—unless (otherwise) he has other wealth of his own from which to pay, even if he spends this amount for the time being. But if everything he possesses has been acquired through scrupulous <note>original: *escrupulo*; here referring to wealth that burdens the conscience because its origin is doubtful or illicit</note> means, he can do none of the things mentioned. 

And even Saint Jerome strictly forbids anyone from receiving presents or alms from anyone who earns by breaking the law of justice in their dealings or by harming their neighbors. And in the legend of Saint Fulceo <note>original: *sant Fulceo*; likely a reference to Saint Fursey, an Irish monk famous for his visions of the afterlife which were widely read in the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>, it is told specifically in detestation of usury that one day the saint was snatched up in spirit, and it seemed to him that he was at his judgment, and the demons accused him of having received a garment to cover himself as alms from a usurer. To give alms from theft is so abhorrent to Him that He judges and holds it as an injury and offense rather than a service. And any usurious interest is theft. 

Thus, the fact that it all belongs to someone else is the reason why he cannot dispose of it, nor give it away, nor can anyone receive it. This is a harsh truth, but reason reveals it so that people may see the great danger in which they place their assets—those who deal either with these usurers, or with money changers, or with merchants whose primary sales are on credit <term>al fiado: buying or selling on credit; the author views this with suspicion as it often hid high interest rates</term>. Concerning this, it should be noted that in ancient times, in the **Old Testament**, the Lord permitted the Hebrew people—due to their greed—to charge usury to foreigners, while prohibiting it among their own kinsmen <note>original: *naturales*; meaning fellow members of the same nation or faith</note>. He governed them in the spiritual and temporal, giving them commandments for their salvation and laws for their political life. Thus, they sinned in doing so as far as heaven was concerned, but this sin was not punished on earth by the law. So when He spoke to them as God through His prophets regarding the salvation of their souls, the first thing He admonished them was that they should not practice usury against anyone, generally: neither kinsman nor foreigner, neither Gentile nor Hebrew. The Emperors sought to imitate this ancient permission by allowing usury with moderation and the strictest possible restriction; the highest they allowed is the **centessima**, followed by another of two-thirds, and another of one, which they call "pious." It was the custom among the Romans to pay back the loans they took every month—just as it is now among us to pay **censos** <term>censos: a type of annuity or ground rent where a person receives a capital sum in exchange for paying an annual percentage</term> in thirds, or exchange rates at the trade fairs. **Centessima usury** consisted of giving the hundredth part of the principal as interest each month, which we would now call one percent every thirty days; this amounted to twelve percent a year. The laws called this interest "very great," and permitted no other higher than it. To this, our Lord the Emperor—may he be in glory <note>Likely referring to Charles V, suggesting he had passed away by the time of this writing.</note>—alluded when he commanded that in currency exchanges, the interest should not rise above ten percent per year, which was the rate of taxes at that time; would to God that this had been observed. And even this rate was not charged except on money that had to be paid in a different kingdom, where the **profiteer** <term>logrero: a usurer who makes an excessive or "filthy" profit</term> would secure and take upon himself the risk of the journey. This is similar to the trickery currently practiced here in the exchanges taken by sailors, as we saw in the previous short treatise. There were other smaller usuries, such as "two-thirds," which meant giving two-thirds of a ducat each month for every hundred lent, which would be seven and a half reales per hundred. This is to take profit from the usury itself, which seemed and seems so evil—and with good reason—that even the Emperors could not permit it. Today, for our sins, there is nothing more commonly practiced. Yet custom never justifies it, for it is always rebuked and blameworthy as a cruel, inhuman vice, contrary to all law. # ON HOW ONE MUST MAKE RESTITUTION

[The law] forbids all usuries, especially those that are clear and manifest. And it commands, under pain of excommunication, that the emperor, kings, princes, and judges of Christendom see that they are returned if they are brought before them; and if they have not yet been paid, they must not constrain the borrower to pay them. If the borrower wishes to fulfill what he promised, he may well do so, but the judge shall not order it. This remedy of justice, as it appears, is specific, for it can only be exercised in cases of public usury, which are rare and few.

In the case of cloaked usuries <note>original: *usuras palliadas*. These were "pallid" or hidden usurious contracts disguised as legitimate sales or currency exchanges to bypass church bans.</note>, which are mixed with other contracts of sales and exchanges—and which are continuous and occur daily—the universal remedy is to wait: either for God to touch the heart of the wretched usurer so that he makes restitution in the manner we have described, or at least for him to die and his heirs to make restitution. For the heirs also remain obligated to restore all of it, whether the usury was express and manifest or hidden and covered, though not in the same degree and generality.

Firstly, by succeeding to the estate of the deceased and remaining, as the law says, in place of his person, the heirs succeed jointly to his obligations; they must pay and fulfill them, not only in the external court <note>original: *in foro exteriori*, referring to the jurisdiction of human law and the Church's visible legal system</note>, but in conscience. They must pay everything that it is clear the deceased gained through usury, in whatever manner or condition that usury took, provided that sufficient wealth remained in the estate for it. For in conscience, the heirs are not obligated to restore more than the total of what was left to them.

Civil law compels them to pay even from their own pockets if they accepted the inheritance outright; for this reason, it is a wise precaution when there are many debts to accept with the **benefit of inventory** <term>benefit of inventory: a legal provision allowing an heir to limit their liability for the deceased's debts to the actual value of the inherited assets</term>. But speaking in terms of **natural law** <term>natural law: a philosophy asserting that certain rights and moral values are inherent by virtue of human nature and endowed by nature or God</term>, it is enough that they spend all that he left, expending it on paying and restoring with the greatest care. But if there is a surplus, and the debts are not so great, and there are many heirs, each one is not obligated by himself for the whole amount, nor for the entirety of what he inherited; rather, the debts are paid first from the whole pile. This is because one is not understood to "inherit," nor is it considered an "inheritance," except for that which was the property of the deceased, and not the property of another.

<summary>This page explains the legal and moral requirements for the restitution of usurious gains, noting that heirs are responsible for a deceased usurer's debts and emphasizing that an inheritance only truly consists of assets rightfully owned by the deceased.</summary>

### ->The Usurer<-

That which remains clearly as one’s own, once debts are paid, is what is and usually remains subject to the division of an estate. However, if there are any goods in the estate—whether movable property or real estate—that are known to be the proceeds of usury <note>original: *interesse de vsura*; the charging of interest on a loan, which was considered a sin and a crime in this period</note>, whoever holds them is obliged to return them entirely to their rightful owner, and the other heirs must contribute to him proportionally. If there were certain gold bars recently acquired as profit from some wealthy currency exchange <note>original: *caudaloso cambio*; large-scale financial transactions often used to hide interest-bearing loans</note>, they must not enter into the division of the estate, and if they are distributed, that division is not valid in conscience. Finally, the clear resolution in this matter is that they are obliged to restore, first, the manifest usuries, and then the cloaked ones, to the full extent of the wealth left behind. I have already noted the method and scheme one must follow in part, but the safest course is to inform oneself by consulting a jurist <note>original: *jurista*; a legal expert or lawyer</note>, as this is their area of expertise.

<margin>Those who do such things are worthy of death, not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them. Romans 1. <note>original Latin: *Qui talia agunt, digni sunt morte, non solū qui agunt , sed qui consentiunt faciẽtibus. Roma. 1.*</note></margin>
Furthermore, usury is so contrary to reason that restitution must be made not only by the usurer or the heirs into whose power the wealth came, but also by those who helped him. This includes those who were the actual or moral causes for him lending with interest or for him collecting it, even if they themselves did not receive or enjoy any part of the profit. For it is not only the thief who must make restitution, but also the one who helped him to be a thief, in the event that the primary actor does not or cannot do so. As Saint Paul affirms, it is not only the principal party in any evil business who is reprehensible and guilty, nor is he the only one punished by justice, but also those who concur with him in committing it or helping him. Speaking to the Romans regarding certain crimes and capital sins, he says: "these are such that he who does them dies, and he also deserves death who consents with the offender." Thus, as a penalty for their fault and as a sign of detestation for the act, restitution must be made by those who were the cause or who induced him to be a usurer, or to provide usuries, or those who—once the loans were given—acted as the means by which they were paid.

# On how one must make restitution

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing from "providencia" or "conciencia" (conscience).</note> [conscien]ce he took upon himself, which is a great burden; but it is with as much reason on our part as it is with injustice that they place it upon their own shoulders. These miserable men should flee from incurring such a great obligation for such a small interest; but if they do not flee and turn away, it is very just that they remain obligated for everything, since they were, in their own part, the cause of all the damage. This is understood to apply if the principal debtor does not pay. For these third parties, factors, and partners, the best means and plan to disentangle themselves, once the harm is done, is to disburse all that they gained in those usurious dealings. And secondly, to beg the principal to make restitution, so that both the one and the other may be freed from the charge; and to send to him some religious persons of authority and sanctity to advise him, if he does not benefit from it. There remains the third step: to agree and reach a settlement with his creditors for the least amount possible. And the fourth: if they do not wish to lower the amount, justice dictates that they pay in full, provided they have the estate <note>original: *hacienda*; refers to one’s total assets or wealth</note> to do so; and if his capital is not sufficient, let him pay as much as he can. Furthermore, as to how much he should reduce from his household and capital, or if he must be left naked <note>meaning completely destitute</note>—in short, what form must be followed in making restitution—we noted and discussed this in the small work <note>original: *opusculo*; a minor book or treatise</note> I wrote on restitution, to which I refer him. 

If he pays, he may take his letters of subrogation <term>letters of subrogation: translated from *cartas de lasto*, a legal document giving a person who pays another's debt the right to recover that money from the original debtor</term> and produce his evidence, and proceed through the justice system to convict him as a usurer—even if this brings infamy upon him—and demand from him what he has restored on his behalf. Likewise, if the usurer sues for his debt before a judge, it being clear that it stems from usury, and if the judges give an execution order for it, those judges who passed the sentence, and the bailiff <note>original: *alguazil*</note> who carried out the execution, and the lawyer who helped and favored him in such a lawsuit <note>original: *pleyto*</note>—all are obligated to restore what they made the other pay, because they are all the cause of him disbursing funds against justice. I said "if it were clear and apparent to be usury," because, knowing these laws, they commonly include the interest along with the principal, and all parties confess they received it in full...

# THE USURER.

[ab]solutely. Thus, judges commonly do not sin by ordering payment: because they are not aware of the deceit; but the scribe <note>original: *escriuano*; a notary or legal clerk who drafted the official contracts</note> who, knowing of it, draws up such a document, through which the other, having been convicted, later pays, is not free from obligation, for he too was the cause of payment being made against reason. The penalties that the law <note>original: *el derecho*; likely referring to the *Derecho Canónico* (Canon Law) or royal statutes against usury</note> imposes on public usurers, I would set forth here, so that by their atrocity and severity, people might understand the gravity of the crime. And if it is true that the hidden and secret sin is of the same kind and nature, let those who provide exchange <note>referring to currency exchange or bills of exchange used in banking</note> and sell on credit see how much they offend God and harm their consciences, since most of the time, in this type of business, secret and disguised usury is committed. But I leave this aside, hoping that through the desire for their salvation they might turn away from such evil, and not merely because of the shame of their temporal punishment, although both are good. Yet the first consideration is the better: that it be for the sake of glory <note>meaning the glory of God and the salvation of the soul</note>.

But since it can be explained briefly, let us not be slothful by keeping silent about what might be of benefit. A public usurer is, first of all, he who in a competent court <note>original: *in foro competente*; a court with the proper jurisdiction over the case</note>, either through his own confession or through judicial proof, was convicted and proclaimed as such. And he who publicly in his house, or in his trade, commits this vice many times. This is found in many ways, as we have seen: sometimes it is blatant usury; other times, it is disguised. And whichever of these he practices in public, he is a public usurer and incurs the penalties of the law. Whether he lends many times with interest, or makes many **dry exchanges** <note>original: *cambios secos*; a "dry exchange" was a deceptive loan disguised as a foreign currency transaction to bypass the prohibition on charging interest</note>, or sells more dearly and above the **just price** on credit <note>original: *fiado*; buying on trust or credit</note> than for cash. And in many other ways that we explained in the seventh, eighth, and ninth chapters. Finally, anyone who manifestly earns true usury is a public usurer, and is subject to and condemned by the penalties. Especially of late, this is much more certain in some contracts of...

<margin>

</margin>

...feigned exchanges, which are disguised usuries. The Pontifical law <note>referring to Canon Law, the legal system of the Catholic Church</note> subjects such money-changers to the penalties of public usurers. From this, it is clearly gathered that to incur these penalties, it is not necessary to practice manifest usury by lending with interest openly. It is enough to commit this sin actually and patently two or more times, for two (as the Doctors <note>learned theologians and legal scholars</note> say) are sufficient. And if we wish to be more lenient, let it be from four or six instances upward. The principal penalties they incur are, first, to be **infamous**. These are persons who, because of their wicked life and habits, cannot acquire any ecclesiastical or secular dignity, along with other privations and prohibitions that the infamous face, as appears in <term>3.q.7. and 6.q.1.</term> <note>These are citations to the *Decretum Gratiani*, a collection of Canon Law; specifically Causa 3, Quaestio 7 and Causa 6, Quaestio 1.</note> Such as not being allowed to testify or bring accusations in criminal cases, nor being promoted to holy orders, nor exercising them if they already hold them, nor being a secure and certain <term>legatary</term> <note>a person who receives a gift or legacy through a will</note> for anyone from whom they are not a forced heir.

Chapter *Quia* regarding usuries. ...for our salvation, restitution.

**Everyone**, our justification and justice will not be perfect, nor even imperfect, without it. For justice cannot be found in pieces, but only as a whole. And the duty of this virtue is to give to each person what is appropriate and belongs to them: a thing that is poorly reconciled with taking what belongs to another, or withholding it. For this reason, it is necessary that we bring reason and order to everything, giving each thing back to its owner.

Let everyone examine, with the greatest diligence, what is in their own power and what belongs to others. Let them be content with the former, even if it be little, if they wish to reach true contentment, which is infinite; and let them restore the latter in good time. They will thus put into practice the words of Saint Paul: that we should owe nothing to anyone, except good will and love. According to Saint Augustine, this is a debt that it is always right for us all to owe one another, as it is a holy and just debt. 

But there are many who have souls full of sins because they do not empty their chests of other people's money, making the truth known through their wicked lives. This relates to what was said one day regarding this matter <note>literally "on this key," a musical metaphor for a recurring theme</note> by the one who is always prone to lying <note>A reference to the Devil</note>. He said that the crime and offense from which a man is slowest to escape is the transgression of the seventh and eighth commandments, which is to steal <note>In the Catholic numbering used here, the Seventh Commandment forbids theft and the Eighth forbids false witness; both require restitution to satisfy divine justice</note>. For even though, moved by holy inspirations or sermons, people often propose to convert, when it comes to the actual deed, the act of paying out <note>original: "desembolsar," literally to take money out of one's purse</note> makes them lukewarm and hardens them. And the enemy boasts that few escape him. 

I remember a notable opinion and response given in years past in Salamanca to a nobleman who came from the court to seek counsel from the Father Master Vitoria—who was a light of our Spain in his time <term>Francisco de Vitoria</term> <note>c. 1483–1546; a foundational philosopher of the School of Salamanca and a father of international law</note>. This nobleman, moved by passion, had falsely accused his adversary of an infamous crime, for which the man had been imprisoned and was about to be executed. Vitoria responded to him: "My opinion is that you should let yourself go to hell." Astonished by such an absolute response, the guilty man asked him: "Is there no means to save me?" Vitoria replied: "The most certain way, in my judgment, is to condemn yourself." <note>Vitoria is likely suggesting that the only way for the man to be saved spiritually is to "condemn" himself legally by confessing his lie, thereby saving the life and reputation of the innocent man.</note>

->How necessary it is<-

having asked and being half-desperate, he went to Master Castro <note>Likely Alfonso de Castro (1495–1558), a celebrated Franciscan theologian and jurist famous for his work on criminal law</note>, a man of most eminent learning, relating to him both the case and the first resolution he had received. Castro said to him: "He has answered you with great prudence; seeing you and your station <note>literally "your dress," implying his social status or clerical state</note>, he sees that what you are obligated to do—which is to recant your statement before the judge—you must do. And if you do not do it, there is no saving you." It is very easy for a man to take charge of someone else’s honor or property <term>hazienda: an individual's total assets, including land, money, and estate</term>, but very difficult to unburden himself of it. Money that was not worked for or sweated over is very sweet to the greedy man. Likewise, it is very tasty and delightful for the foul-mouthed to cut and tear at a neighbor’s reputation—not to speak of the good that is in him, but to exaggerate the bad, and even to invent it. For this reason, understanding how necessary it is for our salvation to satisfy those whom we have wronged in their person, honor, or property, I agreed to treat clearly and concisely in this Little Treatise <note>original: "Opusculo"</note> the cases in which this obligation is usually incurred and how it must be fulfilled. I also did this because in previous treatises I touched upon and explained many matters and contracts where people often incur debt by usurping the property of others under deceptive titles of sale, exchange, and loan. It seems that by stating now how things must be returned, the work will be made perfect and complete in its genre. Therefore, with all brevity and conciseness, I will state where and when there is restitution, who must restore, to whom it must be given, how much must be returned, at what time it must be done, and in what order.

The first mode of teaching is brief and **Scholastic** <term>Scholasticism: a medieval and Renaissance school of philosophy and theology that used strict logical analysis to reconcile faith and reason</term>, suited for Philosophers and Theologians who possess such refined understanding that they can grasp many particular resolutions within a single universal rule. However, such resolution and brevity in this **Little Treatise** <note>original: "Opusculo"</note> would result in shadows and obscurity, falling into the error of **Horace** <note>The Roman poet Horace famously wrote in his *Ars Poetica*: "I labor to be brief, and I become obscure"</note>, who rendered his doctrine more obscure the briefer he was. Because we must speak with people not deeply trained in letters, it is necessary to accommodate ourselves to their intellect, speaking to them with terms and words they understand, and using a style in the discourse of the work that does not confuse or frighten them with its majesty and grandeur, but rather helps and pleases them with its plainness and ease. Thus, we shall proceed by paragraphs, cases, and questions; though the doctrine may be a bit extended, it will be clear and profitable. Nonetheless, I will not fail at the end—following the first style—to provide an **Epilogue** of everything that has been said; once the material has been read, it will be easily understood and will serve almost as a memorial of what has passed.

Restitution is properly the returning to someone of that which was theirs, but which had been taken or withheld from them against justice. Two conditions are required: the first, that one has actually taken what belongs and is appropriate to another. The second, that in taking or withholding it, there is neither reason nor justice. It is also gathered that returning property to its owner is not always "restitution"; for paying for what was purchased, or returning what was borrowed, or a deposit, is not restitution, but simply being faithful. And to hold them against reason is understood principally as being without the consent of the owner, or without the mandate and sentence of a judge. # What Restitution Is, and Its Application

...was not determined, nor disposed to sin. It is evident proof that the persuader, with their flattery, arguments, threats, or gifts, persuaded and inclined them toward it. In this way, many foolish people fall miserably, almost compelling their servants or slaves to be intermediaries <term>intermediaries: go-betweens or accomplices in illicit acts</term> against their will in their shameful deeds. There are also those who hunt, as if for prey, after those who are not looking for them or waiting for them. Their crime and guilt is entirely doubled, not simple; they are imitators of the devil, who not only lost heaven himself but strives to make others lose it as well. Likewise, those who, with vain hopes of great profits, rouse the spirits of many and make them invest their money in prohibited businesses. But if the person was already determined to commit the act, and showed it, or almost professed it as a way of life, it is not "persuading" them to merely say, "do it now." This is why a person is excused if they request a high-interest loan <term>high-interest loan: traditionally called usury, the practice of lending money at interest, which was often legally and morally restricted</term> from someone who usually provides them by custom or as a trade.

<margin>St. Thomas, *Summa Theologica* 2-2, Question 73, Article 3: "The good of the soul, which is the greatest, cannot be taken from someone by another except occasionally—for example, through evil persuasion, which does not impose necessity." <note>original: "homini animæ quod est maximū nō potest alicui ab alio tolli nisi occasionaliter, puta per malam persuasionē quæ necessitatem nō infert."</note></margin>

<margin>Scotus, Book 4, Distinction 15, Question 3, Article 1. Richard <note>Richard of Middleton</note>, in the same place, Article 4, Question 2. Anyone who persuades another to sin incurs the following obligation. First, they must disillusion them if they spoke false words or reasons upon which the sinner relies; they must admonish them to return to God, from whom they were separated, if there is a probable hope that this will be beneficial. If they see that the person does not wish to amend their ways, the first step—disillusioning them—is sufficient. This form of restitution is possible in this matter, whereas returning to them alone what was taken from them (not by the persuader alone, but in company with the sinner) is impossible. Not only did the persuader make them sin, but the sinner himself also participated in the sin; thus, the persuader cannot restore the life [of the soul] that was lost by sinning, unless the "dead" person wishes to be resurrected. Also, if the persuader used threats, they must remove all pressure and leave the person free—and to do it well, they should leave them entirely. That is, they should distance themselves from the person as much as they possibly can. However, regarding temporal harm, if any should result to a third party from such a crime, it will be stated below when and to whom restitution must be made.

# Interior and Natural Goods

...attempted such a devilish deed. And the reason is quite clear: whoever does this causes two very grave harms. First, it deprives him of his judgment <note>original: "juyzio"—referring here to the capacity for rational thought or sanity</note>, which is the greatest of all natural goods and the foundation even of all spiritual ones in terms of their practice. For the exercise of virtues presupposes sound natural reasoning; he who lacks this can neither gain temporal wealth, nor merit eternal life, nor make use of the grace that he possesses in his soul. In short, to deprive a man of his wits is almost to make him a beast <term>bruto: a non-rational animal, lacking the "divine spark" of reason</term>.

Second, it prevents him from acting: he cannot conduct business, earn a living, serve others, or be useful to himself or those to whom he is obligated. In this way, the wrongdoer deprives him of the lesser good he already possessed and snatches away many others he might have obtained.

And if restitution is a returning of all that was taken or damaged, it is easy to argue that the wrongdoer must compensate for all the good that he stole, whether directly or indirectly. He stole not only the judgment he damaged, but also what the victim would have earned or provided for his parents and family through his talent and industry. And let no one be shocked by such a demand for restitution, because the greatest evil one can do to a man is to deprive him of his judgment. In the opinion of the wise, this even exceeds death.

The only difference is that in madness there is some hope of healing. For this reason, the guilty party is primarily obligated to seek, by all human means, for the victim to return to his senses. He must pay all necessary expenses and compensate for all the damages and losses that the victim's house and estate <note>original: "hazienda"</note> suffer in the meantime because his head is infirm. But if other failures occur in such unusual ways that, even if the victim had been sane, he could not have prevented or remedied them, the guilty party is then freed and exempt from those specific losses.

Furthermore, whether the victim recovers or not, and even if his household received no financial detriment—either because he had no house, or because his income came from rents and entailed estates <term>mayorazgos: family lands and titles that, by law, pass intact to the heir and cannot be sold</term> that do not change—the wrongdoer must still pay what prudent persons judge fair for the harm and injury done to his person, having first considered the circumstances of the

# How Restitution Must Be Made

This is not a difficult thing to understand, nor to appraise, by considering what he was earning and the business he managed. For the wrongdoer took all this benefit away, injuriously and illicitly preventing him from obtaining and earning it.

And so as not to repeat them many times, I wish to leave two notable points regarding this matter noted at the beginning.

The first is that the amount of restitution in most of the cases we shall present cannot be determined in general terms. It is necessary to refer it to the judgment and discretion of two or three people who, besides being virtuous, are prudent and expert in that specific type of business. It falls well within the scope of science <note>In this context, "science" refers to the formal study of moral theology or legal theory</note> to determine who must restore to whom, and when; however, the "how much" is often not certain. It depends on so many causes and circumstances that they cannot be understood by any common rules. It may happen that two people commit the same crime, or incur the same charge, yet one must restore much and the other little. This is because they are of different status and wealth, or they had different will and intention in what they did, or their wrongdoing fell upon someone who has no need at all.

For this reason, the doctors <note>referring to the "Doctors of the Church" or learned legal authorities</note> almost constantly tend to entrust the determination of how much must be given to men of experience in those matters. In this case we are discussing, one must consider the victim's estate <note>original: "hazienda" — here referring to his financial standing or business affairs</note>, what he earned in his office, and whether he would have persevered in it or was planning to leave it. On the part of the guilty party, one must also look at his patrimony and means, as well as the malice or simplicity of the act. All of this aggravates or diminishes the debt. These are things that no one could ever devise, much less judge from afar. It is nece-

With the warning that when the damage is such that an entire estate <term>hazienda: the total assets, wealth, or property of an individual</term> is not enough to cover it, it should not be weighed too strictly. For the fact that he cannot perfectly reach the full amount, no matter how much he gives, shows that he must satisfy the debt in such a way that he is not left entirely ruined; for even if he loses everything, it does not equal the damage done. Leave the rest to Divine Judgment, that His mercy may supply our faults, or His omnipotence punish the excessive license with which we wrong our neighbor. Thus Saint Thomas sets down a general rule: When it is not possible of itself to return exactly what was usurped, it is enough to return what is possible. #### How they are to be restored
<meta>catchword: some</meta>

...that was taken, and it cannot be restored either in kind or in its equivalent—such as a hand, an arm, a leg, or life itself—one must make whatever restitution is possible, since a just and equal one cannot be made. This is done either by giving the victim something according to the judgment of prudent men, or by asking for his forgiveness. This declaration or compromise is understood to apply to the matter we are discussing, as well as to the following sections on homicide and infamy <note>Infamy here refers to the legal and social loss of reputation or "civil death."</note>, along with the final section regarding elections for certain offices. 

In the final category concerning property <term>hazienda: refers to wealth, estate, or material possessions</term>, everything is settled in full, as we shall see; as much must be returned as was usurped, even if the offender is left stripped bare. The reason and cause for this distinction is that these first goods—such as knowledge, life, and personal worth—so greatly exceed money in reputation and esteem that if they are compensated with money after being wrongfully taken, it is not because the money reaches their true value, but because there is nothing better with which they can be paid once lost. Their excellent nature makes it impossible for the man who harms them to fully compensate for them; but in the end, by giving money, he gives all that can be given. However, property can never be so great that it does not have its just price; even if a great deal is stolen, it must all be returned, either in kind if it still exists, or in its equivalent.
