# On Making Restitution for Homicide

<margin>
Paul to the Romans 13: "The minister of God bears the sword and is an avenger in wrath." <note>original: "gladiū portat minister dei & vindex in ira"</note> If any man is dangerous to the community, or corrupts others because of some sin, he is laudably and healthily killed so that the common good may be preserved. Saint Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 64, article 2. Homicide holds the first place among punishments, question 13, article 2, reply 1. But it is lawful for princes to kill evildoers, not however for private persons. Question 74, article 3, and question 108, articles 2 and 3 regarding vengeance, and I-II, question 100, article 6, reply 3; and *Against the Gentiles*, book 3, chapter 14. Thomas, book 4, distinction 35, question 2.
</margin>

...[taking] some limb; others crush a person’s ribs with sticks; others—not without cause—whip them or give them slaps; others lock them up or imprison them. All these actions are included in this first category. In none of these cases shall I discuss <term>irregularity: a canonical impediment that prevents a person from entering the priesthood or performing its duties</term>, which is incurred in many of these instances, nor the excommunication that is by law attached to some, nor the gravity of the sin (which is great), but only the compensation that must be made by whoever commits these acts.

These actions create an obligation for restitution only when they are done against justice. However, when there was a legal right to perform them, no trace of obligation remains. Therefore, it will be wise to explain in which cases it is lawful to kill or wound, so that once those are set aside, we can establish a general rule: that in all other cases, restitution is required.

Princes and their ministers hold authority and jurisdiction from the <term>republic: the "res publica" or the common good of the state</term> to deprive of life those who misuse it, according to the laws, and to punish them with lighter penalties according to their crimes. Otherwise, we could not live in this world, seeing as there are many vile and pernicious people who, with their passion and corrupt affection, injure and wrong everyone, and also cause scandal with their bad example—people who are harmful to many and scandalous to the community. It is necessary that these individuals die by violence so that everyone else can live in peace, and that there be authority on earth to remove them from it. 

This means of preservation, being so necessary for universal survival, has been used and is still used by all peoples, putting to death those who give everyone else a miserable life. In the state of nature, from Adam until Moses; and in the Written Law <note>The Mosaic Law or Old Testament</note>; and in our Law of Grace <note>The Christian era following the arrival of Jesus</note>, princes have been and are accustomed to punishing the gravest crimes among the people with capital punishment. This is because it is a natural instinct to cut off a man who is harmful to the common good, sometimes by exile and other times by death, as a part so noxious that, if sustained, he would corrupt the entire body or race with his evil company.

# On Restoring the Murderer

And it is very consistent with reason that the individual interest should be lost for the **common good**, and to preserve the entire body of the people, any part that is already very corrupt and pernicious should be removed and cast away. No true judge, no merciful prince, would ever wish to punish anyone with such severity. God says of himself that he does not desire the death of the sinner—meaning spiritual and eternal death—and no good King, of his own accord, desires the physical death of his subjects.

But it must be done, almost unwillingly, to preserve the health of the community. And there are many of such dissolute habits that they cause more damage to the people than a cancer or a *plague-sore* <term>landre: a swelling or tumor, often associated with the plague</term> would cause in a human body. These must necessarily be cut away with a cauterizing fire and with a knife, like flesh that is already dead and stinking. 

It is worth considering that all nations—Greek, Latin, and Barbarian—always depict **Justice** with a sword; and that kings (who are her supreme ministers) have for many centuries used to have a rapier carried before them as a symbol. This is to make it understood that it is the office of justice to cut off the head of whoever harms the <term>republic: the state or public interest</term>. It is not good advice for a man to keep a part of his own person that brings him no benefit, but only harm. Nor is it any less lawful for a prince to preserve a neighbor who, through his evil deeds, wrongs the entire community—as do murderers, adulterers, and thieves, disturbing the public peace and tranquility that it is right for Citizens to have in their own homes and estates. 

This is something that falls to princes, as the heads of the community, to seek by all means with the greatest diligence. # On the restitution of the murderer

...condemns one who neither did the deed, nor is it sufficiently proven that they did it (two conditions most repugnant to justice). Justice is ordained solely to punish evildoers who have been publicly convicted as such. Thus, no laws permit a good man to be punished; rather, they command and ordain that he be rewarded. Furthermore, a judge does not exercise lawful authority (as I have said) in such a sentence. Because no human jurisdiction extends so far: Only God (says Saint Thomas) and men acting by His particular command and express revelation (something which, until now, He has never done) can take the life of the innocent. And one is innocent in the eyes of the judicial court who does not commit a crime that can be proven according to civil laws, even if they otherwise commit many mortal sins (which, according to divine law, deserve hell). This is because the secular judge must not pass sentence based on the law of heaven, but by the laws of the earth. Therefore, it is the clearest tyranny to condemn the innocent, and a deed most worthy of <term>talion</term> <note>Lex talionis, or the "law of retaliation," where the punishment matches the injury (e.g., an eye for an eye).</note>. And even then, the punishment would not fully satisfy justice, since the judge would die justly for his crime, whereas he had killed the other man without reason.

Secondly, a judge errs if he condemns the true delinquent without the crime being fully proven to him. Regarding secular justice, not having committed a crime is the same as having committed it while the evildoer remains hidden. And just as it would be unjust to punish someone who did not commit a crime, it is also unjust to condemn someone who is not convicted by the facts in the legal record. For this proof, the particular knowledge that the judge has of the deed does not matter—such as if he saw it himself or if his friends told him. Instead (as the <term>Doctor Angelico</term> <note>A traditional title for Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the primary theological authority cited here.</note> teaches), he must judge only by what appears in the legal record and what comes to his ears in that specific case in his capacity as a judge and a public person. And in this rule, "public" is defined as what is established by an accuser and witnesses, and "secret" is what is not sufficiently proven. # On Making Restitution for Homicide

...to avenge an evil by committing another that is worse. It is a most blatant injustice to compel someone to confess what they were not—or when they were not—legally obliged to confess. Thus, if a judge condemns a man based on such a confession, he commits homicide, taking the man's life against the requirements of justice. If he were to condemn him without any confession at all, there is no doubt he would sin in this case we are discussing; however, the fact that a confession was made does not justify his tyranny if that confession was compelled through injustice and grievance. Through such a confession, the judge acquired a right over the <term>defendant</term> <note>original: "reo". In this legal context, it refers to the person standing trial or the accused.</note> contrary to the law. If he harms the defendant in a matter as grave as life itself, what crime can this harm be but homicide? This is a crime into which some fall who are very zealous but very indiscreet, uncovering evildoers through diabolical and tyrannical means.

Furthermore, a judge who subjects a prisoner to <term>torments</term> <note>A reference to judicial torture, which was a regulated part of legal proceedings intended to extract truth when evidence was suggestive but not conclusive.</note> without prior legal proof exposes himself to the risk of condemning an innocent person who, compelled by the torture, confesses to being the culprit. Because of fear, or being overcome by their pains, people often confess to having done what they never actually did. It is certain that by condemning someone who did not commit the crime in this way, the judge incurs true homicide and the obligation of restitution. In substance, it is almost the same guilt to condemn a delinquent by unjustly forcing him to reveal his own guilt. For regarding the execution of a penal law and the suffering of its punishment, the true culprit is just as free—provided he remains hidden and not legally convicted—as the innocent man. It follows that almost the same sin is committed by whoever condemns the defendant based on a confession so unjustly obtained that the Latin speakers call it *extorted* <note>original: "*Extorta*". This refers to a confession "twisted out" or forced from someone through coercion rather than given freely.</note>.

Concerning the sin in all these cases, it is well-established among all learned men, as is the obligation of the judge to make satisfaction to the injured party as their murderer. However, to assess the amount of restitution required, one must examine the <term>indications</term> <note>original: "indicios". ### On the restitution of the killer.

...those who have understanding. Nature gave weapons to all creatures so that they might defend themselves. And if some weapons are offensive, it is for the purpose of offending in their own defense. Thus, most wild beasts do not do harm unless they are attacked. And if some do attack first, it is to sustain themselves with their prey. In this way, all their struggles are for self-preservation; and they never feel, nor find themselves with as much strength, as when they feel half-defeated and close to their own **corruption** <note>In this period, "corruption" refers to the physical decomposition or the end of life; essentially, death.</note>. Remarkable is the **instinct** <note>original: "cognato". In this context, it refers to an innate or natural inclination or impulse shared by living things.</note> that they all then exert in resisting their adversary. This inclination is more effective and vivid in man.

Firstly, because he is such an excellent creature: his being is very sublime, and to everyone—even to his Creator—he is very lovable. Secondly, because he alone among all corporeal beings knows of what esteem and value life is, and as such, he loves it. Others use life without knowing or valuing it, but man understands well what a great good it is *to be*, having not been before. For this reason, when he finds himself with it, he prizes such lovable wealth to the extreme. And from this knowledge and esteem proceeds its protection. Thirdly, because man loves perpetuity more than other creatures, as one who was created to exist forever, whose soul is immortal.

All this makes it very lawful for him to resist, and in resisting, to offend anyone who intends to undo him. Great and beneficial are the licenses that nature gives for the remedy of one who suffers **extreme necessity** <note>A legal and theological concept: in cases of life-or-death need, the law of private property is suspended, and taking what is needed to survive is not considered a crime.</note>. He may take from the people, and even from the temple, what he might need to escape, and he is neither a thief nor sacrilegious in taking it. And there is no greater necessity than when one's life is being taken against justice and with violence. And if, to save his life, he can harm someone who is not harming him—such as by taking from their estate—how much more might he harm the one who does him such great evil? And it is not against this that every person is obliged to look out for their neighbor. For all these obligations cease when the preservation of one's own life is at stake, even regarding one's father, mother, and children.

<summary>This page explores the natural law foundations of self-defense, arguing that man’s unique understanding of the value of life and the immortality of the soul justifies extreme measures for self-preservation.</summary>

# In which cases it is excused.

<margin>
Distinction 1, chapter "natural law" and the Digest on justice and law: this occurs, so that whatever anyone does for the protection of their own body is deemed to have been done lawfully. <note>original Latin: "Dist. 1. c. ius naturale et ff. de iust. & iure hoc euenit, vt quod quisq; obtutellā sui corporis fecerit iure fecisse existimetur"</note>

St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 64, article 2: homicide holds the first place among punishments. Question 13, article 3, reply 1: only princes are permitted to kill evildoers, not private persons. Question 64, article 3, and question 108, articles 1 and 3 on vengeance, and II-II, question 100, article 9, reply 3, and *Summa Contra Gentiles*, book 3, chapter 140. St. Thomas, *Commentary on the Sentences*, book 4, distinction 25, question 2.
</margin>

One can lawfully forget children and wife if one is in danger, and when one cannot help them except by dying. How much more so regarding strangers. All these bonds with one's neighbor are justly broken if they are to cost one's life. And consequently, no one can rebuke someone who kills their aggressor in self-defense. All laws, both ecclesiastical <note>Laws governing the Church.</note> and imperial <note>Civil or state laws.</note>, approve of it. The law says in chapter *Significasti* 2, on homicide, and chapter *Si vero* 1, on the sentence of excommunication: to resist or overcome force with force—that is, to strike back at the offender—all laws and rights approve. And in the unique *Clementine* <note>A collection of decrees by Pope Clement V.</note> on homicide, it is held to be so lawful that it even saves a person from **irregularity** <term>irregularity: a canonical impediment that prevents a person from receiving or exercising Holy Orders or clerical duties</term>, whether they be a cleric or a layman, if they dispatched their offender because they could not escape in any other way. And there is a presumption that they should be believed to be the one attacked and not the aggressor.

The truth is that this is viewed with different eyes in the courtrooms and in confession. Judges will set a man free, as men who judge only by outward appearances, if he proves that the deceased attacked him, and that he begged him and requested peace. They will not interfere, nor is it just for them to interfere, to examine if, despite all that, he could have defended himself without causing harm. But in conscience, as we are speaking now, it is necessary that, being attacked, one has no other safe way or manner to preserve his life except by depriving the opponent of theirs. If two are fighting and one has such a clear advantage that, with a little care, he is certain the other will not touch or reach him, that person has no authority in conscience to harm his enemy, but only to protect himself. For this license that natural law gives to the attacked is not for vengeance, but for defense. And even in the law of men, when there is such inequality, killing him is no more than "passing a dead man" <note>likely a historical idiom suggesting that the act is so effortless or the outcome so inevitable that it is equivalent to stepping over someone already deceased.</note>. The truth is that such a difference in strength and skill is very rare among those who fight, and when it does exist, the inferior person does not dare (unless he is mad) to throw <note>catchword: "a echar" (to throw)</note>

<summary>This page argues that the right to self-defense is so fundamental that it supersedes duties to family and allows for the killing of an aggressor without legal or religious penalty, provided no other means of escape exists.</summary>

# On restitution by the killer

to take up arms <note>Spanish: "echar mano," literally to "lay hand" on a sword or weapon.</note> without being compelled. And when he is compelled, justice and the license we grant are on his side. But in the case where the one who is attacked is doubtful whether he can defend himself without striking back, he is not obliged then to test his valor and luck. He may proceed immediately, without further testing, to remove the one who wishes him ill from his presence.

If one is forced to fight and many people get in the middle of it, it is not lawful for any of those in the quarrel to wound another, provided they can leave honorably. In this way, one only has license to do harm to the aggressor when he cannot save his life in any other way. And it is morally credible that the one who was suddenly attacked acted with such an intention, provided he did not previously have the will to do harm and only intended his own defense at the beginning. 

Once this is established, the confessor <note>The priest hearing the killer's confession and determining their penance.</note> should not trouble or worry himself by questioning and scrutinizing whether the person became inflamed with ire and anger during the struggle and desired to avenge himself. Because in such conflicts, these feelings and movements are natural, and can hardly be avoided. The great danger in which a man finds himself takes away his awareness and the care to repress them. If he should confess that a few hours earlier he suspected, more or less, that they would come to blows and he was glad of it: there one must investigate with what spirit and determination he began to fight. Many times the priest will find sin <note>In the internal spiritual sense.</note>, but never restitution <term>restitution: the legal and moral obligation to pay the victim's family for their loss</term>, if (as we said) he could not otherwise defend himself.

This privilege of preserving oneself at the cost of the aggressor is so general that it is understood even if one has given cause or provoked the other to fight with certain deeds or words. Because no motive or occasion of these gave the opponent the right to seek vengeance with his sword. Thus, the opponent took up arms against reason and forced the other to do so for his own protection; and in protecting himself, he maimed the other. Except if the malice of one were so great that he purposefully provoked with insults

# On restitution by the killer

...one another to unsheathe weapons, or to challenge him, so that under the pretext of defending himself he might finish him off. Such a murderous devil is a voluntary killer, and even worse, since he intended and sought the conflict, and is therefore under the obligation to make full restitution <note>Legal and financial compensation paid to the victim's family.</note>.

Self-defense is so just and natural that it is not right to deny it even to clerics <term>ecclesiastics: members of the clergy, such as priests or monks</term>, although they are otherwise rightly forbidden from staining their hands with human blood. But what natural law grants to all, one's social estate <note>Spanish: "estados," referring to one's rank or vocation in society.</note> does not take away, unless a man specifically renounces a right. And the Church, which defines their profession, has never condemned any of them who killed another while defending themselves; rather, she always saves and exonerates the one who acts out of this natural regard for life.

<margin>Sylvester, on Homicide, 3, paragraph 4.</margin>
What shall we say of the many who, through vice or madness, put themselves in danger of being attacked and killed, or of being forced to kill someone else to escape? These are men who, walking in wicked paths, enter the houses of others where—if the husband finds out—he cannot, humanly speaking, avoid putting everything at risk to take his revenge. Theologians doubt whether this privilege <note>The legal protection and exemption from restitution usually granted to those acting in self-defense.</note> should be extended and given to those who so clearly seem to choose the danger by entering another's house through secret ways and at suspicious hours. Certainly, they deserve to have it denied, as Saint Antoninus <note>Saint Antoninus of Florence (1389–1459), a Dominican authority on moral theology.</note> denies it, and as the law says: he who misuses a privilege should lose it. 

But the desire for self-preservation that every living creature possesses is so great and intense that it seems reasonable to grant it to them. Although many in this regard act like beasts, desiring to live above all else while simultaneously putting themselves, without any necessity, in two thousand obvious dangers of death. But in the end, in my better judgment, it seems to me that such a person sins most gravely by courting such risks. However, once in that position, if he were attacked, he may defend himself with the least possible harm to the sufferer <note>In this legal context, the "sufferer" or "patient" is the person receiving the blow—here, the original attacker who is now being fought off.</note> that he can manage. But if he cannot escape without shedding blood...

# On restitution by the killer

...it would not oblige him to let himself be slaughtered like a lamb.

It is right to note in these cases that when one is attacked, even if he could escape by fleeing, he is not obligated to flee if fleeing would be a disgrace to him; instead, he may stand his ground. And he may harm the attacker in his defense as necessary. For a knight <term>cauallero: a man of high social standing, bound by a code of honor</term> who is attacked, if he were to "put even his horse’s feet to the dusty path" <note>The original Spanish "enpoluorosa" is an idiomatic reference to a hasty, shameful retreat.</note>, it would be a dishonor to him. 

But if it is a person for whom, according to their social standing, turning their back is not an insult, <margin>Soto, *On Justice and Right*, book 5, question 1, article 8, near the end.</margin> they are obligated to do so rather than kill their enemy. This applies to a cleric or a member of a religious order, who have not professed to be brave but rather peaceful and quiet; if they can avoid striking by leaving or moving away, they have an obligation to do so. No loss of reputation follows this; rather, it brings a holy reputation. This also applies to any layperson of modest social status for whom fleeing would not be a disgrace. 

Except in this last case that we determined: when a man, without just cause—and indeed with a very unjust one—places himself in obvious danger of being attacked <note>This refers to the "misguided youths" or adulterers mentioned previously who provoke a confrontation by their presence.</note>. In that case, no matter how much of a knight he may be, or whatever dishonor may follow, he is obligated to flee if he can escape by running or by jumping over a wall to avoid striking a person whose honor and house he has already so deeply wounded. Because by putting himself in such a predicament, he lost all his rights except that of defending his life. Once his life is safe, he is obligated to do everything else to avoid causing further harm. Indeed, it is not truly a disgrace but rather prudence to flee in such cases, especially if he flees to avoid being recognized. The same that applies to these misguided youths applies to any kind of people who, seeking diverse and unjust things, purposely place themselves in locations where it is obvious that, sooner or later, a skirmish must occur.

Neither is he a murderer, nor must he pay restitution, who catches a thief in the very act <term>in flagrante delicto: caught in the act of committing a crime</term>—whether the thief is robbing the house, carrying off stolen goods already gathered and bundled, or attacking him in the field to seize his saddlebags or purse. He may, in such a juncture...

Cajetan on the *Summa Theologica*, Second Part of the Second Part, Question 64.

Law *sed et si*, in the Digest, on the Falcidian Law; and in the Decretals on homicide, chapter *interfecisti*: if, however, without the intent of hatred, but by freeing yourself and your own from such a [threat]...
<note>original: "l. sed. & si ff. ad legem falci. & extra de homicidio."</note>
</margin>

...if he is trying to take the stolen goods from his hands, arrest him, and hand him over to justice, provided there are witnesses with which he can prove his crime. But if the thief does not wish to release what he has stolen, but instead defends it, one must look to see if there are witnesses present to convict him in the evidence <term>prouāça: the formal presentation of proof or evidence in a legal proceeding</term>. If they exist, he cannot harm the thief's person, because since he can recover his property through the justice system, there is no reason to settle it by the blade <note>original: "por la hoja," literally "by the leaf," referring to the blade of a sword or knife</note>. 

But if there is no such certainty of recovery—rather, once this opportunity has passed, he will either not recover the goods <note>original: "la ropa," literally "the clothing," but used here as a general term for possessions or "stuff"</note> or do so only with great difficulty, and even this remains doubtful—he may, in order to take the goods back, take the thief's life. Because to defend one's person and property, everyone possesses a great natural right. 

For this reason, God’s law of old—as seen in the book of Exodus—exonerated the one who wounded or killed a thief who was either breaking down his doors or making a breach in his house. Under these terms, it was understood to mean if he were being robbed. And even now, canon law <term>canon: the body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership</term> absolves from homicide anyone who kills or wounds to defend their property. 

It is true that this usually does not apply except in the case of nighttime thefts, or with highwaymen in the countryside, where the criminal putting up a defense endangers not only the property but also the person of the one trying to recover or protect their goods. Thus, the canonical text deals absolutely with the death of nighttime thieves, and civil law expressly orders that it not be punished; but for daytime thieves, the law sets a thousand conditions to be able to lawfully maim <term>liziar: to injure, wound, or maim</term> them, and a thousand suspicions regarding the act after they are wounded. Because during the day, it is a marvel—at least in a populated area—if it should be necessary to use such means. 

Thus says Saint Augustine: that it is lawful to kill nighttime thieves when they are found stealing and they defend themselves and what they have stolen; and the reason (he says) is because one does not know if the thief came only to rob—

# Of the restitution of the killer

<margin>
You have killed the members of the devil; if he intended to harm you, it will be well for you—that is, you shall not be feared <note>In this legal context, "not feared" means "not held liable" or "not prosecuted by the law." Original Latin: "diaboli mē bra interfe cisti si iū- nare volue- rit bonũ erit tibi (id est) non timeris."</note>.
</margin>

...to steal the valuables, or to harm the person. During the day, it will only rarely be necessary to use this remedy <note>The "remedy" refers to the use of physical force or violence.</note> to recover what was stolen. Firstly, because witnesses are never lacking; and secondly, with a single shout, there is no thief who, seeing himself discovered in the sunlight, is not unsettled and left as if dead. For evil by its nature is a most fearful enemy of light, as the Gospel says; it is so foul that it confounds and shames itself when looking upon the light.

And it is so just and proper for everyone to watch over and guard the life of their neighbor—even if they are wicked—that one must not touch it except almost by force and out of pure necessity. This applies either as in the first case, to escape with one’s own life, or in this case, to avoid losing one’s property. And it all comes down to the same thing, as they say: if the law permits me to protect my property with such harm to the one who steals it, it is because life itself is sustained by that property. 

For this reason, if I can easily defend or recover it, either through the justice system or because the thief immediately drops it and leaves, no private individual may inflict a punishment of blood <note>A "punishment of blood" refers to capital punishment or any physical injury that draws blood.</note>, no matter how much he finds him stealing inside his house. Thus, both laws, ecclesiastical <term>ecclesiastical law: the body of laws and regulations made by Church leadership</term> and imperial <term>imperial law: civil law derived from the Roman Empire and the secular state</term>, consider it a very wrong act to lay hands on a thief by wounding or killing him if he can be apprehended. 

But ultimately, if other means are lacking—whether by night or by day—one may, in order to take the stolen goods from his hands, cut them, and more, if more is necessary and he persists. The contrary—that is, it being unlawful to harm him—would certainly be very damaging and even intolerable. For the thief, knowing that they cannot harm him, would do much—namely, steal and defend the theft with weapons. It would also be a monstrous obligation if a man saw himself being robbed and had to stand by with his hands folded, watching the very light and nimble hands of others in his own property and house. The truth is that neither divine nor natural law binds us to anything except that which is very much in accordance with reason and very worthy of the noble nature of man.

### In which cases it is excused.
<meta>catchword: say</meta>

<margin>Law: *sed & si. ff. ad legem a qui*. If someone, when they could have apprehended a thief, preferred to kill him, they are seen to have acted unjustly. <note>This refers to the *Digest* of Justinian (Lex Aquilia), a foundational text of Roman Law.</note></margin>
But this permission has two limitations. The first is that the theft must be of a significant amount, not so little as to be nothing. For it is a great cruelty to be so fierce and ferocious in recovering a single *real*, or even a *ducat* <note>The *real* and *ducat* were common Spanish currencies; a real was of relatively low value compared to the gold ducat.</note>. This is unless it were in some particular case where letting it be taken with such insolence would cause great loss and shame—either because he is a knight, or being in a place where letting it go would be held as great cowardice and pusillanimity, rather than generosity. So that, as the saying goes, it is not done for the egg, but for the principle <note>original: "no se hiziesse por el ouo, sino por el buen foro." This legal proverb implies that the action is taken to defend one's rights or status rather than the specific value of the item.</note>. He could then, if he fears for his honor or his office some great loss, do as much to defend the little as if it were much. And if it is a substantial amount, this permission is granted and permitted only to the layman.

<margin>And *extra de ho.* regarding the one who killed a thief or robber where he could have been captured without killing, because he was created in the image of God. <note>A reference to Canon Law (Decretals of Gregory IX) emphasizing the sanctity of human life.</note></margin>
For the cleric and the religious person, it would be very wrong to shed blood, much more so to kill for gold or silver. Their state is to profess a forgetfulness and contempt for all temporal things; it sits poorly with their calling, and appears even worse, to value possessions so much that to recover them they put their own life in clear danger, or deprive the culprit of theirs at a time when they would morally be damned <note>The author is concerned that killing a thief in the act of sin sends them to Hell without a chance for confession.</note>. But if, despite all this, an ecclesiastic is so wrathful that he lacks the patience to let it go, he will sin in doing so because of the law and rule that forbid it to him, but he does not sin against justice, nor is he obligated to restitution <note><term>restitution</term>: In this context, the legal and moral requirement to compensate the victim's family for their loss.</note>.

<margin>47. Days do not enter the church. <note>A reference to a standard penance or period of exclusion from the sanctuary for those who have shed blood.</note></margin>
Thus, to defend their person, ecclesiastics and laymen have equal permission, but to protect temporalities [property], they do not have the same power under positive law <note><term>positive law</term>: Laws enacted by human authorities (like the Church or State) as opposed to natural law.</note>. Because, in truth, they ought not to have the same greed, nor the same anger and lack of endurance.

The second limitation is that he be caught in the act <note>original: *flagrante delicto*</note>. That is, that he is currently robbing, or attempting to rob, or carrying it on his back, within the house or very nearby—as they say, "the theft in his hands"—in such a way that the thief cannot with any probability or appearance say...

### CHAPTER FIVE, IN WHICH
->*the aim of the previous chapter is continued, and it is explained how restitution is not required of one who wounds or kills while defending the innocent, or by accident.*<-

<image-desc>An ornamental woodcut initial 'I' depicting a man in a tunic holding a staff or sword in a rural landscape with buildings in the background.</image-desc> Furthermore, he is not required to make restitution <term>restitution: the moral or legal obligation to compensate for a loss or injury, essentially "making it right"</term> in conscience <note>The "court of conscience" refers to one's moral standing before God, often considered separately from secular legal punishment.</note> who, in order to defend an innocent person being actively killed—the victim being blameless—wounds or kills the guilty party. However, He did not obligate them to put themselves in danger to save another. But for anyone who wishes to be so charitable as to risk their life for their neighbor, His Divine Majesty gave them permission, and even a reward, to intervene in their defense, and to wound or even finish off the opponent, if there is no other way for both of them—the defender and the innocent—to escape safely.

## How one who wounds or kills is not bound to restitution

And it is a just penalty that he who, against all reason, intends to deprive of being <note>In this context, "deprive of being" means to take someone's life or existence.</note> one who does not deserve it, should himself be deprived of health, by wounding him, or of life, by killing him. But one must find them in order to do this in actual conflict and strife, not before, nor after, and seeing very clearly that the innocent person will be in danger, or is already in danger, and that if he is not succored, he will be killed. Because if they are equal in the battle, or if he is defending himself sufficiently, only the one attacked has the right to kill the aggressor in his defense, no one else for him. But if he is already being defeated, anyone in such a situation may enter by intervening; and if the adversary were restrained and stepped away, he will have done a heroic work at little cost in pacifying them. But if, having been entreated for peace, he does not desist, one can oppose him by joining with the weak one, and being "two at the mill" <note>The original Spanish idiom "ser dos al molino" (two at the mill) refers to two people ganging up on one, or tipping the scales of power.</note>, since he did not wish to be humane or well-bred.

But it is worth knowing whom the doctors <note>The "doctors" refers to the Doctors of the Church or established legal scholars whose opinions formed the basis of moral law.</note> call innocent, so that it may be understood for whom one must fight. They call "innocent" the one who was attacked and compelled to fight, although (otherwise) he might have given motive. Thus, one must not look to see if he was culpable before the struggle, but only that he is not the aggressor <term>aggressor: the person who initiates the physical violence, regardless of prior insults</term>. Of which the one who enters anew must be certain; for if it is doubtful to him, he cannot take a side for either of the parties. Intervene for peace, yes, and do what he reasonably can in that regard.

Likewise, regarding this point of saving the one who suffers and is in danger, even the aggressor is considered "innocent" in the case that the opponent is patently mistreating him and has him half-defeated. He who comes anew can and should intervene for peace, and if the aggressor were so foolish that, even being in such a bad state, he does not withdraw and persists, he [the newcomer] cannot nor should help him, but rather let him go from bad to worse, so that with the punishment he may become wise and prudent. But if he who attacked at the beginning now restrains himself and withdraws, and the one attacked persists and does not cease, then his failure to cease as he was obligated makes the aggressor innocent and without fault, and gives right...

<summary>This page discusses the ethics of third-party intervention in violent conflicts, defining "innocence" as the state of being the one currently in danger or the one willing to stop fighting.</summary>

# Defending the innocent.

...right so that they can help him, and defend him, and even so that they can wound the aggressor to protect the other. The clear resolution of this matter is that when two are fighting, the one who arrives from outside must try to bring peace, and whoever then makes a gesture of weakening or ceasing his attack, this person is now considered the innocent party. On whose behalf anyone who wishes may fight. But if neither yields nor stops, one cannot fight except for the person who was originally attacked, if, as I say, he is in a bad state. This is permitted only for the duration that the opponent does not desist. Because no one has the right to continue a struggle <note>original: *pendencia*</note> except when forced and compelled. Therefore, the moment the opponent leaves him, he is obliged to stop.

The same license is justly given to defend a **maiden** <note>original: *donzella*</note>, so that she is not shamed, when she cries out and asks for help as one forced and compelled. For if she stays silent, or if her resistance is very weak and lukewarm, it is not reasonable to defend with such rigor one who, as she demonstrates, does not wish to be so rigorously defended. And what I say of a maiden is also understood with the same condition and limitation in the defense of any married lady or widow, especially if she is of honor and reputation in the community.

Sylvester [Mazzolini], *On Homicide*, part 1, paragraph 1: If someone cutting wood in a forest through which people rarely pass, or throwing wood, kills a man, he can be excused from the sin of homicide. *Summa Theologica*, Question 64, Article 8. <note>The marginal note cites Sylvestro Mazzolini’s *Summa Sylvestrina* and Thomas Aquinas to support the idea that accidental death in a place where one does not expect people is not a mortal sin.</note>
</margin>
Likewise, he who kills or wounds accidentally does not have to make restitution, as happens not rarely. For example, if while testing or firing a **culverin** <term>an early, long-barreled cannon</term>, and the artilleryman having performed his due diligence and given warning, the piece happens to burst and its fragments shatter those standing nearby. Likewise, if while firing an **arquebus** <term>a heavy portable matchlock firearm</term> in a forest, one should hit another hunter who is among the myrtles and strawberry trees dressed in green and calling like a deer, which he appeared to be. These are cases that, as they are outside our foresight, do not carry an annexed obligation of satisfaction <note>In canon law, "satisfaction" refers to the penance or restitution required to make amends for a wrong.</note>. The same can be said of a thousand other fortuitous and unhappy tales that happen without the person intending it, provided they have exercised all the care, sense, and diligence on their part that they ought to have used to avoid them. All of which events are disposed by divine providence.

For example, when teaching someone to swim, the <term>master <note>The teacher or instructor.</note></term> must not look away for a moment, or his <term>student <note>original: *ahijado*. While this usually means 'godson,' here it refers to the person under the master's protection or instruction.</note></term> will drown.

The same applies to the use and practice of arms, which are normally intended for real combat, or placing a pregnant woman in a crowded or tight space. In such matters, it is necessary that a man either does not engage at all, or does so with great caution and care. However, when one is engaged in activities that do not naturally lead to accidents, we do not oblige anyone to foresee and avoid every accidental occurrence that might happen in various ways. First, because a man cannot live forever on watch; if he stays awake for a single night, he becomes exhausted. Second, no matter how much he reasons and observes, he cannot anticipate every possibility. These accidents, besides being infinite (as the <term>philosophers <note>A reference to Aristotelian thought, which suggests that accidental events are infinite and therefore cannot be the subject of a systematic science.</note></term> say), do not fall under human providence or science. 

For instance, if someone asks for water at a door, the master of the house is not obliged to suddenly consider whether the water will benefit or harm the person, nor must he recall the rules of medicine. If the other person arrives full of cucumbers <note>In early modern medicine, eating "cold" foods like cucumbers was thought to make the stomach vulnerable to sudden "chills" or death if followed by cold water.</note> and stuffs himself with the cold water given out of <term>charity <note>Acts of mercy or kindness performed for the benefit of others.</note></term>, he may drop dead afterward, as has indeed happened. But the one who gave the water incurs no guilt for his good deed. Likewise, if while sparring with a <term>practice sword <note>original: *espada prieta*, a blunt sword used for training to avoid injury.</note></term>, the more skilled fencer presses his opponent, and the other, retreating by chance and slipping, hits his head on a stone corner where his brains are dashed out, the skilled fencer was not obliged to foresee this disaster, nor was he required to stop using his <term>good maneuvers <note>original: *buenos tiempos*. Having established this, I say that to judge whether one should be held responsible in <term>conscience <note>The internal moral judgment of an individual regarding right and wrong.</note></term> for the death of another—a death neither intended nor sought—one must look at whether the person was engaged in a dangerous activity without the required caution. If so, they shall be held responsible if a death occurs. Thus, one must attend to the quality and nature of the act, and the circumspection with which it is performed, to either attribute or excuse an accidental homicide. 

Although, I will not fail to point out that there are dangers so obvious that no amount of alertness or caution excuses entering into them, as they are inevitable. For example, if a pregnant woman, knowing there would be a great crowd of people—or being in a position where she should have realized it—chose to be present there, she would not be excused if she suffered a miscarriage, unless she was accompanied by enough of her own men to make room for her. 

Returning to our purpose, I say that we must look at the nature of the act and the occupation, rather than whether it was forbidden or permitted, as many do. For even if an act is a <term>mortal sin <note>A grave sin that, in Catholic theology, severs the soul from God's grace.</note></term>, if by its nature it is not inclined to cause physical death, the sinner shall not be held responsible for anything more than the simple sin itself, even if by some "miracle" <note>Used here ironically to mean a strange or unlikely occurrence.</note> an accidental death follows from it. ...and consequently, it is involuntary. For the will does not desire anything unless the understanding knows it in some way. However, not to intend an act at the moment it happens occurs in two ways, which cannot be explained with simple words in <note>original: *romance*. Here referring to the Spanish vernacular.</note> but rather in Latin. Namely, *intrinsically* <note>original: *de per se*. In and of itself.</note> or *incidentally* <note>original: *de per accidens*. By chance or secondary circumstance.</note>. This is to say that the killer did not want the disaster itself by chance, because he did not know of it; otherwise, if he had known, he would have wanted it. Other times, not only did he not want it, but he abhorred it. He did not intend it because he did not know about it, and he would have intended it even less—rather, he never would have committed it—if he had understood it. In both cases, they do not want the outcome when it happens, but one abhors it both before and after it occurs, while the other, had he realized the future harm, would have intended it more willingly.

Let us provide a pair of examples to clarify this obscure distinction. If while hunting, an <term>arquebus <note>original: *alcabuz*. An early muzzle-loading firearm.</note></term> were to burst, or if while aiming at a tree, one were to hit a person who was hidden next to that tree, the hunter did not intend this outcome, for he did not know a person was there; and if he had known, he would have been far less likely to fire. 

But consider if someone determined and sought to kill his enemy, and by chance—having forgotten this intent for the moment—he killed him while shooting at something else. The <term>doctors <note>Legal and theological scholars whose opinions formed the basis of law.</note></term> say that even if he fired with all possible caution so as not to harm anyone, this homicide is attributed to him because of the "corrupt will" he held. This will persists, as we assume, even though he did not actually remember it at the time. Had he already changed his mind and determined not to do it, the death would not be attributed to him. ### CHAPTER VI. ON THE RESTITUTION
#### that the killer must make.

<margin>St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* 2-2, question 62, article 8; question 13, article 4; *Quodlibetal* 7, question 6. Juan de Medina, Distinction 15, question 5. Duns Scotus, in the same place, question 3. <note>original Latin: "quoscumque alebat interfectus, alat interfector omnia lucra debent restitui deductis expensis."</note> Whomever the deceased person used to support, the killer must now support; all lost earnings must be restored, after deducting expenses.</margin>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'P' featuring floral and foliate scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>It is a precept and commandment of both divine and <term>natural law <note>Moral principles believed to be inherent in human nature and discoverable by reason, independent of specific religious revelation.</note></term>: Thou shalt not kill. Because without much argument, and even without any formal education, it is understood to be very just not to deprive anyone of what God has so generously given them. It is a great evil—since we are not the masters of human life—to take it away. Therefore, the transgression of this commandment is a clear injustice and an injury done to the <term>victim <note>The original Spanish uses *leso*, referring to the injured or aggrieved party.</note></term>, as it violently and unfairly dispossesses and strips him of the most excellent good among all earthly things. And if any property belonging to others that is taken against reason must be <term>restituted <note>The legal and moral obligation to restore what was taken or to provide equal compensation to the victim or their family.</note></term> by returning it in its same form to its owners, or its equivalent, then life must be restored with even greater cause, for it is of higher value than all things. And if it cannot be returned in its own form—since it is no longer possible to resurrect the person or call them back (as they say) from the abyss—the killer must provide an equivalent, according to the judgment of honorable men. Truly, comparing it point by point, there is no wealth or treasure that equals the value and esteem of life; however, once it is lost, it is valued and appraised for the purpose of financial restitution. While a man lives, he cannot and should not sell his very being for any amount of wealth. But when he is violently stripped of it by disaster, the wise agree (and their opinion is correct) that the killer should return as compensation—if not as much as he took—at least as much as he is able. ...do as much as he can, and if he were able—even with great labor of his own—to bring the victim back to life, he would give him life. <term>St. Thomas Aquinas, Scotus, Richard of Middleton, and Durandus <note>A group of influential medieval theologians and "Schoolmen" whose writings formed the basis of Catholic moral and legal philosophy.</note></term>, along with the rest, establish two general rules. 

The first: when one cannot restore as much as he owes, let him restore at least as much as he can. The contrary would be very absurd: if, by not having the whole amount to return, he were not obliged to return even the part he does have and is able to give. 

The second: when the temporal goods that are stolen or unjustly taken have no price because of their excellence—such as life and the limbs and parts of the body—restitution must still be made for them. Even if it is not everything the victim deserved, it must be everything that men shall judge appropriate, having considered the status of the persons involved. 

But it is not only the quantity of payment that is obscure in this matter, but also to whom it must be delivered, since to the true owner, who has already expired, it cannot be restored. In explanation of this, it should be noted that one can be a killer in two ways. Either he is the physical cause <note>original Spanish: *real causa*</note>, who causes death by wounding or killing him; or the "moral" cause (as they call it), as if, while not striking the blow himself, he ordered it to be given, or advised it, or arranged it, or assisted in it. 

Among these, the first is commonly more culpable, of whom we will speak in the first place, and then of the second group. He who immediately and physically killed another must make restitution to the heirs, who succeed to the place of the deceased. These people are called, and indeed are, heirs of the estate <note>original: *hazienda*</note> for this very reason. This is because they are judged and counted as another "persona" of the dead man and are—to use the phrase of <term>Alexander <note>Likely referring to Alexander of Imola, a prominent 15th-century jurist known for his commentaries on civil law.</note></term>—his "other self." Thus, to them is owed what was owed to the other. 

However, it is not well established to which specific heirs this applies, because there are two kinds of them. Some are called "natural and forced" heirs, who cannot be excluded from the inheritance, such as father and mother, children, and wife; others are "voluntary" or "legal" heirs, whom the will of the testator, or the law alone, made heirs. Examples of these are brothers who inherit <term>intestate <note>original Latin: *ab intestato*; refers to the legal distribution of an estate when the deceased has not left a valid will.</note></term> when the deceased did not arrange a testament, or when he has...

<margin>Domingo de Soto, *On Justice and Law*, Book 5, Question 6, Article 3. St. Augustine, Letters 54 and 154 to Publicola; *On Free Choice of the Will*, Book 1, Chapter 4: <note>original Latin: "si homicidium est hominem occidere, potest aliquando accidere absque peccato, ut cum miles hostem, iudex nocentem vel casualiter."</note> "If homicide is the killing of a human being, it can sometimes happen without sin, as when a soldier kills an enemy, a judge kills a criminal, or it occurs by accident."</margin>
When there are <term>forced heirs <note>Legally recognized heirs, typically children or parents, who by law cannot be disinherited without specific, serious cause.</note></term>, the <term>Doctors <note>Learned theologians and legal scholars whose interpretations formed the basis of Catholic Canon Law and Spanish civil law.</note></term> hold it as a manifest and clear truth that they must be satisfied. They are considered persons who, in the natural order, were as one with the deceased, such as parents and children. But if these are lacking, and the heirs are "voluntary" <note>beneficiaries chosen specifically in a will</note> or "legal" <note>distant relatives who inherit only because no closer kin exist</note>, the killer owes them nothing in conscience as satisfaction for the life of which he deprived the other. This is because this debt is not "real" <note>pertaining to physical property or assets</note> but personal, resulting from having harmed the person, not from property that the deceased had sold or entrusted to him. Excepting from this rule brothers, to whom—since a brother is such a personal part of oneself—restitution must be made; they should be included in the category of the first group, even if they are not technically forced heirs. 

It is true that all heirs and relatives, according to the law, have the power to accuse him and seek punishment. For this reason, they can and often do reach an agreement to pardon the death for a certain amount, and they will not complain, or they will desist from their complaint if they have already filed it. And they may licitly receive what they agree upon, and the defendant may give it to them to redeem his harassment <note>to settle the legal pursuit or "vexation" of a criminal trial</note>. These are the persons to whom restitution must be made.

Regarding the amount, it should be noted that a killer always causes harm, and with a single act he often harms many, being the cause of two grievances, both of which he must undo—or better said, compensate. The first and most direct cause is natural: namely, depriving the wretched soul of life (a most great evil), or cutting off an arm, a foot, or fingers, thereby maiming him. This follows infallibly from his deed and mischief. And for this, he must give everything that impartial and wise persons shall judge, having looked at the circumstances of the fact, the quality of the persons, their equality and status—whether they are rich or poor, if they were of the same reputation—the malice of the one, and the innocence of the other...

First, whoever kills commits a most grave and detestable **sin**, worthy of the harshest punishment. For it is natural law and the dictate of reason that bad deeds should be punished—even if no harm results from them—and much more so if they cause great damage; while good deeds should receive a prize and reward.

Third, he scandalizes and disturbs the **republic** <note>original: *republica*; here referring to the "commonwealth" or the body politic of the community.</note> with his wicked example, providing a pattern and model for other wicked people to imitate. He wrongs the city and **justice** <note>original: *justicia*; personified here as the legal system and the magistrates who uphold it.</note>, which is the guardian and protection of citizens, whose duty it is to defend and favor them, and also to punish them when they are unruly and scandalous in public, even to the point of removing them from the midst [of society] if necessary, either by death or exile. 

Fourth, it often happens that by depriving the other of his natural being, he takes away the food and honor that many possessed through him, by his authority and office. A killer causes all these damages and wrongs, and he is obligated to compensate for all of them according to their degree and order. Some by force, when judges compel him; others gracefully and by his own will, without anyone asking. 

When justice condemns him to death, he pays for the sin committed, the republic is avenged, and others take warning—for as they saw him do evil, they see him pay—and in some way, his obligation to the deceased is fulfilled, although the loss is irrecoverable. But he does not, by dying, restore to the heirs the temporal goods that the deceased gave or provided for them, nor the loss he causes to their lineage and house, nor the injury that the entire ancestry received in this. <meta>This page continues the discussion from Chapter Seven regarding those who are indirectly responsible for a death. It specifically focuses on the moral and legal responsibility of those in power—rulers and judges—and the circumstances under which their subordinates share in the guilt of an unjust execution.</meta>

->**Of the murderer.**<-

The main ones responsible are those in command <note>original: "mandones," referring here to those who issue the orders for an execution</note>, so much so that many times they alone bear the crime and the obligation of restitution, while the one who committed the act while obeying them is excused and freed from both the guilt and the bonds of the crime. Princes and superior judges who, against justice, knowingly, or out of slander and anger, have someone executed, must make restitution just as if they had done so without the authority of a judge. Sometimes their ministers and executors act rightly and deserve merit by obeying them, while the superiors remain bound by their own command—specifically, when the injustice and cruelty of the act were not manifest and apparent. For if the injustice were clear, the executors would not be excused. It is more reasonable to obey God than man, when man uses the power given to him from on high so poorly. For there is no man in the world, of whatever status he may be, who has the authority to condemn anyone to death except for demerits and sins that he has either committed or that have at least been proven against him. Nor can any necessity arise where it is lawful to deprive the innocent of life. God alone is the Lord and author of life; He gives it and takes it away as He wills, and He disposes of His creatures as it most pleases and satisfies Him. Those who hold high office—Emperors, Kings, and Governors—are ministers of His justice, as Saint Paul says, to defend the good and punish the wicked. Thus, when a criminal case and proceeding moves against justice, it is a sin of conscience, just as if they were acting as private individuals.

### Of those who are indirect causes

...common people who command and entrust it to some servants or slaves of theirs. <note>This continues the thought from the previous page regarding how masters are responsible for the actions of those they command.</note>

In the same state of damnation are those who advise, induce, and sway the minds of princes toward unjust wars, or toward the destruction of a noble house, a family, or—even more seriously—a religious order. They are held responsible for all the harm that results from their influence, which is so immense that they can never fully make amends for it. This applies when they have moved the leader with their wicked and detestable advice, and the leader was not previously determined to act—either because he had not thought of it, or because, even if he were considering it, he was wavering or, as they say, "hanging in the balance" <note>original: "pendiente," referring to a state of indecision.</note>. If, through their reasoning and persuasion, they caused him to make a final decision, they then incur the duty of <term>restitution</term> <note>Restitution is the moral and legal obligation to restore what was taken or to compensate for harm done.</note> for the damage that follows and is carried out.

Also falling into this snare are those who—having the role or the authority to provide a decree to prevent an unjust war or any other injustice harmful to a third party—if asked, do not speak the truth but instead give their consent. In that moment, their consent becomes an approval of the evil being done—an evil they could have easily prevented by dissenting and clearly stating what was right. However, if they are people whose dissent or contradiction would not have stopped the act from happening anyway, they may sin by saying "yes," but they are not bound to pay restitution, because their vote lacked the power or effectiveness <note>original: "virtud, ni eficacia"</note> to change the outcome, as we assume in such a case. But when they are called to a council specifically so that the advice they give may be followed, it is clear that at such a time, staying silent or lying is not just giving bad advice; it is committing the act itself. Consequently, they are obliged to pay for the damages as if they had done it themselves. The same applies to anyone who privately persuaded a friend to fight or commit a similar reckless act. If they incited him with words and inflamed him when he was not already set on doing it, they are the cause of the resulting harm and must provide compensation.

# Of homicide.

Likewise, those who participate in a **brawl** <note>original: "pendencia," referring to a spontaneous fight or public scuffle.</note> and assist in such a way that they were the cause of the homicide [are liable]. For example, if the culprit summoned them to join him, and they had offered their help and went together with a common purpose to do it. But if two or four people are walking with another without any intention of fighting, and the fifth person in whose company they travel starts a fight, and they support him by shielding or even helping him—if the principal actor should mortally wound the enemy, they would not be bound in conscience to make **restitution** <note>The moral and legal obligation to compensate the victim's family for their loss.</note>, because their presence was accidental. 

An exception occurs if, during the conflict of the brawl, one of them performed an act from which the wound resulted—such as if he held the opponent, or blocked his sword so he could not defend himself, or occupied him so the other could strike him from behind. Aside from this, simply taking up arms alongside the killer by chance—even if it were for more than just keeping the peace (namely, to defend him, to strike fear into the opponents, or to make them flee and scare them, which we called "helping him" above)—does not incur the duty of restitution, even though the law has the right to punish them, as we see every day in similar events.

From all these cases we gather (if we care to notice) that many times, many people remain obligated to satisfy a single injury because many cooperated to commit and cause it. It is worth knowing how the restitution must be made: whether they must all contribute proportionately <note>original: "sueldo a rata," meaning a pro-rata share.</note> or if each one is liable for the whole amount <term>in solidum</term> <note>Latin legal term meaning "for the whole"; in this context, it refers to "joint and several liability" where any one participant can be held responsible for the entire debt if the others do not pay.</note>, and what order and rule should be followed. I say that first and generally, the one who was the **principal cause** must provide satisfaction. Because, as he was the first to do the deed, it is just that he be the first, as far as he is able, to undo it. Upon him falls the greatest necessity in conscience; the others are obligated only in the event that he fails, either because he cannot or will not pay. And if, recognizing the spiritual death he incurred by causing the physical death of his neighbor, he wishes to be revived and brought back to life by paying and making restitution, all those of...

# Of those who are an indirect cause

...but they remain free of the burden of restitution. However, it is not easy to discern in all cases who is the author and principal actor; therefore, the following rules will be helpful.

The first is: He who commanded the deed—such as a knight to his squire, a prince to his vassal, or a lord to his slave—finally, he who had authority and command in the matter, is held by **philosophers** <term>scholars of ethics and natural law</term> and **theologians** <term>scholars of religious law and conscience</term> to be the principal cause of the **injury** <note>original: "agrauio," referring to a legal or moral wrong done to another</note> that the subordinates committed by following his instructions, acting almost as his hands and instruments. This person, above all others, must make **restitution**; and if he tries every means to evade this—even if he seeks a dispensation from Rome <note>original: "yr a Roma," an idiom for seeking a distant legal loophole or papal pardon to avoid local obligations</note> and turns a deaf ear—the obligation then falls upon those who executed his wicked desire and vengeance.

Thus, the one who commands and directs is so central to any business that even what he does through the hand of another is attributed to him as the principal, in evil as well as in good. For in terms of the duty to compensate, the person who killed directly is not as much the "homicide" as the one who commanded the act. In all other cases, the principal is the one who actually laid hands on the deceased.

The second rule is: He who was only the motivating and persuasive cause for another to do harm is not judged as the author of the cruelty. Because one or even many pieces of advice—given where there is free will and understanding—do not carry such force and vigor that the act should not be imputed more to the one who followed the advice (for choosing to follow and accept it) than to the one who gave it. Thus, the one who did the evil must pay for it; and in his absence, the one who induced and lured him to it. And in either of these two cases, if those who were less guilty should make restitution, the principal actors remain under the obligation to pay them back, because they effectively paid out on their behalf and in their name.

The third rule concerns those who are participants and companions in the **crime** <note>original: "delicto"</note>. One must distinguish whether they were his servants, subjects, or hired for the purpose. If they were, they are judged by the first rule, where we discussed those who had command over the deed; so that if he does not

<margin>St. Thomas [Aquinas], *Summa Theologica* II-II, Question 73. And regarding esteem, we continue following the distinction established at the beginning. Let us treat the **satisfaction** <term>the act of making amends or providing restitution for a wrong</term> that must be made for fame and honor, things which hold the second place in value. Indeed, they are so lovable in themselves, and held in such high regard by many, that they seem even better to them than one’s very being and natural life. But those men who flourished in wisdom—whose understanding was enlightened and whose souls were free from presumption or passion—exalt honor and fame in such a way that they place them above all riches (following Holy Scripture in this), yet below and at the feet of life itself. It is to life that they give the ultimate primacy. These men I followed, as was right, in the previous section, and I shall follow them in the remainder of this work.

To proceed with total clarity in this matter, it is necessary to know where fame and honor reside and what they consist of, so that it may be known when they are stolen or damaged, and how they must be restored. A man’s fame is the opinion and credit held of him by those who know him. It is the reputation he has in the town or in the kingdom, and it properly and principally consists in being held as good or bad, as virtuous or vicious. **Good fame** is when one has good credit regarding virtue; and **bad fame**, or **infamy** <note>original: "infamia," referring to a total loss of reputation or legal standing</note>, which is the same thing, is when one is considered to have bad habits and vices. In this lies the best and most substantial part of fame; the rest is accessory and accidental. 

Namely: to be held as ignorant or wise, as a rustic or a courtier, as simple or as shrewd and astute, as noble and illustrious or as a plebeian and commoner, as rich or as poor. Because these are qualities which—though they are commonly held, some as good and honorable and their opposites as bad and vile—no one ever achieved true fame with these alone. ...virtuous man, since honor is by its nature the reward of virtue, from which good opinion and credit are born. For many years now, either through our ignorance or malice, these two have become estranged; we give great honor to those who have a very ruinous **fame**. But to explain now how far we have wandered from the true path, and since when and where we went astray, would be to depart from our main purpose. I will not fail to say that this abuse of ours arose because men, not recognizing the internal goodness of each person in order to honor it, applied honor to social stations and worldly pomp—which are visible and perceivable by the senses—in order to make honor certain and firm. This was, perhaps, a wise choice at the time, because usually no one was raised to high dignity except those most outstanding in virtue. But for nearly a thousand years now, all of this has ceased, and of that which was good, healthy, and clean, only this remains: that the offices of the <term>commonwealth</term> <note>original: "republica," referring to the organized body of the state or public interest</note> are honored, both ecclesiastical and secular. 

But as natural law is so firm and stable that it is never revoked no matter how much it is broken, nor does custom ever override it, there is always the strictest obligation to honor virtue (as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> says) wherever it clearly appears; and not to do so is an injustice. Following virtue, one must honor dignity and public office: the prelates, the princes, and the ministers of both, according to their rank and order, whether they be just or unjust. And at times, even when one is lying, one does not fall into the obligation of restitution. Generally, when a person is already infamous and it is not known that they have reformed, but rather they persevere in the same vice, it is not "defamation" to speak of it. Even if the speaker lies this particular time about the person doing the deed, it is considered an **idle or jocose lie**, not a **pernicious one** <note>Theologians of this era categorized lies: "jocose" lies were told for fun, "idle" or "officious" lies were told for some minor benefit, and "pernicious" lies were told to harm someone. They are already so hopeless in their moral illnesses that no one—at least until now—expects any good from them. 

However, if he or she had already begun to amend their ways and had shown signs of it, and they were to slip once more, it is necessary not to "put your foot on them" by exposing it. To do so would be to discourage them, and would consequently be a grave crime. But for the former group, no one is burdened with the debt of restitution for what is said about them "on that same key." This is because no new good reputation is stolen from them, as they had already lost it all beforehand on that particular point. 

On the other hand, if one speaks and publishes a *different* crime regarding someone already infamous for one vice, it is to drag them through the mud, adding sin to sin and giving them a worse name than they had before. But if he is stubborn, and even if I reveal them he will either not believe me or, if he does believe me, he will not desist from what he has started, it is not just to harm the one person without benefiting the other. In all these cases, and many other similar ones, restitution has no place. This is not because reputation is not often lost, but because sometimes it is just that it be lost, and other times (as we have seen), if it is a misdeed...

...doing so, one does not break the law of justice, but rather of charity, by which the offender is excused from retracting, or from compensating and making satisfaction <note>In this context, "satisfaction" refers to the formal process of making amends for a sin or legal wrong.</note>.

### Concerning What Restitution Requires

...admitting clearly that he lied about it. And if it should be necessary to take an oath that he did not speak the truth then, nor is he telling a lie now, he must do so; such an oath will be considered meritorious <note>In religious law, a "meritorious oath" is one that is considered a virtuous act because it serves the cause of justice and truth.</note>. This is something very rarely seen, as we often make poor use of such a great good as the truth. 

Furthermore, one must not retract the lie only once, or only before those who first heard it, but many times, and before everyone for whom it might be necessary. Since the ultimate goal of all this is for the victim to recover their lost reputation, and since the offender's false testimony was spread so many times, the offender must recant as many times as is required so that the injured party is compensated and restored to their former standing and public opinion. 

It often happens that a person lies at first before only four or five people, but each of those five tells it to more than a hundred others, and from each of those hundred, seven more find out—following the fable of the Hydra of Hercules <note>original: "Hydria de Hercules." The author likely refers to the Lernaean Hydra, the mythological monster that grew two new heads for every one that was cut off. Here, it serves as a metaphor for how gossip multiplies uncontrollably.</note>—so that within a single month, the entire town knows. If, at the time of demonstrating the innocence of the wronged party, the slanderer were to recant only once, it would never be established as a fact, nor would the retraction reach everyone’s ears; thus, the evil done would not be undone. It might also happen that the original listeners have died or moved away. Therefore, the most accurate and certain rule for fulfilling one's obligation—which is to return a person’s reputation to them in full—is to recant as many times as necessary, and to suffer shame many times over in exchange for the one time he acted so shamelessly to the harm of his neighbor.

This rule applies unless the slandered person and the slanderer are of such unequal status—such as a king and a vassal, or a prelate <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop.</note> and a subject—which we shall discuss in the following chapter. 

If one defamed another by speaking the truth—meaning the person had indeed committed a sin, but it was a secret one—the only possible <term>restitution</term> <note>Restitution here refers to the moral duty to repair the damage done to someone's "fama" (reputation), even if the damaging information was factually true but shared unlawfully.</note> is to speak all possible good of the injured party from that moment forward. One must honor him and stand up for his honor, undoing and annihilating the rumors and reports circulating about him. The slanderer can achieve this by pointing out how often people are prone to lying in similar cases, adding that perhaps more is being said than is actually true, along with other observations...
