### Of Reputation 154

<margin>
St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 62, article 2: "If, however, someone out of a lighthearted spirit, or without a necessary cause, utters a word so grave that it notably harms someone's reputation—especially in matters pertaining to the honesty of their life—this, by the very nature of the words, constitutes a mortal sin."
</margin>

...[matters] in this tone, but spoken in such a manner that it is clearly seen that he speaks in earnest—not mocking or winking an eye, but weeping in his heart for the harm he did—working both in public and in secret to maintain the other person's good reputation. And if the person’s reputation has already fallen completely, he must work to lift them up from the ground, even if he cannot fully set them upright again. It is not necessary for him to retract the truth (for he would be lying to deny the truth). To do what a man ought, it is not fitting to do what he cannot and should not: namely, to lie and offend God.

It must be understood that whoever defames another, in one way or another, often causes two types of harm through their slander. The first is general: depriving the person of their good name and esteem. The second is that the <term>infamy<note>In this context, "infamy" refers to the public loss of reputation or legal standing.</note></term> acts as an obstacle to obtaining some worldly benefit that they might have otherwise achieved had the speaker remained silent; or the defamation causes them to suffer some actual loss. 

In this regard, two situations are treated equally: whether the gossiper speaks the truth or a lie in their <term>detraction<note>original: "murmuración". In theological ethics, detraction is the sin of revealing another person's real faults without a valid reason, thereby damaging their reputation.</note></term>, they must pay for any worldly harm that follows from it—whether it be <term>actual loss<note>original: "daño emergente." A legal term referring to a direct loss or expense someone incurs because of an injury or act.</note></term> or <term>lost profit<note>original: "lucro cessante." A legal term for the income or gains that a person was prevented from making due to the harmful act.</note></term>. 

If someone says thoughtlessly, "Such-a-woman is an adulteress," and the husband <note>original: "el paciente" (the sufferer), referring here to the person who hears and is affected by the news.</note>, believing it, seeks revenge, the one who maliciously revealed it is obligated to pay for the harm and evil that comes to the woman or the husband, regardless of whether the claim was true or false. Likewise, if by revealing a defect one prevents another from receiving a high rank, a royal office, or some favor they would have received had the speaker not gossiped, it is entirely reasonable that the speaker restore all this benefit to them. As the saying goes, it was "nearly snatched from their hands"—for even if they did not possess it at that moment, they almost did. 

It is true, however, that because of this "almost," and because the achievement of that office could have been blocked in many other ways, the restitution does not have to be so complete that a portion—sometimes a large portion—is not deducted, especially...

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion on the restitution of reputation, specifically focusing on cases where gossip or "murmuring" causes tangible loss, such as being passed over for a prestigious office or being drawn into a violent conflict.</meta>

# He Who Requests Restitution

<margin>If anyone by words diminishes the reputation of another, unless it is for some good purpose and with the proper circumstances observed, he commits detraction. St. Thomas Aquinas, as cited above. <note>original Latin: "Si quis verbis diminuat famam alterius præter aliquod bonum debitis circũstãtijs obseruationẽ detrahit. S. Tho. vbi supra."</note></margin>
...especially if the loss is so great that it cannot be repaid. If someone's gossip prevented another from obtaining a bishopric or a governorship, there is no amount of wealth sufficient to compensate for that value. It cannot be appraised in general terms; instead, it must be left to wise and discreet persons to assess and moderate the damages each time such a thing occurs. Nothing more can be said here, other than that he who caused temporal harm to his neighbor through his <term>murmuring<note>original: "murmuracion"; in this context, it refers to gossip, slander, or speaking ill of someone behind their back.</note></term> is obligated to make satisfaction. This is understood to apply when he spoke with bad intent, with the purpose of preventing the other from being given the dignity or office—and in short (as they say) against justice: not at the proper time or for a proper reason, nor to the proper person.

I say "with bad intent." Because if, moved by good zeal, a person prudently reveals the defects of someone who is truly unworthy—with the intention that these defects be known so the benefice or office is not granted to them, since they do not deserve it—we have already said this is very lawful and a work of charity, especially when one is asked for their opinion. Also, it is permissible if he says it to prevent some evil, advising his friends and relatives about the character and bad habits of certain persons whose company might harm them. 

But it is very important to note that if he reveals something without considering or remembering the harm that might result—if it was clear and manifest that harm would follow once the matter was revealed—he is just as obligated to make satisfaction as if he had revealed it knowingly and with malice. For in such matters, he ought to have noticed and considered the consequences. If he reveals an adultery, or says, "So-and-so says of you that you are a <term>Hebrew<note>During the Spanish Inquisition, accusing someone of being a Jew or a "Mahometan" (Muslim) was not just a social insult but a legal accusation that could lead to trial, loss of property, or death.</note></term>, or a Mahometan, or another fault of this kind"—which is a most manifest occasion for a quarrel—it is no good excuse to say, "I did not think he would take it so to heart," or "It didn't occur to me," or "I never imagined such a misfortune." He could, and should, have anticipated and imagined it. 

Thus, one becomes responsible for everything just by speaking. Because words often harm more than fistfights. But if he did not intend the harm, and some harm followed later that was far outside the common course of events, or through a thousand other detours and causes, he shall be excused.

### CHAPTER . X . HOW ONE MUST RESTORE another's reputation, with the loss of one's own, but not of life. And particularly, regarding those who make defamatory libels, or accuse, or testify falsely.

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut initial 'L' with a floral and acanthus leaf design within a square border.</image-desc>

**FIRST, IT OFFERS** itself to treat how necessary it is to keep these rules, and how much effort and work one must put into fulfilling them. It is asked: if a person retracts their words to restore another's reputation, and by doing so they themselves become <term>infamous<note>original: "infame"; someone who has lost their legal standing or social honor due to a public crime or shameful act.</note></term>, are they still obliged to restore it with such detriment to themselves? I answer that one must look at and weigh the quality of the persons: whether they are equals—two Princes, two Knights, two Citizens—or at least not very unequal, such as a squire compared to a laborer, or a merchant, and even also an official. If they are equal, or not very unequal, there is no doubt that he is obliged to take back what he said; and if from this there should come to him any **diminishment** <note>original: "mēgua" (mengua); a reduction in social status or honor.</note>, let him take the blame and let it be a lesson for another day. If this inconvenience were to be considered, reputation would never be restored...

On this point there is no doubt: one must suffer and endure any evil lesser than death to spare it for someone who does not deserve it; whether, by revealing oneself, one must face public shame, have teeth removed <note>Physical mutilation was a common punishment for perjury or libel in the 16th century, intended to mark the offender for life.</note>, or be exiled. And as I say, most serious authors obligate the accuser to put himself at risk, so that the innocent may never be shamed again.

Cajetan, *Opuscula*, 16, response 9. Adrian, *Quodlibetal Questions*, 11, question 1. Soto, *On Justice and Law*, Book 5, Question 10, Article 2. Silvestro, "Detraction," paragraph 4. Scotus on this matter, 4, distinction 15, question 4. Cajetan on the *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 73, article 2. Soto, *On Justice and Law*, Book 4, Question 6, Article 3, response 4. **The fourth way of defaming, which is as pernicious as it is common.** <note>original Latin: "quartus modus infamandi tanto perniciosior quanto usitatior."</note>

...if they were known; in this case they were not known. There are two customs among men, not only scrupulous but pernicious and hateful. The first and most common—especially among women <note>The author reflects the common gender prejudices of the era, associating gossip specifically with women's social circles.</note>—is that with this excuse, "I did not see it, but I heard it said," they publish the secret faults of another. And with this "hearing it said," the miserable patient <note>meaning the victim or the person being talked about.</note> goes about, being defamed from mouth to mouth, and is left dragged through the mud in the opinion of all. There is no one who says "I saw it"; everyone says they heard it. 

In this way many sin who think they are in a state of grace, yet they are in great disgrace with God for having wronged their neighbor in their conversation and visits. And since they take such broad license to sin in this kind of **detraction** <note>original: "murmuracion"; in this context, it refers specifically to the sin of spreading truths or rumors that damage someone's reputation.</note>, I believe they must think that by saying "I heard it, I did not see it," there is no sin, nor any need for **restitution** <note>the moral requirement to give back what was taken, in this case, a person's good name.</note>. Because with that excuse they say, without any scruple, everything they heard—and may it please God that it was not something they themselves imagined. 

But they ought to take heed: for he who affirms what he saw sins in saying it—for no other reason than that by saying it, he defames him. Therefore, if they also defame him, and the same effect follows, how shall they not sin? Even if they say "I heard it," if saying "I heard it" is enough to defame him. And those who presume to be religious and devout must watch how they speak, for at times the **evil tongue** <note>original: "mala lengua"; a common biblical and moral metaphor for malicious speech.</note> harms more than the evil deed. 

In this species of gossip, those who first divulged the crime under that title of "hearing it" sin gravely. The second are those who followed and imitated them, and so on in their order for the rest—except for the last ones, who came to say it when it was already known to everyone. And the restitution required is greater than we think. 

One must take heed of the following: First, if what they heard is true or not. If it is a lie, it is clear that they are obligated to return his honor and credit to him. If it is true that they were told it, one must consider if he heard it from some boy, or a person held to be a gossip and a liar. To affirm it afterward, having heard it from such people, is a great fault...

...therefore, although he may say, "I heard it," he should act as if he had not heard it at all. Secondly, if he does not believe the rumor, it is a great pity that he defames the other with his words regarding what he himself considers a lie. To determine the requirements for restitution, one must distinguish whether the person was defamed by a judge’s sentence, or if it was merely evil tongues spreading the burning poison that stings their honor. If he was legally condemned for some shameful crime, it is not a sin of restitution to speak of it, regardless of where in the world it is told. The law gives permission for such matters to be published and divulged.

And in whatever particular penalty a judge condemns someone, there is mixed in—as a common and universal penalty—the loss of reputation. Thus, the law judges as infamous all those who are corporally punished for criminal causes.

<meta>This page continues the legal and moral discussion regarding the restoration of a person's reputation. It specifically addresses the nature of judicial punishment and the ethics of spreading news about a person’s public shaming.</meta>

->...being accused.<-

And in truth, the true and primary punishment for a human being is not the whip, the amputation of a hand, or the loss of one's head, but rather the stripping away of their reputation and honor. Because to die, to be wounded, or to feel pain is common and natural to every animal. But to feel shame, and to possess honor and a good name, is proper and unique to man as a rational being. For this reason, the most rational—and indeed the most irreproachable and justified—penalty is to deprive him of his standing and credit. To this end, it is ordered and commanded that wrongdoers should not be punished in prisons, nor at night, but that they be led through the public streets on the days when there is the greatest crowd of people, so that they might experience greater shame and dishonor.

Therefore, one does not rob them of their reputation anew by recounting their crime in other places, since they have already been deprived of it by the law—provided that one does not recount a different story, nor add a single jot <note>original: "jota," meaning the smallest detail or letter</note> to what happened. To speak of different crimes, other than those for which they were punished, would be to do them a grievance, as they might still hold a good reputation in those other matters. It does not follow that if someone tripped or slipped into one pit, they must necessarily fall into them all. If a person did one evil deed, one should not immediately believe, or speak, every possible evil of them. Thus, while divulging the judicial infamy <term>infamy: a loss of legal standing or "civil death" resulting from a criminal conviction</term> that someone suffered here to people elsewhere is not an act of injustice requiring restitution, it could still be a sin against charity in two cases.

<margin>

This appears clear and evident if we turn our consideration to the past. If a murderer fulfills his obligation by restoring a life through money <note>The author refers to the historical legal practice of "blood money" or "wergild," where a killer paid a financial settlement to the victim's family to satisfy the debt of the crime.</note>, how much more will he who stole someone's reputation <term>reputation: "fama," referring to one's social standing and public honor, which was a legally protected asset</term> fulfill his obligation? And sometimes there is no other better way to fulfill it. 

For if someone persuaded his friend to defame his enemy, whereby he takes upon himself the burden of the infamy that follows for the third party, which he cannot restore by revealing the plot—as that would be to defame the actor <note>the "actor" here is the friend who performed the defamation at the speaker's request</note>—he has no other means but to pay, if only in coin. And sometimes, even if he could restore the same reputation, he fulfills his duty with money in the case that the defamed person is a private individual and is satisfied with it. And if the person is satisfied, it is in the defendant's discretion to exit his obligation either by recanting or by paying out.

Many other cases are usually proposed in this matter. For example: whether one could defame himself by raising some testimony, especially under torture, or by revealing his own faults; or if, defamed by another, he could forgive the injury; along with two thousand other cases of this kind. But as our intent is to treat only of those cases where restitution is required, it is not necessary to determine these. Because in none of them—whether they are done lawfully or unlawfully in common course—is there satisfaction. In the cases proposed and resolved, I believe it has been said concisely how and when a person is obliged to return the reputation which he unjustly and violently stole, although in the final chapter we must treat of many who, even if they do not defame someone themselves, do not prevent the defamation when they are able, or (what is worse) persuade or command that one be defamed.

# How it is restored

...neither more nor less, there follows this horrible confusion that we see with our own eyes, and Wisdom <note>Likely referring to the personification of Wisdom in the biblical books of Proverbs or Sirach</note> weeps and mourns—namely, that the wicked are exalted, the virtuous are cast down, the wise are commanded, and the ignorant govern. In short, we do exactly what Solomon himself asks—wondering how it can be done—when he says: "Who will honor him who dishonors himself?" <note>referencing Sirach 10:29: "Who will justify him that sinneth against his own soul? and who will honour him that dishonoureth his own life?"</note> Thus, very few, or none at all, follow virtue or the labors of *good letters* <note>meaning the study of literature, philosophy, and the liberal arts</note>, except for those that serve to earn a living, which are the lowest and least noble among them. Because they do not see or expect honor from studying the primary sciences, but only poverty and abasement, from which everyone flees.

So it is of the highest importance that the prince and governor honors human graces and gifts with the utmost attention, each one according to what he deserves, and applies great rigor so that his subjects do the same. For it is the most certain means and the easiest plan to kindle virtue in the people, and to preserve them in order and governance <term>Governance: original "policia," referring to the civilized administration and orderly conduct of a city or state</term>, if they have it, or to establish it if they do not. That which there is no hope of reaching, nor seems possible to achieve—which is that rectitude and ancient truth of our ancestors, and that wise and prudent simplicity of our progenitors that we read about and praise in their histories—could very easily be revived now in our times if our leaders would follow this rule with even moderate care. Whatever they honor and esteem, the people would immediately follow.

For as the Gospel says: "Where the body is, there the eagles will gather," <note>A reference to Matthew 24:28 or Luke 17:37, here used metaphorically to mean that people flock to wherever rewards and status are found</note> and where the governor leans, there the citizens run. How infallible and certain that celebrated sentence of Wisdom shows itself to be in this teaching: "As the prince is, so usually are his vassals and ministers." At the very least, without exception, as he is, so is the harmony and order of his republic. ### Of Restitution

We are now set to emerge from this labyrinth into which we have entered—the matter of **restitution**. This obligation is usually incurred by usurping those external and bodily goods that are so loved and sought after: states, towns, or cities; dignities, <term>prebends <note>A stipend or portion of revenue granted to a member of a cathedral or collegiate church</note></term>, and benefits; public offices, gold, and silver; houses, inherited lands, <term>entailed estates <note>Spanish: *mayorazgos*; property restricted by law to a specific line of succession, usually the eldest son</note></term>, rents, tributes, harvests, fruits of the earth, slaves, livestock (both large and small), jewelry, ornaments, and clothing. Finally, all assets, both real and movable. For no property is possessed with such security that it is not at risk of being lost, even during one's lifetime.

In this matter, it is difficult to write about and resolve every case, doubt, and difficulty found within it. This is partly because the subject is inherently broad and extensive, and partly because it is obscure and tangled due to the great deceits that are practiced and mixed into it. I consider it a mark of great skill to write with brevity and clarity, especially when writing for persons whose intellects have not been enlightened by the precepts and teachings of **philosophy**.

I confess for my own part that, looking at the magnitude and subtlety of the subject, I did not find it as arduous and laborious to strike upon and determine the truth of it as I did to treat the whole matter and each part on its own with clarity, resolution, and conciseness. Not only must one say what is certain and true, but one must do so with a style that is understood and does not cloud the mind of the reader. And since we have so much to deal with in this section, it is only right that we spare ourselves from that which neither our intention nor this <term>Opuscule <note>A minor work or small book</note></term> demands.

Our profession here is to declare in which cases a man incurs the obligation to restore property, and by what means he must do so. Thus, we are not speaking directly of lawful contracts, nor of the equity and justice that must be observed for them to be valid, but rather of **unjust and illicit** acts where one's neighbor is aggrieved and harmed in his <term>estate <note>Spanish: *hazienda*; refers to a person's total wealth, property, or assets</note></term>. We shall discuss how the damage received must be compensated and satisfied. Thus, we are primarily teaching how to undo evils, rather than how to

St. Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologiae* II-II, question 62, article 4: A person is harmed in two ways: in one way, because that which they actually possessed is taken from them, and this harm must always be restored according to an equal compensation; in another way, they are harmed when they are prevented from obtaining what they were in the process of acquiring.

There are two ways one takes what belongs to another. The first is by stealing it in person and with one's own hands, such that he is the principal actor—a category that also includes those who command the theft. For the masters are always the authors, while those who actually take it are their ministers. The second is when, though he does not steal himself, he advises another to do so, or persuades him, or acts as a third party or mediator, providing the plan and means by which it is carried out. We will treat the first group as principals, and later we will briefly touch upon the second.

Also, so that we may proceed with greater distinction and clarity, it should be noted that robbery and theft sometimes involve what is already the property of the aggrieved party, which they possessed and held—such as when a hundred ducats are stolen from someone’s chest, or their cloak is taken from them. At other times, the item is not yet actually theirs, but they have a right to it and are seeking it, and they would undoubtedly have obtained it if they had been left alone and not hindered. For example: burning someone’s field while it is in bloom or ripening is like stealing their wheat; for even though they do not have it stored in the granary yet, very little was lacking for them to have it. Likewise, when someone worthy and possessed of the required qualifications applies for a <term>benefice <note>A church office that provided the holder with a guaranteed income or "living"</note></term>, not giving it to them or preventing them from obtaining it is almost like stripping them of it. It is true they did not yet possess it, but they have such justice on their side that very little was missing for them to hold it. In this way, one is also wronged even in what...

# On Restitution

...[one] does not yet possess, if according to justice it is owed to them and they were soon to have it. Of these two modes or thefts, it is inherently more serious to take from someone, against reason, that which they have already acquired, rather than that which they merely seek to gain (even if they deserve it); it is worse to take what is in a person’s hands than what is only in their hope. Therefore, the order of our subject will be that, before all else <note>original: "ante omnia"</note>, we speak of those who take what another truly possessed; then, of those who, also acting as principals, deprive someone of what according to reason should have been given to them. Thirdly, we will speak of those who usually act as ministers, advisors, or third parties in both these cases—people so reckless and blind that, without putting almost anything in their own pockets, they become obligated to restore in full <note>original: "insolidum," a legal term meaning that each individual is liable for the entire amount of the debt or damage, regardless of their share of the profit</note> all the damage that has been done simply for helping to do it, which is a more than sufficient reason to obligate them to such restitution.

A person is a thief in two ways: either a secret one, who takes another's property stealthily without the owner seeing it; or a public and open one, who snatches it before their very eyes. This is the sin the philosophers call robbery <term>robbery: the original Spanish "rapiña" refers to theft by force, which was legally and morally distinguished from "hurto," or stealthy theft</term>, and it is much more serious than the first. This is because, in addition to the material loss, it adds a kind of contempt and violence. However, the laws divide both types of theft into five species. If the theft involves a sacred object or something consecrated for divine worship—altars, chalices, crosses, sets of vestments <term>ternos: a set of three matching vestments worn by the priest, deacon, and subdeacon during High Mass</term>, chasubles, altar fronts, hangings, images, books, or any other thing dedicated to the worship of God—even if it is currently in the home of a particular clergyman or a layperson, by the mere fact of being consecrated, it is sacrilege. Likewise, even if the item does not belong to the church but to some private ecclesiastical or lay person—as there are many who keep chapel furnishings in their homes—if any of these are stolen, it is sacrilege. For a chalice or ornament belonging to a private individual, if it is consecrated, is just as dedicated to divine worship as those kept in the sacristy. If one steals within a church, even if the object is secular <note>original: "prophana," referring to non-sacred or mundane objects like money or tools</note>, it is sacrilege. In such a way—

# On Temporal Goods

...ry, <note>The text completes the word "robbery" or "rapine" from the previous page.</note> so that for the robbery to be sacrilegious, it is necessary that either the stolen object or the place from which it is stolen be sacred. If one steals any goods from the commonwealth or the council—which are called the "private assets" <note>original: "proprios"</note> of the city or town, whether they be movable goods or real estate—this crime is called embezzlement <term>embezzlement: the original Latin term "peculiatus" refers specifically to the theft of public or state funds</term>. In this crime, the councilmen and officials of the commonwealth (or, what is the same, of the King) have frequent occasion to fall. These men collect and manage the state’s revenues; they sin if they appropriate any of them for themselves, or if they profit from them against justice by withholding them when the people or the prince have need of them, or by usurping some portion of them, thinking they can do so without being noticed. If one takes livestock grazing in the field—cows, sheep, or horses—it is called cattle-rustling <term>cattle-rustling: "abigeatus" in Latin, a specific legal category for the theft of livestock</term>. If one steals human beings, men or women, to sell them—a heinous wickedness—he is a kidnapper <term>kidnapper: the original "plagiario" refers to the Roman law "plagium," the crime of stealing or selling a free person as a slave</term>. If outside of these categories one steals other things, such as books, jewels, or tapestry, the act is called simply theft <note>original: "hurto"</note> and the one who does it a thief. This is not because the others are not also thieves, but because those acts have other specific names in the law that are more atrocious and ugly.

They must give it to its owner, or to his heirs if he should be dead, or to the poor if neither the one nor the others can be found or known. One must consider the quality of the debtor: whether they are a prominent person or a commoner and ordinary person, the amount of the debt, and the capacity of the creditor or their level of need. THE SECOND CASE IS, IF ONE HAS
Bought certain estates, or jewels, or clothing, or any saleable thing, and possesses it quietly and peacefully: what will he be obliged to do if he later finds that they belong to someone else? So that the resolution of this question may be better understood, it should be known that—considering the various occurrences and human affairs, and how temporal goods pass from hand to hand, disappearing many times and reappearing after many days have passed, having been bought and sold not a few times in the interim, only to be found at last in the power of someone who acquired them with good money—the laws agreed (in order to avoid lawsuits and insoluble, difficult cases, and to encourage and require men to guard their property with care and vigilance and to seek it out quickly when it is lost) to establish and ordain <term>prescription: a legal rule where a right or liability is created or extinguished by the passage of time</term> regarding property. This means adjudicating and granting the goods to the one who possesses them, even if they originally belonged to another, provided he has possessed them with <term>just title: a legal basis for possession, such as a valid purchase or inheritance</term> for a certain span of time that the laws specify. In this way, the original owner loses the ownership and lordship over them. # When he must make restitution

in one place, or if in several, for a period of four years. And if it should be immovable property <note>original: *rayzes*, literally "roots"; a common legal term for real estate or land</note>, ten years, or twenty if the owners are absent, these things remain his; he may possess them and dispose of them from then on as his own, with a good conscience. <term>For example</term> <note>original: *V.g.*, abbreviation for the Latin *Verbi gratia*</note>, a man inherited from his parents certain houses that they truly believed to be theirs, though they were not; and the son possesses them for ten or twenty years. If it should later appear that they belong to someone else, simply by having held them for all that continuous time under this just title of inheritance, and with a healthy conscience—believing they were his own until now—they remain his, and the original owner loses them. This is so to such an extent that neither in conscience nor in justice is the other person obligated to return them. Although, in truth, if the deceased held them with a bad conscience, the law says that the bad faith of the deceased harms the heir. But who shall prove this bad faith? <term>Also</term> <note>original: *Item*, a Latin term used to introduce a new point or example</note>, if someone bought a pitcher or a cup from a silversmith and holds it for three or four years, and after that time it is learned that it was stolen, there is no obligation to return it to its owner, because the ownership of the pitcher has been established by prescription. This law requires and asks for two conditions: the first is that the things be possessed for the full time declared, according to whether they are movables <note>personal belongings like jewelry or tools</note> or immovables, whether one person possesses them throughout or many possess them successively with a good title, holding them and believing them to be their own, as appears in the examples we provided. For this reason, a thief never acquires ownership by prescription, no matter how long he possesses the item, nor does the usurer, whose titles are unjust, nor the person who buys from a thief if he knows who he is or strongly suspects it. In this, silversmiths and second-hand clothes dealers <note>original: *ropauiejeros*; merchants who bought and sold used clothing, often a trade where stolen goods might circulate</note> often err, as they can see more or less that a piece might be stolen. <term>Also</term>, [this applies to] whoever acquired possession through an unjust legal sentence that he himself understands to be so. But if the time has not passed, he must return it to the owner, even if he loses the price he paid for it, as we shall soon declare. Regarding the **fruits** <note>In a legal and historical sense, "fruits" (*fructos*) refers to any natural or financial profit produced by an asset, such as crops from land, offspring from livestock, or interest and rent from investments.</note>, which it is also often necessary to restore, I say that anyone who held with a bad conscience any estates, or houses, or towns, or <term>annuities</term> <note>The original term *juros* refers to fixed annual payments, often state-funded debts or pensions common in early modern Spain.</note>—in short, **real estate** that naturally produces fruit and yields rent—either through a suspicious sale that he knew or probably believed belonged to others, or inherited from someone of ill repute who was suspected of holding it against reason and justice, such an heir or buyer must restore not only the principal, but also all its fruits and rents, deducting the costs, whether he has already spent and used those goods or still possesses them.

In such a way that if he possessed them for four or five years, he owes in conscience everything they yielded during that time, because it is established that they belong to someone else. And if he has worked and cared for the administration of it, such as if they were farming lands, he may <term>deduct</term> <note>The original Spanish *escalfar* means to subtract or offset expenses from a total sum.</note> the expenses from the total, but not what his labor deserved; for he chose to work where not only was it not appreciated, but where he was doing an injustice.

If he lived in the houses, he must pay what the rent would probably be worth. If they were orchards, olive groves, fields, and vineyards, and he provided his household with fruit, olives, wheat, and wine, he must pay for it all in full. This is understood to apply when the person who bought them knew for certain at the time of the sale that they were not the seller's, or at least, if it was not fully proven, there was already a strong suspicion, or a lawsuit was pending over it, and it was common knowledge that the other party had justice on their side. All these reasons, or any one of them, obligated him not to get involved nor buy it; and consequently, he never has secure or peaceful possession in conscience until the truth is determined and clearly established.

It is enough for the person being dispossessed <note>The author refers here to the good-faith possessor who is now losing the property.</note> that they are left with the obligation to maintain that lifestyle and toil for it, or, if they lack the strength to endure the cost, to step down from it and lower their status.

# When one must restore

Due to the formal requirements of the law, these rules are not understood in similar cases, nor is it always necessary to return the **fruits and rents** <note>In legal terms, "fruits" refers to the natural produce of the land (crops, offspring of livestock) or the income (rents) generated by property.</note>. Other rules must be followed, which we will set forth in the discourse of this work. We could provide one here that is brief, true, and universal: namely, that whenever a sale is "true" <note>Meaning the legal forms and signatures were correctly executed.</note>, even if it is unjust, by the rigor of justice, the **estate** <term>hazienda</term> yields fruit for the one who bought it until the contract is undone. This is because, in buying it, he became its true master, and it remains at his own risk. 

However, in this work, I have deliberately included very few of these so-called "universal rules." Firstly, because there is almost none without some exception; and secondly, because of how poorly greedy people, blinded by their own avarice, usually apply them to specific cases—the truth being that success or error consists entirely in how such rules are applied.

By these same rules, another very significant case is determined and resolved, which occurs not infrequently. A **colt** was stolen from a meadow; it is broken and trained in such a way that it turns out to be a fine horse, with a very graceful gait and stance, and a beautiful presence. It comes time to restore it at a point when it is worth much more, beyond comparison, than when it was stolen. Is it enough to restore what the colt was worth then, or everything it is worth and valued at now, having become a horse? 

Likewise, ten **bushels** <term>hanegas</term> <note>A Spanish unit of volume used for grain, roughly equivalent to 1.5 bushels.</note> of wheat were stolen when they were worth five **reals** <note>The *real* was a silver coin and a unit of currency in Spain.</note>, and now the price has risen to ten. The same applies to those who purchase something that improves many times over while in their possession and through their industry; when they finally have it in its state of perfection, the truth is discovered. What will they be obligated to restore? Because this case is obscure and often involves significant interests, I will endeavor to answer with distinction and clarity. First, we shall speak of those who acquired such goods with a **just title** and a good conscience, and then we shall move on to the others.

# What belongs to others

...[consumed] <note>The original Spanish text begins with the suffix "-caron," likely part of a word like *gastaron* (spent) or *consumieron* (consumed).</note> whether it was wheat, or barley, or clothes, they owe nothing to anyone, even if it later becomes known that the item belonged to another and that the person who sold it to them had stolen it. This is because they spent it in **good conscience**, and having already consumed it, no property belonging to another remains in their possession to be restored. If, however, they still have it in their power and possession, one must examine why it is worth more now than before. If the increase is solely due to the passage of time or because that specific type of clothing is now scarce—and not because they improved it through their own industry and skill—then the item belongs entirely to the first and true owner. 

For example: someone bought a hundred *fanegas* <term>hanegas; a unit of dry volume, about 55 liters</term> of wheat four months ago at three reals, and finds now that it is worth eight because it is a bad year. If it is discovered that this wheat had been taken from someone else's silos or granaries, all of it must be returned, whatever its current value, provided they still have that same wheat. But if they have already consumed it, even if they have other wheat in stock, they owe nothing for the reason stated above. The same applies if one bought a horse for a hundred ducats and it is now worth two hundred due to some accidental event—such as a war, which makes horses more valuable. In such a case, one must return the horse to its owner once it is proven to be theirs. 

But if the item bought or obtained is now worth more because of the work the possessor put into it, they may, in **conscience**, deduct everything that the estate has gained through their ingenuity, diligence, and skill, and restore less. The true owner will also be obligated to pay the possessor for these improvements if they want the property itself and are certain of the possessor's innocence. 

Let us provide an example. Someone bought a hundred *alanzadas* <term>alançadas; a unit of land area, roughly the amount a pair of oxen could plow in a day</term> of land that was entirely uncultivated, wild, and mountainous, or at least a large part of it. They clear the land and plant it as a **young vineyard** <term>majuelo</term> or with olive stakes, which makes it of much greater value than when they first acquired it. If it is later discovered to belong to another, and it was sold through either ignorance or malice, it is enough for the possessor to restore what the land was worth at the time the first master lost it. This is understood to be the rule in **conscience** <note>Meaning the moral or religious obligation (the "Internal Forum") rather than strictly the civil law.</note>; for if the case is brought before a judge, he will perhaps sentence adversely, judging according to the civil laws. # When one must restore property

[jud-]ges <note>The Spanish text begins with "zes," the suffix for *juezes* (judges).</note> rely on presumption and do not examine good or bad intentions as is done in confession. And thus, [a judge] will presume a theft was acquired in bad faith and will require that it be returned along with all its profits. What shall we say, then, if the item has not only failed to improve but, on the contrary, is worth less than it used to be? I respond that, speaking as we are of one who obtained it with **good title** <term>good title; a legal possession acquired in good faith, where the buyer believes the seller is the rightful owner</term>, it is enough that they return it in whatever condition it may be in. The same must be said of someone who purchased a horse or any other trainable animal and taught it fine skills; it is not right that a person who thought they were working on their own property should lose the value of their labor.

Speaking now of one who acquired it illicitly, either by stealing it or by buying it while knowing it was stolen: if they have already spent it (supposing they were goods consumed through use and service), they must pay not only what they were worth at the time of the theft but also the damages caused to the owner by the theft. For perhaps the owner was keeping the items for a time when they would be worth more. This potential profit must be satisfied. The same must be done if they have already sold the items. But if they still have the item in their possession, no matter how much it has been improved or how much more it is worth—whether the increase was due to their own **industry and skill** or through natural growth—they must return everything and lose all [their investment] because of their wickedness and malice. 

And even if they have made use of the item, they must pay for its labor and service. It is not just to benefit for free from another's property. And if the "piece" <note>original: "pieça"; in this period, this term often referred to a "piece" of property, including livestock or an enslaved person</note> has decreased in value or has died (supposing it was an enslaved person or livestock), even if the death was accidental and not their fault, it is just and reasonable that they pay for it simply because they stole it. For if they were at all at fault or negligent regarding the death, and it died due to their poor care, it is a most certain thing that they are obligated to pay for it in full. If the item still exists but is diminished—if it diminished through their negligence—it is at their expense. But if they do everything possible to remedy the situation, the **confessor** may decide what seems merciful to him, [considering...]

[...or damaged,] considering the quality and gravity of their fault.

To conclude and perfectly close this question, I believe only one doubt remains. If someone, purchasing from a thief or from any other person some kind of clothing in good faith and innocence <note>original: "con simplicidad, y virtud"</note>, were to sell it to another, and afterwards it were discovered to whom it had belonged and from whom it was taken, what must this middleman do—he who neither took the property from anyone nor currently possesses it?

Here (as is clear) we are no longer discussing the person who either stole it or bought it knowing it was stolen. We have already stated how much those individuals are obligated to make restitution. Instead, we speak of those who bought it while being deceived. My sound advice is: if he is a man of honor, let him speak quickly to the one who bought it from him, making him aware of the truth and offering to undo the sale so the item may be returned to its owner. For if he remains silent, and the wronged party finds out who has his property (as is to be expected), he will demand it, and the buyer will respond, "I bought it from so-and-so," about whom—at least at that moment—nothing good will be suspected.

If he does not follow my advice, his strict obligation <term>mere obligation; a term in moral theology referring to the minimum requirement to avoid sin, as opposed to a recommendation for higher virtue</term> is to be prepared, when the other person returns the clothing to its master, to return the price he received. This is because his initial sale was not actually valid <note>In this period of law, one could not legally transfer ownership of a stolen item, even if the sale was made in good faith</note>, even though his ignorance excuses him from sin. He might respond to this by saying that he obtained it in the same way and was himself deceived, but it is not right that he should deceive others just as he was deceived. Rather, recognizing (as he must) that the one who sold it to him did him a wrong—if the seller knew what he was doing—or at least, if the seller was ignorant, that he must now make amends upon finding out, he must convince that person to do the same with his own buyer and merchant.

He is also obligated to spare him from all harm, trouble, and costs. For instance, if a lawsuit is brought against the buyer regarding the recovery of the item, and the buyer defends himself and "spends and suffers" <note>original: "gasta y lasta"; a traditional legal idiom referring to paying court costs and enduring the financial damages of a trial</note> in the process, the one who sold it to him is certainly obligated (if the truth is clear to him) to reveal the truth and spare him all that toil, labor, and expense, and to undo the sale. And if he remains silent and allows him to suffer the loss, he incurs the obligation to pay for it.

THE THIRD case concerns what one destroys or acquires in war, either by oneself or through one’s agents <term>ministers; in this context, subordinates or officials carrying out orders</term>, such as burning fields, looting places, or capturing men—specifically when and to what extent one is obligated to satisfy the damage done. In this section, we must necessarily speak of three types of persons. The first are those who initiate the war, publish it, and proclaim it, having the jurisdiction to wage it. The second are the captains and soldiers who pursue and continue the war until the end, which is victory. The third are the merchants who follow the army and are present at battles and lootings to sell their goods or to buy spoils and captives. These three different classes of people are those who commonly participate in these affairs and either succeed or err in them. 

Regarding the princes, kings, and emperors who initiate war as the primary authors—although there are many things to note and say regarding just wars <note>original: "justa bella"</note>—several reasons excuse me from touching upon them. First, these rulers possess scholars of all faculties whose advice and decrees they follow. When the substance and circumstances of the matter are considered, these advisors tell the rulers (at least, I should hope and it is right to think so) what is lawful and what can or should be done. Second, even if something could be said in general, there is no need even to point it out (as it is notorious). Namely: how heavily obligated these rulers remain if they initiate an unjust war—not for the sake of justice, but out of a desire for vengeance or an appetite for glory—to satisfy <term>restitution; the act of making amends or paying back for all deaths and damages caused</term> all the deaths, robberies, violence, damages, injuries, and wrongs

### On Restitution in War

A harmful crime, and deserving of capital punishment, is the great disorder and corruption of military discipline, disrespect, and insolence toward the captain when, once a city has surrendered, the army mutinies (as sometimes happens) because the general denied them the right to sack the city, and they enter by their own audacity alone, killing and stealing.

<margin>The art of war requires three things, namely: knowledge, strength, and practice. <note>original: "Ars bellica requirit tria scilicet scientiã, robur, & exercitium."</note></margin>
Aside from this ruinous behavior, there are certain "business dealings" of captains to be noted, which are certainly not becoming of their office and preeminence. They receive more pay from the paymasters and overseers than they have soldiers, inserting friends or their own servants at the time of the muster <note>The formal inspection and counting of troops</note> to fulfill the required number of their company, and taking their pay with a bad conscience. This is because that money is His Majesty’s property, which he does not give to you, but to the soldier whom he believes—based on your information and report—you have in his service. When the soldier is not there, it is stealing from the King; furthermore, you are unfaithful to him by not maintaining the number of soldiers that he thinks he has in the <term>tercios; the primary administrative and tactical units of the Spanish infantry during this period</term>, frontiers, and companies, from which some disaster might one day occur.

They are also responsible for the restitution of parts of the pay belonging to many whom they keep in their company. This occurs because they appoint sergeants and squad leaders, and distribute other honorable offices to their servants and relatives, not giving them their bonuses and wages in full, but only what they secretly agree upon with them. These captains have no jurisdiction nor authority to assess or shorten the wages and pay of military officers. In this, they err more gravely than they think, and incur more obligations of restitution than they imagine—and perhaps more than the value of what they distribute. First, it is to the ruin and damage of the entire army to distribute these offices to vile and most unworthy men, lacking in courage and prudence, just to save that small portion of money—which, in actual truth, they do not save. Beyond this, if the person he appointed was unworthy of the post, the captain must pay the King, not only what he kept for himself,

Augustine against the Manicheans. 23. q. 1. c. *quid culpatur*.
<note>original Latin: "uendi Aug contra Manicheos. 23. q. 1. c. quid culpatur." This refers to a famous passage in St. Augustine’s writings, later incorporated into Canon Law, which discusses what is actually blameworthy in war—not the act of killing itself, but the desire to harm, cruel revenge, and the lust for power.</note>

For example: someone sold three or four thousand **ducats** <note>A gold coin used across Europe as a standard of trade.</note> of cloth on credit, and added two hundred **escudos** <note>Another common gold or silver currency.</note> to the prices, which he keeps for three or four years before he can bring himself to return them. If he later wishes to be restored to grace and life, he must pay the two hundred with interest; it is not enough to return the principal, because the same sin he committed in taking them is found in retaining them and not restoring them so that their true owner may make use of them. Therefore, just as he became obligated to return them by usurping them, so too by withholding them is he obligated to satisfy the owner for what he ceased to earn with them. 

However, if he did not achieve this understanding nor realize the injustice, the quality of his ignorance must be examined. For there are persons who are ignorant of things they ought to have known or have forgotten—things so patent and manifest that even a child would not be ignorant of them—which certainly excuses them not a bit of guilt, much less of restitution. When giving exchange with excessive interest while seeing merchants in distress, there is no room to plead ignorance; nor is there in these **dry exchanges** <term>cambios secos: a predatory lending practice where a loan was disguised as a foreign currency exchange to bypass laws against usury (charging interest).</term>, which have always been so criticized. But if the ignorance is reasonable—of the kind <term>Theologians</term> call **invincible** <note>Ignorance that cannot be overcome by ordinary diligence, thus potentially excusing a person from sin.</note>—such as if he were ignorant of some subtlety of the law or some circumstance of the fact, and while ignorant he profited, thinking with a healthy conscience that it was lawful, it is enough that upon being disillusioned he pays back what he originally pocketed.

By this rule and distinction, **disguised usuries** must be judged. As we saw in the treatise on that subject, there are not a few species nor a few differences among them. If they were very obscure and hidden, they shall restore without delay what they gained from them. But if they were such that they were plain to see, and if they did not see them, it was not because they were well-covered but because the traders closed their eyes and wished to make themselves blind, it is necessary to return what they caused the other to lose in profit.

The Doctors of the Church agree: whoever has taken another's property wrongfully or for their own benefit is bound to restore it, even if they have lost it.
<note>original Latin: "Doctors qui cunq; rẽ alienã accepit injuriose vel ad sui vtilitatẽ tenetur restituere etiã si amiserit eã"</note>

There is this difference between those who possess another's things with a **just title** <note>A legal right to ownership, such as a fair purchase or inheritance.</note> or without one: he who holds something with a good title and conscience is free from restitution if the items are lost through no fault of his own or pass to a third party. Because the sea and its shores, and even the harvest of both (which are these things it produces), are—as the law says—common to everyone and for everyone. Whoever happens upon them, finding them without an owner, makes them their own. Likewise, all gold and silver mines that the earth and the heat of the Sun commonly engender are, by common law, the property of the one who discovers them.

# Of captains and soldiers.

...the treasure was not the property of anyone, nor does it have an owner, as we assume—and as its antiquity clearly shows. This is especially true if the treasure consisted of such currency, or if the coins were so shiny and clean, that it appeared to have been recently placed and hidden; in such a case, it does not belong absolutely to the finder until they perform the same due diligence as they would if they had found it on the earth's surface <note>The author is distinguishing between ancient "lost" treasure (which often belongs to the finder or the landowner) and recently hidden items, which are treated as lost property requiring an effort to find the original owner.</note>.

<margin>As seen in paragraph 8: although they were in someone's property, items like pebbles and gems found on the seashore are granted to the occupant; the same reasoning applies to treasures hidden underground for a long time, except that according to civil laws, one is required to give half to the owner of the land. St. Thomas [Aquinas], as cited above. <note>original Latin: "ut. parra. 8. Quāuūquā fuerūt in bo nis alicuius ut lapilli & gēmereper tæ in litore maris, occu pāti cōcedū tur & eadē ratio est de thesauris ā tiquotēpore subterra oc cultatis ni- si quod se- cundum le ges ciuiles tenetur da- re medietatem domino agri. S. Tho. vbi supra."</note></margin>
Regarding these prosperous findings, which the law says are favors that God grants to those who receive them, it is worth noting that in many places there are **positive laws** <term>leyes positiuas: man-made laws enacted by a government, as opposed to natural or divine laws</term> that, due to particular and good reasons that move the Princes, forbid and prohibit them. In some places, it is commanded that no one may fish for **Pearls**, except for a specific person to whom that privilege is granted; in others, that no one may search for **Amber** <note>original: "Ambar." In this context, it refers to ambergris, a valuable waxy substance produced by sperm whales, often found washed up on beaches and used in luxury perfumes.</note> on certain islands where whales often spawn or purge themselves; in others, that no one may work gold mines, and in others, not even silver mines. All these laws can be just and reasonable, and subjects are obliged to keep and fulfill them as they are understood. It is understood that judges should not consent to or permit these acts, but rather forbid them when they come to their attention, and punish the transgressor with such penalties—whether they be fines or the loss of rights.

For example, in **Fuerteventura** (one of the Canary Islands, which the ancients called the "Fortunate Isles"), a certain person holds a **privilege** <note>A legal grant or monopoly given by the crown to an individual.</note> stating that only he, and no other, may go out to search for Amber on the coast, under penalty of forfeiture. If others should go out and find it, they could lawfully take it <note>This suggests that while the person has a legal right to the find, the act of picking it up is not inherently "sinful," though it is legally risky.</note>, but the judge has the authority to seize it if he becomes aware of it, and he does the finder no wrong in doing so. The same applies to the fishing of pearls or fish: it is not the intention of Princes to bind the conscience of the people so that others may not fish at all, but rather that they do not do so publicly. This same exposition and interpretation applies to the law of **Treasures** that are found, the ruling of which is that if it...

This refers to a person's moral standing before God, as opposed to a legal standing in a public court.</note> and the law concerning treasures found in another’s field is not a penal law—which would require a judge’s sentence—but rather one establishing the ownership of things. Since the ownership of things is a matter of **positive law** <term>positive law: man-made laws enacted by a government or ruler</term>, therefore, where Imperial law holds force, the finder of a treasure...
<note>original Latin: "Inst. de rer. di. parr. thesauros. c. li. 10. de thesa. l. vnica. & l. nō intelligitur. ff. de jure fisci. parr. si inlocis. ...found in a meadow, or in a forest, or a communal mountain, or in one’s own houses or estates, it shall be theirs. If it was found in a vineyard, an orchard, or in a neighbor's house (so says the law), let it be seen and examined whether the person went there on purpose to seek and discover it. This will be easily inferred by the circumstances: whether they were going there to do, or were doing, something else and found it by chance; or if they sought it on purpose with the intention of finding treasure. If it was sought intentionally, the law says they shall lose everything, and it shall belong to the owner of the pasture or the estate. 

This law appears to be very ancient, and the Holy Gospel alludes to it in that parable of the merchant seeking pearls <note>The author here conflates two parables from Matthew 13: the Parable of the Hidden Treasure (v. 44) and the Parable of the Pearl of Great Price (v. 45-46).</note>. Finding one of incomparable price beneath the earth in another's territory, he covered it and, dissembling, sold all that he had to purchase the ground. He did this so that he might have the stone for himself with secure legal right, and so that the owner of the field where it lay would not claim it from him. From this, it clearly appears that this law is most ancient. 

However, if by chance while making a trench or digging a grave someone found it, the law says they shall split it in half with the owner. And it should be noted that it is the same whether one is the owner in property or in possession. The same calculation must be made regarding this treasure whether the land is one’s own property or if one possesses it through rental or **tribute** <term>tributo: a form of long-term lease or land tax where the occupant pays a fixed fee to the owner</term>, provided that the digging does not cause damage. 

In this way, if someone, while laboring, found some treasure in their sown field or in the orchard they hold from another by tribute, by civil law it is theirs. This law is most just and most holy, and it must be observed in the judicial forum <note>original Latin: "in foro judicial." This refers to the public legal system and courts.</note>. It is founded upon presumption, as are many others: for when one purposely seeks treasure in another's possession, the law presumes and judges it to be larceny and a type of theft. For this reason, the law requires that they lose everything, so that no one dares to trespass upon another's estate under the pretext of any title. If they found it by chance, the law commands for the sake of peace and equity that it be shared, and thus

These serious scholars have great probability and appearance of truth in what they say, because the law expressly determines it so—just as in <term>prescription</term><note>The legal principle of *prescripción* (usucaption), where ownership is gained through continuous possession over a set period.</note>, as we saw, it grants ownership of goods after three or four years of possession. Thus, in the case of a find, the law intends that after fourteen months have passed, the items remain with the finder. It is understood that this applies provided he has performed public, manifest, and sufficient efforts; for without them, the law gives him nothing. 

My opinion in this case consists of two points. The first is that either of these opinions is good and safe, and the finder can follow either of them with a clear conscience. And I suggest that most of the time, the second should be followed. The other point is that, in my judgment, no one acquires ownership or right in the find (according to conscience); rather, whenever the owner appears, one is obliged to return it to him. The law that says he may keep it, I always understand as meaning that the person who lost it no longer has a legal action from that point forward to request it before a judge. For if one lost something, he can also recover it through justice within a year and two months, but once the term has passed, he cannot demand it. # Of restitution in war.

These merchants have a most disordered condition and ordinance in their insurance: that no goods whatsoever be removed if there is a shipwreck. Thus, the sailors and owners let it all be lost so that the insurers might pay the full amount in cash.

Now, I do not meddle in examining this statute. I only say that whenever a ship is thus left and forsaken, this abandonment gives the right and full authority for anyone to enter, take, and profit from the best, and from all that they can. If ancient treasure belongs to him who finds it, it is because its antiquity is an evident sign of having no owner; and as a vacant and ownerless thing, it is granted to the first who finds and seizes it. And it is the same for a thing to have no master, or for the true master to give it up for lost and abandon it. For this reason, it shall belong to the first who enters it, like the <term>Behetria towns</term><note>Communities in medieval Castile that had the right to choose their own lord, often used here as a metaphor for things that are not subject to a fixed master.</note> in Spain. Thus, everyone may take possession of the goods which, though they could be salvaged, are abandoned; as in a thing that by that very act is left, it also ceases to have an owner, and consequently, he who takes it takes it from no one. Although the circumstances of the case must be weighed heavily, for a ship is not always given up as lost or abandoned just because it is forsaken. For if it is taking on water from a breach, or if it has caught fire, and the people jump into the boat, leaving the ship alone, for the benefit of...

# Of captains and soldiers.

<note>original: "Instit. de rer. diui. para. vlt..."</note> Institutes, on the division of things, final paragraph: another reason for those things that are thrown out for the purpose of lightening ships in a sea storm. And in the Digest, on the <term>Rhodian Law</term><note>Lex Rhodia: An ancient maritime legal code that governed Mediterranean trade, specifically addressing how cargo losses should be shared among the shipowner and merchants if goods were jettisoned to save the vessel.</note> regarding jettison: those who throw certain things out to lighten ships do not have this intent. ...the winds, it is not to give the goods up for lost, but rather to strive to escape with one's life. Therefore, if others from their convoy and fleet should arrive and, finding it lacking, should secure it, the property does not cease to belong to its original owners. Everyone knows this, and thus it is done when such a danger occurs. The certain sign of the abandonment we speak of is when they are able to provide aid and yet let it be lost. Aside from this, if in a storm they should <term>lighten</term><note>original: "alijassen"</note> the ship of any goods, even throwing them into the sea with their own hands and by their own will, it is not to give them up for lost, nor can they be taken by anyone who, coming behind, might find them upon the water. Nor if they fell overboard through carelessness. He who collects them among others is obliged to restore them, should the truth of the business come to his notice. Concerning this, the law of the kingdom says: "If a ship or galley, or any other vessel, should be in peril or be broken, we command that the ship and all things found from it be given to those neighbors to whom they belonged before the ship broke or was imperiled. And let no one be so bold as to take any part of them without license from their owners, if they can be found, or from the justice in their absence, with a registry. And let this same apply to the things that were thrown from the ship to lighten it, or that fell or were lost in any manner."

And <term>Cajetan</term><note>Thomas Cajetan (1469–1534), an influential Italian Dominican theologian. His writings were frequently cited in early modern Spanish legal and ethical debates.</note> says: the estate or goods of those who suffer shipwreck are not held, nor ought they to be judged, as abandoned or lost. The first part will be the primary focus here. What should one do who encounters some hidden theft, or some corsairs? ## CHAPTER XVI. ON THE GREAT OBLIGATION there is to fulfill promises, and on the restitution that is owed for not fulfilling them; regarding the rights of ministers of justice, Judges, Secretaries, and Notaries; and on Simony and the Office of the Huntsman.

<margin>St. Thomas, Summa Theologica II-II, question 88, throughout; Cajetan, ibid; Silvester, on contracts, paragraphs 3 & 4, and the word "promise" (pollicitatio); Digest, book 1, on agreements (de pactis); and in the Institutes, on verbal obligations, at the beginning, and book 1; and the law on agreements in the Digest, on promises (de pollicita).</margin>
THE SIXTH Case and question concerns the obligation that one incurs when promising something: whether one must always fulfill it. As a general rule, it is usually said:
> Every promise is a debt. <note>original: "Omne promissum est debitū."</note>
That is, any promised thing is as necessary to give as if it were already owed. The promise makes it a real debt, and it is an injustice not to give it. If there were no obligation to make a promise true through action, there would be no man who would trust or believe another; trade, credit, and the faith that exists—and must exist—among people would be lost. And if it is right to be faithful to man and keep one's word to him, how much more in accordance with reason it is to be faithful to God and keep the vows that man makes to Him. But speaking of human promises that people make to one another: <image-desc>Decorative initial capital E, featuring a woodcut illustration of two seated figures in a landscape context inside the frame of the letter.</image-desc>

The natural obligation <note>A legal and moral concept referring to a duty that arises from fairness or nature rather than just civil law.</note> resulting from these in the one who makes them is understood in this way: First, in matters of quantity and value, where fulfillment or failure to fulfill is significant. Such as promising a hundred ducats, or lending a thousand; marrying off one’s daughter; backing someone in their business dealings; or paying all or some of their debts. These are the promises that carry an inherent necessity to be fulfilled and carried out. Daily and common promises made out of courtesy or triviality—such as not leaving without saying goodbye, returning by St. John’s Day <note>June 24th, a common benchmark for seasonal contracts and social appointments in Early Modern Europe.</note> when the return is of no consequence, or sending the first...

The second requirement is that the man be free to promise and to fulfill it. He must have the liberty and permission to act and to speak. # On Obligation

<margin>
Promises are not to be kept if they are useless to the person to whom they were promised, or if they harm the promisor more than they benefit the recipient. Cicero, *On Duties*, book I. For who does not see that those promises should not be kept which someone made under the compulsion of fear or was deceived by fraud? (the same source).
<note>original Latin: "Nec promissa seruanda ea quae sunt his... non videt, ibidem." This refers to Cicero’s *De Officiis*, a foundational text for Renaissance ethics.</note>
</margin>

...ble. Fourth, if it were either impossible to do, or extremely difficult; for some people are so generous and powerful with their words that they promise things that exceed their own strength. The same applies if, due to some new occurrence, there is no longer a way to perform what was previously feasible. Also, if the promise is harmful, either to the person who promised or to the one who was promised. For example, if at the beginning it was—or was thought to be—useful and convenient, but is later seen to be harmful, or at least not at all profitable; provided that the "harm" is not simply the act of having to pay out or fulfill what was promised.

In all these cases, there is no obligation in the promise. Nor is there an obligation when the parties were previously friends and that friendship was the cause and root of the promise, but later the other person proves to be a traitor and performs bad deeds. It is not necessary to be very faithful to the unfaithful, nor to keep one's word to someone who violated and broke a good friendship. However, if the promisor were to break the word on his own part because he is seeking (as Wisdom says) an occasion to distance himself from the other, he remains obligated and bound to make true what he said.

Furthermore, any promise made under violence—made through fear or force—has no strength at all. It is of no value if one promises a thief one hundred <term>ducats: gold coins used as a standard currency</term> so that he might let him go freely on his way or leave his house. Unless he swears an oath on it, he is not obligated. Likewise, if a man promises to marry a woman because her brothers cornered him <note>The Spanish "tomaron entre puertas" literally means "took him between doors," implying they trapped or ambushed him in a confined space.</note> and threatened him with death, there is no necessity in conscience to marry, as long as there was nothing more to it than the promise itself.

Finally, it is required that the other party accept the promise. It is through their acceptance and consent that the obligation is perfected and finalized. But it is also necessary that they accept it at such a time that, according to custom and use, the promisor cannot reasonably back out. For if one promises a person one hundred <term>doblas: an Iberian gold coin</term> and they take too long to accept them, a time will come when the promisor can say "no" for himself. In all business matters, it is necessary not to lose the opportunity and the moment, especially when receiving favors. But

In that case, not only would the cause itself be bad, but the donation itself would be as well; thus, they would be excused by the third paragraph and condition mentioned earlier, where we said that no promise of a vice should be fulfilled, and in that instance, the act of giving would itself be a vice. In this matter, truly, there is more need to understand than to speak and explain.

Thus I say in general, that any person, whether man or woman, free or captive, who promises another some moderate little thing according to their status, is obligated to fulfill it, and the third party may also receive it.

However, the law gives him a <term>legal action<note>original: "action," a formal right to sue for recovery.</note></term> so that he can later demand what he paid out—though I believe it would be poorly thought of to use this license—but the other person, without being asked, is obligated in conscience to restore it to him. This is because they can neither keep it, nor could they even receive it. What reason is there for one to receive a price for ceasing to do what they were already obliged by justice to cease? And for doing what they ought to do anyway? This includes certain swindlers who, when they finally come to pay after a long time, ask the poor <term>creditor<note>The person to whom the money is owed.</note></term> for a gift of trout or some laborious service, as if they were doing them a favor by paying what they owe.

They can receive none of these things. And if they should receive them, they must return them. In short, any promise made to another to steer them away from some vice is valid. And it is necessary to fulfill it, although the other person does not always have the right to receive it, nor even less to keep it, if they should receive it.

## ->On Fulfilling Promises<-

<margin>
Law *generaliter*, Digest, regarding the obligation of words: we know generally that shameful stipulations are of no consequence. <note>original Latin: "L.genera. ff de verborũ obligatio, generaliter nouimus ſtipulationes turpes nullius eſſe momenti." There are other promises that fail on both sides and are invalid; namely, those made to the contrary of the aforementioned, intended to cause some vice against justice to be committed. For instance: to kill someone, to defame them, or for a judge to pronounce an unjust sentence. Or perhaps to be a false witness, to forge a document, or the gifts and bribes given to the ministers of justice. On this subject—which is broad and far-reaching—everything it touches is illicit, and everything promised is invalid. To give a salary or reward so that one may harm another or act as an evildoer is a thing against nature.

One of the natural principles we hold is that evils deserve punishment, not reward. Such a promise or donation is so hateful that, if it becomes known, justice rightly punishes both: the one who offered the price and the one who accepted it. All these services rendered to judges are great grievances and disservices done to the commonwealth <note>original: "republica," referring here to the state or the public good</note>. Reason does not permit such promises (if any should be made) to have the virtue or force to be binding. On the contrary, ministers are disqualified from receiving gifts, and litigants from offering them. Both parties—the one giving and the other accepting—commit a sin, though the ministers sin more gravely. They are obligated in conscience to return the gift immediately, without waiting for a judge or a **judicial review** <term>residencia<note>A formal audit and review of a public official's conduct at the end of their term of office, common in the Spanish Empire.</note></term> to command it. This is because the recipient acquires no more lordship or ownership over the gift than if they had stolen it. For the law not only forbids and prohibits them from taking anything, but it also disqualifies or makes it legally impossible for them to do so.

In such a way, even if they receive it, it is not truly received. **Nor does the act hold** <note>original Latin: "Neque factum tenet"</note>. This is like what is said of first cousins: no matter how much they marry or cohabit, they do not remain married if there is no dispensation, because they are incapable and unfit to contract [marriage]; in the same way, judges are unfit to receive [gifts].
