->### on fulfilling promises.<-

Greed reveals itself for what it is; it is clearly seen to be called "liberality" <note>In this context, *liberalidad* refers to the virtue of being generous or giving freely, which the author argues is being used as a mask for bribery.</note> when a legal process is transferred or dispatched with more diligence and speed than expected. To give a couple of **toſtones** <term>toſtones [silver coins worth four reales]</term> beyond the **official fee schedule** <term>aranzel [a government-regulated list of prices for legal services]</term> when there are many pages involved may seem like a reasonable show of gratitude. However, when a **judicial order** <term>prouiſion [a formal administrative or judicial decree]</term> must be dispatched—and even after it has been requested—if five are owed and twenty are given, to say that this is a "gift" is something they should only try to convince the convalescing or those entirely ignorant of legal practice.

They say: "I did not ask for it in words." This is true; but you asked for it, and even made it a necessity, through your actions. For if one does not grease your palm, the case would sit there and be eaten by lice before you would ever dispatch it. Knowing what **novices** <term>boçales [originally a term for newly arrived enslaved people who did not yet speak Spanish; here used to mean people inexperienced in the ways of the court]</term> and newcomers go through, they agree to negotiate like **street-smart experts** <term>ladinos [individuals fluent in the language and customs of the colonial system]</term> just to redeem themselves from such harassment. And so that everyone may understand how frivolous all these excuses and replies are, and so that they themselves may be convinced of their illicit acts, it will be convenient to insert here, word for word, the laws that they themselves profess and swear to keep when they are granted their offices.

In Title 5, Law 56: We command all **Judges**, **Presidents**, and **Appellate Judges** <term>oydores [literally "hearers," the senior judges of the Royal Audiencia]</term> of our Council and Chanceries, and the magistrates of the high courts, and the court magistrates, and the Judge of Vizcaya, and the magistrates of the nobility, notaries, reporters, chamber scribes, attorneys, prosecutors, nor any other scribes of the said courts: That from this day forward, they may not take nor receive for themselves, nor through intermediaries, any present or gift of any value whatsoever, nor things to eat or drink, nor other things of any value from any council, university, or person who currently has—or who it is likely will soon have—a **lawsuit** <term>pleyto [a civil or criminal legal dispute]</term>. Nor may they receive such things from those who have had a lawsuit before them during their term of office; nor can their wives or children receive them, in small or large quantities, **directly or indirectly** <note>original: *directe ni indirectamẽte*</note>.

# On Restitution

Neither the **Legal Counsel** <term>Letrados [university-trained lawyers]</term>, nor the **Advocates of the Poor** <term>Procuradores de los pobres [court-appointed representatives for those unable to afford legal fees]</term>, shall receive anything from the poor. # On Obligation

A man, by not doing it, would not be required to do it, either because it is difficult or because it is not necessary. For example <note>original: "V. g." (verbi gratia)</note>, if one promised a highwayman <term>salteador [a bandit or thief who robs travelers on the road]</term> that he would give him one hundred ducats <term>ducados [gold coins used as a standard currency in the Spanish Empire]</term> so that he might let him go free on his way: if there was nothing more than a promise, he is not obligated to fulfill it, as it was made under such necessity and violence. But if he swore an oath to him, he must pay him. Because the reverence owed to the divine name is of greater force. Thus, given that it is very arduous for a man to pay the legal penalty without being condemned to it by the judge—so much so that perhaps the common and universal law alone cannot compel him to do it—if he swears to it, he is obligated to fulfill it, because of the force and strict obligation with which he bound himself in swearing it. 

And this is true not only in the case of monetary penalties, but also if one swore to return to prison, or to another place, city, or kingdom where he was a captive. For instance, if a prisoner swore to the jailer <term>alcayde [a warden or governor of a prison or fortress]</term> that he would return in the morning, or at a certain time; or if a captive asked for permission to go to his own land and swore to his master to return. Both are obligated to return, even if one loses his liberty upon his return and the other loses his life, if he is imprisoned for a capital crime. How much more, then, will judges be obligated to make restitution or pay their penalty for breaking this law, if they take the oath according to its tenor.

Likewise, in Title 14, Law 2, it is commanded that the chamber scribes <term>escriuanos de camara [secretaries responsible for judicial records and court proceedings]</term> must swear to uphold their fee schedule <term>aranzel [a fixed list of official fees and taxes for legal services]</term>. This schedule is set down in Law 18 of the same title. It is modern, made and established by King Philip <note>King Philip II, who ascended the throne in 1556 and was known for centralizing the Spanish administration.</note>, who now reigns: the year 1556. This is so they cannot say that the laws are ancient. And in Title 20, Law 8, Lord Philip says: We command that neither the servants of the scribes, nor the officials, shall take rewards <term>albricias [traditionally, a gift given to one who brings good news, here used as an illegal tip for a favorable ruling]</term> for the sentences of the litigants, nor any other thing, even if they say it is given to them for the transcription of the sentence, under penalty of four times the amount. And the scribes who know of it, or understand that their servants are taking it, shall also pay four times the amount.

# On Obligation

The Schedule of Fees <term>Aranzel [a fixed list of legally permitted prices or taxes]</term> for the Scribes of the Chamber is located in Title 20, Law 40. It is quite modern; and that of the Public Scribes <term>Escriuanos [notaries or court clerks responsible for documentation and legal records]</term> is in Title 27. From all of this, our resolution is clearly shown. Namely, that they cannot carry off or receive more than their legal fees, nor does any reason remain that they might allege, nor any pretext they might give of "donations" or "presents" to cover their hidden robberies. For the law prohibits and forbids all of these, specifying them clearly. But because this resolution concerns what *should* justly be done, rather than what *is* done, let this section be about what is so unjustly practiced. This is the fact that these gentlemen who are officials of the courts <term>audiencias [high tribunals or courts of justice]</term> and seats of judgment live in a state of most obvious condemnation. Their father confessors—whom they seek out in the densest shadows of ignorance—absolve them without requiring restitution <term>restitucion [the moral and legal obligation to return stolen goods or illicit gains]</term>. Nevertheless, they do not cease to be obligated to make restitution in the same way we pointed out for hucksters <term>regatones [retailers or street vendors often accused of small-scale cheating]</term>, who little by little, through small overcharges, become burdened with the debt of great sums and quantities.

It is common, although very rare, for some of these ministers to also excuse themselves by saying that they have a license from their King to receive presents and favors <term>mercedes [grants, gifts, or honors bestowed by a superior]</term>. For this reason, it will be a useful and timely question to discuss whether a supreme prince can license them or grant them a dispensation to receive whatever people might give them; and if he can, what effect this license has and how far it extends.

The first sense of this question is whether it is appropriate to grant a dispensation from this law. I respond that such a dispensation is never appropriate or reasonable; rather, it is always prejudicial to many and scandalous to all. This is because it only serves the convenience of one—the official—and works to the detriment of all the litigants <term>negociantes [persons involved in lawsuits or legal business]</term>. It is a very poor decision to harm many to benefit one. What is intended by exempting him, other than enriching him with the property <term>hazienda [wealth, estate, or assets]</term> of the litigants?

This rightness is not maintained when receiving gifts. Therefore, whoever grants them license is, in their own degree and order, the cause of all the grievances they commit. Just as the one who lifts the gate that held back the water is the cause of the mill grinding, so also does the one who grants an exemption from this law—which prevented them—cause these injustices and grievances.

And just as a prince would sin by not establishing the laws necessary in his kingdom, so too does he sin who does not repeal those already established when they are still necessary, or who grants exemptions from them without cause. # On Fulfilling Promises

<header>->on fulfilling promises.<-</header>

...as is the custom, and as the law itself commands, they swear to uphold it. The question is whether a secular prince can grant a <term>dispensation [a formal exemption from a law or obligation]</term> to his official so that he may receive presents, even though the official has sworn—according to the tenor of the law—not to receive them. To understand the resolution of this matter, one must assume that there are two ways to swear an oath. The first is absolute: "I swear to God to keep this, or to do it, or not to break it." The second is to a specific person or community: "I swear to God to perform this business for you tomorrow as you ask." When one swears in this second manner, the other party can release them from their word and promise; once released, the oath is dissolved. But when one swears an absolute oath, they cannot be exempt from the obligation they undertook except by the authority of the <term>Pontiff [the Pope]</term>.

Second, it must be assumed that the ministers of whom we speak do not make their oath to the King. Instead, they swear absolutely to God and upon the holy Gospels to uphold this law. In truth, this oath is not made in favor of the King—to be sworn to him personally—but rather for the benefit of those conducting business and for private citizens.

Third, it must be assumed that an oath, according to <term>Divine Law [laws believed to be ordained by God, distinct from human-made laws]</term>, is such a strict obligation that no power on earth has the authority to relax or dispense it when it concerns a grave and necessary matter—especially one involving the utility of the <term>republic [the "res publica," or the common good of the state]</term>—unless just reasons and causes concur. Without these, any relaxation or dispensation is of no effect in one's conscience. Among theologians, these first and third assumptions are so certain and evident that they serve as infallible principles and foundations upon which many truths rest.

Given these assumptions, I say first that no Emperor can dispense or relax this oath once it has been made by his ministers. This is because granting a dispensation in this matter is a spiritual and ecclesiastical jurisdiction, just like the act of absolving one from...

# On the Obligation

<header>->on the obligation<-</header>

...sins in the <term>court of penance [the internal forum of confession and conscience]</term>. <note>original: "foro penitenciæ"</note> Second, I say that no <term>prelate [a high-ranking church official]</term> can licitly relax or grant a dispensation for this oath we are discussing. This is not because the supreme authority lacks the power to do so, but because just causes are necessary to exercise that power rightly. As far as I can reason now, such causes cannot be found in this case. Chiefly, this is because to grant a dispensation for an oath that causes harm to another party without their consent, great, extremely grave, and most urgent causes must coincide. To grant a dispensation in this matter is to cause harm to many—especially to all those engaged in lawsuits—and thus it can never be relaxed or dispensed with any safety of soul. From this, it is inferred that after the oath is taken according to the letter of the law, any license granted by the prince to receive presents is of no effect in one's conscience.

I imagine people will laugh to see with what diligence I write these rules for people who—I will not say with permission, but even without it—so openly break the <term>fee schedules [official lists of set prices for legal services]</term> <note>original: "aranzeles"</note> and receive presents, refusing to conduct any business without them. But those who laugh are those who do not know how profitable it is to write the truth clearly, even when no particular individual seems to benefit from it. Divine Majesty desires that His justice and equity be preached in every matter; thus, even if no one takes advantage of it, He is justified on the day He executes judgment upon those who, knowing the truth, did not obey or follow it. 

Furthermore, I am not so devoid of hope that I do not trust in His mercy; I expect that more than a few will benefit from this declaration of His justice. For in places where we least expect it, God has His chosen ones, who beneath steel armor wear the armor of virtue, and beneath rich brocade wear a rough <term>hairshirt [a garment of coarse animal hair worn against the skin as a self-imposed penance]</term>. <note>original: "cilicio"</note>

...right; the other is the cutting of wood in the forests of others, or hunting in enclosed and guarded woods, as if the wild beasts that are raised and graze there were protected maidens. This is a most singular vanity, which the whim of many madmen has introduced. Regarding <term>simony [the buying or selling of spiritual things or church offices]</term>, there is so much to say; and regarding hunting and forestry, there is so little to <term>restitute [to legally or morally restore what was taken]</term>, that it would be a just middle ground to remain silent on both extremes, since we have always followed the middle path here. This is especially true since simony usually involves people so well-educated that they have no need to look up their rights in these small treatises. 

However, we will very briefly point out what could be discussed in this matter, leaving it in general and broad terms, either for another place and language, or for another author. Simony is the selling of spiritual and divine things, which for many reasons are not for sale. First, because of their excellence and their value is so great that no human price can equal them; if they were sold, the sale would always be unjust, for less than the true value would be given. Second, and most importantly, because they are the goods and property of God—gifts and mercies that He created and distributed most liberally to the human race, as Saint Paul says. He desires that they also be distributed and shared for free, and communicated without envy. Because they are the property of another, whose Owner does not wish to sell them but to give them, no one who holds them as a <term>steward [mayordomo]</term> (and all who possess them do so in this way) can charge a price for them. 

Spiritual things are the graces of the Holy Spirit "given freely" <note>original: "gratis datas"</note>. As for those other graces that <term>justify [the process by which a person is made righteous in the eyes of God]</term>, it is madness to even think or speak of selling them. Justification, wisdom, understanding, piety, prudence, counsel, and fortitude cannot be transferred or communicated to another through human industry. Those which *can* be communicated are the gift and grace of preaching, the performing of miracles, healing the sick, raising the dead, and interpreting the scripture, along with others that the Apostle [Paul] lists...

# On Obligation

...ordered and given for the utility of the Church. Also considered spiritual goods are the ecclesiastical sacraments, which the Redeemer established and instituted, as well as ecclesiastical <term>benefits [offices that provided an income to the holder]</term>, such as bishoprics, dignities, and canonries, along with other prebends, whether simple or <term>curatas [offices involving the "cure of souls," or direct spiritual care of a parish]</term>. Furthermore, all things dedicated to divine worship are included insofar as they possess consecration: images, chalices, altars, and vestments. Although one may certainly sell the material they are made of—the gold, silver, brocade, or velvet—and the workmanship and labor, it is forbidden to charge more for them than the value of the material and labor simply because of their consecration. All these things are unsellable, and no price may be taken for them. It is called a "price" not only when there is an express agreement under the terms of "sale" and "purchase," but also when it is disguised and hidden, just as we previously described regarding <term>disguised usury [interest-bearing loans hidden behind other legal contracts to avoid religious bans]</term>. 

However, since our profession in these small treatises is to deal with profane and secular business, and having kept this rule inviolable until now, it is not appropriate to break it here at the end of the work. For this reason, it is suitable to leave the temple and head out to the fields, the forests, and the hunt. It is enough to have pointed out the vice of <term>simony [the sin of buying or selling sacred things]</term>, as it is understood among learned people.

### On Fulfilling Promises
<center>-> On fulfilling promises. <-</center>

...if it was at first very cleared and harvested, and the <term>commonweal [the community or public interest]</term> wishes to let it sprout and grow, so that it does not become bare and cease to be a woodland, I certainly consider it to be for the common good and utility. This obliges one in conscience to guard it, and I would not dare to cut firewood in such a place, at least in any quantity, no matter how secret it might be. If it should belong to some particular neighbor or a monastery, no one has permission to cut and steal from another’s estate, for perhaps its owner maintains himself by selling it, or holds it leased and subject to <term>tribute [a form of tax or rent]</term>. In the middle are the woodlands and forests enclosed by certain princes and lords, where hunting or the cutting of firewood is prohibited. It is a just thing to have respect and subjection to superiors, and it is also just that they have some places particularly designated for their recreation and relief, where they may unburden themselves from the many affairs of the people. But commonly they also place such a guard over it that it is enough, and it is not necessary for there to be an obligation in conscience not to enter and hunt, since they do it so without obligation, merely fulfilling it through the fear of the penalty. Finally, there are many things that it is right to do, though it is not a sin to fail to do them. If one looks to <term>natural law [universal moral principles thought to be inherent in nature]</term>, game was created for everyone, and thus the laws command that it is common property, and no one should hold as his own anything except what he might hunt or buy with his money. If someone should have a quantity of wild animals for breeding in his vineyards or estates, which had cost him his own money, it is not lawful to take them.

How will He not condemn the occupation of so much land for a single <term>hunting party [monteria]</term>? Secondly, regarding <term>restitution [restitucion - the moral obligation to repair a finished wrong]</term>, he is obligated to satisfy all the damage that the game animals cause to the fruits and neighboring harvests, especially if it is the reason that the people, having lost heart, stop sowing. One ought to take as much heed of this as one understands that the lesser folk have less permission to say it to him: let him not wait for our Master to come and say it to him with the rod of punishment in His hand.

<margin>
Saint Thomas Aquinas, *Summa Theologica* II-II, question 62, article 4, in its entirety; <note>original: "S. Tho. 22. q. 62. ar. 4 per totum"</note> Cajetan on the same. <note>original: "Caie. ibidem"</note>

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'H' set within a square woodcut border featuring floral and vine motifs.</image-desc>

HITHERTO we have dealt with the first part of this subject—or of this third part—which is the restitution that must be made by those who, acting as principals, have taken or deprived others of the wealth they actually possessed. In this second part, we must speak of those who also deprive others of that which, although not currently theirs, was very soon to be so, or at the very least, they held a right and justice for it to be theirs, and these people are the cause of them losing it. Here one can set down a general and clear rule, though I do not know if, because of its generality, it will be well understood, and it is this: Whoever has wronged his neighbor in this manner and form must restore as much as he took or hindered, according to how certain it was that it was to be his, and how close he was to having it. 

But its truth will be made manifest through examples. If someone burned a <term>sown field [sementera]</term> where a poor farmer had planted a hundred <term>hanegas [a unit of dry measure or the land required to sow it]</term>, which was already sprouting and heading, he certainly did him a greater wrong than if he had stolen the grain from the <term>granary [troxa]</term> or the <term>unthreshed heap [parua]</term>. He damaged him—or to speak more accurately, he took from him—almost all the wheat he hoped to harvest, according to how the year was progressing. And even if it had not yet produced grain, it had sprouted and was on its way to being harvested; thus, the person owes him more or less depending on how near and close the <term>harvest [cosecha]</term> was, and how certain the multiplication and increase of the crop appeared to be. If one were to destroy the entire fertile plain or all the boundaries of a village, so that no wheat, or very little, could be harvested—which causes the price to be high in that place—he is not only indebted to the farmers, but also to the <term>neighbors [vezinos - residents with full civic rights]</term>. # On the Restitution of Goods

...wise effect, such that even Aristotle, a pagan <note>original: "gentil"</note>, says that every sinner is ignorant. And since sin consists in man turning away from God, who is the highest good: what goodness of being, esteem, or value can remain to him, if he is without God? All that remains to him is dust and ashes, and therefore, he who remains in sin is not truly and morally wise, nor illustrious. Thus, in all these states, it is required that—both in public and in secret before God and men—he be virtuous, although the people cannot give testimony except of outward acts. These [virtues] must shine forth with such power, especially in prelates <term>prelate: a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop, who holds authority over others</term>, as heads of the Church (which is the spouse of Christ), that they invite and draw others toward virtue, being irreproachable in everything, as commanded by St. Paul, whom they succeed in office.

Following holiness, wisdom is required, which is the light; he must be a theologian, as the Catholic Church commands in its decrees and councils, for this is the proper science of bishops. Secondly, until now, the business still proceeds by election and presentation, even though much simony <term>simony: the illegal and sinful practice of buying or selling church offices or spiritual things</term> is mixed in. In short, the electors or those who present candidates are obliged in justice to choose the most worthy person, according to the quality of the benefice. And if there should be two who are equally rich in these true riches—which I have explained—one may licitly choose either.

If they are unequal, both being sufficient, but one more so than the other, there is a divine precept to give it to the one who has the known advantage. In doing the opposite—namely, placing it in the hands of the other who is not equal (even if he is sufficient)—the elector sins most gravely because of the injury done to the person who so superiorly deserved it. He also sins against the church and the people, for although he was able to give them such a fine minister and priest, he did not. It was a kind of infidelity, not being as faithful in their election or presentation as they should have been.

The unworthy man collects and spends them, but the electors are obligated to pay them back out of their own pockets. # Concerning the Restitution of Goods

Saint Thomas <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a foundational philosopher and theologian.</note> holds one view, and Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), another influential medieval theologian who often debated Thomas’s ideas.</note> another. Yet the truth is that this is not merely a matter of opinion, but a certain science, where there is no disagreement among the Church Fathers, but rather the highest conformity, as it is a manifest natural and eternal law. And so that these gentlemen might recognize their error, I will state briefly and clearly everything that all the theologians say on this matter. 

All agree that the patron or the elector is obligated under pain of **mortal sin** to choose the most worthy candidate. And so the holy Council of Trent <note>A major 16th-century council of the Catholic Church that addressed reform and defined church doctrine.</note> now determines and defines it. Thus, having named an adequate person, the elector does not fulfill his duty if there is another who is more worthy. 

Secondly, all agree that if he presents an unworthy person, he sins mortally and must restore nearly all the revenue the office earns. In these two points, there is no difference of opinion; no one contradicts it, no one doubts it, and everyone consents. Where there is a difference of opinion is in this: some say this restitution and satisfaction must be made to the church that was poorly provided for; and this is the view I follow here, and have followed, as it is most in accordance with reason. To others, it seems it should be made to those who, despite deserving the office, were not named. 

There is also an opinion that even when they choose a worthy person, if he is not the *most* worthy, the elector must also compensate the candidate for the grievance caused by not proposing and choosing him. I do not follow this, because it seems too rigorous; I follow that which everyone agrees upon, which are those two principal obligations. 

So it is a most thoroughly verified doctrine among all the <term>theologians: scholars of sacred scripture and doctrine</term> and <term>canonists: experts in church law</term>, without exception of any who are of name and account. For it is divine, eternal, and natural law, without exception or failure; nor can there be a dispensation from any living man, regardless of how supreme a station he holds (that is to say), that if the elector or patron names an unworthy person—especially for a <term>benefice with cure of souls: a church office, like a parish priest, responsible for the spiritual care of people</term>—he remains obligated in conscience to pay back the fruits and rents of the office, if, as I noted, he knew and understood his...

St. Thomas, II-II, question 62, article 1, reply 3.

In this way, it is not enough to say, "I thought he was worthy," or "they told me so," because saying "I thought so" provides no remedy afterward for either the people or the clergy. He was obligated to inquire—not superficially for the sake of ceremony with a few general questions—but very specifically into his life, customs, and scholarship. To be negligent in this investigation, if the candidate later proves useless, is the same as having chosen such a person on purpose. 

However, if after performing a full investigation, he should be deceived as any man might be, and the person who was thought to be skilled in the office turns out to be coarse and dull, there is neither sin nor restitution, nor is it a wonder that this should happen. For one of the final reasons that moved our Savior, according to Saint Thomas, to choose Judas Iscariot as an apostle—knowing how wicked he was to be—was to comfort future electors <note>Those responsible for choosing people for leadership roles.</note> if the person named should turn out very differently from what they expected. This holds as long as this failure in the chosen candidate did not arise from the elector's own evil and corrupt intention, or from his carelessness in gathering information at the beginning.

Regarding the one who confirms the choice, he is less obligated than the patron. This is because he trusts the patron and the report he provides, provided it is not evident to him that the chosen person is unworthy. He can and should confirm him; however, if the candidate's unworthiness were evident to him, he cannot and must not confer the dignity <note>In this context, a "dignity" is a high-ranking church office or benefice.</note> upon him. If he does grant it, he commits the same sin and incurs the same duty of restitution as the elector. Thus, the patron must choose the best person, while the confirmer may be content with one who is merely sufficient, as the law determines; otherwise, no election could ever be finalized. Furthermore, it is enough for the confirmer to have no knowledge that the candidate is unworthy. In this way, it is necessary for the elector to know the candidate's merits are the greatest, while for the Pontiff <note>Referring here to the Pope or a high-ranking prelate acting as the confirming authority.</note>, it is enough that he does not know of any demerits and that the patron assures him that the individual deserves it.

# Of Restitution in Matters of Property

And because the answer and resolution are almost the same, it will be appropriate for us to treat secular offices and dignities: viceroyalties, governments, presidencies, courts, councils, and mayoralties, along with the rest. These positions, which princes and lords of subjects distribute, are of two kinds. Some are officials of their private estate and household, such as treasurers, stewards, accountants, factors <note>A commercial agent or business manager.</note>, headwaiters, and chamberlains; these they may freely give to whomever they please. This is because in choosing correctly or erring, they act only to the benefit or harm of their own estate, of which they are the owners. This is provided they do not entrust them with any jurisdiction or the administration of justice, but only that they guard and spend their rents and treasures according to their instructions and warrants. For to make them executors of their decrees and mandates is to make them judges in some part, and then they fall under the following paragraph.

Others are offices of justice, such as those named above. Here it is worth noting that princes, kings, and emperors, when they accept or inherit the crown and dignity, obligate themselves in conscience to their people, towns, cities, provinces, and kingdoms to maintain them and administer justice to them, defend them from their public enemies, and hear their lawsuits, causes, and disputes. And because a prince cannot be present in every part of his lordship, he must appoint others to hear and sentence them according to law and reason. In such a way, in recompense for such great honor and so many millions <note>original: "cuentos de renta." A *cuento* was a term for one million maravedís, the currency of the time.</note> in revenue, he takes charge of this administration of justice. For this reason, he is obligated to appoint upright and severe judges. Failing to do so in this manner—instead distributing offices by whim and favor, rather than by merit—they remain obligated to make restitution for the damages and grievances that such unworthy governors may commit. And if a cross-examiner <term>pesquisidor</term> <note>A special judge commissioned to conduct a *pesquisa* or inquiry into specific crimes or administrative misconduct.</note> is sent who is quick-tempered, impulsive, biased, self-interested, and greedy, whatever injustice he may commit—whether against persons by punishing or insulting their honor, or by penalizing their purse—it is at the account of the prince, to re-

...to the injured party, restoring what is theirs. This is also a most certain doctrine, and one from which there is no dispensation, because it is not a law of emperors, but of God, to whom all supreme powers—even celestial ones—are subject. This is understood alongside the previously mentioned moderation and restriction (namely): if the ruler knew of the lack and inability of the person he appointed as a judge <note>original: "oydor." Literally a "hearer," a high-ranking judge in the Spanish legal system.</note> or magistrate, or if he failed to conduct the necessary inquiry to discover it. For certainly, giving these offices out indiscriminately to the most favored, or to those of the highest lineage, provides no excuse.

The first thing required in a man to be a fit minister of justice is goodness and virtue; it is impossible for a man of vice to administer it well, for vice will make him bend and twist a hundred times the staff <note>original: "vara." The wooden staff carried by officials as a symbol of their judicial authority.</note> that he carries. There is no law so clear that a corrupt mind cannot obscure and confound it. Nor is there greater blindness in an understanding than a disordered love—especially for pleasures or possessions—within the will, which immediately blinds it and covers the eyes of reason. An example of this is from the Psalm where David affirms that the fool <note>original: "incipiente," referring to the "insipiens" or the fool from Psalm 14</note> has said in his heart that there was no God. But if someone were to cut this sentence and say, "David says there is no God," they would be bearing a great false witness against him. 

In this manner, these men respond to their princes with half a truth, which truly and realistically is a pernicious lie for them. And ultimately, they respond to them in a way that they do not understand. For this reason, I resolved to do them the service of clarifying the response of their lawyers, so that they might understand how insufficiently they sometimes choose them. 

A work is illicit in one of two ways: either because it is evil in itself, which can be done in no way and under no circumstances; or because it is the cause of great evils and a clear occasion for many sins. ### That they are not yet possessed ###

...distinctions very well suited to this same subject, which occur to me now. For a man to know a woman who is not his own is, in itself, most illicit; there can be no respect, nor consideration, nor intention that could make it good. This is a most clear crime against the sixth commandment of the Decalogue: Thou shalt not commit fornication <note>original: "No fornicaras"</note>. This is because it is a most manifest occasion for great inconveniences, both interior (that is, bad thoughts and impulses) and exterior. Regarding this, according to St. Augustine, with just a look and being looked at, the fire of concupiscence <term>concupiscence: an intense desire or lust, particularly sexual, that overpowers rational thought</term> is kindled in a soul. In this manner, while fornication is an illicit straying in its very nature, loose conversation through words and hands among the unmarried is illicit because of the great spiritual and physical evils that almost continually follow from it.

It is now necessary to know that among the public offices of the Christian people, the ecclesiastical ones—such as bishoprics, canonries, dignities, along with other prebends <term>prebend: a portion of a cathedral's income granted to a clergyman</term>—are in themselves unsellable. No one can sell anything except their own estate. If one sells another’s property, the consent of the owner is necessary; without it, the sale is void. And as these benefits <term>benefices: permanent church appointments with guaranteed income</term> are the patrimony of Christ and His Church, which forbids with all rigor that they be sold—commanding instead that they be distributed for free among those who can worthily serve and administer them—no one can sell them. # On the restitution of goods #

...public and common, where they are sold: which is a mortal sin, commonly to sell them. Because a prince must strive so much for the common good of his **vassals**: that he sins gravely by doing things from which harm almost always follows. And he necessarily wrongs them (as **St. Thomas** <note>Reference to St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), a hugely influential philosopher and theologian whose *Summa Theologica* shaped Catholic views on law and ethics.</note> says) by giving royal offices of justice for money. Because where they are saleable, they are given to whoever gives the most, and most of the time, the one who deserves them least gives more for them, moved by his **ambition**. And since no account is taken of the excellence in merits, but rather of the money, the one who does not seek them to serve and benefit the **commonwealth** achieves them, but rather seeks his own **honor** and **utility**.

And since **justice** is so holy that no one can administer it except the righteous and holy: justice is not administered where offices are sold. Because it is administered very poorly. And to administer justice poorly is to **tyrannize**, it is to rob, it is to wrong, it is to wound the subjects in the soul and in the purse. **St. Augustine** says: if justice is set aside, what are great kingdoms but great robberies? <note>original: "Remota itaque iustitia, quid sunt regna nisi magna latrocinia?" from St. Augustine’s *City of God*.</note> Every evil can be feared and expected: and every evil will follow where public offices of governance are bartered.

Even when they are given by favor and blood <note>A reference to nepotism—giving jobs to relatives.</note>, and not by character and personal value (which are the gifts that **justice** asks for and the people need), great universal evils follow. What will happen where they are given for money, which is a thing more base than nobility and antiquity of **lineage**? Someone will say: "At least when it is sold to someone who deserves it, it will not be a sin." I respond that this is what we teach: and experience shows that out of a hundred times, it will not be sold to the worthy ten times, but rather to the unworthy. Men whose principal intent is to increase their wealth, improve their house, establish their children <note>Usually meaning to provide them with a dowry or a social position.</note>, and when for this it should be necessary to bend the rod <term>rod of justice: a physical staff carried by judges representing their authority; here used metaphorically for the law itself</term>, not only to bend it, but to break it into pieces. ### On Restitution of Property

<meta>catchword: war</meta>

...offices for that which has no price. Everyone asks what is being sold when these offices are sold, or what is being bought? If we look at the office itself, it is a post in which a man obliges himself to work, administering justice and enduring a thousand annoyances from subordinates. Is it not, then, contrary to reason to take money from a man simply so he may be obliged to work? Is it not enough that he obliges himself to be a common servant to all, losing sleep (as they are obliged to do) while thinking of the welfare and peace of all? Must he also purchase his own slavery? I do not mean his way out of it, but his very entry into it. 

Even serving the **commonwealth** <note>original: "republica," referring to the state or the public good.</note> at one’s own expense—**Saint Paul** asks who has ever done such a thing <note>Referring to 1 Corinthians 9:7: "Who serves as a soldier at his own expense?"</note>—how much worse is it to have to purchase the right to serve it? Furthermore, if one looks at the commonwealth or its prince who sells such offices, it also seems they cannot sell them, being themselves obliged to establish and distribute them. It is the obligation of a king to provide judges for a people to govern them with wisdom and hear their causes. How, then, can he sell what he is already obliged to give? 

To these arguments, everyone responds that the offices themselves are not being sold—not when considering the weight of their obligations (since, according to natural equity and universal custom, the commonwealth provides a public salary to the one who receives and administers them). For as the Gospel says, **the laborer is worthy of his hire** <note>original: "digno es el trabajador de su estipendio." A reference to Luke 10:7.</note>. 

Then what is being sold? They say it is the "excessive salary"—that is to say, when the annual salary and the daily profits of the office are substantial, exceeding what the labor deserves or at least what an honest livelihood requires. In such a case, the commonwealth can take for itself a portion of these revenues from its ministers. Just as the **Apostolic See** <note>The central administration of the Catholic Church in Rome.</note> can and does impose a certain pension on a **benefice** <term>benefice: a church office that provides an income</term> for itself or for others. This means taking away a part of the fruits—a fourth or a fifth—provided that a decent living remains for the one serving the **prebend** <term>prebend: the portion of the revenues of a cathedral or collegiate church granted to a canon</term>. In this same way, the commonwealth can also demand from its ministers some portion of the profits and annual salary. And this portion, which could be refer...

# Of Restitution in Property

...henna. <note>In this context, the author likely uses "henna" as a metaphor for something of negligible value, continuing from the list of minor salaries on the previous page.</note> In this category are sometimes the **dignities** <note>High-ranking offices within a cathedral or collegiate church.</note> who are the heads of **ecclesiastical chapters**, who have the power to propose and receive those nominated by superiors. All these people are prone to committing this crime, and they have a need to see this doctrine, which I will set out in three paragraphs for greater clarity.

<margin>He who, by hindering the honor of God or the utility of the Church, hinders an unworthy person, does not sin. St. Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Second Part of the Second Part, question 62, article 2, response 4.</margin>

Whoever hinders a **benefice** <term>benefice</term> <note>An ecclesiastical office that provides an income to its holder.</note> through their words or actions must look at the merits of the person being hindered or pursued to judge the good or evil they have done. If the person was **unfit** <note>original: "inhabil"</note>, there is no requirement for **restitution** <term>restitution</term> <note>The act of restoring something to its rightful owner or compensating for a loss.</note>, although one must take great care that their own ill-will does not deceive them into thinking a truly worthy person is unworthy. Therefore, a person should not judge the matter themselves when they feel they are acting out of passion, but should ask others who will judge more accurately. Ultimately, if the candidate truly lacked the necessary qualities, there is no obligation to make amends for taking the office away from them—especially if one was seeking it for someone who actually deserves it. In such a case, the person does what they ought to do, which is consistent with the law, and incurs no charge. Even if they used bad means to achieve their goal, such as telling certain lies, they might be required to restore the honor they took away, but they remain free of obligation regarding the office and its property.

If one took the office from a worthy and deserving person to give it to another who was equally qualified, and did so with sincerity by plainly stating their opinion, there is no obligation. However, if this involved bribes, pestering, illicit mediation, or false testimonies, there is certainly a sin. In that case, there might be a need for restitution—either of **reputation**, if it was damaged against justice, or of **property**, if the elector or patron had already decided to give it to the other person.

If one were to hinder someone who deserved the office without seeking it for another, they wrong that person by taking away what was rightfully theirs, because it clearly appears to be a bad intention and a bad act to prevent someone from obtaining what they deserve. ### On the Right of Regression and Resignation

...then admit him even if he be **unworthy**. Because I am not so much giving him the **benefice** <term>beneficio</term> <note>A church office, such as a parish or chaplaincy, which provided the holder with a guaranteed income from church lands or tithes.</note> as I am acquiring it for him under that condition or restriction. However, when someone who possesses their benefices petitions His Holiness for the **regression** <term>regresso</term> <note>A legal mechanism in canon law allowing a person to designate who will succeed them in an office, or to reserve the right to return to it.</note> of them to a certain person, they are obliged to propose a **worthy person**. This is because, in truth, to grant a regression is a form of **resignation**. 

The difference is that the former gives possession immediately, while the latter gives it to the other person after his own days <note>Meaning after the current holder's death or retirement.</note>. One distinction exists on this point between the one who **resigns** <term>resignante</term> and the one who grants **regression** <term>regressante</term>: this second person can more easily grant a regression—believing they will live a long time—to someone of a young age whose character and merits cannot yet be known for certain. In such a case, there is only a **pious hope** that the youth will become what he ought to be; and since the **prelate** <term>perlado</term> <note>A high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop or abbot.</note> grants it to the boy, there would be no doubt about it. 

However, one who resigns, having to give immediate possession, cannot make use of this long-term outlook without creating some kind of **monstrosity**, such as these "child-canons" and "child-beneficiaries" <note>The author is criticizing the corrupt practice of appointing young children to prestigious church positions to keep the income within a family.</note>. And it is very important to note that when granting a regression to someone of age who currently has **wicked habits** and already shows bad signs, the person proposing the regression cannot be excused by saying, "I believe he will mend his ways." The demerits he currently possesses carry more weight than the merits one merely hopes for. 

In these two cases of **resignation** and **regression** involving an **unworthy** <term>indigno</term> person—where it is evident that the one resigning or regressing commits a sin and must make **restitution**—it is a matter worth knowing whether they are obliged to resign or regress in favor of the *most* worthy person, or if it suffices that the candidate be **suitable** and **fit** for the office, even if there are others who deserve it more. 

In my poor judgment, it is enough to name one who is **well-deserving** <term>benemerito</term>. This is because the resigning beneficiary is not bound to the same level of loyalty and distribution as an **elector**. Thus, he fulfills his duty as long as he does no harm, which he achieves by resigning in favor of a good person; he would not be obligated to provide for the "best" candidate, as a **patron** <term>patron</term> <note>A person who has the legal right to nominate a candidate for a church office.</note> is obligated to do by virtue of his office.

### CHAPTER XVIII. ON HOW THOSE WHO ARE THIRD-PARTY CAUSES OF HARM MUST MAKE RESTITUTION, EVEN IF THEY DO NOT PROFIT FROM IT.

<margin>
Whoever consents to a sinner is burdened not by the sins of others but by his own; granting consent to the sin of another already makes that sin your own. <note>original: "Quisquis consentit peccatori, non alienis sed suis grauatur peccatis, concessio ad peccatum alterius peccatum jam tuum facit."</note> Psalm 1
</margin>
It is very natural for a man to help himself through the virtue and strength of another in his actions, and to admit him and take him on as a partner in them. It is also a very ancient custom for a person to gain or lose in such partnerships. This is because not only is what he does by himself imputed and attributed to him, but also what another does if he assists him; so much so that to judge who each person is, it is enough—according to our adage—to know who their companions are. And because, given that each person is defined by their works, one’s own works are also (according to Saint Augustine) those which a companion performs with one's consent. Even if he did not execute them with his own hands, he caused them by consenting that they be done by the hands of others. All this the most serene King David understood when he said, "with the holy you will be holy, and with the wicked, perverse," and when he supplicated God to forgive him even the "sins of others," wisely judging them as his own. For we often sin when others sin, whom we either helped to sin or to whom we gave scandal and a bad example. And if the offense and crime in which we concur with another is an act of injustice, we are not only partners in the guilt <term>culpa</term>, but also in the **restitution** <term>restitucion</term> <note>The legal and moral obligation to restore stolen goods or compensate for damages caused to another party.</note>, as we have exemplified in many parts of this **treatise** <term>opusculo</term> <note>Literally a "little work"; a short scholarly or instructional book.</note>. Thus, it is very famous in law and very common among doctors to note, when treating restitution, two types of people who usually incur it: some who, by their own person, cause harm and injury; and others who, through indirect paths, morally caused the injury. Of these latter people, we shall briefly treat in the first part of this final chapter; in the second part, we must teach at what time and with what speed one must return what is to be restored.

In one of five ways, a man commonly falls under the obligation to satisfy the evil that another did, or...

<margin>Sylvester, *Summa Summarum*, under "Restitution," volume 3, paragraphs 6 and 7.</margin>
This is a general rule: any judge who, against the law, condemns someone to corporal or pecuniary <note>financial</note> punishment, or orders someone to pay what is not owed, or to return what was lawfully possessed, or removes from possession the one who justly held it, is obliged in conscience to compensate the harm that the inferior suffers because of his sentence, or to return to him the good he lacks. Sentencing "against the law" is understood to occur when the judge breaks the substantial order of the legal process, or when he determines and defines the cause knowingly against the legitimate sense of the laws, whether he knows them or is ignorant of them. If he knows them, it is clear wickedness not to follow them. If he is ignorant of them, he is not without fault—regardless of how great his desire to be right may be—since, without the light of letters <note>meaning formal legal education or literacy in the law</note>, he dared to adjudicate the lawsuits <term>pleytos: legal disputes or trials</term> of others and, being blind, took upon himself the office of head and political guide. 

And in this matter, not knowing the laws is the same as having known them once but not studying them presently, nor constantly leafing through the books. This is because human memory is weak, and the distinctions and notations of the law are many. It is an easy thing for our human condition to forget and overlook—in three or four months without studying a specific title—three or four nuances <term>subtilezas: fine points of law or logic</term> upon which, perhaps, the resolution and clarity of the business currently being decided depended. By failing to look closely, they will err in their judgment, especially in difficult cases that fall outside the common course of things. I would greatly wish for these gentlemen <note>referring to judges and magistrates</note> to take notice of this at length (though it is said here in brief), understanding that they must not only give an account <term>residencia: a formal review or audit of an official’s conduct at the end of their term</term> to His Majesty—who cannot personally oversee all these defects—

# How they must make restitution
<meta>catchword: restitution</meta>

Saint Augustine in Letter 54 to Macedonius <note>Saint Augustine (354–430 AD) was a foundational Christian theologian; Letter 153/154 to the magistrate Macedonius discusses the ethics of legal advocacy and the forgiveness of sins.</note>. I spoke of <term>civil cases</term> <note>Lawsuits involving private disputes between individuals, such as property or inheritance, rather than crimes against the state.</note>, where the matter concerns either taking property away from the person who possesses it with justice, or not giving it to the one to whom it rightfully belongs. In such matters, if someone helps the party who contradicts justice—using apparent but false reasons, or citing texts poorly and interpreting them even worse—and a sentence is given in favor of their client, the lawyer remains obligated to restore not only the salary they received, but everything the other party lost. For through their advocacy, they were the cause of that loss.

And I truly believe that, speaking with those learned in this matter, it is enough to speak in these general terms, without further defining what we call an "unjust case." For there are two types of them: some where the injustice is clear and obvious—in these cases, our rule applies without exception—and the obligation to <term>make restitution</term> <note>The moral and legal requirement to restore what was taken or compensate for damages caused by an unjust action.</note> falls upon whoever defends them, and even more strictly upon the judge, if he passed sentence based on them.

There are other cases that are doubtful, either <term>in law</term> <note>original: "in jure"; referring to cases where the legal interpretation of the statutes is debated.</note> or <term>in fact</term> <note>original: "in facto"; referring to cases where the actual events or evidence are unclear.</note>, regarding whose truth and justice there are various opinions among scholars. In such lawsuits, a lawyer may lawfully represent any party, and it is not necessary (though it is the safest course) that his side always be the most probable one; it is enough that it has an absolute probability based on reasons and precedents, even if there are more effective or weightier ones for the opposing side. Any interpretation from legal commentators that is accepted among good scholars is sufficient.

To some, though to few, it seems a matter of glory—as this holy doctor says—to defend and advocate in illicit lawsuits, but it is not a glory that is sung at the end. Because it is false, vain, and not true. However, to defend and protect a defendant in <term>criminal cases</term> <note>Legal proceedings involving acts against the state or public order, often carrying physical or capital punishment.</note> who is guilty and deserves death—this is (as the law itself says) a glorious act for a lawyer as a man of letters, and a merciful work for a good Christian. For defending him to set him free, or to lighten his punishment, does not cause harm to anyone else and is beneficial to human nature. As much as we say, they are obliged to resti-

Into this pit fall the agents of **Cape Verde**, in the **trade of Black people**, when they do not perform the examination they ought to, investigating if the Black people are of <term>just war</term> <note>original: "buena guerra." This was a legal and theological requirement of the era, asserting that people could only be rightfully enslaved if they were captured during a "just war" rather than through kidnapping or illegal raids.</note>.

After this group, which is large, follow those who **participate in theft**. This happens in two ways: the first is by assisting in the act of stealing—giving advice, acting as backup, or "watching their backs," as they say, or receiving the thief in one's home and protecting him. In such cases, they are obligated to <term>restitution in solidum</term> <note>original: "in solidum"; a legal term meaning that each individual is responsible for the full amount of the debt or damage, not just a portion.</note>, even if they have taken only a small part of the proceeds. There are others who participate in the theft after it is done, who were either given the goods for free or in some other manner. For such people, it is enough to restore the part that fell to them or that they acquired. This difference arises because the first were guilty in the theft itself and participated in the act according to their rank and order, and consequently were obligated for the whole; the second participated only in what had been ill-gotten. Therefore, they fulfill their duty and give satisfaction by simply returning what they have.

The last are those who, being by office obligated to prevent evils, do not prevent them; and it is incomparably worse if they concur in them through dissimulation or by a "negative" presence. Among these are **parents** who do not restrain their children who are under their governance when they know they are walking in bad paths, or involve themselves in reprobate dealings, or cause damage to the property of others. For this reason, God rigorously punished **Eli**, the High Priest, who did not forbid or prohibit the wicked deeds they committed in the temple and among the people <note>Referring to the biblical story in 1 Samuel, where the High Priest Eli failed to discipline his sons, Hophni and Phinehas, for their corrupt behavior.</note>

...tion is a general duty of the prince: to maintain his subjects in peace and defend them from their enemies. And true enemies are the thieves and highwaymen on land, and the corsairs <note>original: "cosarios"</note> at sea. For he owed them by right and natural law this protection and support, with which they would have been safe. However, if he does all that he ought and can, and by chance or adverse fortune a robbery occurs, he is not bound to pay for it, because not everything is in the hands of men. And it should be noted that when the high authorities provide sufficient defense, whether by sea or by land, they fulfill their office; they place and transfer the obligation they held onto the captain-generals of the fleet, and onto the presidents and governors <term>corregidores</term> <note>Local administrative and judicial officials representing the Crown.</note> to whom they entrust it. In this rule are included those who elect and appoint as judges men who are unruly, greedy, biased, impulsive—in short, unworthy of the office and of governance. For all the grievances that such ministers commit against the subjects, the rulers are required in conscience to undo those harms using their own revenues and treasures. The same applies if, after they are elected and appointed, the rulers discover incompetence and inability in the administration of their charge, and yet they still tolerate them and leave them in power. The second is the time and the opportunity in which he must execute and put this intention into action. For this business is not only one of good desires and purposes, but of timely and suitable acts and deeds.

Regarding the first point, I say that every time it comes to memory what is owed, and that it is indeed owed, and one proposes and determines within himself not to pay, he sins. For in substance, it is to confirm oneself in the past ill will and in the sin committed. Which, besides being a new offense, is even somewhat more grave. ### Third causes of harm

If it is natural for us to set ourselves right, so in writing <note>original: "eſcriptura"; this can refer to sacred scripture or legal records</note> the evil is less reprehensible than its constancy and duration; and he who perseveres in the offense <term>offenſa</term> is much more culpable than he who offended in passing. And he who—having damaged the reputation or diminished the estate <term>haziẽda</term> <note>In this context, wealth, property, or a neighbor's livelihood.</note> of his neighbor—resolves in himself not to make equality or provide compensation, is "virtually" persevering in that harm. 

Therefore, the second general rule is that as soon as one is aware of the harm he did, he is obliged to resolve in his soul to satisfy the debt when he is able. And what some very speculative people say—that he may suspend the act <note>The "suspension of the act" refers to a theological debate about whether one can delay the mental intent to repay without committing a fresh sin.</note>—I do not consider to be a learned or serious resolution. Not because, perhaps, by suspending it he does not fulfill his duty, but because these metaphysical <term>methaphificales</term> subtleties are as difficult for plain people <note>original: "gente llana"; referring to common folk or those without formal theological training.</note> to understand as they are impossible to practice. 

And it will be, in my judgment, a miracle if any of them succeeds in such a suspension. The common and universal experience is that when one remembers some unjust sales or exchanges, he either rejoices in them or regrets his guilt. And therefore, our distinction is sufficient without adding more parts or members. 

In such a way that if we speak of the heart that a man who holds what belongs to another ought to have, it is necessary that he keep it good: that he be prepared and determined to pay when there is the possibility and opportunity. For to have "bad property" and "bad faith"—which is said when one possesses something badly and simultaneously has a bad will—is to be altogether and in everything bad. 

Regarding the interior of the soul, and what a man ought to want, it is to owe no one anything through an unjust title. Solon <note>Solon (c. 638–558 BC), the famous Athenian lawmaker known for his moral and political reforms.</note> used to say: *I would well like to have money, but not ill-gotten.* I add that he who acquires it badly is obliged to want to give it up. 

But it often happens that while desiring to restore <term>reſtituyrlos</term> them, either there is no occasion, or the possibility is lacking to put his desire into execution. The will <term>voluntad</term> is a very different thing from the work. There is no one who cannot "will," and there are many who cannot...

->### On how they must make restitution<-

...to carry out their will. Especially in this matter of restitution. Although in truth, a prompt restitution <note>original: "restitucion corta"; literally a "short" restitution, meaning one that happens quickly.</note> is more profitable to the poor creditor than a long-delayed intent <note>original: "voluntad larga"; referring to a person who has many good intentions but takes a long time to act on them.</note>. For this reason, it is necessary that we speak not only of the spirit and intent of the debtor <term>deudor</term>, but of his actual follow-through.

It is also a general rule: pay as soon as you are able. Because just as it was not right to usurp <term>vfurpar</term> <note>To take or use something that belongs to another without right.</note> what belongs to another, so it is not lawful to retain it. Everything is on one weight and scale—both the one and the other. That is, taking it and keeping it are both theft; an act that is at all times and in all nations condemned.

The delay that is permitted in such a matter is only that which is necessary to seek some hidden means, or to wait for an opportunity, if the restitution must be secret. It is right that if a man can keep his reputation and esteem whole and unharmed by paying through a third person, or by waiting for a less suspicious moment, he should wait twenty or thirty days. He should be allowed this time and not be so rushed that he loses more by making restitution than he gained by stealing.

Beyond this general obligation that always runs—to repay immediately—there are certain articles, or "narrow passages" <note>Critical circumstances where the moral stakes are higher.</note>, where the debt grows so much that it is a new sin <term>peccado</term> to let them pass without paying. The first is when the injured party is in such great need that he would almost count the payment as a gift, given how distressed he is; he would be completely or largely helped if he were repaid now. He who owes him must pay him immediately and not let him suffer. To fail to pay him at such a juncture is to do him a particular harm and injury. 

For while it is an offense at any time to deprive a man of his estate <term>hazienda</term> <note>This refers to a person's wealth, property, or means of living.</note>, it is a much greater offense to prevent him from using it in his time of need. Thus, to keep it from him then is a new malice on the part of the one who has usurped it and does not return it. This also applies to a lost reputation <term>fama</term> <note>In this period, "fama" or public honor was considered a form of property that could be "stolen" via slander and must be "restored."</note>. If an opportunity for business is offered to the defamed man, where he would have an advantage if his reputation were intact, the debtor is obliged...

->### Third causes of harm<-

<meta>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the identity of a thief.</meta>

...identified then the one who robbed them, and they must restore it to them, without delaying the restitution any longer, because delay in such a situation is a particular and notable grievance to the injured party.

The second article <note>A specific point or condition of moral law.</note> is when the debtor <term>deudor</term> currently has the means to fulfill his obligation, and believes he will likely lack them later—either because he is becoming overwhelmed by so many business affairs <term>negocios</term> that he will be continually short of funds, or because he does not know how his ongoing ventures will turn out. Such a person is obliged to pay before he spends or employs the money he currently holds. This is so that if he fails, he does not fail to make restitution; and so that if things go poorly for him, he alone bears the cost <note>original: "lo laste"; meaning to suffer the financial penalty or consequence oneself rather than letting the creditor suffer the loss.</note>.

Many argue against making restitution based on how much of their estate <term>hazienda</term> <note>Referring to one's total property, assets, or wealth.</note>, reputation, and esteem they will lose or diminish by doing so. Because they owe so much that it constitutes almost their entire possession, or a large part of it, they imagine they will be left naked and very poor if they pay. For this reason, it is common to assess and determine when and how much a man owes, even lowering himself from his social standing if necessary to make restitution. Everyone agrees on this resolution: if the wealth <term>caudal</term> <note>Capital or accumulated funds.</note> with which he maintains his splendor was ill-gotten—whether gained in peace, in war, or any part thereof—he is obliged to return it, even if he must leave his house and his vanities <note>original: "fantasía"; here referring to an ostentatious lifestyle or social pretensions.</note>. And this is not "losing" his status, but rather reclaiming his own proper and former state of poverty, which he had abandoned through illicit means and almost through betrayal. If a man, having enriched himself through thefts <term>hurtos</term>, robberies <term>robos</term>, usury <term>vsuras</term>, and currency exchange, and having dressed himself in fine cloth <note>original: "puesto en estofa"; a metaphor for achieving high social status or luxury.</note>, were excused from making restitution until he had traded and increased his wealth with someone else’s property, then being a "great thief" would be a true profit and benefit. It would be "good advice" to steal a great deal if, by stealing much, one could keep it, or use and profit from it for a longer time. On the contrary: as the debt is of a greater amount, there is an obligation to restore it more quickly, because it will be more missed by its owner. One must dismount <note>To "dismount" or "step down" from a high horse/social position.</note> and walk upon the ground...

## How they must make restitution

...to the level ground where they were, since without a sturdy ladder they climbed to the pinnacle of the temple <note>A biblical allusion to the Temptation of Christ, used here to describe someone who has risen to a high social position through pride or ill-gotten gains rather than merit.</note>. In this rule are included many people who, yesterday, neither were anyone nor had the merit to be so, because they were poor; yet in a few days, through sales and purchases—the nature of which they well know—and other dealings we all know about, they emerge like someone surfacing from a dive with fifty or a hundred thousand <term>escudos</term> <note>Gold or silver coins used in Spain and its colonies.</note> in movable and fixed assets. Others come from the Indies <term>Indias</term> <note>The Spanish Americas.</note>—at least they used to in times past—of whom I do not say that a tenth <note>original: "diezmo"; a religious tithe.</note> as the fruit of the land, or a fifth <note>original: "quinto"; the royal tax on silver and gold.</note> as silver, but rather half of what they bring is tied to the obligation of restitution. Others who, in public offices of government and judiciaries along with their ministers, believe they have not judged well if they do not leave a good income to their heirs—even though they would not have enough to spare if they had lived honestly.

If all these people are told to make restitution, they respond, "Am I to be left at the door?" <note>A phrase meaning to be left homeless or destitute.</note> If it were two hundred doubloons <term>doblas</term>, they would give them, but they say, "almost my entire substance belongs to another." Justice and reason say the opposite: If it were little, little would be lost in keeping it; but since it is much, it is a matter of great importance that they return it at once, as the saying goes. Thus, they cannot delay it if they wish to be prepared for death, nor can the prudent confessor <term>confeſſor</term> <note>A priest who hears a person's sins and determines if they can be forgiven.</note> overlook it, nor grant absolution in any way, if they do not first pay out. 

And let it not seem harsh to them to dismantle the wheel <note>A reference to the "Wheel of Fortune" or perhaps a peacock's display.</note> that they had built with artificial—and even false—feathers <note>An allusion to Aesop’s Fable of the bird wearing borrowed feathers to appear more beautiful than it is.</note>. Rather, it is shocking that men have ears and tolerate hearing that someone triumphs with another’s estate <term>hazienda</term>. Upon hearing such a thing, our ears ought to close to avoid hearing something so detestable. Let it not seem rigorous to us to command him to return it to its owner and cease to be a "personage" <note>original: "perſonage"; meaning to stop maintaining a high social facade or "character" played on a stage using stolen wealth.</note>. And it is very important to note that it is not within the liberty or discretion even of the confessor to absolve the debtor <term>deudor</term> if he does not restore, especially when it is a large amount, even if the debtor says he will restore it when he can. The confessor is obliged to inform himself of the status and capability of the penitent, and he (that is)...

### Third causes of the damage.

->Ee 3<-

...the priest is the one who must judge and verify whether the other person can or cannot pay immediately, rather than leaving it to the will and opinion of the debtor. And he <note>The priest, acting as a confessor.</note> must compel him to descend (if there be a need) into poverty by suspending the supernatural benefit of **absolution** <note>The formal forgiveness of sins granted by a priest, which in Catholic theology is necessary for a person in a state of mortal sin to return to God's grace.</note>. And let the priest not soften, nor let compassion move him upon seeing the man fall; rather, like a true doctor and father, let him release his hand and help him fall. Because to be exalted and to rise [through sin] is to destroy oneself, while to descend [into poverty] is to avoid falling into the abyss forever. Compassion should instead be felt for the true owners, who for so long have been dispossessed of what this man holds. This is what the **doctors** <note>Refers to the "Doctors of the Church," authoritative theological scholars such as St. Thomas Aquinas or St. Augustine.</note> understand: when a large part of the **estate** <term>hazienda</term> <note>A broad term for wealth, property, or a landed estate.</note> must be restored, and even more so when it is a small matter, he should restore it without delay and embrace poverty. 

But if all of it is someone else's—if it is public knowledge that it is not his, and it is known to whom it belongs—no one can hear his confession until he either actually pays or reaches an agreement with the **creditor** <note>The person to whom the money or property is legally and morally owed.</note>. For by granting him confession, a grave scandal would follow in the **Church** (as sometimes happens) upon seeing someone confess and receive communion while holding so much usurped property. If the matter is secret, the greatest mercy that the most pious wise men approve is not to oblige him to remain so naked <note>A metaphor for being totally destitute.</note> that he goes from door to door [begging]. Instead, out of three parts, he should restore two at once, and with the remaining part maintain himself poorly, paying the rest as he earns it. In this way, he should never be flush with money, nor grow his wealth, nor prosper until he is entirely free of the debt. And it is quite a **license** <note>A formal permission or relaxation of a strict rule.</note> to permit him not to beg when, according to reason, he ought to be begging.

This permission applies mainly when the creditors are not certain <note>Meaning the specific individuals who were robbed or defrauded cannot be identified.</note>, and the money must instead be distributed to the poor, in accordance with the previously mentioned documents. In such a case, it seems this **relaxation** <note>A technical term in canon law for the loosening of a strict requirement.</note> can be used, allowing him to keep some part of it to live as a poor man. For when the wronged party is known and recognized, it is a harsh thing to maintain oneself na-
