### How they must make restitution

...of the **estate** <term>hazienda</term> <note>A broad term for wealth, property, or assets.</note> of another. In the end, it is left to two or three elderly **theologians** <note>Scholars who study the nature of God and religious belief; in this context, they act as moral arbiters.</note> to designate and assess only what is deemed necessary for a simple life without luxury. For it is very much against reason and **natural law** <note>A system of right or justice held to be common to all humans and derived from nature rather than the rules of society.</note> that anyone should enjoy or profit from what is ill-gotten. I believe that, in fact, such gains are never truly enjoyed, no matter how deaf or stubborn one becomes. For either in his own life, or in that of his children, God ordains that he shall lose it where he least expects, even if he holds it in immovable property or **entailed estates** <term>mayorazgos</term> <note>A legal arrangement where an estate is kept intact and passed down to the eldest son to prevent the fragmentation of family wealth.</note>. For God uproots, changes, and transfers these things, because there is nothing of greater power—as the child **Daniel** <note>A reference to the biblical story of Daniel, often cited as a paragon of wisdom and justice even in youth.</note> said—than truth and justice, which in the end achieve their effect by making all things equal. Justice may indeed be delayed, but like the current of a river, it eventually breaks through with its invincible force; and when it breaks, there is no tower so firm that it does not topple.

The conclusion is that restitution must not be delayed because the amount is large, nor because one will be left poor, nor even to avoid losing the profits one used to make, nor to avoid losing the honor and status one had attained. Rather, one will regain their own natural state, which perhaps came to them by direct line from their ancestors. It is only just to defer payment when, by paying a little, one would lose a great deal. If two hundred **ducats** <note>A gold coin used as currency across Europe during this period.</note> are owed, and because of a scarcity of cash to gather them, one would have to lose a third of the value of their clothing, it stands to reason—provided the creditor is not in extreme or great need—that one may wait until they can be found without such great loss. With this permission, we include those conditions we set down in Chapter 7: that it was not necessary to make restitution at the cost of one's life.

What shall we say of those who do not wish to unburden themselves in life, despite knowing their great obligations, and instead save the unburdening for death by leaving it in their **will** <term>testamento</term>? Certainly, if one did not make restitution while living, it cannot be denied that they lived a very burdened life; and if death is usually as the life was, their death cannot help but be very heavy.

### Third causes of the harm

...and consequently painful. Any death, even a light and easy one, is horrible and frightening; how much more so is dying with a great burden of conscience. Furthermore, if one who owes money does not make **restitution** <term>restitución</term> <note>The act of returning something to its proper owner or making amends for a wrong.</note> and avoids his obligation to pay, how can he expect his **heirs** <term>herederos</term> to make restitution? And will the payment not seem even more grievous to them, given that they were not the cause of the harm?

It is very believable that he who intentionally delays restitution until his **will** <term>testamento</term> <note>A legal document expressing a person's wishes regarding their property after death.</note> neither made amends in life nor truly wants them to be satisfied in death. For it seems like madness to think that if the person who owes and is able to pay does not do so, the heirs must; for even though they may be legally obligated, their moral obligation is not founded on as many reasons as that of the original debtor. 

In short, one should feel about those who save their satisfaction for the clauses of a will exactly what the Saints feel about those who delay their conversion until death. Namely, that it is a very harmful decision to wait to convert in the midst of such mental confusion <note>The original "desacuerdo" implies the disorientation and loss of faculties common during the process of dying.</note>. Yet, when the point of death arrives, they do no wrong in turning back to God, even with their "soul between their teeth" <note>A traditional Spanish idiom for being at the very last gasp of life or the threshold of death.</note>, although according to **Saint Augustine** <note>A 4th-century theologian and philosopher whose writings were foundational to Western Christianity.</note>, there is no guarantee of their salvation.

Thus, he who could pay his **debts** <term>deudas</term> and did not, errs most gravely; it is not a new error, but a simple obligation, to declare them in the will. But no one can assure him that the amount will actually be satisfied. For it is very probable that, just as he did not wish to pay, his successors will wish to do so even less. THE LAWYER, OR attorney <term>procurador</term>, who in civil causes helps those who do not have justice on their side, must restore the damage that the opposing party receives. It discusses what unjust causes are, and whether he is obliged to follow the best opinion, there being disagreement among the doctors. 6. 18.

He who absconded <note>Referring to "alçarse," the act of hiding assets or oneself to avoid paying creditors</note> while being able to pay, sins, and is obligated to all the debts, and to the damages suffered by the creditors because of the extensions <term>esperas</term> they grant him: which in conscience he cannot enjoy, and much less if they forgave him any of the principal. But if he went bankrupt <note>original: "quebro"</note>, being unable to do more, he remains obligated to the principal, and may use the extensions.

An exchange from fair to fair <term>feria</term> <note>These fairs, such as those in Medina del Campo, were the primary international financial and trading hubs of the period</note> is conducted in two ways (that is to say): from fair to fair when both fairs are to be celebrated within the same town—in which case no interest may be charged—or in different towns, where a profit can almost never be made. 4. 8.

One who provided money for exchange <term>cambio</term> <note>refers to the purchase or sale of a bill of exchange</note>, suspecting it likely that the settlement <term>quitança</term> would not be fulfilled, cannot profit from that exchange if it was not actually carried out and the letter was returned; however, one who provided money with sincerity, truly thinking it would be fulfilled, and was later not paid, may take part of the initial interest, though not all of it. 4. 10.

How the first contract that existed among the human race was exchange. 4. 1.

How the Law of the Caesars <term>ley de los Cesares</term> <note>original: "ley de los Cesares"; refers to Roman Civil Law, specifically the concept of *laesio enormis*, which allowed a contract to be rescinded if the price was less than half the "just price"</note> is understood, which dictates that a contract should be undone when there was deceit involving more than half of the just price; here many beneficial resolutions are provided. 2. 10.

The just price in the sale of shipments in the Indies is the price set when the fleet <term>flota</term> arrives at the common deadlines; how much one sins in this type of sale, regarding the time for which credit is extended. 2. 17.

Two types of bills of exchange <term>cedulas de cambio</term> or settlements: some in the bank and others outside of it in cash. 4. 4.

Three conditions are required to justify an exchange: that it be true and not feigned, plain without deceit, and equal without injustice; these are explained at length. 4. 7.

It is not appropriate for a General Council <term>concilio general</term> <note>an ecumenical meeting of Church leaders, such as the Council of Trent</note> to deal with matters of exchange, nor should the money-changers wait for their resolution and decree, for that would be like waiting for the dead to be resurrected. 4. 11.

...serving me, it is sufficient that their equivalents are returned. 5. 5.

**The loan of the first kind** <note>original: *préstamo de la primera especie*; this refers to *commodatum*, where a specific, non-consumable item—like a tool or a horse—is lent and must be returned.</note> always remains the property of its original owner who lent it, but the loan of the second kind <note>original: *préstamo de la segunda especie*; this refers to *mutuum*, where consumable goods like grain or money are lent, ownership transfers to the borrower, and an equivalent amount is returned later.</note> is now the property of the one who received it on loan. 5. 5.

**If I sent a borrowed horse to its master** with a person of trust, and the messenger happened to take it for himself, I am released from the obligation to pay for it; but if it were money that I was returning and it was lost, the loss is mine. What is the cause of this difference? 5. 5. <note>In legal logic of the time, since the borrower "owns" the specific coins in a cash loan until they are handed back, the risk remains theirs until the transaction is complete.</note>

**Which am I more obligated to protect**: my own property, or that which has been lent to me and is in my possession? 5. 5.

**Regarding what was lent, if it is a thing of measure**, the same quantity must be returned, even if the price has changed. It discusses how payment should be made when it is not returned in the same kind, but in money: whether at the price it had when it was lent, or at the price it has when it is returned. 5. 5.

**The loan is an act of no price or value.** 5. 6. <note>This means a loan is, by definition, a gratuitous act of charity; charging for the act of lending itself was considered a moral failing.</note>

**Lending and doing good to others**, without regard for personal interest: the ancients called this a "work of kings," but we call it a "divine work." 5. 10.

**In order for a lender to receive something**, it is necessary that it be given to him freely, not for interest, and that he receives it as a favor and benefit, not as payment: if either of the parties has bad intentions toward the other <note>i.e., if they intend to hide an interest-bearing loan as a gift</note>, they can receive nothing. 5. 10.

**Giving money to vassals so that they produce salt**, or something else, while obligating them to sell it to the lender, is usury and injustice. 5. 9. <term>usury: The practice of making unethical or immoral monetary loans that unfairly enrich the lender, often by exploiting the borrower's need.</term>

**Lending to farmers**, obligating them to sell their sowings and harvests, even if it is for a fair price, is usury. 5. 9. <term>fair price: *justo precio*; the ethical value of a good as determined by common estimation and the public good, rather than price-gouging or forced sales.</term>

**A penalty may well be imposed on someone who does not pay** on time what is lent, and it may be collected if they fail to pay, provided it is a moderate penalty. 5. 4.

**The harshness that money changers exhibit** in demanding payment on the very day a debt falls due is highly reprehensible. 4. 10. <note>Money changers often acted as private bankers; the author criticizes their lack of mercy regarding deadlines.</note>

**How the secrets of religion**, whether sacred or secular, have never been shared with the common people. 4. 11.

**Whether it is necessary to risk one's life and reputation** in order to restore worldly goods. 6. 13.

**Goods thrown into the sea** to lighten a ship do not belong to whoever might find them. 6. 15. <note>original: *alijar*; this refers to the maritime practice of jettisoning cargo to save a ship during a storm. The law protected the original owners' rights to such property.</note>

**Those who resign a church office** in favor of a specific individual are obliged to propose a worthy person to the prelate; the same applies to those who return to an office. If they fail to do so, they incur the obligation of restitution. This section discusses whether they must present the most worthy candidates or if they fulfill the requirement by pointing out suitable ones. 6. 17. <term>prelate: a high-ranking member of the clergy, such as a bishop, who has the authority to oversee appointments.</term>

**The various ways** in which one is obliged to restore that which they did not even take with their own hands. 6. 17. <note>This entry explores legal liability for damages caused by others or the receipt of ill-gotten goods.</note>

**How much one saves** by making restitution immediately. 6. 18.

**How a debtor is obliged to make restitution**, even if they lose their luxury and social standing in doing so, if they were maintaining that lifestyle with another's property. 6. 18.

**How scrupulous and dangerous a thing it is** to delay restitution until the writing of one's final will and testament. 6. 18. <note>The author warns that waiting until death to settle debts endangers the soul.</note>

**The many and powerful reasons** that show it is illicit to seek profit from lending. 5. 6. <note>Lending with interest was traditionally viewed as the sin of usury.</note>

...[tax] of the city, and the laws established regarding this, with many useful documents for this purpose. 2. 7. <note>The text likely refers to the "tasa" or official price ceiling set by municipal authorities.</note>

**How pernicious it is** not to set a price control for the merchants who, in the Indies, are called "from Castile." 2. 6. <note>In the colonial context, "merchants of Castile" referred to those importing goods from mainland Spain to the Americas; the author argues that without price caps, these importers exploit the colonial markets.</note>

**How it is natural and divine law** to observe the price controls of the commonwealth, for which reason everyone, even if they are clerics, is obliged to observe them. 2. 6.

**The price control of the commonwealth**, or of the king, must not be permanent, but rather changed according to the times and circumstances; and how much error is committed by not varying them. 2. 7.

**Ancient treasures that have no owner**: the act of finding them makes them one’s own property. How the division mentioned in the laws—which they say must be shared with the owner [of the land]—is to be understood. 6. 15.

**Treasures that appear to be new** do not belong to the one who discovers them, unless the procedures required for a discovery found upon the land are first carried out. 6. 15. <note>Legal distinction was made between "ancient" treasure (hidden so long the owner is forgotten) and "new" lost property, which required public notification to find the rightful owner.</note>

**With what limitations** the justifications for "lost profit" and "accrued loss" are validated, and how they never apply to merchants. 2. 11. <term>lost profit: (original Latin: *lucrum cessans*) the profit a person fails to make because of another's debt or delay; accrued loss: (original Latin: *damnum emergens*) the actual loss or damage someone suffers.</term>

**These subjects** are treated very thoroughly in the treatise. 5. 10.

**How hateful and evil a practice it is**, both in Spain and in the Indies, to corner an entire class of goods—which means buying it all up so as to have the sole sale of it. How much obligation those who do this incur at every moment, and even more so those who live by it. 2. 19. <note>This entry condemns the creation of monopolies through "forestalling," where a merchant buys all available stock to force prices up.</note>

**How moderate and quiet** those who find themselves with a sick person at the time of making a will should be. 6. 17.

**When someone, by hindering the sick person**, prevents them from ordering in their will what they wished to command, that person is obliged to pay it themselves. 6. 17.

<meta>This page continues the alphabetical index of a moral and theological treatise. It completes an entry regarding restitution and then moves into the letter 'V' (historically interchangeable with 'U'), focusing on "Vendedores" (Sellers) and "Usura" (Usury). These entries provide a summary of the ethical obligations of merchants and the strict prohibitions against exploitative lending practices.</meta>

...or ill-gotten. 6.14.

**Merchants, bankers, and money-changers** who command their servants to sell for more than the <term>just price</term> <note>The "just price" (pretium iustum) was a central concept in Scholastic economics, referring to the current market value of a good, free from monopoly or manipulation.</note>, or to enter into any usurious contract, must make restitution; they are more responsible for this than the servants who actually performed the deed. 6.18.

**Selling on credit** for more than the just price is usury; however, if one sells for more than a thing is worth when it is paid for immediately, it is an act of injustice, but not usury. 5.9.

**When selling goods**, one should not take into account what the items cost, but rather what they are worth at the present moment. 2.10. <note>The author emphasizes market value over the "cost-plus" model, a sophisticated economic view for the period.</note>

**It is always a sin** to sell goods for more than they are worth, and restitution must always be made, however small the excess may be, even if the state does not always punish it. 2.10.

**It may happen** that a sale is valid in one's conscience, yet the judge may rightfully annul it. 2.12.

**A person who loses much** by selling their goods may charge more than the intrinsic value if they sell at the request of the buyer; the same applies if the goods cost them more than the current valuation and they sell only at the petition of the other party. 2.12.

**The distinct manner** in which merchants sell in the Indies <note>Referring to the Spanish Americas.</note> compared to how they sell in Spain. 2.17.

**Which things are valued** among men by money, and how in none of them can one <gloss>take interest</gloss> through usury. 5.7.

**How in usurping the property of another**, two evils are sometimes committed—which are harm and injury—and sometimes only one. 6.3.

**The vice of usury** is to take interest for lending that which is consumed by its use, such as wheat, wine, or money. 5.6. <note>In traditional theology, charging for the use of "fungible" goods (items consumed when used) was considered charging twice for the same thing.</note>

**God, and the whole world**, call and have always called the usurer a thief. 5.6.

**Cato**, when asked what it was to be a <term>usurer</term> <note>original: "logrero" — a profiteer or someone who seeks illicit gain.</note>, responded that it was to be a murderer. 5.6.

**What specifically constitutes** "mental usury." 5.10. <note>Mental usury refers to the intention or expectation of receiving a gift or benefit in return for a loan, even if no contract is signed.</note>

**The professional usurer** is not favored at all by the justifications of <term>lost profit</term> <note>original: "lucro cessante" — the profit a lender misses out on because their money was tied up in a loan.</note> or <term>accrued loss</term> <note>original: "daño emergente" — the actual financial loss suffered by a lender due to the loan.</note>. 5.10.

--- Page 809 ---
<meta>This page continues the index under the letter 'V' (for Usura/Usury), concluding the rules regarding restitution for usurious gains and the different types of illegal lending practices. It marks the end of the alphabetical table of contents for the volume.</meta>

All usury must be restituted, along with all the damage the aggrieved party may have incurred due to the usurer withholding their money. Likewise, if any real estate was obtained directly from usurious gains, one must restore all the fruits and rents from them; however, if with ill-gotten money one purchases properties that bear fruit for the usurer, 5. 11. <note>The text discusses whether the "fruits" (profits or crops) of a property bought with stolen money belong to the victim or the buyer.</note>

God permitted the Hebrews, in His role as a secular prince and legislator, to lend at usury to foreigners; however, as God and Savior, He forbade it in conscience, 5. 11.

Civil law, as established by Emperors and Kings, permits usury, but Ecclesiastical law prohibits and punishes it, 5. 11.

How many types of usury were permitted in ancient times. 5. 11.

The usurer is obliged to make restitution, as are his heirs to the extent that the estate allows; likewise, his <term>factors</term> <note>A "factor" was a business agent or manager who acted on behalf of a merchant or financier.</note> incur the same obligation, along with many others who are explained therein, 5. 11.

It is usury when a prince requests a sum of borrowed money and is forced to take all or part of it in <term>clothing</term> <note>In this period, "clothing" (ropa) often referred broadly to dry goods or merchandise. Forcing a borrower to accept overpriced goods instead of cash was a common way to hide interest charges.</note>; moreover, great outrages and inconveniences follow from such an agreement. 5. 7.

It is also usury when a needy merchant asks for an exchange and is forced to take part in clothing, along with many other ways and contracts in which this vice is committed, 5. 7.

There are two types of usury: some are manifest, others are <term>palliated</term> <note>Palliated or "masked" usury (usuras palliadas) refers to loans disguised as other types of contracts, such as simulated sales or partnerships, to evade the Church's prohibition on charging interest.</note>, which are more frequent than the overt ones. 5. 9.
